en: The *Account of the Novice’s Discipline* (*Śrāmaṇera-vinaya*) is a compendium that clarifies the ritual procedures; the *Essentials of Yunqi* (*Yunqi yaolüe*) is a treatise that reveals the underlying principle.

Ritual procedure refers to the characteristics of the precepts and dignified deportment; principle refers to the mind of unconditioned precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*). Without principle, ritual procedure is not clarified; without ritual procedure, principle is not realized.

It is not manifest; phenomenon and principle are as one, and the intent of the precepts is clear. It is because the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, preached this Sūtra on the Precepts so that those who have left the household life might be without worldly action or desire, maintaining themselves in purity.
However, the Sūtras and Vinaya are profound and abstruse; their meanings are vast and difficult to clarify.
Therefore, the Great Master came forth by the power of his vows; he excised the redundant and extracted the essentials, providing a concise commentary.

He explained supramundane dharmas through mundane dharmas, and manifested mundane dharmas through supramundane dharmas. Within this work, there is little investigation into the characteristics of offenses, while there is much exhortation to uphold [the precepts].

His intention was that since *śrāmaṇeras* have only recently entered the gateway of the Path, they should not yet be expected to hear of the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* categories [of offenses]. I...

Our original teacher, the Venerable Master Jianyue, revitalized the practice of ritual observances (*zhizu*). Observing that his essential compendium was elegant and fluent in its literary style, it inspired those at the beginning stage of their practice;
thus, he transmitted the precepts for over thirty years. For all who received the precepts, he invariably required them to contemplate deeply and recite thoroughly.
He caused their deportment to be orderly and composed so that they knew what to practice; only then did he ascend the platform with them to receive full ordination.

For this reason, this book has flourished widely in the world. Yet, for a master of such talent in the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals) to interpret the characteristics of the precepts, and to compile rules of deportment using the methods of the *Liji* (Book of Rites)—this could not have been achieved unless one had thoroughly investigated the sūtras and vinaya, and possessed broad mastery of the commentaries and histories.
I have sought to understand its origins and development. For several decades, I have constantly held this in mind;

thus, with diligent effort morning and evening, I have searched exhaustively through all internal and external texts, analyzing their meanings and clarifying the phrasing, compiling them into two volumes, upper and lower, entitled *Shuyi* (Exposition of Meaning).

This is to recount the essential points of its great meaning. Should future readers, by taking even a single step, ascend the mountain, or by entering at the first ford, enter the sea, they will immediately reach the realm of the Tathāgata.
When phenomena and principle are thus perfectly manifest, one will know that all worldly speech and written characters are entirely non-contradictory with the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Written on an auspicious day in the month of Gui during the Wuzi year of the Kangxi era by the practitioner Yu Daozhe of Fuan in Pilu,
at the Farnu Hall of Zhaokong Temple on West Lake.
General Principles:
The ten precepts of the śrāmaṇera constitute the foundation for the five sections and three groups [of the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*].

The twenty-four categories of dignified conduct (*viniya*) are the root of the thirty thousand and eighty thousand [rules of discipline]. One must maintain them with purity as the essential core of the eight virtues.
In receiving the precepts, one must not be negligent.
The preceding ten precepts have already been categorized in sequence; the subsequent rules of deportment (*vīryā*) have their articles listed first, so there is no need for further classification.

Nevertheless, regarding the methods of interpretation within them, there are differences in practice: some provide direct explanations of the characteristics of the precepts, while others [rely on] worldly...

Regarding the analogical inference (*upamāna*) of the Dharma: there are those that manifest karmic retribution, those that establish vows, and various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), each of which has its distinct characteristics.
If these were not categorized and explained, they would be difficult to identify and point out.
Therefore, I have now added topical headings (*kośa*) to each section, so that even those who have not yet seen the full text may first understand the general meaning.
The characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*), the dignified deportment (*airyāpathika*), and the titles should all be written with the first character aligned at the top margin (*dingge*).

When explaining the method, lower it by one space; for the analytical commentary (*keshi*), lower it by another space; both of these should be written in large characters. When expounding the meaning (*shuyi*), write in small characters in double columns.

This serves two purposes: first, to show reverence for the monastic discipline (*vinaya*); second, to ensure that the explanation and description are clear and distinct. Within the section on deportment, although several matters are combined—
This constitutes one section. Nevertheless, beneath each item, a circle (○) is used to distinguish the individual entries, and a triangle (△) is employed to mark the exposition of their meaning;
thus, the structure remains clear and distinct, ensuring there is no confusion or overlap.

To explain this interpretation of the text, its original purpose was to clarify the fundamental intent therein. Therefore, the Sūtras are cited according to the Sūtras and the Vinaya is elucidated through the Vinaya.
Furthermore, upon encountering the admonitions of ancient worthies, several of their words have also been recorded to serve as aids for clarification.
As for the external texts cited, these are likewise explained using secular classics; none of this is based on arbitrary views or personal speculation.

The matters concerning the *śrāmaṇera* precepts differ from those for *bhikṣus*; therefore, the gravity of the offenses and the permissions or prohibitions established therein are presented here only as a general outline.

Furthermore, human hearts are not as they were in antiquity; when people hear of a permission (*anujñā*), they take it to heart with urgency, yet when they see a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), [they disregard it].
Otherwise, it would be regarded as mere scrap paper. Had I foreseen this, I feared it might become a cause for obstructing the Way; therefore, I shall not elaborate further here.
These rules of monastic decorum according to the Vinaya are like the "Elementary Learning" (Xiǎoxué) of the Confucian tradition.

Beginners and those of lesser capacity should all practice and uphold them. Through gradual refinement, the vessel for the Way will easily be formed, so that one may avoid the fault of skipping over stages.

In traditional examination formats, there were "suspended" (xuán) sections and "attached" (tiē) sections. If there were two or three suspended sections, one was required to complete each one in full before marking the beginning of the first section with its attached text.
Nowadays, for the sake of brevity, if a sub-section is divided into three parts, one simply begins with the first part and does not write out the subsequent ones in full;
this constitutes one method. For each section, labels such as "A," "B," and so forth are used.

The characters have been clearly demarcated so that readers may distinguish between mother and child, and avoid confusing ancestors with descendants, thereby ensuring the continuity of the lineages for easy consultation.
As this collection has circulated for a long time, it has been re-carved many times; consequently, there are inevitably omissions in the wording and errors in the calligraphy.
Errors and corruptions have not been entirely avoided. For instance, "chuppu" (摴蒲) was erroneously written as "chupu" (樗蒲); "tiaojiao" (絛) was erroneously written as "tiaojiao" (縧);

and "jiaojiao" (屩) was erroneously written as "jiaojiao" (脚). All such instances have now been collated and verified. Furthermore, passages such as those concerning "discourse on traversing the Way" that benefit body and mind have also been included.
It is hoped that nothing has been omitted or mistaken.
This is a summary of the meaning; it should be read in conjunction with the *Xiangru ji* (Record of Fragrant Milk).
For those passages within it that correspond to daily practice—such as the verses on "arising upon hearing the bell" and the "three ladles and five contemplations"—all have been abbreviated.
These are merely indicated as being explained in detail in the *Xiangru ji*, and thus are not re-explained here.

Since the time of the Sage has long passed, people have largely been fond of seeking victory over one another. They hold the three characters of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya across their chests, each clinging to their own views.
Little do they realize that Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya all emerge from the single nostril of the Tathāgata;

how could the Buddhas and Patriarchs ever have delineated them as three separate pegs? Therefore, I have composed this exposition of the meaning, following the public truth in its entirety, without any partiality or dogmatic attachment.

A Brief Exposition of the Essential Meaning of the *Śrāmaṇera-vinaya-vidhi*, Volume One. By the Vinaya-transmitting Śramaṇa Shuyü, of the Wanshou Precept Platform at Shaoling Temple in Ancient Hangzhou. Explanation of this Vinaya-vidhi is divided into two main parts: first, the title; second, the commentary on the text. Within the first part [there are three sections]; first: [The title] "A Brief Exposition of the Essential Meaning of the *Śrāmaṇera-vinaya-vidhi*" is explained as follows: "Brief exposition" (*yào lüè shù*) refers to the concise explanation of the essential meaning of the Vinaya-vidhi for śrāmaṇeras. "Essential meaning" (*yào yì*) refers to the core principles of the precepts for śrāmaṇeras. "Śrāmaṇera" (*shāmí*) means "one who seeks to be disciplined. "Vinaya" (*lǜyí*) means "to discipline. "Vidhi" (*yí*) means "method" or "rule. "Volume One" (*juàn shàng*) indicates that this work consists of multiple volumes and this is the first. "By the Vinaya-transmitting Śramaṇa Shuyü" identifies the author. "Of the Wanshou Precept Platform at Shaoling Temple in Ancient Hangzhou" specifies the location where the author resided. "Ancient Hangzhou" (*gǔ háng*) refers to the capital of the Southern Song dynasty. "Shaoling Temple" (*zhāoqìng sì*) was a famous temple in Hangzhou. "Wanshou Precept Platform" (*wànshòu jiètán*) was the site where the author received the full precepts. "Vinaya-transmitting" (*chuán lǜ*) means one who has inherited the lineage of the Vinaya teachings. "Śramaṇa" (*shāmén*) is the general term for a Buddhist monastic. "Shuyü" (*shūyù*) is the author's personal name. "Explained" (*shì*) means to interpret and elucidate. "This Vinaya-vidhi" (*cǐ lǜyí*) refers to the specific text being commented upon. This is the brief commentary on the title of the *Śrāmaṇera-vidhi*.
This title is named after both the person and the dharma. "Śrāmaṇera" refers to the person; "vidhi" (disciplinary code) refers to the dharma. The meaning will be explained below.
Explanation: Generally speaking, when the Tathāgata appears in the world, the temporal teachings he expounds throughout his entire life must be upheld and sustained by seven classes of disciples;
only then can the Buddha-dharma endure for a long time. These seven classes refer to the five groups of renunciants.
These are the two assemblies of householders. Within each, there are differences of seniority and juniority. Therefore, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he thought to himself:
"I have attained wisdom, yet none are able to believe and accept it. If I remain in this world, it will be of no benefit to the world;
it would be better for me to enter nirvāṇa. At that time, the Great Brahmā King immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the ocean of Dharma is already full; the banner of Dharma has already been raised. Now is the very time for moistening, saving, and guiding.
Why do you wish to abandon all sentient beings and not preach the Dharma? At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the request of Brahmā.
Initially, at the site of the tranquil path of enlightenment (śama-maṇḍala), he first established the Prātimokṣa and preached the Brahmajāla Sūtra for the sake of bodhisattvas of sharp faculties;

this was the beginning of the Mahāyāna. Subsequently, at the Deer Park, he called out "Come, O Bhikṣu" to Kauṇḍinya and the others, turning the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; this was the beginning of the Hīnayāna. At that time, the three...
The requisites for the jewels are complete. Regarding the *śrāmaṇera*: it originally began with the initial ordination of Rāhula as a novice.

As for the *śrāmaṇerī*, this refers to the observance of the precepts. Regarding the "code of discipline" (*vinaya*): there is both the general and the specific. The general sense is that the entire Great Canon of Teachings is collectively termed the code of discipline.
The specific sense refers to these ten precepts and various rules of decorum. A *śrāmaṇera* is one who is capable of learning.

The *śīla* (restraint) is that which is to be studied. Because the object [the precepts] and the subject [the practitioner] are combined, it is called the "Śrāmaṇera-śīla. As for its essential summary:
the Great Master extracted from within the *Vinaya-piṭaka* those matters that must necessarily be practiced in daily life; hence they are called "essential" (*yāo*).

In contrast to the thirty thousand and eight hundred thousand rules, they are called "abbreviated" (*lüè*). This was because the Great Master embodied the Buddha’s vast compassion and made them convenient for beginners.

This study is intended to cause every person to believe and accept the Buddha’s words, to read them thoroughly and practice them, and to progress from the small toward the great so as to enter the ranks of the Sangha Jewel.
Such is the general meaning of this *Essentials for Śrāmaṇeras*. The title is hereby concluded.
Next, the names of the individuals are indicated:
compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhuhong, a disciple of the Bodhisattva precepts at Yunqi Monastery. Regarding "Bodhisattva" (菩薩):
it is a term from the Sanskrit language, which in full is *bodhisattva*. "Bodhisattva" is translated here as "one on the path to Buddhahood. "Sattva" (薩埵) [is...]

*Satva* is translated here as "sentient being" (*sattva*). Furthermore, *bodhi* is wisdom (*jñāna*), and *satva* is compassion (*karuṇā*). Because of wisdom, one seeks the Buddha-way above for one's own benefit;
because of compassion, one transforms sentient beings below for the benefit of others. Thus, the four vows become ever more firm.

Because they benefit both themselves and others, they are called *bodhisattvas*. Alternatively, they are translated as "Openers" (*kaishi*), meaning that by means of the Buddha-way, they open and transform sentient beings so that they may give rise to faith.
Or they are translated as "Noble Persons" (*gaoshi*), meaning that they transcend ordinary people and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Since these translations are not fixed, the Sanskrit term is retained. As for "precepts" (*śīla*), they are the primary chapter for mobilizing the good and for repelling evil.
The former refers to the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*). The Sanskrit name is *pratimokṣa*, which here means "guaranteed liberation.

This signifies that by strictly maintaining the pure precepts and practicing the bodhisattva path, the Tathāgata guarantees that one will certainly attain liberation from afflictions and realize nirvāṇa.
The Sanskrit name is *śiṣya*, which here means "disciple"; this refers to one who studies following after the teacher.
My brother, those who understand that one follows a teacher to become a "disciple" (śiṣya) know that this Great Master studied the supramundane Dharma and took the precepts as his teacher.
He was given the title by which he guides and transforms sentient beings through the compassion and wisdom of a Bodhisattva. Yunqi is the site where the Great Master revived the Way;
it is located over twenty li from the provincial seat. The mountain is named Wuyun (Five Clouds). In the past...
There were auspicious clouds of five colors that swirled above his head; subsequently, they flew and gathered at the western ravine, remaining there for a long time without dispersing.
The people of the time marveled at this, and thus it was named Yunqi (Cloud Dwelling). As for "si" (temple), it means succession;

it refers to ordained disciples who, therein, serve the Buddha-dharma and practice according to the teachings. "Shamen" (śramaṇa) has the meaning of "one whose virtue is real," referring to one who diligently cultivates [the path].
"Precepts, concentration, and wisdom extinguish greed, anger, and delusion; by knowing the mind and reaching its source, one is called a śramaṇa—this is not a mere common title.
Zhu Hong was the master’s given name; his courtesy name was Fohui, and his style name was Lianchi.
He was the son of the Shen family of Hangzhou. At the age of seventeen, he passed the local school examination; at thirty-two, both his parents passed away. Because of this—
Realizing that human life is impermanent, he entered the Wumen Cave. There, he took ordination under the Dharma Master Xingtianli.

He requested the Vinaya Master Muchen Yu of Zhaokeng Temple to confer the precepts upon him before the Diyong Altar. Subsequently, after traveling extensively to visit various masters, he returned to Wulin.
While begging for alms in Fancun, he saw that the mountains and waters of Yunqi were secluded and tranquil, and thereupon built a thatched hut.
He gradually established monastic centers and cultivated pure deeds with diligence. His spiritual influence spread throughout the world.
He lived to the age of eighty-one, having completed fifty years of ordination (*saṃgha-lakṣa*).

He was born on the twenty-second day of the first month in the year Jiājìng Bǐwèi (1535) and passed away on the fourth day of the seventh month in the year Wànlì Bǐmǎo (1615). As for the compiler, "Jí" means to collect; it refers to gathering and compiling these chapters.
This is the transmitted study. The designation of the person has been completed.
Third, the explanation of the meaning of the title (divided into two parts). First, regarding the meaning of "person" in the title:

the Sanskrit term for *śrāmaṇera* is translated here as "cessation and compassion" (*xīcí*). This means to cease evil and practice compassion; it signifies ceasing worldly defilements while providing compassionate salvation.
They are also called *śrāmaṇera* (勤策), and also called *śramaṇoddeśa* (求寂).
To explain: according to the *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra*, when the world was first formed, there was only a single ocean of water.
Stirred by the wind, it gradually solidified into earth. The hosts of the Light-Sound (*Ābhāsvara*) Brahmā Heaven looked down upon the mountainous earth and saw its "earth-fat" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*).
His complexion and fragrance were beautiful. He tasted it with his finger, and its flavor was like *ghṛta* (clarified butter). As he ate it incessantly, his body became coarse and robust;
he lost his celestial radiance and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), and could no longer ascend. He subsequently became the progenitor of humanity and resided for generations in India.
Since then, as people have moved across different lands, their pronunciations have each become distinct; only that of India remains as it was.
Therefore, its sound is the *Brahma*-sound and its speech is the *Brahma*-language. As for the term "śrāmaṇera," there are three translations; the meaning is derived from the biography of Yaśas.
Regarding the term "Xici" (息慈): the Patriarch Xuan of Nanshan translated the Indian title *śrāmaṇera* using the Chinese name "Xici.
"Xi" (息) has the meaning of "ceasing," and "ci" (慈) has the meaning of "acting. "Evil" refers to conduct that is not in accordance with the pure precepts (*brahmacarya*).
"Worldly defilement" means that this matter is something for which worldly people harbor greed and attachment; yet, this very greed and attachment is...
It is the root of birth and death and the source of all evils. By leaving the household life and departing from defilement, one cultivates the path to liberation;

thus, one should weed out its root and block its source, and for this reason, one ought to cease evil. However, although evil may be ceased, if one does not practice compassion, [the cycle will continue].
Otherwise, one would fall into partiality and the Lesser Vehicle, and thus would not possess the faculties of a Mahāyāna vessel; therefore, one must further compassionately save all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Vairocana is translated as "Pure and Full": it is called "pure" because evil never fails to cease, and "full" because compassion never fails to be practiced.
It should be understood that these śrāmaṇera precepts are the fundamental cause of Vairocana. In the Sanskrit language, they are called *śrāmaṇeraka*;
Master Xuanzang translated this as "Diligent Encourager" (*qínsè*). "Diligent" (*qín*) means not being indolent; "Encourager" (*cè*) refers to advancing in cultivation.

It is like a fine horse that advances upon seeing the shadow of the whip. Therefore, in the subsequent explanatory text, there are many citations of karmic retribution and other conditions to warn against and avoid all evils;
this is precisely the meaning of "stilling and compassion" (śikṣā). In Sanskrit, it is called *śikṣāmaṇi*.
The Vinaya Master Yijing translated [the term śrāmaṇera] as "seeking tranquility" (qiú jí). "Tranquility" (jí) refers to *nirvāṇa*. *Nirvāṇa* is translated as "perfect tranquility" (yuán jí):
it is called "perfect" (*yuán*) because there is no virtue that is not complete, which is the fruit of practicing compassion and diligence in goodness;

it is called "tranquility" (*jí*) because there are no obstacles that are not exhausted, which is the fruit of ceasing evil and exerting oneself in conduct. When a śrāmaṇera is untainted by the ten branches [of misconduct], he is then endowed with the precepts.

One attains perfection. When a bhikṣu is pure regarding the five categories of offenses, then nirvāṇa can be realized; thus, he is called a "seeker of tranquility" (*śramaṇa*). Although there are three names, in meaning they are actually without distinction.
Furthermore, "tranquility" (*śama*) refers to *pratigraha* (observance through restraint), which is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint).

"Compassion" (*maitrī*) refers to *kriyā* (observance through performance), which is the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint). This is the teaching. "Diligence" (*udyoga*) is exhortation to action, and "exertion" (*vyāyāma*) is admonition to cessation; these constitute...
The *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the human standpoint) refers to practice; "perfection" (*yuan*) is the fruit of cultivation, and "quiescence" (*ji*) is the fruit of cessation.

This is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint), which is both principle and fruit. As in the three translations above, the four *siddhāntas*—teaching, principle, practice, and fruit—are all fully encompassed.
If one examines this carefully, the meaning becomes manifest.
Next, regarding the "Dharma-meaning and Vinaya-restraint" in the title: this refers to the ten precepts and all modes of decorum (*īryāpatha*).

To explain: the ten precepts begin with the prohibition against killing and end with the prohibition against handling precious objects. As for "all modes of decorum," this refers to those that follow.
There are twenty-four items; these follow the dignified deportment (*airyāpatha*) prescribed by the Vinaya. Furthermore, "precept" (*śīla*) refers to the *vinaya* (discipline), which means "stopping.

This is because it stops all evils so that they do not arise. "Deportment" (*iryāpatha*) refers to physical form and conduct, which means "acting. This is because it causes one to practice all manner of virtues. By means of this *vinaya*, one is able to stop all evils within the physical form;
therefore, it is called "discipline-deportment" (*vinaya-airyāpatha*). For if the *vinaya* lacked physical deportment, then the *vinaya* [would be incomplete].
[Otherwise, it would be] a hollow pretense. If outward appearance lacks discipline, then the observance of precepts will have no basis for verification.
When there is both appearance and discipline, such that the internal and external are one and the same, the title of *śrāmaṇera* manifests both its essence and its function.
Second, the explanation of the text (divided into two). First, the precepts; second, the deportment. First, the precepts (further divided into two):
first, the general heading of the gate name (further divided into two). First, the heading of the name "Gate of Precepts."

"Śīla" (Precepts) refers to the ten precepts; they take the restraint of the mind as their foundation. "Vinaya" (Discipline) refers to the legal code; it takes guarding [the mind] as its primary principle.
As for "gate," it carries the meaning of being able to pass through. Although these are called the "Ten Precepts of a Śrāmaṇera," they are in fact capable of leading one through to Nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have emerged from this. Why is this? Although people are divided into great and small, the person is but one.
If, regarding this *vinaya*, one is able to hear it and contemplate it, this is "entry"; if one is able to cultivate it and practice it, this is "emergence."
It is like a great mansion: one must enter through its gates. As it is truly said: "He who finds the gate is equal to a Buddha in a single day;
he who loses the gate labors in vain for ten thousand kalpas. If one receives the precepts but does not practice and study them, then there is no gate through which to enter the Way.
Therefore it is said: "Although the precepts are received all at once, their realization must be cultivated gradually. This is from the *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-sūtra*.
Within this [text], there are passages concerning both the precepts (*śīla*) and dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). Therefore, the Great Master also divided it into two sections, upper and lower.
This is to show that if the precepts were not distinguished from dignified deportment, one could not perceive the essence (*tattva*) of the precepts;

and if dignified deportment were not distinguished from the precepts, one could not establish the function (*vṛtti*) of dignified deportment. Nevertheless, since function issues forth from essence, [dignified deportment] is listed at the beginning.
II. Explaining the Meaning (divided into two parts). First, a general preface summarizing the essential origins (divided into four sections).

First, describing how the Buddhas of antiquity established the rules for those who leave the household life: for five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*) or less, one must focus exclusively on the Vinaya; only after five summer retreats is it permitted to study the teachings and engage in Chan meditation.
Therefore, when a *śrāmaṇera* shaves his head, he first receives the ten precepts, and subsequently ascends the altar to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Commentary: "The Buddha's regulations" are like the ordinances of a sage-king. The Tathāgata is the Great Teacher of the three realms;
all his teachings are observed by living beings, who receive them with faith and practice accordingly. Hence, they are called "the Buddha's regulations.

As for "those who have left the home life," this means that those remaining at home are immersed in the turbulent waves of worldly toil, like galloping horses without reins. Even if they possess the aspiration to transcend the mundane and advance toward the Way...

[Such a state of] contemplation—how could it possibly be attained? Therefore, the Tathāgata provisionally established the "transformed city" (nirmita-pura) to lead [beings] back to the "place of jewels" (ratna-sthāna).
Thus, the Sūtra says: "There is no one living at home who can cultivate the path of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

This is precisely what is meant. Now, there are two kinds of renunciation (pravrajyā): first, leaving one's kin and severing attachments, shaving the hair and donning the dyed robes; this is called "leaving the secular household. Second, [severing]...

To eliminate delusive afflictions and realize the fruit of non-arising is called "leaving the home of the triple world. As the ancients said: "Leaving the home [to become a monk] is the business of a great man;
it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. The *Sutra on the Merit of Leaving Home* states:
"If anyone creates obstacles for this, they sever the seed of the Buddha. In the present life, various illnesses will gather in their body, and after death, they shall enter the dark hells."
Even after passing through thousands of millions of kalpas, one cannot escape [suffering]. If one can release another person to leave the household life, the merit is immeasurable.

For example, if one were to provide the four requisites to as many arhats as would fill the four continents for a full hundred years, it would not equal the merit of someone who, for the sake of nirvana, leaves the household life and receives the precepts for even a single day and night. Those who have completed five summer retreats are [equivalent to] five...

This concerns the year. The text appears in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. It means that when one leaves the household life and departs from secular society, one does not calculate [seniority] by the years since birth;

rather, one counts the *varṣa* (rainy-season retreat) and *kṣapaṇa* (years of ordination) to establish one's status as a venerable elder. Furthermore, "summer" (*xià*) signifies "flourishing," referring to the time when all things grow lushly.
The Buddha ordained that those who have received the precepts, upon reaching the summer season, should increase their efforts in practice and cultivate with diligence.

It is maintained that this is also like the flourishing of all things. Therefore, from the sixteenth day of the fourth month until the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the ninety-day period is fulfilled and the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is completed.
Calculating this as one *laba* (winter retreat), this is precisely what is meant by the ancient term "sitting the summer" (*zuòxià*).
Furthermore, the fifth [category] refers to a person who has first received the precepts and has practiced them for five years; such is the category of the precepts.

"Steadfast" means not being shaken or carried away by the winds of external objects; it is like a tree that has been nurtured for five years, whose branches and trunk have become thick and sturdy, such that it does not fear frost, snow, or hail.
"Specialized" refers to focusing on the phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) while extensively investigating what is permitted and what is prohibited.
"Refined" refers to minutely examining the underlying principles (*artha*), fully elucidating the subtle and profound. Furthermore, "specialized" implies non-duality, while "refined" [implies]...

If one is not focused, one will be distracted; if one is focused but not refined, one will be unable to penetrate the monastic laws (*vinaya*). If one is refined but not focused, one’s practice will be unable to remain constant.
Therefore, one must study for at least five summer retreats (*varṣa*) until the five dharmas are accomplished and one is capable of reciting the *prātimokṣa* and performing the *karmavācanā*;
only then may one leave the teacher. If it is otherwise, one must never leave one's reliance (*niśraya*) for as long as one lives.

Even if one possesses wisdom surpassing others and, within three or four years of ordination, is able to understand the Tripiṭaka and realize the Three Insights (Traividya), they are still not permitted to leave their preceptor.
Why is this? Because the Buddha ordained that one must not do so until five years have been completed.
This is why the Vinaya Patriarch Daoxuan attended ten lecture seats to study the Vinaya, and why the Dharma Master Huixiu spent his entire life following the assembly to hear the Vinaya.
This is truly a model for later students. Regarding the phrase "after five summers" and so forth:

it means that once one has mastered the rules of observance and violation (*dhāraṇa* and *atikrama*) and the five-year period has elapsed, one is permitted to listen to the teachings and practice Chan. To "listen" means for the consciousness to arise through the faculty of hearing.

"Teachings" refers to the words spoken by the Buddhas for the sake of those below them. "To practice" (*can*) means to investigate; "Chan" (*dhyāna*) is the method for investigating the mind. Thus, the teachings are the basis for Chan.
The ladder to it. Chan is the very marrow of the teachings. Because practice arises from understanding, one must listen to the teachings. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"If the Buddha-dharma is not explained by someone, even those with wisdom cannot comprehend it. To awaken to and clarify the ground of the mind, one must certainly engage in Chan.
Therefore, in the past, people traveled thousands of li to seek teachers and visit masters of learning (*kalyāṇamitra*) to resolve the matter of birth and death. Chan is...
The Buddha’s mind is the teaching; the teaching is the Buddha’s speech; and the precepts are the Buddha’s body.

If one holds this within one's person, hears it with the ears, and contemplates it with the mind, then the fundamental source of the mind-ground will be thoroughly penetrated. If one practices Chan meditation without relying on such guidance, [the goal cannot be attained].

Yet they merely sit there piling up their own deaths; the ancients derided them as "dead men whose spirits have not yet dispersed" or as "those who have fallen from the holy and entered the ranks of external paths.

Thus one knows that if the contemplation of principle is not yet clear, one must listen to the teachings; if one wishes to initiate practice based on the teachings, one must engage in Chan meditation.

To be proficient in the Teaching (Jiao) but not the Principle (Zong) is like a snake boring through a bamboo tube; to be proficient in the Principle but not the Teaching is to speak with one's mouth open and yet fall into confusion.

To be proficient in both Teaching and Principle together is like the sun shining upon the void: every dharma and every aspect manifests clearly. Even the paths through mountains and rivers have their passages.
Furthermore, the Teaching is a verbal expression; even if one’s cultivation and realization are not yet pure, one cannot avoid being deluded. Thus, the *Lengyan*...
Yan said: "Though one may possess much learning, if one does not practice, it is equal to having heard nothing at all.
It is said that those who possess true precepts must necessarily possess true wisdom. This is the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata, which possesses both the provisional and the real:

first, one uses the *vinaya* to gather and restrain the beginner's mind; later, one gathers them back into the non-action (*avijñapti*) of the One Vehicle. First, one uses phenomena to realize the principle; later..."
One attains the principle and forgets words. If the initial mind does not maintain the *vinaya* (precepts), it will become unrestrained and result entirely in false views;
if the subsequent mind does not penetrate the true nature (*dharmatā*), diligent cultivation will ultimately remain within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

If one practices Chan without upholding the precepts, even if one possesses empty intellectual understanding, one cannot avoid falling into ruin. Thus it is said: "If there is no true precept, there will certainly be no true wisdom. Apart from the precepts...
Cultivating concentration and wisdom is called the cause for [becoming] a Māra or an outsider. Cultivating precepts apart from concentration and wisdom is called the cause for humans and devas.

To possess all three trainings together is the cause for attaining Buddhahood. Therefore, those who listen to the teachings and engage in meditation for five years or more do so fundamentally with the desire to increase their mind and wisdom, practicing the three trainings in unison.
Because the precepts are pure, wisdom is pure; because wisdom is pure, the precepts are pure.
Purity. It is like washing two hands together; there is no distinction between before and after. That is to say, one need only return home by way of the path at hand;
it is unnecessary to change the route or alter the tracks. There is no separate method for practicing the precepts of renunciation outside of the five years [of study].
Whether listening to the teachings or engaging in Zen meditation, the principle is clear. "For this reason" means because of this. Thus, he received...
These are words used when one of higher status initiates someone of lower status. Regarding the tonsure of a *śrāmaṇera*, the *Duren jing* (Sūtra on Delivering People) states:

"Whenever one wishes to leave the household life, they should wear their original secular clothes. First, instruct them to take leave of their sovereign and parents, and then recite this verse for them:

'Wandering through the three realms, one cannot escape the bonds of affection; to abandon the secular world and enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the true way to repay one's debt of gratitude. Thereafter..."
"Shaving the hair. "To shave" means to remove or to sever; it refers to severing and removing the beard and hair, with the wish that afflictions (*kleśa*) may likewise be severed and removed.
"Falling away" (*luò*) refers to the falling away of the hair. When people of antiquity shaved their hair, they called it "falling away. Regarding those who first receive the ten precepts:
this is likened to ascending a multi-storied tower in four stages, one after another. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "First receive the five precepts to discipline oneself..."

Prostrations. As their faith and delight gradually increase, they next receive the ten precepts; as their wholesome mind deepens further and their deportment becomes orderly and dignified, they finally receive full ordination.
Following this sequence, they attain a portion of the Buddha-dharma. Their aspiration becomes firm and steadfast, and they give rise to the Great Mind by receiving the Bodhisattva precepts.
Just as one travels across the great ocean, which gradually becomes deeper and wider, so too is it when entering the ocean of the Buddha-dharma.

Now, it is not the five precepts that are being discussed, but the ten precepts. This is because the five precepts apply to both the laity and the clergy, whereas the ten precepts pertain exclusively to those who have left the household life.
Since one’s hair and beard have now been shorn, only the ten precepts are mentioned.
If they were received all at once, the proper sequence would be lost and the Buddha’s regulations violated; as the saying goes, "that which is obtained with ease is easily lost."

It is not difficult. Furthermore, there may be sentient beings who attain the fruits of the Path without receiving the five precepts, or who attain the fruits of the Path by receiving the ten precepts.
Because of these various causes and conditions, the Tathāgata speaks of receiving them in sequence.
Regarding "ascending the altar to receive full ordination": to ascend from below to above is called "ascending"; this refers to the bhikṣu as a member of the Saṃgha.
"Jewel" (*ratna*). It serves as the banner and sign for humans and devas; it distinguishes the faculties of individuals. Thus, the Vinaya states:

"In a mere moment, I shall cause you three to reach the most supreme state. As for *śrāmaṇeras* and *bodhisattvas*, with the sole exception of those hindered by the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), all are universally included;
therefore, they are not mentioned [separately]. "Altar" (*maṇḍala*) means a site. This site is established through the collective performance of legal acts (*karmavācanā*) by the Saṃgha.
Were it not for this assembly, the precepts could not be obtained. "Complete" means being fully endowed;

that is to say, upon receiving the two hundred and fifty great precepts, one immediately becomes complete with the sublime cause of *nirvāṇa*. It is also called "full ordination" (*upasampadā*), meaning the reception of these great precepts.
The *jñapti-karman* (white *karman*) having been concluded, the matter at hand is accomplished in accordance with the Dharma; one is not far from the state of *nirvāṇa*.
Now, regarding the bestowal of the *śrāmaṇera*, *bhikṣu*, and Bodhisattva precepts, they are collectively termed "platforms" (*tán*).
This is analogous to the three stages of examination in the secular world. Inferring from this, there is no need for further discussion regarding the designation of the "Three Platforms."
Second, it is lamentable that those now called *śrāmaṇeras*—regarding the precepts originally received—are either ignorant and bewildered by them, or heedless and neglectful in their study;
they instead seek to leap over the stages, having no regard for loftiness or the distant goal. This too is truly lamentable.
Commentary: Now is the age of the Final Dharma (*mofa*). As for "name," it means they merely possess the name of a *śrāmaṇera*. Regarding "the precepts originally received":
"originally" refers to their fundamental portion—that is, the ten precepts which constitute the fundamental portion of a *śrāmaṇera* that they have received.

As for "fools," they lack the eye of wisdom. As for "bewildered," they are obscured in their will and nature. Because of this, they are unable to study the precepts; instead, they take pleasure in remaining base and inferior. And...
The Dharma has become increasingly remote. The "insane" give rise to false views; the "negligent" treat the *vinaya* with contempt.
Some, possessing a modicum of knowledge, claim to be highly capable; when urged to study, they instead reply, "This is merely taught for beginners.
Or, when teachers fail to instruct according to the Dharma, disciples are unwilling to request such guidance.
Questioning a single word, they stubbornly cling to their delusions and ignorance, leaving their minds in a state of chaotic negligence. Master Yuán of Gūshān said:
"Though a person may be utterly foolish, how could they not be able to record one word a day? In a month there would be thirty words; in a year, three hundred and sixty words.
Accumulated over several years, it would naturally form a body of work. If one merely feels ashamed of their lack of talent and wisdom, it would be better to abandon [the practice] altogether."
If one does not study, then one should likewise feel shame regarding food and drink; it would be better to abandon them and not eat at all.
Since eating is something we must do in common with others, why should the Dharma be treated with such negligence? If one does not practice and study, what is the purpose of receiving the precepts?
As the ancients said: "Through learning, the son of a commoner becomes a high official; through lack of learning, the son of a high official becomes a commoner. If you wish to...
"Are they high ministers? Or are they commoners? Master Yongming Shou said: "One who captures birds uses a single mesh of the net;
yet one cannot discard the other meshes because of that one. One who achieves success relies on a single move of chess; yet one cannot discard the other moves because of that one.
Master Yueku said: "The high is founded upon the low; the vast arises from the minute."

Arise! From the Yu and Xia dynasties up to the Sage [Confucius], even they underwent trials and tests; could it be that the Two Ancestors [the Yellow Emperor and Yao] still served with diligent labor?
As it is said: "If the cause in a single thought is true, the fruit in a thousand lifetimes will be real. If the cause is not true, how can the fruit be real?
If one eats to satiety all day long without applying the mind, then it is truly difficult indeed. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "All who possess a mind..."
All shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If one lacks faith, it will only serve to increase black karma (*kṛṣṇa-karman*).
Therefore, the Buddha admonished Rāhula with this verse: "The Bodhisattvas of the worlds in the ten directions Have already realized the fruit of the Sugata in every thought-moment.
Since they are great beings (*mahāpuruṣa*), so too am I; I should not disparage myself or succumb to despondency."
The *Samādhi Sūtra* states: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is unfathomable. Those who cling to partiality and ignorance fail to penetrate the principles of the Truths;
they do not practice the Three Studies and do not receive instruction from a teacher. Misinterpreting what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, they call themselves wise, yet this is not true wisdom.
The harm of狂妄 (mad arrogance) is even greater than that of the ignorant and unworthy. The sūtra further says: "Humility is like the great ocean."
They accommodate the hundred rivers yet remain as haughty as a high mountain; the water of the Dharma does not abide within them.

Of a single flavor yet possessing great ambition and grandiloquence, they treat the Buddha’s words with contempt and disregard the *vinaya*. They disparage the study of the precepts as the "Lesser Vehicle" and slander the practice of observance as trivial and pedantic.
If one stubbornly clings to the conceit of "I" and refuses to follow the good, then salvation is difficult to achieve.
Yet we have never heard that when Kumārajīva was first studying the Hīnayāna, he prostrated to Paṇḍulata; this was respect for those superior to himself.

Later, when Paṇḍulata studied the Mahāyāna, he in turn prostrated to Kumārajīva; this was honoring the worthy. Thus it can be seen that from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old, [this has been the practice].
There has never been one who achieved success without study. Once a śrāmaṇera has ascended to the level of the precepts, how can he not study?
If, with a mere fragmentary understanding, one considers a little attainment to be sufficient, then one will fail to respect those above and fail to honor the worthy among one's superiors;
to wish to equal the sages of antiquity under such conditions is impossible. To "propose" (*ni*) means to desire. To "leap over" (*lie*) carries the sense of crossing over or skipping grades.
"Equal" refers to the rank. This means that as soon as one has received the ten precepts, one immediately wishes to be equal to the fully ordained monks (*bhikṣu*).

To have "no intention for loftiness" is also something to be lamented. "No intention" (*wǎngyì*) refers to being dark-minded and ignorant; "loftiness" (*gāoyuǎn*) refers to falsely exalting oneself to an excessive degree.
When one hears such wild and unrestrained speech, even sages and worthies would find it beyond their reach. If one asks about the characteristics of their precepts and their majestic...
[The Master] was utterly bewildered, not knowing a single dharma. He sighed with lamentation, saying: "To be thus mad and foolish—how can one not feel sorrow and regret?
The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "If one does not first study the Hīnayāna and subsequently study the Mahāyāna, one is not a disciple of the Buddha."
Part Three: An Abridged Exposition (divided into four sections).

First, regarding the initial instruction for beginners, ten precepts are selected and briefly explained in a few words so that those who have begun their studies may know the direction they should follow.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "selecting the ten precepts," this refers back to the preceding text. It means that because of such madness and folly...
For this reason, I have selected the Ten Precepts to explain them. This is so that those who are reckless may be led to study, and those who are ignorant may be made to understand.
Being concise rather than extensive, they are called "a few words. For those who have newly entered the Way, these are called "elementary studies" (*mōngxué*).
"Toward" (*xiàng*) means to incline toward; "method" (*fāng*) refers to the method for entering the gateway of the Way. Thus, it is the method for entering the Door of the Way.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "One uses the finger to point at the moon. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

"The burning fires of the three evil realms, the heavy torments of camels and donkeys, and the hunger and thirst of hungry ghosts are not what is called suffering. Only the darkness of ignorance, the lack of learning, and the failure to recognize one's direction are called suffering.
Because the Great Master lamented that the deluded and foolish do not understand the precepts and the Dharma, he has provided this brief explanation here to enable beginners...
For one who has resolved their mind [on enlightenment], there is a proper way to enter the Path, so as not to stray onto divergent paths like those who are blind and deaf.
It is like when a sprout first emerges; it must depend upon rain, dew, and human effort to be able to grow and reach maturity. Thus, if the initial resolve is once lost...
The harm wrought is no small matter; even if a skilled physician were present, it would be difficult to regulate such a potent poison. It is truly as the saying goes:
"If one does not encounter a master at the very outset, one will end up as nothing but a worn-out relic in old age."
Second, regarding those who leave home with a sincere resolve to practice: you must follow this intent with all your heart and be careful not to violate it.
Master Nanshan explained: "Those who leave home with a sincere resolve do so because they fear the manifold sufferings of the four enemies and loathe the three realms."
Recognizing impermanence, he bid farewell to his most beloved kin, renounced his deep attachment to the five desires, and was not led astray by fame or profit, nor coerced by royal power,
nor did he seek a livelihood through improper means, nor did he act out of laziness or a desire for idle comfort.
It is not for the sake of fleeing debt or seeking refuge; rather, it is for the sake of transcending birth and death, and for the sake of Bodhi.

Because they maintain faith and leave the household life, the Great Master Zhiwei divided those who leave the household into four types: first, those whose minds have left the household but whose bodies have not, such as Vimalakīrti and Pang Jushi;
second, those whose bodies have left the household but whose minds have not, meaning those who, although they have entered the Gate of Emptiness, [have not yet realized its truth].

First, because they do not practice the deeds of a Buddha. Second, because although they have left home physically, their minds have not; this is because the roots of goodness have not yet arisen. Third, because neither body nor mind has left home;
this is because the roots of goodness have not yet arisen. Fourth, both body and mind have left home; this is what is meant by a "good heart. "Urgent" (切) means truly earnest.
This means that once one has resolved to take the precepts, one’s intention must be truly earnest. The precepts are the swift vessel for crossing the sea of suffering and the adornment of the Dharma.
Regarding the ornaments of the body, if one loses mindfulness for even the duration of a hair’s breadth, it becomes a cause for suffering in the three miserable realms.

One should therefore follow these precepts without deviation, practicing them without indolence, being cautious and avoiding intimacy or contempt, and remaining refined and solemn without transgression.

With the fundamental nature thus pure, one’s movements and stillness shall be composed and dignified. If one has not yet reached the required age, there is no harm in waiting; once it is fulfilled, one may naturally ascend the altar.

The Three Stages (Sanjie) are first, and then [the monastic precepts]: they serve as the steps for the bhikṣu precepts in the near term, and as the foundation for the bodhisattva precepts in the distant term.
Commentary: "Then" refers to ascending from the lower to the higher; that is to say, when the preceding ten precepts are pure and the period of probation has been completed.

This refers precisely to ascending the altar to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Regarding the two terms "near" (*jin*) and "far" (*yuan*), there are both a practical (*shi*) and a principled (*li*) sense.

In the practical sense, a *śrāmaṇera* is called "near" because he is in immediate succession to the *bhikṣu*; yet he is called "far" because he is still separated from the *bhikṣu* by one further stage of the ordination platform.
In the principled sense, a *bhikṣu* is called "near" because he seeks only his own benefit and aims solely to exhaust the remainder of his physical life in this present existence. A Bodhisattva...
The vow is to benefit sentient beings until the end of the future; therefore, it is called "distant. As for the "stages," they are the paths of ascent and progress.
One travels a long distance starting from what is near, and one climbs to a high elevation starting from what is low. Thus, the Vinaya states:
"It is impossible for one who has not received the full precepts (upasaṃpadā) to receive the bodhisattva precepts. "Root" refers to the root of grasses and trees; that is to say:
These ten precepts are the very foundation for both bhikṣus and bodhisattvas. If the initial stage is destroyed, it is difficult to ascend to the subsequent levels.
If the root is once impaired, the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will all fall away. Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"If one breaks a grave precept among the five precepts, there is no possibility of receiving the five precepts again, nor even the bodhisattva precepts. If...
If one has broken the grave precepts among the ten precepts, and yet wishes to receive the ten precepts, the bhikṣu precepts, or the bodhisattva precepts,
there is likewise no such possibility.
This is the fourth noble cause.
Through precepts, concentration arises; through concentration, wisdom is developed. In this way, one may hope to accomplish the Noble Path and not fail the aspiration for renunciation.
Regarding "through precepts, concentration arises": the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* records the Buddha telling Ānanda, "To restrain the mind is the precept. Through the precept...
Birth arises from concentration; through concentration, wisdom is generated. For the mind is the root of both purity and defilement;

by means of precepts, it is restrained so that nothing enters from without and nothing issues forth from within. When these are unified into a single whole, it is called concentration (*samādhi*). When stillness reaches its ultimate limit, luminosity penetrates everywhere, giving rise to wondrous function;
this is called wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, precepts are the foundation of concentration, and concentration is the substance of wisdom. Wisdom...

This is the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Hence it is said: "Based on ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration arises; based on concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) is developed. "Shujie" (庶幾) means "to approach [the goal].
"The Way of the Sages" refers to the path of the sages. In Sanskrit, this is *bodhi*; here it is translated as the "Way of Awakening.
This means that this path is the way traversed by the thousands of sages. There was not a single *śrāvaka* who did not strictly observe the precepts. There was...
If a bodhisattva does not cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), there is not a single Tathāgata who has not fulfilled the essence of the precepts.
It is said that when one refines and purifies the precepts, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) will arise, whereby one no longer indulges in worldly defilements.
Practicing in this manner, one may soon achieve *bodhi* and avoid betraying the original aspiration for which one shaved one's head and donned the black robes.
If one wishes to examine it in detail, those who delight in broad study should consult the complete Vinaya-piṭaka themselves.

*Śī* means "to delight"; *ruci* means "to prefer. *Guǎnglǎn* (broad study) means to observe extensively. *Jiǎn* (inspect) means to examine; *yuè* (read) means to look closely. *Zàng* (piṭaka) means to contain.
This encompasses the meaning of the *piṭaka* (the scriptural collections). When the Tathāgata taught the Dharma, he divided it into the Three Piṭakas, namely the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.

Since this work is specifically intended for those receiving the precepts, it refers exclusively to the Vinaya Piṭaka. The entire text is precisely for the purpose of revealing the essentials in brief;
the Great Master has selected a few words for beginners so that they may easily practice and uphold them.
If there are those who are intent upon the *vinaya*, they should examine the *vinaya* section in its entirety; only then will they understand the meaning of the whole *piṭaka*.
Second, the source of the establishment of the precepts is presented in two parts.
First, the names of the ten precepts are described as they appear in the *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-sūtra*.
Explanation: Regarding the names of the ten precepts, they refer to the ten matters, namely, abstaining from killing, stealing, and so forth.

This is established by the *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-sūtra*, which demonstrates that this is not a mere speculative theory and shows that there is a scriptural basis for it. That is to say, the Vinaya was personally proclaimed by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata.

From the Bodhisattvas below the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambuddha) downward, none dare to increase or decrease even a single word. This is why the Great Master cites this as scriptural evidence.
"Sūtra" is a general designation, for the entirety of the Great Canon of Teachings is collectively termed "sūtra. Thus, the specific name is made manifest through the general.
This refers to the *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-sūtra*, cited here to distinguish it from other sūtras.
Second, regarding the person:
the Buddha commanded Śāriputra to expound [the precepts] for Rāhula.
Explanation: "The Buddha’s command" is like an imperial decree issued by a Son of Heaven. "To preach" means to transmit the teaching.

Since the Buddha is the Dharma King, he established the precepts and commanded Śāriputra to preach them to Rāhula. In Sanskrit, Śāriputra is called Śāriputra; here it is translated as "Son of the Śāri.
He received this name from his mother because her eyes were as clear as those of the śārika bird. His father...
This was the Brahmin of India, the master of treatises Tiṣya, also known as Śāriputra. The *Wenju* (Exposition of Words and Phrases) states: "Śāriputra’s mother possessed a beautiful body;
because he was born from her body, he is called 'Body-Son' (Śarīraputra). Upon entering the city of Rājagṛha, he encountered Aśvajit on the road, who spoke this verse for him:
"All phenomena arise from conditions; when conditions cease, phenomena likewise pass away. My teacher is the Śākya...
Kāśyapa constantly spoke in this manner. Upon hearing this, Śāriputra immediately realized the first fruit [of the path], entered the Buddha’s order, and left the household life.
In the Sanskrit language he is called Rāhula; here it means "Seizer of the Sun. He was the son of the Buddha.
At the time of his birth, he coincided with an asura who obstructed the sun with its hand; he was named for this reason. He is also called "The Obstructor. Formerly, when the Buddha was a prince—
He requested his father’s permission to leave the household life. His father said, "Do not sever the lineage of my kingdom. If you have a son, I shall allow you to renounce the world.
The Prince then pointed with his finger at Yaśodharā’s womb, and she immediately became aware that she was pregnant. He remained in her womb for six years before being born;
thus, he was obstructed by the turning over [of the fetus]. The *Adbhutadharma-sūtra* states: At that time, the Buddha was in the city of Śrāvastī and entered the city.
While begging for alms, Yaśodharā and Rāhula were on a high terrace when they saw the Buddha entering the city.
At that time, Rāhula was seven years old; Yaśodharā, having awakened to faith, spoke to Rāhula, saying, "This bhikṣu who has come here—"
"This is your father. The Tathāgata possesses immeasurable wealth of the Dharma; you should receive your portion. You must go there and claim your remaining inheritance.

Rāhula immediately descended from the tower and went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet. The Tathāgata, observing his faculties and providing instruction according to his needs, stroked the crown of Rāhula’s head with his hand.
Rāhula awoke from his state and thought to himself: "Since birth, I have never before experienced such softness."
Experiencing the pleasure of soft, fine, and smooth sensations, he subsequently realized the nature of the tactile object (*spraṣṭavya*) and attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
The Buddha then asked Rāhula, "Are you able to leave the household life? Rāhula replied, "I am able. The World-Honored One then extended a single finger and led Rāhula back to the saṃghārāma.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Śāriputra, you must ordain Rāhula and let him enter the monastic order. Śāriputra...
He said: "How shall I be ordained? The Buddha taught him to speak thus: "I, Rāhula, take refuge in the Buddha;

I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Saṅgha. I, Rāhula, having completed my taking of refuge in the Buddha, having completed my taking of refuge in the Dharma, and having completed my taking of refuge in the Saṅgha, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill living beings.
This is the śrāmaṇera precept. Are you able to uphold it? And so on, up to the [eighth].
Tenth: Not to grasp or hold gold, silver, or precious objects, whether raw or refined.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept. Are you able to uphold it? Thus he asked three times. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha commanded Śāriputra to teach this to Rāhula.
There are five reasons why the Tathāgata did not act as Rāhula’s upādhyāya: first, for the sake of equality; that is to say, the Buddha...
The mind is equanimous; it is entirely without partiality. One does not act as a preceptor for that person, nor does one act as a preceptor for this person.
Second, it is for the sake of stopping strife and contention. If one acts as a preceptor, there will be favoritism and distance; once favoritism and distance exist, [conflict arises].
Consequently, disputes will arise, and the Buddha-dharma will be difficult to practice. Third, it is to prevent slander. If one acts as a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), outsiders will say:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama claims to be compassionate toward all; why does he act as a preceptor for one person and not for another?
In that case, he is no different from an ordinary person. Fourth, it is to bring [the teaching] to fulfillment.
Because of the three refuges. If one acts as an upādhyāya, one then falls into the category of the Saṃgha; if there is no Buddha Jewel, then the three refuges cannot be established.
Fifth, it is for the sake of fulfilling the six recollections. If one acts as an upādhyāya, there is no recollection of the Buddha.

Furthermore, if one acts as an upādhyāya, when a disciple falls ill, one ought to attend to them—providing food, drink, clothing, medicine, and all other necessities. How could this be [if one were not a monk]?

Is this what the Sovereign Dharma-King ought to do? For instance, there was once a bhikṣu who was destined to attain the fruit of arhatship, yet because he had previously possessed the merit to become a Cakravartin King, that karmic fortune acted as an obstruction, preventing him from reaching the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Out of compassion for him, the Tathāgata, for the sake of that sick bhikṣu, performed a single *puṭa* of medicinal herbs, whereby the Cakravartin’s merit was instantaneously exhausted.

One will immediately attain non-attachment. If the Buddha were to act as the *upādhyāya*, there would be harm and no benefit. Furthermore, the Buddha is but a single person, whereas the *saṃgha* encompasses both ordinary beings and sages.
If a member of the *saṃgha* acts as the *upādhyāya* and the disciple receives the precepts, those near and far can all obtain them;
this does not cause sentient beings to undergo much hardship. This is why the Buddha would not act as the *upādhyāya*. Moreover, if he were to act as the *upādhyāya*...
"When the Buddha was in the world, the Buddha served as the *upādhyāya*. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, who would act as the *upādhyāya*?
For these various reasons, [the Buddha] did not appoint an *upādhyāya*. As for the command to Śāriputra, it was for the sake of symbolic representation.
Among the ten great disciples, Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom; because he possesses such wisdom, he alone is able to act on his behalf."
The Buddha taught the precepts. Rāhula was foremost in the secret practice; because he was able to practice them, he was fit to receive the precepts.
Thus, one who receives the precepts and is able to practice them is a true son of the Buddha.
II. Detailed Explanation of the Precepts (divided into ten): First, the precept against killing, up to the tenth, the precept against handling precious objects.
Regarding the first, the precept against killing (divided into two):
first, the title—namely, "Abstaining from Taking Life."
Commentary: This refers to the precepts established by the Tathāgata. The subsequent nine precepts are the same. "First" (*dī-yue*) signifies the intent of uttering words and proclaiming a statement.
"Killing" (*sha*) means to sever. "Life" (*sheng*) refers to vitality.

That is to say, regarding all life—whether past and already gone, future and not yet arrived, or present—all that exists in a single *kṣaṇa* continues in an uninterrupted succession; this is what is called [life].
"Birth. To sever that continuity now is therefore called "killing. The Preface to the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhi-sūtra* states:

"All things belonging to the realm of blood and breath must possess consciousness; all who possess consciousness share the same essence. All have the mind that desires life and fears death. Thus, the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* says:
'Because the sons of the Buddha lack compassion and filial piety, they recklessly take the lives of other beings to satisfy themselves.'"
I find their flesh savory and sweet, yet I fail to realize that these are beings whose lives were taken and whose flesh was eaten.
Their love for life is identical to my own love for life. Since every person cherishes life and every creature craves existence, how can one harm them? As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
The Buddha said that there are ten kinds of offenses for killing living beings: 1. One’s mind constantly harbors poison, which persists without end from lifetime to lifetime.
2. Sentient beings detest one; they take no pleasure in seeing one with their eyes. 3. One constantly harbors evil thoughts and contemplates wicked matters.
4. Sentient beings fear one, as if seeing a snake or a tiger. 5. One’s heart is filled with dread while sleeping, and remains uneasy even upon waking. 6. One is perpetually beset by evil...
7. Dreams; 8. At the time of death, the terrors of a violent and evil demise; the eight causes and conditions for a short life; 9.
Upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life, falling into hell; 10. If one emerges as a human, one will always be short-lived.
As stated in the sutras, how could one not strictly observe these precepts? For a śrāmaṇera, compassion is the foundation; therefore, the precept against killing stands first.

Third, the Explanation of the Meaning (divided into three parts): First, the exposition of the precepts; second, the citation of scriptural evidence; third, the summary exhortation. Within the first [part], there are four sections. First, clarifying the objects of the precepts:
from the Buddhas and noble sages above, and teachers, monks, and parents, down to the smallest crawling and wriggling insects.
"Minute insects. Explanation:
To analyze the meaning based on the text is called "interpretation" (jie). "Supreme" (*shàngzhì*) means the most exalted. The Buddha is the God among gods and the Sage among sages;
because he is the most honored and supreme within both the mundane and supramundane realms, he is so designated. "All" (*zhū*) refers to those of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

One who is fully endowed with the three types of awakening is called a Buddha. One who has already attained the perfected fruit is called a Sage. One whose spirit transcends all things is called a Human. One who serves as a model for later students is called a Teacher.
Those whose six harmonies are pure are called the Sangha. Those who are the root of one's wood and the source of one's water are called Parents.
For the Buddha is able to reveal the Dharma, the teacher is able to transmit the Dharma, and the Sangha is able to propagate the Dharma. Parents labor in their efforts to nurture and raise us;
their kindness is equal to that of the Buddha. Yet, worldly parents give birth to and raise the physical body, whereas supramundane parents give birth to and raise the Dharma-body.
As the Vinaya states: "One should mindfully reflect upon the kindness of one's parents and teachers, and diligently practice the Path to repay them."

As for virtue, since one is said to "mind the kindness" [of others], how could there be any intent to harm? What is being discussed here concerns Devadatta’s act of pushing a rock to crush the Buddha, thereby injuring the Buddha’s toe;
therefore, among the methods of repentance, there is the inclusion of the single *ānantarya* offense of shedding the blood of a Buddha.
For this reason, the Great Master placed the seven heinous offenses at the forefront because they are the most grave. "Sage" refers to one who has attained the stage of fruition;
"Master" refers to the Upādhyāya; "Ācārya" refers to the Karmācārya; and "Saṃgha" refers to the Saṃgha that turns the Wheel of Dharma. Regarding parents, their physical birth is paramount.
Should one commit an offense against them, it is termed a "heinous act" (ānantarya); it does not admit of repentance, and the offender falls into the Avīci Hell.
They undergo immeasurable suffering. "Down to" means reaching the ultimate limit; it refers to arriving at this subtle state, having reached the very extremity.

*Quyan* (flying insects) are those of the aerial class born by transformation (*huasheng*). *Ruan* (crawling insects) are those of the aquatic class born by moisture (*shisheng*). *Kun* is a general name for insects; they are also called "insects" (*kunzhong*). There is the mosquito (*meng*).
In Jiangnan there is a bird that spits out mosquitoes, and in the north of the Great Wall there is the "mosquito-mother" (*mengmu*) plant.
In this region, mosquitoes are born within the fruits of the *puk* tree, and gadflies are born within the pods of the elm tree;
these are the most minute and smallest. All that can be seen by the naked eye is included herein.
This means that not only sentient beings of large form must not be killed, but even those that are extremely minute must not be harmed. That is to say:
Because all sentient beings, down to the most minute insects, possess Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, out of his great compassion, has prohibited killing in all circumstances whatsoever.
These circumstances are categorized into three grades: Buddhas, sages, teachers, monks, and parents are termed "superior"; all humans and devas are termed "middling";
and sentient beings of the four realms of existence are termed "inferior. If one causes injury to any of these, the gravity of the offense is determined according to the specific case.
Second, it is shown that regarding the precept against taking life, one must not intentionally kill.
"But" (但) means "generally" (凡). This concludes the preceding section. "Those who possess life" (命者) refers to all sentient beings. All...
Because consciousness (*vijñāna*), breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), and warmth (*uṣman*)—these three—are interconnected through matter and mind, they are termed "life.
The word "intentionally" (*hetoḥ*) indicates that it was done on purpose, thereby excluding the possibility of error. "Not permitted" (*na labhyate*) is a term of prohibition;
it means that anyone possessing a physical form and endowed with life must not intentionally give rise to a murderous intent and take that life. However, there is also unintentional injury.
Regarding the retribution for inflicting injury, it is recorded in the *Chao-ya-qian-zai*: Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty was habitually devoted to and trusted the Master Kētō.
At one time, he dispatched a messenger to summon him while the Emperor was in the midst of playing go with someone else. Desiring to kill a piece, the Emperor shouted, "Kill it!
The messenger consequently executed the master. When the Emperor finished his game and called for the master, the messenger replied, "Just now, Your Majesty commanded me to kill him."
The Emperor asked the Master, "What were your final words before you died? The messenger replied, "The Master said:

'In a previous kalpa, when I was a śrāmaṇera, I used a spade to dig the earth and accidentally injured the leg of a lizard; the present Emperor is that very being. This retribution is indeed fitting. It is truly as it is said:
'Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created is not forgotten. When causes and conditions meet, the fruit of retribution ripens.'"
One must return to receiving [the precepts] for oneself; one must know that the ten realms are of one and the same mind-substance. When deluded, they become the wriggling and crawling insects;
when awakened, they become the Buddhas and sages. Therefore, out of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, he has prohibited all [evil deeds] for everyone alike.
Regarding the three types of killing:
either one kills oneself, or teaches another to kill, or sees someone being killed and rejoices in it.
"Or" (*vā*) is a term indicating indefiniteness; that is to say, although acts of killing are numerous, they are summarized into these three types according to how they are performed.

The offense is established; therefore, it is called "indeterminate. Regarding "killing oneself," this refers to performing the act of killing by one's own body—whether by striking with the hand, using a blade or staff, pushing someone into a pit or trench, or using poison and the like.
This constitutes a transgression created through bodily action (*kāyakarman*), while also involving the mental faculty (*manas*).
Regarding "inciting another to kill," this refers to instructing another to strike with the hand, and so forth, up to the use of poison and the like. Or...
To instruct another to take their own life according to the aforementioned methods constitutes a transgression of verbal karma, which is also accompanied by mental karma.

Although the killing is performed by another, the guilt falls upon oneself. Regarding "rejoicing in the act of killing": this refers to seeing another person commit a killing and one’s own mind following along, giving rise to joy.
Although one has not personally committed it through body or speech, among the three karmas, it is the mental...
Karma is the primary factor; therefore, all incur guilt. The details are as found in the Mahāvibhaṅga.
As for the width of four finger-breadths, it is as described in the Vinaya; the text is too voluminous to be recorded here.
Explanation: "Extensive" refers to that which is contrasted with the "concise.

This means that while this [text] merely provides a brief presentation of the three factors, the various other instances of killing—whether intentional, partial, or accidental—and the varying degrees of gravity of the offenses are as clarified in the *Bhikṣu-vinaya-piṭaka* and the *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-sūtra*.
Those who require them should consult these sources; however, as the texts are voluminous, they cannot be recorded in full here. The same applies to all subsequent cases.
This section consists of two parts citing scriptural evidence (divided into three sub-sections).
First, the *Sūtra on Protecting Living Beings* records that lice were born in winter; they were taken and placed inside bamboo tubes, warmed with cotton wool, and nourished with oily substances.
This is because he fears they might die of hunger or cold. Even such acts as filtering water, extinguishing lamps, and not keeping cats or wildcats are all part of the path of compassion.
Regarding the phrase "as recorded in the sutras" (*śāstra*), this refers to the supramundane methods for protecting living beings, which serve to manifest the śrāmaṇera’s cessation of evil.
This is the practice of the Way of Compassion. Although the text originates from various sūtras, its meaning is in fact detailed and complete within the Mahāvinaya.

"Lice" (śi) is the original name; they are popularly called *bàn-fēng* (half-wind). Their honorific designation is *dān-hóng*. Those born in winter are so called because they easily breed in heavy clothing and warm garments.
"Greasy substances" refers to the oily impurities on the body. They are frozen using cotton and silk floss.

They warm their bodies; when hungry, they sustain their lives with oily substances. When neither hungry nor cold, they await the coming spring to be born by transformation upon blades of green grass as mosquitoes and gadflies.
During the months of spring and summer, they transform as soon as they are released.

Even if they pass through winter until summer arrives, they are still born when the time comes. The Vinaya states: "If one discards fleas, lice, and the like, one must not do so according to one's own whim."
One must not simply discard them on the ground. One should place them upon old cotton cloth, observing whether the time is cold or warm.
If there is no cotton cloth, one should place them in a crevice in a wall or a hole in a pillar, allowing them to survive on their own. One must not discard bedbugs haphazardly anywhere;
they should instead be placed upon green grass or in a cool, shaded spot. The *Caturvargika-vinaya-khandaka* states: "The case of the elderly and the infirm..."
The Buddha said, "Kauṇḍinya, you have repeatedly picked up lice and placed them on the ground until you were utterly exhausted.
