I allow you to use a vessel—whether made of wool (*vāla*), cotton (*karpāsa*), rags, or cotton絮—to pick them up and place them inside. If the lice run away, I allow you to make a tube from bamboo to contain them.
When you take them out, cover them with a lid. If you have no bamboo, stalks of sugarcane, wood, or reeds may all be used."
Nowadays, there are many who do not understand the teachings. [They place fish] stored for a long time inside bamboo tubes until they die of distress;

though they claim to act "in accordance with the teachings," they utterly lack any intention to protect life. How, then, can they escape the sin of killing? The *Record on Preserving Life and Prohibiting Killing* states:
Xue Hao was compassionate by nature and observed the precept against killing; he would not harm even a tiny louse.
One night, he dreamed that there were many lice upon his robe, which gradually grew to about an inch in length. The lice said to Hao, "We have received your bounty for no fewer than a day.
Now that you face this peril, it is precisely our season to save our lives. Thereupon, they formed a line; on the robe were silk threads and bloodstains.
It was about a foot wide and was the carcass of a dead louse. Xuǎo gazed at it for a long time, not knowing the reason why.
That very night, an assassin came to harm Xuǎo. This man possessed a sharp sword that caused one to die instantly upon seeing blood.

That night, when the man saw blood under his blade, he thought [Xuǎo] was dead and reported it to his master with great joy. The next morning, when he looked at him, Xuǎo was unharmed. He then went to inquire...

Regarding the matter of finding lice, he first realized it was his dream; this is a manifestation of protecting living beings (*husheng*). The phrase "and so forth" (*nàizhì*) serves to cite what precedes and follow what comes after, thereby encompassing the meaning of that which lies between.
This means that while the preceding section clarifies the coarse aspects of killing and harming, the subsequent section clarifies the subtle practices of protecting life.

The intermediate instances of both coarse and subtle acts are not limited to one; they can be understood through reflection but are difficult to enumerate exhaustively. Therefore, [one must] filter water.
This is an essential duty of maintaining the precepts: because water contains minute insects, it must be filtered. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"Regarding water that has been kept overnight, if one does not examine it closely, one fears that minute insects may have arisen; if one does not strain and filter it..."
Not drinking [alcohol] and not using [forbidden items]; this is called the subtle observance of the precept against killing. Furthermore, the *Yize jing* (Sutra on Ritual Rules) states:
"Even regarding grasses and trees, or cow dung used for smearing altars—when utilizing such things, one must protect sentient beings.
Whether within beds and seats, or amidst fields, manure, and soil—one must examine each thing with great care; this is called the practice of a renunciant."
"Covering the lamp" means using gauze, silk, paper, or other materials to cover the lamp in order to protect against insects and moths. "Keeping" refers to raising animals;
the cat is a beast that catches mice and is also called a "land-walking rākṣasa. Regarding the etymology:

field mice damage the seedlings, and since the cat can eat these mice, its character is derived from the word for "seedling" (miao). The *li* is the fox; it is a beast that seizes prey, and all such creatures are... [omitted].
One must not keep things that harm living beings. An ancient saying goes: "For the sake of mice, one always leaves food;
out of pity for moths, one does not light the lamp. From the moment the green grass sprouts, one no longer steps down the stairs. Such is the utmost intensity of the thought of protecting life.
The Way of Compassion is the Great Path by which Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings.

Because loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness, one warms them with cotton-wool and nourishes them with fatty substances. Because compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to extract suffering, one filters water and extinguishes lamps.
One does not keep cats or wildcats.

Second, by citing this as an illustration, it is evident that even such minor creatures are treated thus; one can infer that the same applies to larger beings. Yet, people today are unable to practice compassion in this way, and furthermore—
"Is it permissible to cause injury?
[The Master] explained: "If even those of the most minute kind are thus [treated], this concludes the preceding passage by means of an analogy.
It means that if even the smallest insects can protect themselves in such a manner, then sentient beings with large bodies will naturally refrain from killing them. Now...

"Human beings, etc. is an expression of sorrow and regret. It means that since one has already failed to practice the aforementioned acts of protecting living beings, thereby violating the precepts of a śrāmaṇera, how could one possibly inflict further harm? "Is it permissible?
is a phrase used for inquiry; it means that one must strictly refrain from doing so again.

Regarding the third practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the Sūtra states: "Bestow favors and relieve the destitute so that they may attain peace. If you see one who is being killed, you should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.

[This is] explained within the commentary on these ten precepts; wherever the term "the Sūtra says" occurs, it all derives from the *Śrāmaṇera-saṃvara-sūtra*. Hereafter, [such citations will not be repeated].
Detailed Explanation: When a Bodhisattva sees all sentient beings being killed, they immediately redeem their lives;
this is called "bestowing grace. When they see those who are destitute, they bestow gifts of wealth and Dharma; this is called "relieving poverty.

This is truly because all sentient beings suffer from great scarcity regarding these two kinds of things: wealth and Dharma. If they see sentient beings oppressed by the need for food and clothing, [they do not...]
That which can satisfy their wishes should be given according to one's capacity to benefit and assist them.
If one sees sentient beings who lack the means to support themselves and have not attained self-mastery, one should explain the Dharma to them according to one's capacity to rescue and deliver them.

Thus, the gift of material wealth settles the body, while the gift of the Dharma settles the mind; since there is no lack in either body or mind, it is said that they are made to obtain [what they need].

This is peace. To see one being killed and give rise to compassion is the heart of sympathetic concern (*cāruṇya*). If you have the power, you should exert yourself to rescue and deliver them, liberating them from their suffering and hardship.

If you lack the power, you should silently recite the name of the Tathāgata Ratnaśrī or maintain the *Wǎngshēng* (Transmigration) mantra and dedicate the merit, so that they may hear the Dharma, transcend [this world], and forever leave the realms of suffering behind.
May it be so in future lives... [not]... (Note: The final portion of the provided text appears to be truncated.)
Seeing sentient beings afflicted by such suffering, it is said that one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Third, the exhortation to conclude:
"Alas! How could one not exercise restraint?"
"Shi" (釋) means "to explain. "Yi" (噫) is a sound of grief and pain; it is a word used when speech is exhausted, and it is also an exclamation of lamentation.

It signifies that the retribution for the sin of killing is immeasurable, and one shall suffer its calamities throughout kalpas; it is truly pitiable and must be regarded as a matter for urgent admonition.

The *Sūtra on the Wheel-Turning through the Five Realms* states: "Those who take pleasure in killing will, in their future lives, become insects such as earthworms or mayflies, born in the morning and dying by evening.
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: "If one kills the lives of others in jest, they shall enter hell wailing in grief;
foul filth and molten copper shall be poured upon them in an unceasing succession; they shall rush toward blades and leap into flames, being split, torn, and shattered."
Bitter and agonizing; for ten billion years, sufferings of myriad kinds. Heart-wrenching, beyond all recording. The *Xi bao jing* (Sutra on the Retribution of Habitual Actions) says:

"Those who kill enter the four realms of existence. Having exhausted their suffering in the three miserable paths, they may be reborn among humans, yet they shall have short lives, much anxiety, and many illnesses.

They will be afflicted by epidemics and hardships; their lives will be brief and they will long remain submerged [in suffering]. If there is a person of wisdom and discernment, how could they ever allow their murderous intent to be heedless? (8)

The Master’s Scripture says: "The killer's heart lacks benevolence; the strong and the weak injure and maim one another. When one kills a living being, one shall pass on into the future, accumulating enmity over many kalpas.
One will suffer punishment through a short life and die in terror, encountering violence and evil. It is because I fear this that I [refrain from killing]."
The mind of loving-kindness subdues the palace of Māra. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When you practice samādhi, its purpose is fundamentally to transcend worldly toil.

If the intent to kill is not eliminated, you cannot transcend the world of dust. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not cease killing, you will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits.
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "Human beings attain long life as the retribution for abstaining from killing."
The Second Precept on Stealing (divided into two parts): First, the title; second, the explanation.
It is called "not stealing. Explanation:
All things have their respective owners. To take what has not been given is termed "stealing. As for the fault of stealing, its harm is as follows:
This is not a trivial matter. It is because those who have received their forms within the six realms of existence all have greed and desire as their source;

those who have been granted their natures within the three modes of being all take attachment to wealth as their foundation. To seek gain at the expense of propriety when confronted with wealth is not the mark of a wise man;

to forget righteousness for the sake of profit—how could such a person become a gentleman? Su Shi said: "If it is not mine to possess, I shall not take even a single hair's breadth of it. For this reason:
Gavāmpati, having damaged the grain, was inevitably reborn as an ox; when a bhikṣu smelled the fragrance [of his body], the deity of the pond rebuked him.
That sins have their own origins and that cause and effect do not deviate—this is why strict prohibitions are established so that no one may transgress them.

Fearing that once one falls into such a state, there will be no end to the search for liberation, the Great Master, in his commentary on the Ten Precepts, has in every instance included the intent to cease evil and practice compassion.

[This concludes the preceding section. Second, the explanation of the meaning (divided into three parts): first, the exposition of the Vinaya; second, the citation of scriptural evidence; third, the summary exhortation. Within the first [section] (divided into four), first, the clarification of the object.
The explanation states: Regarding precious objects such as gold and silver, down to even a single needle or a blade of grass—*śulba* in Sanskrit means "gold," and *rūpya* in Sanskrit means "silver.

As for "precious objects," it means that although the items may be numerous, they are all subsumed within four categories. First, those heavy in both substance and value, namely gold, silver, and the seven [treasures].
1. Jewels and the like: these are heavy in value but light in substance. 2. Silk fabrics such as *zhou*, *ling*, and *ge*:

these are light in substance but heavy in value. 3. Wood, stone, and the like: these are heavy in substance but light in value. 4. Grasses, leaves, and the like: these are light in both substance and value.

Here, because those of high value are mentioned first, they are termed "heavy objects. The phrase "up to" (*zhì*) serves to indicate the range from the heaviest to the lightest, thereby encompassing those in between. One.
"Needle" refers to that which is most minute; "a single blade of grass" refers to that which is most light. The Tathāgata’s great compassion prohibits all instances of theft within his domain.
There are three grades of such domains: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha—both the local monastic community and the universal Saṃgha of the four quarters.
The property of parents and teachers is termed superior; that of humans and devas is termed middling; and that of ghosts, spirits, and animals is termed inferior.
Should one commit an offense against these, the penalty shall be determined according to the specific matter.
Second, the prohibition against taking what is not given. Explanation:
"Not permitted" (*na labhati*) is a term of prohibition. "Taking what is not given" (*adattādāna*) means that while the preceding person has not given it, one takes it.

To take it away is precisely to seize what belongs to the owner. Thus, the Vinaya states: "If an object belongs to another and is guarded by that other, and the former owner does not give it, yet one moves it from its original place, one immediately commits the offense of theft.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "If an object belongs to another, one should maintain the perception that it is another's property;
one must never give rise to a thieving mind toward it. Even regarding a blade of grass or a leaf, if it is not given, one shall not take it."
How much more so for other articles of livelihood? Thus, one should know that both the Sūtras and the Vinaya prohibit [the taking of] these:
whether they be the property of the Three Jewels, permanent assets, offerings made out of faith, the property of the Saṃgha, or the property of officials or the common people—all such things.
Regarding "objects":

the commentary states that "permanently established objects" (chángzhù wù) is the Sanskrit term *cāturdiśika*, which in the Tang language means "objects belonging to the Sangha of the four directions.

The Vinaya states that there are four types of permanently established objects: first, the permanently established for the permanently established, referring to the monastic kitchen, storehouses, and temple buildings.

First, regarding items such as utensils, flowers, fruits, groves, fields, gardens, servants, and livestock: their substance is restricted to their specific location and does not extend to other realms;
they may only be used and may not be divided or sold. Second, regarding those belonging to the ten directions that are permanently held in common (*śāśvata-sāmānya*):

these are like the constant meals provided for the Sangha in a monastery; once the *ghanṭā* is struck, their substance extends throughout the ten directions, yet while they pertain to the four quarters, they are restricted to ordinary monks within those ten directions.

It applies to both the noble ones (*ārya*) and the ordinary (*pṛthagjana*). In this world, the ordinary are many while the noble are few; therefore, it speaks only of the four directions, being restricted to the local area and not extending beyond it.
Third is the "present and permanently established" (*pratyutpanna-sthiti*), meaning that when the Saṃgha receives offerings, they are obtained solely by the present Saṃgha of that specific location.
Fourth is the "present and permanently established of the ten directions," such as the light personal belongings of deceased members of the five groups (*pañca-varga*).

One acquires ownership through a formal act (*jñapti-karman*) performed in one's presence. If the formal act has not yet been performed, a thief incurs an offense against the Sangha of the ten directions;

if the formal act has already been performed, he incurs an offense against the Sangha present before him. These two aforementioned types are called the property of the Sangha of the four quarters (*cāturdiśa-saṃgha*).
If there is any encroachment or damage to this, it is termed the commission of theft; for even a single grain or a single thread belonging to the Sangha is [the property of the Sangha].
The donor gave with a pure mind; now you take it by theft with an impure mind. The sin is extremely grave. The *Zhuāngchūn Lù* states:
"If one steals even a single coin from the monastic community (sangha), for one day and night, the interest on the principal accrues at three fen and seven li.
On the second night, interest is added to the interest. In a future life, one must repay this with cattle and horses. If even a single coin enters [the treasury]..."
Regarding property belonging to the Sangha (*saṃghika*), the merit gained from its long-term preservation is twice that of the aforementioned. The *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states:

"The transgression of stealing property belonging to the Sangha exceeds the sin of killing eighty-four thousand parents. The *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra* states: "The sin of stealing property belonging to the Triple Gem is exceedingly grave;
even if a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, it cannot be absolved through repentance. If one employs such property improperly..."
To privately provide [monastic property] to lay families is a most grave offense. The *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* states:
"If one steals the property of the Sangha—be it grain, food, clothing, or anything else—and takes what has not been given, one shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
Master Daoshi stated: "If one takes the property of the Sangha and gives it for the personal use of laypeople..."

If one does so, the dragons and devas will reprove them with anger, and the guilt shall fall upon the administrators. The permanent assets managed by the stewards—whether money, grain, or property—none of them belong to the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha;
what right has one to them? If even a hair’s breadth of these things is defiled by personal use, it is the cauldron of boiling water and the furnace of glowing coals.
If within these matters the distinction between the pure and the turbid is maintained with clarity, it is the treasury of the blue lotus. Thus says Tieshan Qiong.
Whatever belongs to the permanent endowment (*sāṃghika*), whether it be a single grain of tea or rice, a single *fen* or *li*, is all given by donors seeking merit;
therefore, it should be offered to the Triple Gem. How can one dare to use it privately? The relationship between sin and merit, cause and effect, is as clear as looking at one’s own palm.
As the Chan Master Cishou said: "Not even a fraction of the permanent endowment may be stolen; were it to increase ten-thousandfold daily, one would surely fear [the consequences]."
It is difficult to repay. The heads of pigs and the feet of donkeys are clearly manifest; even in this present life at the stage of Buddhahood, one has not yet finished sweeping them away.

Viewed from this perspective, that which is permanently entrusted must not be violated by even a hair’s breadth; for this reason, the sages of both past and present have exhorted us with bitter urgency.
Regarding "objects of faithful offerings" (śraddhā-deya): these refer to items brought to a temple by a donor out of faith to be offered as alms. And...
Regarding those things not yet distributed to the Saṃgha that belong to the community: these are items for the use of the assembly present before them.
If one should secretly take even one of the four requisites from among them, this is called stealing the property of the *saṃmukha-saṃgha* (the present Saṃgha).
It must not be used privately; even if there is a shifting or borrowing of goods, using the surplus to cover the deficit, one must inform the assembly before moving anything. Hereafter...
If one comes forward to compensate as before, it is not termed an offense of theft. The Vaipulya Sūtras state: "The Bodhisattva says:
'I am able to save those who commit the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds; however, I cannot save those who steal the property of the Sangha.
Regarding 'official property,' this refers to the goods belonging to the nine grades of officialdom. Under heaven, there is nothing that is not the King’s land; even if buried beneath the earth..."
"Treasury" (zàng): Even items left behind in open spaces, as they reside upon the King’s land, are all termed "official property.

"People's property" (mín wù) refers to the goods of the common people—the merchants, artisans, farmers, and the general populace. "One" (yī) is a term signifying universality; "all" (qiè) is a phrase denoting the totality of things.
Taken collectively, this encompasses all things in the world—whether large or small, heavy or light—including spirits, ghosts, deities, birds, beasts, and so forth.
The four types of taking what is not given— whether by force, by stealth, by fraud, or even by evading taxes and crossing ferries without payment— all constitute stealing.
Commentary: "Taking by force" refers to seizing through reliance on power and violence. "Stealing by stealth" refers to pilfering while waiting for someone not to see one.
"Deceptive taking," also called "false taking," includes such acts as guileful trickery and swindling, borrowing with no intention of returning, or fraudulent over-drawals based on one's influence.
The phrase "and so forth" (乃至) means from the beginning to the end, indicating that which lies between them.

This refers to various forms of deception, such as falsifying weights and measures—using the *gui*, *he*, *zhu*, and *liang* units—to shift ancient boundary markers, privately concealing entrusted goods, consuming communal property (*changzhu*) in excess, and evading taxes.
Regarding taxes: taxation is a fundamental state decree; if one possesses goods...
One must necessarily declare it to them; one may not pass by concealing it, nor may one conceal taxable goods for another.
"To cross under false pretenses" means to falsely claim another's name while passing through a customs post or ferry crossing.

The term "etc. (*ādi*) is an expression indicating that [the list] is not exhaustive; it means that although the specific instances have not been fully detailed, other related dharmas can be understood by extension.
"All constitute theft" summarizes the aforementioned rules. The remainder is as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Great Vinaya).
II. Citing Scriptural Evidence (divided into two parts).
First, as recorded in the *Karmavipāka-sūtra*: One novice stole seven fruits belonging to the permanent endowment; another novice stole several portions of cakes belonging to the community of monks;
and another novice stole a small portion of stone honey belonging to the community of monks—all fell into hell.

Commentary: "As recorded in the sutras" means that this citation of scriptural text serves as proof that a śrāmaṇera who violates the precept against stealing will consequently incur great suffering throughout the long night [of saṃsāra].
Regarding "stealing fruit," the *Sūtra on Great Requital of Kindness* states:
"One sees a sentient being with a glowing iron ball entering through the top of their body and exiting from the bottom; it travels through the void, and the pain is unbearable."
Maudgalyāyana asked the Buddha, "By what offense was this brought about? The Buddha said, "In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a śrāmaṇera who guarded the fruit orchard of the Saṃgha.
He stole seven fruits and offered them to his teacher. By reason of this cause and condition, he has incurred this retribution."
Regarding those who steal cakes, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka Sūtra* states: [The Buddha] saw a sentient being with two glowing iron wheels beneath both armpits;
his entire body was scorched and rotting, and the suffering was unbearable. Maudgalyāyana asked the Buddha, "By what offense was this caused?
The Buddha said, "In a previous life, when he was a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), while making cakes for the assembly, he stole two portions and tucked them under both [armpits]."
Under the armpits. For these reasons, he incurred this punishment. Regarding those who steal "stone honey" (*śarkarā*): stone honey is also called *tangjing* (crystallized sugar).
According to the *Guangzhi*, it is the candied juice of sugarcane; its form is like rock candy, and it is as hard as stone.

The *Book of Tang* states that the Stone Honey is produced in the kingdoms of the Western Hu, and it was highly prized in China. The *Han Wudi Neichen* records that the Queen Mother of the West said to the Emperor:
It is said: "The supreme medicines include the purple honey of China, the vermilion honey of the mountain clouds, and the rock honey of the kingdom of India.

The *Cinnabar Scripture* (*Xianjing*) states that honey is the 'mushroom of the mouth. The *Pharmacopoeia* (*Bencao*) states that cliff honey, when consumed, prevents hunger, clarifies the eyes, and prolongs life.
According to the Vinaya, one does not eat after midday; yet those who open [the vessel of] rock honey do so because its essence, when boiled in water, becomes formless and serves as medicine."
Because of this stone, the *Āgama* Sūtras state: A certain sentient being was seen with a long and broad tongue;
there was a blazing, sharp axe that cut his tongue as he traveled through the air, wailing and crying out in unbearable agony.
Maudgalyāyana asked the Buddha, "By what offense was this caused? The Buddha said, "In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a śrāmaṇera who used an axe to [cut...]"
Stone honey was offered to the monks; [a person] smeared honey on the edge of an axe and stole a small portion to eat—it was not much.
Because of this offense, after emerging from hell, he received this residual retribution.

Regarding those who "all fall into hell," this is a general statement used to warn against three things. "Earth" (di) means the bottom; among all things, earth is at the very lowest, hence it is called "hell" (yu).
This refers to being restricted. It means that the offender is confined and unable to find peace and happiness.

Although the three aforementioned matters do not occur simultaneously, the cause for the theft is one and the same; therefore, they all result in retribution in the hells. That even a single coin or a single blade of grass brings this about is truly beyond doubt.
Second, because of making a vow, a sutra says: "I would rather have my hand cut off than take what is not rightfully mine.
Explanation: "I would rather have my hand cut off than take what is not rightfully mine" means that one deeply fears the suffering and pain of hell more than anything else.
To lose one's hand is a matter that chills the heart when spoken of; therefore, the Tathāgata earnestly exhorted and warned, leading me to take a vow and resolve never to accept it.
For a person possesses hands and feet only then may they be called complete; a monk possesses precepts and virtue only then can he serve as a source of auspicious protection.
As for "non-wealth," this refers to wealth that is contrary to righteousness. An ancient said: "A person does not associate with those who are not good; as for things..."
One should not take what is not right. According to worldly laws, taking wealth that is not right brings about extraordinary calamities.
As for the Buddhist Canon, it states that by consuming things that should not be shared, one consequently incurs the retribution of the Avīci Hell.
Third, the exhortation to refrain from stealing: "How can one not be cautious? Explanation:

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When you cultivate samādhi, it is fundamentally for the purpose of emerging from worldly toil. If the mind of theft is not eliminated, you will not escape the dust [of the world]."
You may go forth. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not cease stealing, you will inevitably fall into deviant paths.
It is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup; though they seek to fill it, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be restored to fullness.
The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states: "It would be better to eat one's own flesh than to steal the property of the Triple Gem.
Chan Master Dongshan Jia said: "The permanent endowment must rely on the power of the precepts for its support; do not squander it through reckless use or indulge in greedy schemes.
When managing the goods within the gate of the Triple Gem, cherish them as you would your own parents' two eyes. Though one might be able to calculate with clever artifice in secret,"

In the underworld, spirits and deities naturally inflict punishment. If one takes even a hair’s breadth of anything without private intent, one will avoid becoming a horse or a donkey in a future life.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "If a person steals the property of another..."
Seized by the authorities, they are sent to the officials for investigation and punishment.

They are confined in prison, where they may be beaten with clubs, have their hands, feet, ears, or noses cut off, or have their heads severed. Subjected to such various tortures, they die and are reborn in the hells.
There, fierce fires burn their bodies and molten copper is poured into their mouths; they undergo unspeakable suffering for hundreds of thousands of millions of years. Only then are they released.

There is no fixed time for their release. When their retribution in hell is exhausted, they are born among animals—such as elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, camels, donkeys, and dogs—and for hundreds of thousands of years they repay their debts through the power of others.
When their retribution as animals is exhausted, they are born among hungry ghosts, where the suffering of hunger and thirst is beyond description;
they endure such misery for hundreds of thousands of years. Once their retribution is exhausted, they become human beings and obtain two [faculties].
There are two kinds of retribution: first, poverty such that clothing does not cover one's body and food does not suffice for one's mouth;
second, being constantly plundered by water, fire, kings, ministers, or evil bandits, thereby failing to obtain peace and happiness. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"If a person is very wealthy, they receive the retribution of not stealing."
The third precept on sexual misconduct (divided into two parts): First, the title is stated as "the third:
abstaining from sexual misconduct.
Explanation: "Sexual misconduct" refers to impure conduct; that is, performing defiled and evil acts with a stained mind, and is therefore called "abstaining from."
It is pure. Even in secular society, there is the instruction that men and women should not touch one another when giving or receiving gifts;

for those who have left the household life to distance themselves from defilement, it is especially appropriate to maintain solemn vigilance. Now, having received your compassionate instructions so earnestly, I must engrave them upon my heart and never allow them to violate the Buddha’s precepts.
I shall deeply contemplate sensual desire as being like a venomous serpent. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "If one is pursued by women..."
Forms intoxicate the mind with passion, like an infant who lacks insight into its own nature; it is also like a plain garment that takes on the color of the dye applied to it.
One is submerged by desire and cannot escape, like a worm in dung that delights in dwelling among filth, or like a filthy pig that adorns itself with impurity.
The *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* states: "The renunciant śramaṇa severs desire."
Abandon attachment. Clarify the source of one's own mind, penetrate the profound principle of the Buddha, and awaken to the unconditioned Dharma; only then is one called a child of the Buddha.

The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "It would be better to cast this body into a blazing, fierce fire, into a great pit, or onto a mountain of blades, than ever to violate the sūtras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods by engaging in impure conduct with any woman, even an eight-year-old novice nun."

The *Mìkāijiě Guówáng Jīng* (Sūtra on King Aśoka’s Further Enlightenment) states: When King Aśoka first took refuge in the Buddha, a plague broke out among the people. He invited the Saṃgha to offer prayers.
The holy assembly dispatched the novice Śrāmaṇera Miaoyan, who was only eight years old but had already attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
He flew into the royal palace; when the queen and her handmaidens saw him, there was none who did not feel love and reverence. The queen raised her hands, wishing to embrace him.
Miaoyan (Wondrous Countenance) declined her advances. The lady said, "Your age is still young; you are like my own son. What harm is there in drawing near?
Miaoyan replied, "Matters arise from the minute; it is like a spark the size of a grain of millet that can burn a wilderness of ten thousand *li*."
"A single drop of water can penetrate solid rock; from little comes much, and from small comes great.
Therefore, the wise distance themselves from suspicion and avoid doubt to prevent what has not yet occurred. At that time, the sound of the śrāmaṇera reached the royal palace.
When the King heard it, he came to see him and said, "You are still as young as my own son; why do you harbor such suspicion when I embrace you? Yan replied, "The ancient sages..."
Establishing ritual decorum is to anticipate what has not yet sprouted; it is also to maintain vigilance from beginning to end. A girl of seven years should not play upon her father’s armrest;
a boy of eight years should not squat upon his mother’s bed. One should not reach up to touch one's head while beneath fruit trees, nor reach down to touch one's feet in a melon field.

By distancing oneself from suspicion and avoiding doubt, one closes off the gradual and eliminates the incipient. Although we are currently equal as mother and son, this is intended for those who might be unable to do so in the future.
Giving. At that time, the king, together with his consort and five hundred court officials, all attained the fruit of the Path.

[The Exegesis of the Two Śākyas (divided into three parts): first, the exposition of the Vinaya; second, the citation of evidence; third, the concluding exhortation. Within the first [part] (divided into three), first, the manifestation of the precepts.

The commentary says: Regarding the five precepts for laypeople, only sexual misconduct is prohibited; regarding the ten precepts for those who have left the home life, sexual desire is completely severed.
Explanation: The "five precepts for laypeople" refers to the precepts for upāsakas and upāsikās. That "only sexual misconduct is prohibited" means:

Since the time of primordial chaos, when the Sovereign of Yu [Shun] sat with hands folded while Qi served as Minister of Instruction, he taught the principles of human relations (*ren-lun*), declaring that "between husband and wife there must be distinction.
Where there are husband and wife, there are father and son; thus, among human relations, the union of husband and wife is primary.

Among acts of unfiliality, the failure to have descendants is the greatest. This matters above all for social transformation and below all for the continuation of the ancestral line. Therefore, it is not...
Prohibition. As in the *Guanju* (Cranes Crying at Dawn) ode, which is joyful yet not licentious, it serves to rectify the fundamental principles of human relations.

Therefore, when receiving the precepts while living at home, with the exception of husband and wife, all other [sexual] acts are strictly regulated. The *Da guobao diyu jing* (Sutra on the Great Retribution of the Hells) states:
Furthermore, there was a ghost who said to Maudgalyāyana, "I constantly cover my head with a cloth or net because I fear people coming."
He was killed. Fear arose in his mind. "By what sin has this been caused? Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, you committed adultery with another's wife.
You were constantly afraid of being seen by others, or feared that her husband would seize, bind, beat, and kill you. Because your mind was perpetually terrified, you have incurred this retribution.
This is the 'flower reward' (the immediate karmic fruit); the actual result lies in hell. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "When a Bodhisattva, regarding himself..."
Even a wife should know contentment; how much more so regarding sexual misconduct. Furthermore, these five precepts are called the Five Stars in heaven;
they are called the Five Elements on earth; they are called the Five Relationships among humans; they are called the Five Viscera within the body; they are called the Five Peaks among mountains;
they are called the Five Punishments in the state; and they are called the Five Constant Virtues in Confucianism—namely, Benevolence (Ren).
The precepts such as non-killing and so forth are the very path of practice.

It was because of Yaśoda’s father that [the Buddha] first received the request from fifty people to accept the Three Refuges and Five Precepts; thus, the Tathāgata opened the teachings for humans and devas to gather the two assemblies of householders.
As for the ten precepts for those who leave the home life, they are the life-preserving float for crossing the sea of suffering. To transcend...
This is the direct cause for nirvana. Regarding the total severance of sexual desire: it means that sexual activity is not the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*);
it is a base, evil, and unbearable matter. Furthermore, within the supramundane Dharma, there is no distinction between the improper and the proper.

However, because the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was taught for householders, it says, "one should even be content with one's own wife. Because the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* was taught for those who have left the home life, it says:
This means the total severance of sexual desire.
Second, it clarifies that the objects [of this precept] consist of all men and women in the mundane world who one might offend.
Commentary: "To violate" means to transgress against names and meanings; it refers to committing impure acts with those one honors, defiling those one is close to, and practicing unwholesome conduct.

"All" is a comprehensive term, meaning that human females, non-human females, female animals, human males, non-human males, male animals, and even eunuchs or those with dual sexual organs are all included as objects (*viṣaya*). As it says:

Come, O Great Compassionate One. Regarding all objects of lust, they are entirely prohibited. These objects are of three grades: one's mother, daughter, sister, and other close relatives are termed "superior";
all men and women, as well as those involved in illicit sexual conduct, are termed "middling"; and for a layperson, one’s own wife when approached at an improper time or place is termed "inferior.
If anyone violates these precepts, the penalty shall be determined according to the specific circumstances. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One should contemplate sensual desire."
It is more terrible than a fierce fire. A fierce fire burns the body and harms only this single lifetime; the fire of desire burns the body and its calamities fall upon one for countless kalpas.
The wise fear it; the foolish bind themselves to it.
The three types of offenses involving defeat are all termed "breaking the precepts.
Explanation: "All" means "entirely. "Breaking" means "violating. One does not say "violating," but rather "breaking," because when one first receives [the precepts],...
When one observes the precepts, the essence is complete. If one violates these precepts, it is like a person whose head has been severed;
the body is destroyed, just as a great rock shattered cannot remain whole. The destruction of the body of precepts is likewise so.
One should know that lewdness is not a sword or blade that can sever the life-force of wisdom; rather, craving and desire are a fierce fire that consumes the forest of merit from within.
The Buddha said: "A person who has broken the precepts cannot, while alive, digest even a single drop of water from the faithful offerings made to them;
their feet may not tread upon even a cubit’s breadth of ground within a monastery; and after death, they fall into hell, where they undergo retribution without end.

Yet, the faculty of desire within the mental ground is most difficult to uproot and most easily defiled by gradual infection. If even as much as a mote of dust remains therein, it is already [a cause for downfall]."

Birth and death are the womb of calamity. If the habit of lust is difficult to exhaust, one should practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), or dwell in a cemetery (*śmaśāna*) as an antidote.
Alternatively, one may touch one’s own crown with the hand, gaze at the *kāṣāya* robe, and reflect:
"Having consumed the faithful offerings of others, one should not give rise to such thoughts. Or, one may pay homage to the Buddha and recite mantras to rectify the mind. Thus...
Greed will naturally be extinguished.
Second, citing evidence (divided into three parts): First, revealing the retribution as recorded in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
The bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā engaged in secret sexual misconduct. She herself claimed that sexual desire is not killing.
It was not theft; there was no karmic retribution for that act. Consequently, he experienced his body emitting fierce flames and fell into hell alive.
[Commentary: The account in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is cited here to demonstrate that sexual misconduct carries such grave consequences that it must not be committed.
As for Bāoliánxiāng (Jewel Lotus Fragrance), she was a bhikṣuṇī who was initially excellent in upholding the Bodhisattva precepts.

This is the title. It means that because the essence of the precepts is inherently noble, it is called a "jewel" (*ratna*). Because the essence of the precepts is inherently pure, it is called a "lotus.
Because it is noble and pure, its fragrance pervades all things, and thus it is called "incense" (*gandha*).
Later, due to a single moment of deluded movement, one fails to guard one's own mind; violating this precept against sexual misconduct, one conversely feels no shame or remorse—this is an error.
They give rise to false views and deny the existence of cause and effect, speaking recklessly that there is no retribution for killing or stealing.
They fail to realize that engaging in illicit sexual desire is indeed stealing, and that once the act of lust is consummated, the life of wisdom is severed—is this not killing?
"Fierce fire" refers to the fire of desire; having spoken these words, fierce fire immediately arises, burning them limb by limb, and they fall alive into hell.
This means that without waiting for the death of the body, one falls directly into Avīci. Its Sanskrit name is Avīci, which here is translated as "Uninterrupted" (Mújiàn).
This refers to falling into this hell where one undergoes the suffering of being burned and boiled without any interruption.
Second, to provide an illustration:
because of desire, worldly people lose their lives and ruin their families. Having left secular life to become monks, how could one further transgress?
Desire is the foremost root of birth and death.
Commentary: "The people of the world" refers to kings, ministers, scholars, and commoners. Regarding those who have lost their lives and ruined their families:
for example, in the Xia dynasty because of Mei Xi; in Jin because of Li Ji; even the outbreak of the fire at Mount Li caused by Bao Si; and the dust-raising on the road to Shu due to Taizhen.
That families were ruined and states brought to ruin—all was for this reason. From antiquity to the present, those who have been deluded are not limited to a single instance. Therefore...
It is said: "From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, all must take the cultivation of the self as their fundamental task.

Having left the secular world to become a monk, how could one again commit transgressions? This means that because one recognizes the faults and afflictions of the five desires, one abandons them to leave the household life;
one ought not to be further swept away by the cycle of birth and death. How, then, could one again engage in the impure conduct of birth and death?
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If you love my heart and I cherish your form, by reason of these causes and conditions, you shall remain in bondage for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
One should know that while a red furnace or white blade may destroy the physical body in a single moment, a flower-arrow or honeyed barb sinks the life of wisdom for ten thousand kalpas.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Those who enter the Way with a sense of shame and remorse hold their alms bowls and gather the assembly."
Born [into this world], how can one indulge in the objects of desire and become submerged in the five sensory faculties?
Having already abandoned the pleasures of the five desires and cast them aside without looking back, how could one wish to obtain them again? It is like a fool eating his own saliva.
Among the roots of birth and death, desire is the foremost; that all sentient beings possess bodies is entirely due to the initial moment of inverted perception.
He engages in union; with a lustful mind, he enters the mother’s womb and thereby forms the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). Therefore, it is called "birth.
That which all sentient beings undergo—namely, that their very life and nature are established through sexual desire—is what is meant.
Where there is birth, there must inevitably be cessation; therefore, it is called "death. Thus, one knows that the root of birth and death is primarily sexual desire. Hence it is said:
First: To eliminate birth and death, one must sever the lustful mind. Thus, a sutra says:

"If the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor a lustful mind, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death. If the lustful mind is not eliminated, one cannot transcend the dust of the world;
one must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind, so that even the nature of severance is absent within the Bodhi of the Buddha.
This is indeed something to be hoped for.
Third, because of the vow, a sutra says: "To live a life of lewdness is not as good as dying with integrity."

"Shi" (release) and "yi" (excess) refer to licentiousness and dissipation; this means acting with sexual license due to a mind given to unrestrained indulgence. "Zhenjie" (chastity) refers to maintaining integrity and purity;
this means upholding the precepts with such purity that one remains as if alive even in death. Conversely, one who gives rein to a dissipated mind is as if dead while still alive.
Therefore, a sutra says: "To live a life of licentious excess is not as good as to die in chastity. This is as stated in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.
It is said: There was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment whom a certain elder supported for his entire life, sending him food every day.
Another elder brought a son to seek ordination; the bhikṣu observed the boy and saw that he could maintain the pure precepts, so he ordained him as a śrāmaṇera.
When the former elder arrived at the assembly with his whole family, he left behind only one daughter to guard the house.
The food was forgotten. The bhikṣu thought, "The sun has already passed the meridian, yet the food has not yet been sent. He then dispatched a śrāmaṇera to fetch it.
There he saw only a young girl at the gate, displaying various seductive gestures. The śrāmaṇera thought to himself, "Will this woman not destroy my pure conduct?
He then firmly maintained his dignified demeanor. The woman immediately prostrated herself with her five limbs touching the ground and said, "This house..."
"It is filled with rare treasures; you may be its master, while I am willing to serve as your handmaid.

The śrāmaṇera thought to himself, "I would rather sacrifice my life than violate the pure precepts. He immediately entered his room, closed the door, knelt with palms joined, and made a vow not to forsake the Three Jewels or the true precepts.
"May I be born into a tranquil family, exhaust all outflows, and attain the Way," he prayed. He then cut his own throat and died.
The daughter’s lustful desire immediately subsided; overcome by grief and distress, she fainted. Just as her father returned, she regained consciousness and related everything that had occurred.
When the king heard of this, he praised her, piled up various fragrances upon the ground, and performed the cremation rites in her honor.
Third, the exhortation to refrain from sexual misconduct: "Is it not necessary to observe the precepts?
Explanation: According to the *Aṣṭācārya-sūtra*, the Buddha told a brahmin: "Regarding women who are unchaste, whether they belong to their husbands or to others..."

One will know that at the appointed time, calamity shall strike; punishments of sword and staff shall be inflicted, and hands and feet shall be severed. The disaster shall extend to one’s family and clan.

Or, one may be arrested by the royal law and cast into prison, where one is subjected to cruel and poisonous torture. One must personally bear the retribution for one’s crimes and, upon death, enter the hells.

They lie upon iron beds or embrace copper pillars; the hell-wardens kindle fires to burn their bodies. When the retribution for their hellish offenses is exhausted, they shall receive the form of an animal.
Even if they should obtain human birth, they will be lewd and disorderly within their households, distancing themselves from the Buddha and violating the Dharma.

They will not associate with sages and worthies, constantly harboring fear, and will experience much peril with little peace. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If a person who has broken the precepts..."
To don the dharma-robes is to wrap one’s body in sheets of molten copper and iron.
To hold an alms bowl is to carry a vessel filled with boiling bronze. Whatever one eats is to swallow hot iron balls and drink molten bronze.
To receive offerings and provisions from others is to be attended by the ox-headed jailers of hell. To enter a vihāra is...
This leads one into the great hells. If one sits upon a monastic bed, it is as if sitting upon a bed of glowing red-hot iron.

Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-sundarī-sūtra* states that when Śākyamuni was a prince, having become weary of and detached from the five desires, he sought to leave the household life and spoke this verse:
"In this world, there is nothing more impure, delusive, and perverse than the nature of a woman's body. [He then removed] his garments...
Because of the adornment of necklaces and ornaments, delusion gives rise to desire and greed at its extremes.

If there are those who can contemplate in this way—that [all things] are like illusions and dreams, lacking true reality—they will swiftly abandon ignorance; do not be negligent! They will surely attain the body of liberation and merit.
The Fourth Precept on False Speech (divided into two parts). First, the title:
The fourth is "not speaking falsely. Explanation:

To speak falsely means to speak in contradiction to one's own mind. For a disciple of the Buddha, a straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Regarding the four [unwholesome actions]...
Regarding dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*): among all modes of conduct, to speak without falsehood is essential.

If one’s mind and speech are discordant due to impurity, such that the words uttered are untrue, this is termed "false speech" (*mṛṣāvāda*). The root of falsehood lies in the mind, while its expression issues from the mouth.

By turning one's back on the truth and pursuing delusion, one inverts right and wrong, causing the True Path to remain obscure and allowing perverse words to agitate the masses. This is [the nature of] cultivation...
One should sever the conditions that obstruct the Path. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "By nature one does not speak falsely;
a bodhisattva always speaks words that are real, true, and according to reality. Even in dreams, they cannot bear to utter words of concealment."
If one has no intention to commit them, how much less would one intentionally transgress them? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"In this world, although the sentient beings of the six realms may have perfected the three practices of non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexuality within their bodies and minds, if they engage in great falsehood, their *samādhi* will not attain purity;
they will become demons of craving and views and lose the seed of the Tathāgata."

Second, the explanation of the meaning (divided into three parts): first, the description of the rules; second, the citation of scriptural evidence; third, the summary exhortation. Regarding the first [the description of the rules] (divided into four parts):
first, minor false speech; second, major false speech; third, the allowance; fourth, the application by analogy. Regarding the first of these [minor false speech] (further divided into three):
first, the general heading and explanation. There are four types of false speech.
Commentary: "There are four kinds of false speech" is the initial enumeration of their names.
This means that when conceptualization arises falsely, one utters words that are empty and deceptive.
These may arise from joy, or from inducement, or from anger, or from jealousy. Since the circumstances are not uniform, the speech [varies accordingly].
There are distinctions of magnitude; offenses have degrees of gravity. Therefore, out of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, he prohibited all instances of false objects of perception.
These objects are of three grades: parents, teachers, and the Sangha are called "superior"; humans and devas are called "middling"; ghosts, spirits, animals, and so forth are called "inferior.
If one commits an offense against these, the penalty is determined according to the specific case. Now, first we shall clarify four types, investigating their fundamental source.
All arise from delusion; it is as the saying goes: "When a single film is in the eye, a thousand flowers fall in confusion.
When a single delusion resides in the mind, the sands of the Ganges are born and perish. If the sovereign of the mind is correct, then the six ministers will not be perverse.
II. Detailed Explanation (divided into four parts). First, False Speech:
This refers to taking what is true to be false, and taking what is false to be true; seeing something and saying one did not see it, or not seeing something and saying one saw it;
being deceptive, unreal, and so forth.
Explanation: "Speech" (yan) refers to the sound of the mind. When the mind is correct, speech is correct; when the mind is deviant, speech is deviant.

Furthermore, that which issues directly is called "speech" (*yan*), because it is produced from one's own intention. That which is proclaimed and recounted is called "discourse" (*yu*), because it is produced by recounting what has been seen or heard.
The discourse of the Tathāgata is nothing other than that which benefits sentient beings; therefore, it possesses true speech and reality.
Speech refers to right speech. Yet the speech of sentient beings is nothing other than that which harms them;
thus there arise false speech, frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, and harsh speech. Because they take what is right to be wrong, they claim not to have seen what they have seen.
Because they take what is wrong to be right, they claim to have seen what they have not seen. Due to such falsehood, it is unreal. Now, although false speech—
There are eight kinds [of false speech], which do not go beyond seeing, hearing, touching, and knowing—these four factors. That is to say: to claim not to have seen what was seen;
to claim to have seen what was not seen; to claim not to have heard what was heard; to claim to have heard what was not heard; to claim not to have touched what was touched;

to claim to have touched what was not touched; to claim not to have known what was known; and to claim to have known what was not known. If one wishes to deceive another, committing any one of these constitutes lying. Furthermore...
To say one has seen when one has not seen is deception; to say one has seen when one has not seen is falsehood.

This refers to the fact that the discriminative consciousness functions as "seeing" when it resides in the eye, as "hearing" when in the ear, as "touching" when in the nose, tongue, or body, and as "knowing" when in the mind.
Because these three faculties—seeing, hearing, and knowing—are sharp in nature and their functional power is particularly predominant, they are each designated by distinct names. As for the nose...
The tongue, the body, and the three faculties share similar natures; their functional scope is narrow, and they can apprehend dull objects. Therefore, they are combined into a single designation.
Here, only the single factor of "seeing" is mentioned. The term "and so forth" (等) collectively includes the three factors of hearing, touching, and cognizing.

The second [unwholesome path of action] is frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). This refers to ornate, empty, and flowery words, licentious songs, and amorous expressions that incite desire, increase sorrow,
and agitate the minds and wills of people.
Explanation: "Gaudy" (*kīrṇa*) refers to brocade and fine silk; it is a metaphor. "Frivolous" (*mṛṣā*) means beautiful and ornate.

It refers to words that are artificially embellished and decorated, empty and unsubstantiated, yet beautiful—like weaving brocade and embroidery, clustering flowers and patterns to dazzle the eyes and minds of people.

Furthermore, even if the words are true, speaking them at an inappropriate time or speaking when it is not the right occasion is also called frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*). It is "vulgar" (*yaṃtra*)... [text fragment].
As for "melodies," this refers to the skillful composition of lascivious and beautiful songs that delude the human ear and mind, such as the "Mimi" and "Yang'e" melodies.
Generally speaking, regarding the compositions of the ancient *Yuefu*, none were as refined and elegant in their phonology and rhythm as those of the Han and Wei dynasties.

Subsequent imitations gradually became more ornate and beautiful; by the time of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang, he was so infatuated with *faqu* (court music) that he selected three hundred courtesans.
The person was taught in the Lìyuán (Peach Garden). The *ōuqǔ* (songs) of today that are called "Lìyuán" originate from this.
The *Zuǎnyào* states: "Singing in unison is called *ōu*; the songs of Wú are called *yú*; licentious songs are called *wā*; and the songs of Chǔ are called *yàn*.

Regarding "erotic lyrics," these refer to words that are flowery and beautiful, the speech of the seductive and charming. It means that the rhythms and tones are winding and turning to exhaustively convey what the mind intends to express.
They incite carnal desire; all are capable of leading people toward attachment and prolonging their sorrow.

Nevertheless, as for lyrics and melodies, there is no lack of shifting scales and changing modes, with slight variations according to the times. Roughly speaking, the Han and Tang dynasties favored *yuefu* (ballads), while the Song and Yuan dynasties favored songs and lyrics.
These are the works of poets and literary men, not something for scholars to occupy themselves with.
That which "disturbs the human mind and will" refers to the aforementioned passionate lyrics and erotic songs;

these proclaim and describe the fetters that lead into attachment, capable of altering one's ordinary nature, causing one to lose right mindfulness, and leading practitioners to forfeit the seed of the Tathāgata.
Hence it is said they "disturb the human mind and will. The term "and so forth" (等) comprehensively includes all states of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure. The *Bishan* (Pen-can) says:
Li Bashi was skilled at painting horses. Xiu Tie-mian rebuked him, saying, "You are a scholar-official who has gained fame through painting;
moreover, you paint horses merely to boast of your own excellence. To have such mastery as to penetrate into the belly of a horse is truly enough to cause alarm.

Li Bashi thereupon abandoned his brush. The Master encouraged him to paint Avalokiteśvara to atone for his transgression. Huang Lüzhi was adept at writing erotic verses; the Master likewise censured and rebuked him.
Huang laughed and said, "Are you going to place me inside the belly of a horse again? The Master replied, "Such seductive speech stirs the lustful hearts of all people under heaven;
it is not merely a matter of being in a horse's belly—it is truly feared that one will be reborn in the hells. Huang was struck with awe and apologized in regret.
Thereupon, he exerted himself with diligence.
Regarding the three types of harsh speech: "harsh speech" refers to using coarse and evil words to revile others and so forth.

Commentary: As for "harsh speech," it refers to words that are as abrasive as an owl, lacking any consideration for another's feelings, and consisting of coarse sounds and foul breath used to revile and slander others.
Thus, once the fire of anger arises, it gushes from the mouth and burns the heart, inflicting injury upon the person before one such that the pain exceeds being cut by a blade.
This truly contradicts the virtuous mind of a Bodhisattva and violates the Tathāgata’s...
This is the compassionate instruction [of our predecessors]. Thus, the *Fayuan* states: "Anger is the root of losing wholesome dharmas and the causal condition for falling into the evil realms;
it is the enemy of the joy of the Dharma, a great thief of the virtuous mind, and the internal organ of foul speech.
To 'revile' means to directly denounce; to 'abuse' means to slander indirectly—meaning to rely on one's own strengths while seeking out the shortcomings of others. Evil...
They revile one another with their mouths. Such reviling is of seven kinds:

reviling by means of physical marks, or by means of the sense faculties, or by means of transgressions, or by means of illnesses, or by means of arts and crafts, or by means of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), or by means of caste (*gotra*). The word "etc.
collectively subsumes the aforementioned methods of reviling. Upon the death of the body and the departure of the soul, they fall into the three miserable realms, as described in the sūtras.
If they fall into hell, their tongues will be cut off and made to eat them; if they fall among the hungry ghosts, maggots and pus will flow from their mouths;
if they are born as birds or beasts, they will feed on filth and excrement, and people will find their cries strange.

When their retribution ends and they become human, their countenances will be ugly, their breath will always be foul, and their lips and teeth will all be missing. The Buddha said: "It would be better to have one's tongue severed with a sharp blade..."
One must not, even for a single word, revile or slander a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts; the retribution for such evil is difficult to exhaust, lasting through the accumulation of kalpas.
There are two kinds of people who invariably fall into hell: first, those who do not practice the holy life (brahmacarya) yet claim to practice it;
second, those who truly practice the holy life but are slandered as not practicing it.
The fourth is divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
This refers to speaking about one person to another and about that person to this one, thereby creating estrangement between those who share affection and duty,
inciting strife, and so forth.
Explanation: "Divisive speech" refers to fanning discord between two parties.

"Speaking to this person about that person" means conveying the words of that person to this person, and conveying the words of this person to that person. All such acts arise from resentment and jealousy dwelling in the heart;
thus, through idle talk, cold remarks, and the proliferation of suspicion and slander, those who were united are made to part, and those who were close are estranged.
This causes estrangement. It causes the bond of gratitude between teacher and disciple to perish and the righteousness between friends to be severed.

Even if one does not repeat the words of either party, but merely speaks in order to cause a rift between the two sides, this is also double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*). The *Guǎngzi* says: "To analyze friendships and alienate kin is to be a traitor.

"Li" (離) means separation; "bie" (別) means parting; "jian" (間) means interval; and "ge" (隔) means obstruction. Regarding "en" (恩), the commentary specifically explains it as the grace of a sovereign, a father, or a teacher.

Brothers, friends, and those who provide wholesome benefit are called "righteous" (*yi*). To "instigate" means that before the other party has spoken, one provokes and incites them, causing their words to lead to conflict and strife.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "If one teaches with a virtuous mind, even if it results in separation, no offense is incurred.
However, if one uses an evil mind to cause others to quarrel and create discord, this constitutes divisive speech (*paiśunya*)."
The offense committed is profound and heavy; one will fall into the three evil realms and, in birth after birth, obtain wretched, malicious, and ruined kinsmen.
This is because, in the present life, one has caused separation and sowed discord among others.
The three types of fetters,
up to praising someone in one's presence and disparaging them behind their back, as well as exposing the faults of those who have realized the truth or proclaiming the shortcomings of others—
all these belong to the category of false speech.
Commentary: "Up to and including" (*yāvat*) is a term indicating succession; it means that these four factors are all the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of false speech.
Regarding "praising in front and disparaging behind": this refers to commending someone in their presence and then, having withdrawn, reviling them. This arises from attachment.

To "hate someone to the point of death" means to agree with them to their face while contradicting them behind their back; that is, to follow along with what is publicly right in one's presence, yet privately disapprove in secret.

Without having seen, heard, or even suspected anything of the matter, they speak recklessly and confusedly at will, seeking only to vent their own resentment, regardless of whether others live or die.
The *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "When people are born into this world, calamity comes from..."

What issues from the mouth must be guarded against more than a fierce fire. While a fierce fire blazes up and burns away worldly wealth, malicious speech blazes up and burns away the seven noble treasures.

Regarding "proving the guilt of another": this refers to making a firm, sworn testimony with a malicious mind, regardless of whether the person before one is guilty or innocent, thereby establishing the guilt of another. To proclaim [the faults] of others...

The "shortcomings" refer to exposing another's private secrets and proclaiming their faults. Knowing only oneself and disregarding others, one employs a hundred forms of deceitful artifice to cause others to fall into ruin;
therefore, it is said that these are all varieties of false speech. The *I Ching* says:
"A single word of goodness will be responded to from a thousand li away; a single word of evil will be opposed from a thousand li away. Thus, the ancients—
To seal one’s mouth is to provide a mirror for posterity. The Duke of Tai said: "If you wish to measure others, you must first measure yourself.
Words that wound others are those that wound oneself; to spit blood at another first defiles one's own mouth.
Marquis Ma Yuan of Xinxi of the Han dynasty, in a letter admonishing his elder brother’s sons, said: "I desire that you all hear..."
The faults of others are like hearing the names of one’s own parents; they may be heard with the ears, but must not be uttered by the mouth.
To delight in discussing the long and short of others and to recklessly judge the correctness of the True Dharma—this is what I greatly detest.
I would rather die than hear that my descendants have engaged in such conduct. As stated in the *Wheel of Five Realms Sutra*, the Buddha said that people take pleasure in spreading [such tales].
If one harbors hatred toward others, upon death they will enter hell. Molten copper is poured into their mouth; their tongue is pulled out and plowed with an ox-oxen.
Thereafter, they fall among the evil birds; when people hear their cries, there is none who is not struck with terror. [The practitioner] then recites mantras to cause them to die.
Second, the two types of great false speech (divided into two). First, clarifying the object:

if an ordinary person claims for themselves that they have realized the state of an arhat, such as saying, "I have already attained the fruit of a srotāpanna" or "the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin," and so forth.
Commentary: "An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who claims for themselves to have realized the state of a sage (*ārya*)"—this first phrase designates their name.

The preceding discussion concerned matters of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); this refers to supramundane false speech. One is called an "ordinary person" because they dwell within the outflows (*āsrava*) and their mind remains at the level of the common masses.
One is called a "sage" because they clearly understand the Four Noble Truths and abide in their final body. In Sanskrit, this is *ārya*.
This term is translated here as "sage" (*ārya*). Formerly, the Grand Chancellor of Shang asked Confucius, saying, "Master, are you a sage?

He replied, "I, Qiu, am merely one who hears much and has a strong memory; I am not a sage. [The Chancellor] asked, "Were the Three Kings sages? He replied, "The Three Kings were adept at employing wisdom and courage;
being a sage is not something I know. [The Chancellor] asked, "Were the Five Emperors sages? He replied, "The Five Emperors were adept at employing benevolence and righteousness."
"The Sage is not something I know," [the Master] said. The Grand Minister was startled and asked, "If that is so, then who is the Sage?
Confucius paused for a moment, then with a change in his expression replied, "In the West there is a Sage. He inspires confidence without speaking; he brings order without governing;
he acts spontaneously without transforming. How vast and boundless he is! No one is able to give him a name. However, as for all Sages—
They are distinct. There are ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) arise through defiled conditions;

that is to say, all sentient beings, upon the basis of true nature (*tathatā*), differ in their own emotional conceptions, and thus there are the six ordinary realms. Sages realize [the truth] through pure conditions;

that is to say, the Buddhas and the three vehicles, within the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), differ in the loftiness or inferiority of their wisdom, and thus there are the four noble realms. This can be seen by ordinary people.

The distance between this and sainthood is as vast as that between heaven and an abyss. To claim now that [these practitioners] have attained realization is the height of delusion. As the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* states:
"It is like an ordinary person who falsely claims to be a sovereign; he brings his own execution upon himself.

A *srotāpanna* (須陀洹) is translated here as "Stream-enterer," meaning one who has severed the eighty-eight *kleśas* (afflictions) of the three realms and has completely exhausted the delusions of view, thereby entering the stream of the Dharma of the Noble Path.
Therefore, it is also called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because one sees the True Truths (*satya*).

It is also termed "flowing against the current" or "entering the stream," because one flows against the current of birth and death and enters the stream of the Noble Dharma (*āryadharma*). It is further named the "Noble Stage" (*āryāvasthā*); this refers to the first fruit of the Hīnayāna, the *Srotāpanna*.

As for the *Sakṛdāgāmin*, this is translated as "Once-returner. This means that among the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned through cultivation, [one has already...]
Having completely abandoned the first six grades [of afflictions], yet with the final three grades still remaining, one must still return to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) once more to undergo birth;
such individuals are the *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer) and the *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner). "And so forth" refers to the remaining three fruits and the fourth fruit.

Furthermore, it may be said that they have attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), samādhi, and right reception (*samāpatti*), and that devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits come to take refuge in them.
Because the speech was not finished,
the offense of the two concentrations is termed a great lie; its retribution is extremely grave.

Commentary: Regarding "great false speech": this refers to those who, having no knowledge or insight whatsoever regarding the aforementioned four fruits of the path, as well as the dharmas of meditative concentration and so forth, falsely claim to have attained and realized them; hence it is called "great false speech.

Because they deceive and delude the world in this way to seek fame, profit, and offerings, they fall into the Avīci Hell after death; therefore, it is said that their transgression is extremely grave.

Third, it is permitted to speak other kinds of false speech if it is for the purpose of rescuing others from urgent distress, employing skillful means and expedients out of compassion and a desire to benefit them; in such cases, there is no offense.
Explanation: "Other kinds of false speech" refers to false speech excluding those mentioned above. "Rescuing others from urgent distress" refers to...

Originally, he had no intention of seeking profit, as his sole concern was to uproot suffering. As the Vinaya records: A hunter was pursuing a rabbit, which fled and took refuge beneath the Buddha’s seat.
Shortly thereafter, the hunter arrived at the Buddha’s location and asked, "Did you see the rabbit?
The Buddha replied, "I did not see it. The hunter then departed. Later, a disciple asked, "The rabbit was clearly under the Buddha’s seat; how can you say you did not see it?"
He replied, "I did not see it. The Buddha said, "It was for the sake of saving the rabbit. Furthermore, it was like King Prasenajit, who ordered the execution of his kitchen supervisor.
When Queen Mallikā learned of this, she had him hidden away until the king’s intoxication had worn off and he felt regret; she then sent him back to the king, who was greatly delighted.
Although the queen had received the eight precepts, because she saved another from distress, she did not violate the precept against lying."
This is what is called skillful means and expedient wisdom; it is that which brings benefit through compassion.

Fourth, citing an analogy from the ancients, they said that the essential principle for conducting oneself begins with not speaking falsely. How much more so, then, for one who studies the Way of transcending the world!
Commentary: "The Ancients" refers to Sima Guang, the Duke Wen. "Essentials" (*yào*) refers to the essentials for establishing one's character.
The *Tongjian* records that Lord Liu Zhongding asked Sima Guang: "May I hear the essentials for exhausting one's heart in the conduct of oneself?
The Duke replied: "It is sincerity. He asked again: "What is the starting point for the essentials of conducting oneself? The Duke replied: "From not being deceptive..."
Regarding the beginning of these words: both gentlemen were Confucians of the Song dynasty, yet they still took sincerity and integrity as their foundation.
How much more so for those who have transcended the world—how could their words and deeds possibly be at variance? For the preservation of the Way and its virtue, utmost sincerity is paramount;

for the essentials of establishing one’s character, speech and action come first. This is why Nanrong [Zhuzi] repeated the lines of the "White Fang" three times, intending thereby to exercise caution and vigilance.
Regarding these words: for this reason, the ancients cautioned against negligence at the beginning and were careful about the end; they began with the precept against false speech.
Lingsuan said: "One must not fail to examine one's conduct; one must not fail to verify one's words and deeds.
One who speaks little is not necessarily foolish, and one who has a ready tongue is not necessarily wise."
II. Citing Scriptural Evidence (divided into two parts).
First, as recorded in the *Karmavipāka-sūtra*: A novice monk mocked an elderly bhikṣu whose recitation of the scriptures sounded like the barking of a dog.
That bhikṣu was an arhat. Because he instructed the novice to perform an urgent confession, the novice narrowly escaped hell, yet still fell into the state of a dog.
A single harsh word from the body causes harm to such an extent.
[Commentary: This cites past events to prove the fault of false speech. A dog’s cry is called "barking";

that one fell into a dog's body because of a single word demonstrates that the fruit does not obscure the cause. Arhat; this is translated as "One Beyond Training" (Wuxue), meaning that which has been accomplished.

"The task is accomplished; the holy life is established; there will be no further existence. There is nothing more to be learned. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the *Mahāpratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* (Great Sūtra on Repaying Kindness) states:
In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a wealthy elder who, at the age of eighty, fathered a son named Kunti.
At ten years of age, he left the household life and went to Mount Indradhanu in the region of Rājagṛha, where he arrived at the place of the Tathāgata.
He came to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him; he immediately attained the fruit of the Path. Ānanda, harboring a doubt in his mind, addressed the Buddha.

The Buddha said, "It is not only now that Cūḍapanthaka [the Śrāmaṇera] has been so. In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a young śrāmaṇera who was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka.
He saw an elderly bhikṣu who lacked the physical marks of a man, yet who delighted in praising the Triple Gem with a melodious voice."

His voice was muddled and dull; he could not chant the hymns. When the youth insulted him, saying his voice was like the barking of a dog, the elderly bhikṣu called out to the young man, "Do you recognize me?
