My holy life is established; I shall not undergo further existence. Upon hearing this, the youth’s heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end.
He immediately sought forgiveness, saying, "Out of my folly, I did not recognize a noble sage. May I—"
In a future life, he will see a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). At that time, while still young, he reviled an elder with harsh abuse;
consequently, for five hundred lifetimes, he constantly took birth in the body of a dog. When the assembly of hundreds of thousands heard what the Buddha had said, they all made this vow:
"Even if a glowing iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of our heads, we would never utter evil words because of such suffering. Even if..."
An iron wheel revolves above my head; yet I shall never, for the sake of such suffering, slander the noble sages.
At that time, Śāriputra, throughout the six periods of day and night, observed all sentient beings with his divine eye and delivered those who were ready to be saved.
At that time, between the two kingdoms of Magadha, five hundred merchants were leading a white...
There was a dog that would cook meat for its food during the first watch of the night; then, during the last watch, it would steal and eat it.

On the following day, the merchants, suffering from hunger and thirst, became enraged; they took up knives and cut off its four paws, throwing it into a pit of excrement where it crawled about on its belly, enduring endless suffering.
When Śāriputra entered the city to beg for alms, he passed along that road and came to where the dog was. He took hold of it...
He gave him food and taught him the Dharma to benefit and gladden him. After one week, his retribution was exhausted and he was released.
He was reborn among humans. The Buddha told Ānanda: "Was that white dog at that time anyone else? It was none other than the śrāmaṇera Cunda.
Because in a past life he had reviled and abused the noble ones, he fell into the evil realms; yet because he initially vowed to repent, his transgressions were exhausted."
He was reborn in the human realm and, upon encountering the Buddha, the World-Honored One, immediately attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Because these were two fruits of karmic retribution, the Sūtra says: "When a man dwells in the world, an axe is in his mouth; it is by means of evil speech that he cuts his own body."
Commentary: Although this passage originates from the *Mūlasūtra*, it is identical in the *Dharmapada*, the *Āgama*, and the *Mahāvinaya*.
The *Fayuan* states: "The mouth is a gate; the tongue is a weapon. If one utters words improperly, one will instead injure oneself. The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states:
"Weapons are instruments of inauspiciousness, used only when there is no other choice. Speech is a thing that is not true [to reality]."
I present this against my will. Furthermore, the axe serves as a metaphor for the tongue; malicious speech is likened to the striking of the axe.

It is like a person throwing an axe to strike the sky; when the axe falls, it instead injures one's own body. When worldly people wish to harm others with malicious speech, they instead bring harm upon themselves.
As stated in the *Mahā-vinaya*: "In the past, Devadatta reviled Śāriputra, [saying] 'You are evil.'"
A lustful bhikṣu, at that moment, had warm blood flow from his nostrils and immediately fell into the great Avīci Hell with his living body.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke this verse: "When a man dwells in the world, an axe is in his mouth; it is that by which he cuts his own body."
Because of such evil speech, one who should be reviled is instead praised, and one who should be praised is instead reviled; thus one brings calamity upon oneself and ultimately finds no happiness.
As the *Sūtra-samuccaya* states: "Ambrosia and poison both reside within the human mouth.
Ambrosia refers to truthful speech; false speech is poison. Poison does not necessarily cause death, but false speech is certain [to do so]. False speech—
It is not beneficial to oneself, nor is it beneficial to others; it is not beneficial to both self and others. Why, then, speak falsely?
If it is harmful to one's own person, what harm is there in being cautious with one's speech?
Third, the exhortation to refrain from speaking falsely: "How can one not observe this precept?
The *Śīlapaṭala* (Chapter on Ethics) of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The sin of false speech can cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born [there]..."
Among human beings, one receives two kinds of retribution: first, being frequently slandered; second, being deceived by others.
Why does false speech cause one to fall into the three evil realms? It is because such speech is unreal and causes others to undergo suffering and affliction in vain.

Therefore, after death, one undergoes the suffering of hell. Because of that deception and falsehood, which violates the sincerity and trustworthiness of humanity, one thus receives [this retribution].
The retribution of animals. Because of their false speech, they all deceive themselves out of greed; due to the sin of such greed and deception, they further become hungry ghosts.
Because their false speech is not truthful, they are slandered by others; because their false speech deceives and entices people, they are in turn deceived by others.
Now that one knows that false speech brings these four great bitter retributions, how can one not exercise restraint?
The Fifth Precept on Abstaining from Alcohol (divided into three parts). First, the title:
Fifth, "Not Drinking Alcohol.
Explanation: Alcohol is a fountain of calamity. Drinking it causes one’s spiritual wisdom to become clouded and confused, leading to the inversion of right and wrong, and [the body] to rot.
The sprout of bodhi that destroys the fruit of perfect enlightenment should be eradicated. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"A bodhisattva should give rise to the wisdom of clear realization toward all sentient beings; one should not give rise to a mind of perversion toward any sentient being."
Furthermore, in the past, Meditation Master Yuanjian frequently undertook construction projects, employing a great many craftsmen.

Whenever someone sent him wine, he would invariably say, "Regarding what I am building, I must ensure it is done according to the Dharma; I would rather let the work stop than allow myself to drink wine.
At that time, while Qinghua Temple was renovating its Buddha hall, the local prominent figure Sun Yi presented two carriages of wine to Yuanjian. Yuanjian immediately broke the wine.
The vessel overflowed onto the ground. The Master [Dao]yi was greatly incensed, fearing that Ming would inflict harm upon him. That night he dreamed of a divine being who pointed a sword at him;
upon waking, he went in person to offer repentance. The *Sacca-nirgrantha-sūtra* states: "Drinking alcohol leads to much negligence."
In this life, one is perpetually deluded and forgets all matters; one is constantly rebuked by the wise.
In future lives, one remains perpetually dull-witted and loses many merits. Therefore, the person of keen wisdom avoids the faults of drinking alcohol.

Second, the explanation of the meaning (divided into three parts): first, the exposition of the Vinaya; second, citing scriptural evidence; third, the concluding exhortation. Regarding the first [exposition of the Vinaya] (divided into four parts), the first is the clarification of the object and its interpretation, which states:
"Drinking alcohol" refers to drinking any kind of intoxicating liquor. In the Western Regions, there are many varieties of such liquor.
Sugarcane, grapes, and various flowers can all be used to produce wine; in this region [of China], however, wine is made only from rice.
The commentary states that the term "drinking alcohol" is a general designation, for there are many kinds of wine; hence it says "all. This refers to the Western Regions.

This refers to India (Tianzhu). Regarding the various types [of wine], the *Shenxian Fushijing* (Scripture on the Elixirs of the Immortals) states that one gathers the *nanzhu* herb (*uncaria gambir*), boils it to make wine, which reflects a divine radiance of five colors like azure jade.
The *Fusangji* (Record of Fusang) states that in the kingdom of Donxun, there is a tree.
Its shape resembles that of the pomegranate (*dāḍima*). By taking the juice of its flowers and storing it in a basin for several days, a fine wine is produced.
The *Dongming ji* states: "Nine ten-thousand *li* from the royal gate of Yaoyan, there is a herb; when cut, it is used to brew wine. Drinking one *he* of it causes one not to wake for three days;
drinking water from the Dayi River restores consciousness. The *Nanshi* records that in the kingdom of Kulu, there is the "Water Fairy" (*shuixian*).
There is a tree whose trunk contains water called "Immortal Nectar" (*siddhārtha*). Those who drink it remain intoxicated for seven days. The *Gujin zhu* (Notes on Antiquity and Present) states:

"In the kingdom of Wusun, there is the 'Green Field Stone' (*qingtian he*). When it encounters water, it becomes wine of pure flavor; once it is drunk, it regenerates. It is named 'Green Field Wine' (*qingtian jiu fu*).
The *Yiwuzhi* (Record of Strange Things) states: "Wine made from 'Patterned Grass' (*wencao*) is of exquisite taste; people purchase it with gold and will not accept anything else."
This is considered noble. Now, although there are many varieties of alcohol, they generally do not exceed two types.

The first is grain liquor (*dhānya-madya*), which is brewed by mixing the five grains with *qū* (fermenting agent). The second is wood liquor (*vṛkṣa-madya*), which is distilled from the stems, branches, flowers, and fruits of various trees, combined with medicinal herbs;
this includes liquor made from sugarcane, grapes, various flowers, lotus roots, sugar, honey, and so forth.
This is so. "This region" refers to Zhendan (China). It is said that because Zhendan has not yet produced [the specific medicinal preparations], both types of manifest precepts prohibit drinking.

Commentary: "Neither [type] may be drunk" refers to the aforementioned kinds of liquor; even if they possess color, fragrance, and fine flavor, yet have the power to intoxicate a person, none of them may be drunk.
If one does not refrain from doing so, one will be held in contempt by others in this present life.
One who falls into the evil realms after death shall not even place a drop of wine upon the tip of a blade of grass to let it fall into the mouth;

for even a single drop, if not removed, gradually becomes a river and an ocean. It is likewise forbidden to consume food from a trough, to eat fermented grain (*maku*), or to cook food mixed with wine.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "If you take me as your teacher, you must not drink wine, nor must you store it."
[The Buddha] permitted [the consumption of] fermented liquids for three reasons:

to provide relief, to treat those with serious illnesses, and when there is no remedy other than wine. In such cases, one may consume it only after informing the assembly; otherwise, not even a single drop may be taken.
"Touching the lips.

Explanation: "A person with a grave illness" refers to one whose condition is not a minor ailment. How could a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jun weight be used solely against a field mouse?
Regarding the phrase "nothing but wine can cure it," this is as if a physician were to say that no other substance can provide salvation, and only wine will do.
Regarding those that can be treated as medicine: one should follow the Vinaya by informing the assembly before consuming them; only then will one be free from the fault of self-indulgence.

However, one must not harbor the intention of acting "sick" when not yet ill as a pretext for drinking. If one feigns illness as an excuse to plot the indulgence of drinking, this is called breaking the precepts.
Even for the sake of illness, one should consume the medicine only if it is effective, and stop immediately once the illness has been cured.
When drinking, one must not enter the assembly; one should instead pay respects from afar at the lee side of the Buddha hall.

Furthermore, one is not permitted to recite sutras or hold mantras. Only after seven days have passed, having bathed and changed clothes, is it allowed to do so. Regarding "without cause," this refers to the absence of any medical necessity;
one must not drink otherwise. In the Vinaya, the Buddha said: "Alcohol has many faults; it opens the gateway to heedlessness."
"Drink [liquor] like *tṛṇaja* (mustard seed): once the transgressions have accumulated, it is not as if one can first eliminate them by curing the suffering of illness.
Furthermore, the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* says: "Liquor is the root of heedlessness; by not drinking, one closes off the evil paths.

It would be better to abandon hundreds of thousands of bodies than to violate the teachings of the Dharma; it would be better to let the body wither away than to ever drink this liquor. Even if one were to..."
One who violates the precepts may live for a full hundred years; yet this is not equal to one who guards the prohibitive precepts, even if that person’s body perishes at once.
Such a person is certain to be healed. "I still do not drink [the medicine], much less now when it is uncertain whether I shall be cured or not.
Having formed this resolute mind, great joy arose in his heart, and he immediately attained the vision of the Truths; thus, his ailment was instantly eliminated.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "The bhikṣu Sāti had nourished his body and sustained his life with alcohol since childhood.
After he went forth into homelessness, because he could not obtain alcohol, the four great elements of his body became unbalanced. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
'For one who is ill, I permit smelling it from atop a jar. If he does not recover by smelling it, I permit mixing alcohol with flour to make cakes and eating them. If..."
As for those who have been assigned [this task]: they are not permitted to smell food again;

they are protected from censure in these four respects, up to and including not being allowed to sniff alcohol, not being allowed to stay in a tavern, and not being allowed to give alcohol to others to drink.
Explanation: "Xiù" (to smell) refers to smelling with the nose. "Zhǐ" (to stop) means to pause briefly. "Jiǔshè" (wine-house) refers to a tavern;
it is one of the improper modes of conduct (*akuśala-saṃvara*). Although one does not drink when smelling wine or stopping at a wine-house, there are two great dangers:

first, it causes others to harbor suspicions; second, it gradually perfumes the senses until it becomes a habit. This is also a method for preventing small evils from becoming great and stopping gradual corruption before it spreads. As the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: [With]...
One who gives alcohol to others shall be handless for five hundred lifetimes; the prohibition against it is extremely strict.

This is because while breaking the precept of abstaining from alcohol oneself results in no more than the fault affecting only one's own person, if one provides it to others to drink, the harm caused does not cease there.
II. Citing Scriptural Evidence (divided into two parts): A. Non-Buddhist Texts; B. Buddhist Sūtras. A. Non-Buddhist Texts (divided into three parts):
First, Yu’s Prohibition against Yi Di’s Brewing of Wine; Yu, consequently, lamented and cut off [the practice].
Commentary: The *Renwu Kao* (Investigation of Men and Things) states that Yi Di was the younger brother of Yu’s consort and was skilled at brewing wine.

When Yu drank it and found it sweet, he said, "In future generations, there will surely be those who cause their states to perish because of wine. He subsequently distanced himself from Yi Di and renounced fine wines.
Formerly, when Bing Yuan of the Han dynasty refused to drink wine, someone asked him why. Yuan replied, "I was originally able to drink, but..."

Wasteful thoughts cause one to neglect their vocation; therefore, I have severed them. If Confucian scholars of the world still fear neglecting their vocations, how much more so for those studying the Way that transcends the world?

Furthermore, according to the *Book of the Restoration of Jin*, Emperor Yuan was by nature fond of wine. Wang Dao deeply admonished him against this, and when an attendant brought a cup of wine forward, he overturned it.
The *Book of Jin* states that commoners were not permitted to privately brew or sell wine; however, in cases of marriage...
This applies to those who are ill; others who violate this shall be fined eight *liang* of gold. Furthermore, Mei Cheng’s *Qi Fa* (The Seven Triggers) states:
"Wine is a medicine that rots the intestines. Since antiquity, sagacious rulers and worthy ministers have feared it would bring hardship upon the people, and therefore they prohibited it."
Second, regarding the ruin of Zhou:
Zhou constructed a wine pool, and the state perished because of it.
The *Shi ren wu kao* states: Zhou’s name was Xin. He was the youngest son of Emperor Yi. He had three brothers; the eldest was named Wei.
Zi Qi was the next; his successor was Zhong Yan; both were born of concubines. The third was Xin, born of the legitimate consort; he was Zhou.
He possessed quick-witted eloquence and strength sufficient to wrestle with fierce beasts. His wisdom was such that it rejected all counsel, and his speech was sufficient to gloss over his errors.
He made a forest of meat and a pond of wine, ordering men and women to pursue one another naked within them; at a single drum-roll, three times as many drank like oxen.
He maintained a thousand concubines in his palace and held nine markets within it. He indulged in drinking bouts throughout the long night and devised the "frying-iron" torture.
He剖開ed pregnant women and hacked at people's shins. When Prince Bi Gan remonstrated with him, he said in a rage, "I have heard that the heart of a sage has seven apertures."
He then killed Bi Gan and cut open his chest to examine his heart. Thereupon, King Wu addressed the feudal lords, saying, "The Yin dynasty has committed grave offenses;
it must be punished. He then marched east to attack Zhou. Zhou fled and ascended the Luk Tai terrace, where he dressed himself in pearls and jade, set himself on fire, and died.
This is what Yu meant when he said that future generations would lose their states because of wine. Thus, the *Shi* and *Shu* [criticize] such excess.

The warning against disorder originates entirely in wine. Thus, when King Zhou was steeped in the dregs of liquor, the Viscount of Wei composed a *Gao* (Admonition) and departed for the sake of Jizi and Bigan.

Duke Mu, following the example of King Li of Zhou who was immersed in wine, composed a *Daya* (Elegant Ode), sighing with lamentation until his tears flowed incessantly. Later, the Qin ruler Fusheng drank without restraint...
Day and night, he slaughtered many while intoxicated; his ministers and subjects feared him. Fu Jian, the King of Koguryo (Haedong Wang), led an army to attack him.
While Fu Jian was still sleeping drunk, the soldiers killed him. Fu Jian subsequently proclaimed himself Emperor.

As for Emperor Jingzong of the Tang, at the age of eighteen, he drank heavily and played ball with eunuchs one night; suddenly the candles went out, and he met his assassination. Thus, he lost his life and his kingdom perished.
All this is due to alcohol.
For three monks to pass by other monks while drinking wine is even more shameful.
Commentary: As for the term "Sangha," it refers to those who uphold the prohibitive precepts and preserve the truth; whose dignified deportment transcends the mundane;
who perpetuate the lineage of the Sages; and who terrify the armies of Māra. They serve as the banner for humans and devas, and are the beams and rafters of the Dharma-gate.
If one drinks alcohol, their speech will mostly lack foundation and their transgressions will be immeasurable—resembling a mad elephant without a hook, like a playful monkey...
Because it is under a tree, it is said that the shamefulness is even more extreme.
Part Two: The Inner Scripture (divided into three). First, explaining the cause:
formerly there was an upāsaka who, because he violated the precept against intoxicants, subsequently broke all the remaining precepts as well, resulting in thirty-six faults.
A single drink [of alcohol] is sufficient to prepare for this;
how could the transgression be anything but minor? "Śramaṇa" is a Sanskrit term; in this [Chinese] language, it is translated as *upāsaka*, which means "male lay follower.

This refers to one who, by receiving and upholding the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, is able to dwell in close proximity to the Triple Gem. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Formerly, there was a certain lay follower whose innate nature..."

The benevolent and worthy one had received and upheld the five precepts, observing them with single-minded diligence and without transgression. Later, at another time, he returned home from a long journey.
His family members were attending a gathering, and being oppressed by thirst, he saw wine in a vessel that appeared like water;

he took it and drank it, thereby violating the precept against intoxicants. At that moment, a neighbor’s rooster entered his house; he stole and killed it for food, thus further committing the offense of theft and killing.

Second, regarding the precepts: A neighboring woman followed a rooster into his house and forcibly compelled him to engage in sexual intercourse, thereby causing him to violate the precept against sexual misconduct.

When the neighbor reported this to the authorities, he refused to acknowledge it and remained silent, thereby further violating the precept against false speech. Thus it is said: "He subsequently broke all the remaining precepts as well.
As for the thirty-six faults, they refer to being unfilial toward one's parents, showing disrespect to teachers and elders, lacking faith in the Triple Gem, and failing to revere the scriptures.
They slander the Dharma; they revile śramaṇas; they expose the shortcomings of others; they constantly speak falsehoods; they falsely accuse others of evil deeds;
they engage in divisive speech by conveying rumors; they use harsh words that wound others. These are the root of illness and the foundation of strife;

they cause an evil reputation to spread, are despised and loathed by others, disparage the sages and worthies, bring resentment upon Heaven and Earth, neglect their duties and vocations, and squander their family wealth.
Constantly lacking shame and remorse, they know not how to feel abashed. They beat their servants and slaves; they kill living beings wantonly;

they commit adultery with the wives of others; they steal the property of men; they distance themselves from virtuous people and associate closely with evil friends. Always harboring anger and resentment, they are filled with sorrow day and night.
Tugged eastward and pulled westward, held south and pinned north, they fall prostrate in the streets and lie down in the alleys; they tumble from carts and fall from horses. When they encounter...
One falls into rivers; one holds lamps and loses them to fire; one perishes from the heat in the summer months; one freezes to death in the depths of winter.
These thirty-six calamities are all brought about by a single drink. Therefore it is said: "The transgression is no small matter."
Second, those who crave and indulge in intoxicants will, upon death, fall into the Hell of Boiling Excrement; in every lifetime they shall be born dull-witted and foolish, losing the seed of wisdom.
This delusive drug that maddens the soul is more virulent than arsenic or poison.
Commentary: "Those who greedily drink" refers to those who crave its fragrance and flavor, finding pleasure in drinking it.

Little do they realize that this very pleasure gives rise to perversion (*viparyāsa*), and through perversion, one loses right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Once right mindfulness is lost, the seed of the Buddha is lost.
As the *Sūtra on the Five Paths of Rebirth* states: "Those who take pleasure in drinking alcohol will, after death, enter the Hell of Boiling Excrement. Hereafter...

They fall among the *xingxing* apes. Later, when reborn as humans, they are foolish, dull-witted, and thus possess no knowledge. The *Jiaohua didiyu jing* (Sutra on Teaching and Transforming the Hell Beings) states:
"The Bodhisattva Xinxiang addressed the Buddha, saying: 'Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are either dazed or insane.'"

"Sometimes they are deluded or foolish, unable to distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly. What sin has caused this? The Buddha said, "In a previous life, while intoxicated and disordered from drinking wine, they committed thirty-six transgressions.
Consequently, they have now obtained a body of delusion, like a drunken man who does not recognize the honorable from the lowly, nor the beautiful from the ugly;
thus they incurred this retribution. Nevertheless, good and evil do not fail to correspond; there must be a result for every cause."
Because of greedy drinking, one falls into the Hell of Boiling Excrement; because of drunken confusion, one loses wisdom. Regarding "drugs that delude the soul and cause madness":
this is because alcohol can cause people to become inverted and disordered, losing outward decorum and internally forfeiting their true nature.

Regarding "more virulent than arsenic or poison": arsenic refers to white arsenic (*pīśāca*); if one consumes it, the mind and spirit become disturbed and one dies. "Poison" (*dūṣī*) refers to the *dūṣī* bird; [it is] large...
It is like the *pārāvata* pigeon, which feeds on snakes; when it stirs food with its bristling feathers, anyone who consumes it dies immediately.
"Fierce" refers to the bitterness of wine, which is even more severe than the poison of arsenic or the *viṣa* of the *śatapatra* bird. Yet, as for the poison of arsenic and the *viṣa*...
It does not destroy one's physical body; yet in the future, one may again obtain a human body. The poison of drinking alcohol, however, can destroy the body of precepts.
Once the body of precepts is destroyed, it is difficult to restore.
Regarding the three vows, a sutra states:
"I would rather drink molten copper than venture to violate the prohibition against alcohol. The commentary explains:
"As for 'I would rather drink molten copper,' this is because one contemplates the faults of alcohol; since its harm is such as this, one makes a solemn vow: 'I would rather...'"
"Drink molten copper; let it corrode and rot my body, yet I shall never drink alcohol.
Based on these sutras and treatises, as well as various historical records and their diverse expressions and metaphors, the general intent is to exhort one to abandon the faults of alcohol.
Indeed, among all poisons in the world, none are more violent than arsenic, lethal toxins, and molten copper; therefore, these are cited as analogies.
One must restrain oneself by means of the precepts. As a disciple of the Buddha, can one afford not to be sober?
Alas! After these three exhortations, can one not exercise restraint?
The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: At the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery, a certain bhikṣu was gravely ill and nearing death.
Upāli asked him, "What medicine do you require? He replied, "I need wine. [Upāli thought,] "This truly violates the Vinaya;
rather than exhausting my life, I would never permit the consumption of alcohol. Upāli then said, "If it is for the sake of illness, the Tathāgata has granted an exception."

This man had taken wine to cure an illness. The bhikṣu felt ashamed and, still considering himself to have committed an offense regarding alcohol, went to the Buddha’s dwelling and earnestly repented his transgression.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the path of an Arhat. The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) by Liang states: "Fayu was at Changsha Temple in Jiangling.
A certain monk drank wine and neglected the evening incense offering. Fayu merely punished him but did not expel him; such was the teacher's way."
An placed thorns in a tube and sent them to Yu. Upon receiving them, Yu prostrated himself toward the tube in respectful homage and ordered the *karmadāna* to administer the staff [of discipline].
He shed tears and reproached himself.
Sixth, the precept against wearing garlands of fragrant flowers (divided into two parts). First, the title.
The sixth is: not wearing fragrant flowers or garlands, and not anointing the body with perfumes.

Explanation: "Not wearing" fragrant flowers and the like means severing craving and attachment. If craving and attachment are severed, one is identical to the Buddha-body, and the adornments of both the primary and secondary bodies are spontaneously and fully perfected.
If one wishes to attain such perfect adornment, one must first distance oneself from perfumes.

This refers to the two types of objects of contact. Indeed, all people in the world know that the adornments of the Tathāgata’s physical body and his environment (the *āśraya* and *sambhoga*) are beyond compare;
yet they do not realize that these adornments were accomplished through the cultivation of ascetic practices over vast eons and are the result of having severed craving and attachment.
Today, people fail to cultivate ascetic practices and do not sever their craving and attachment, yet they desire to imitate the Tathāgata’s physical body and environment.
This is like a poor man wearing the robes of a sovereign; his calamity will swiftly arrive.

Second, the explanation of the meaning (divided into three parts): first, the statement of the rule; second, the citation of evidence; third, the summary exhortation. Within the first [part] (divided into two), first, clarifying the object.
The commentary states: Regarding "flower garlands" (*mālā*), people in the Western Regions string flowers together to form garlands with which they adorn their heads.
In this land [of China], it refers to such items as silk, wool, gold, and jewels used to fashion turbans, crowns, and similar headwear.

Regarding "anointing the body with incense," the nobility of the Western Regions use famous incense ground into powder, which is rubbed onto the body by attendants dressed in blue. In this land, it refers to wearing perfumes, burning incense, and using fragrant oils.
This refers to items such as powdered [incense].
Explanation: In Sanskrit, it is called *mālā*, which means "to remove" or "flower garland," or it is called *kaṇṭhikā* (necklace).

In India, people frequently use flowers such as the *sumana* and others, stringing them in rows to adorn their heads; this is termed a *mālā*. This applies regardless of whether one is male or female.
Women all adorned themselves with these. *Zēng* refers to fine silk; *róng* refers to spun silk, which is silk thread processed by scraping and refining.
"To fashion and decorate" means to embellish necklaces, bracelets, and armlets with gold, silver, and the seven treasures, as well as to manufacture items such as headscarves and crowns.
As for the manufacture of these headscarves and crowns, it began in the time of the Yellow Emperor. Ancient...

According to the rites, at the age of twenty one begins the practice of capping; for the scholar-officials (*shiren*), a formal cap (*guan*) is used, while for the commoners (*shuren*), a turban (*jin*) is used.
Since then, figures such as Zi Yun and Dongpo have each devised their own styles. As for the names of incenses, they are not fixed;

those termed "precious" (*mingxiang*) refer to highly valued fragrances such as agallochum, sandalwood, musk, camphor, benzoin, frankincense, and white resin. The practice of anointing the body with these is the custom of the kingdom of India.
Noble men and women all prefer fine incense ground into powder; either after bathing or at other times, they have youths apply it to their bodies.
This is like the "fragrant soap" (fāng zhāopí) and similar items of this region.

The "youths in green robes" (qīngyī shìtóng) are like the youth Qiáoqīng mentioned by Xuánzhēnzǐ, who was ordered to brew tea within bamboo tubes. In this region, there are also those who wear incense sachets (xiāngnáng), or alternatively...
Incense tubes. This includes the incensing of robes and bedding, as well as the application of rouge, face powder, and the like; all such acts are subsumed under this precept. The *Er-yi-lu* states:

"The use of rouge began with King Zhou [of the Shang dynasty]. It was made from the juice of *honglan* flowers and was used as 'peach blossom makeup' (*taohua zhuang*), which originated in the state of Yan.
Regarding silver powder (*yinfen*), the *Gu-jin-zhu* says that during the Three Dynasties, lead was used for powder. This...
These are all merely worldly manners.
For one who has left the household life to manifest the precepts, how could such things be appropriate?

Commentary: This refers to those who have left the household life. If one uses silk, wool, gold, jewels, or the like to fashion and decorate hats or canopies, it is just as in India, where one strings flowers to make garlands to adorn the head.

If one wears incense or applies perfumes, this is simply using fragrances to smear the body. These are all practices of laypeople and are not for the use of monks. Since they have already departed from the secular world...
One should distance oneself from ornaments and cultivate the supramundane path by wearing dyed robes.

Adorning the Dharma-body with precepts and concentration serves as the incense that perfumes the untainted essence. How could one act like a worldly person, indulging the mind in greed and attachment?
Therefore it is said: "How could it be appropriate to use these? If one possesses a heart of greedy attachment and clings to such things, one is not a disciple of the Buddha. Why is this so?
The mind of greedy attachment is the root from which desire arises. If the thoughts of desire are eliminated, then no evils will be produced.

The *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "If one takes pleasure in garlands and scented ointments, it is the same as taking pleasure in garlands of glowing red-hot iron, or taking pleasure in having one's body smeared with excrement and urine."
II. Citation of Scriptural Authority (in five parts).

First, reflecting on the ancient Buddhas' regulation of the three robes: they were all made of coarse hemp; [using] animal fur or silk from silkworms would harm living beings and violate compassion, and is therefore not appropriate.
Explanation: The Buddha’s regulations are as stated above. Regarding the three robes: the *antarvāsa*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *saṃghāṭī*.
"Coarse" means not fine or sparse, nor is it dense. This is stated by citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to admonish against coveting what is beautiful.
This includes animal hair, such as furs and coarse wool; and silk from the silkworm's mouth, such as *zhou* and *juan* fabrics. All of these...
It is produced from the act of killing; therefore, it is called "harming living beings. It detracts from the mind of compassionate salvation; therefore, it is called "injuring compassion.
Since it violates the Buddha's precepts and further harms benevolence and mercy, it is said to be "that which ought not to be done. The Great Master Zhao of Dazhi said:
"The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that in the past, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa bestowed upon our original teacher, Śākyamuni, his robe..."

The thirteen-fold *saṃghāṭī* made of coarse cloth is this very one. When [the Buddha] was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he personally entrusted it to the Venerable Kāśyapa at Mount Kukkuṭapāda, saying:
"Wait for Maitreya; this is the robe worn by every Buddha. It is a garment of coarse cloth.
Second, as for the allowance of exceptions:
this applies to those over seventy years of age whose physical decline is so extreme that they cannot remain warm without cotton clothing; for such individuals, it may be permitted.
For all others, it is not allowed.

Explanation: When the vital energy (*prāṇa*) weakens and declines daily, and one’s strength diminishes, it is called "decline" (*tūi*). In its extreme form, one cannot endure even the most basic tasks;

this refers to the period after the age of seventy, when the blood and vital energy have become feeble and physical power is insufficient. One is unable to move about even with coarse clothing; therefore, [the Buddha] provisionally permitted [this practice].
This Great Master [Vasubandhu] did so out of compassion by means of worldly attire, and thus it is not the three robes (*tricīvara*). Some say...
It is not fixed. That is to say, if one’s physical decline is not severe, it is not permitted [to wear them]. The *Gantong zhuan* states:
In the second month of the second year of the Qianfeng era of the Tang dynasty, the Four Heavenly Kings said to Vinaya Master Xuan:
"From the time Śākyamuni Tathāgata first attained enlightenment until his parinirvāṇa, he wore only coarse cotton *saṃghāṭī* robes and the three white woolen garments; he never..."
They wore silks and fine fabrics as their "silkworm robes.
Three were frugal by worldly standards:
Yu of Xia wore coarse clothing; Gongsun Qi used a cloth blanket for a bed; and even those of noble rank among the king's ministers did not do what they ought to have done.
Commentary: "Evil" refers to the loose-fitting garment; it celebrates the virtue of Yu. The *Tongjian* records that Bo Yu, the Xia Hou Shi, was named Wenming and styled Gaodi.
According to the *Shifafa*, one who succeeds by abdication and achieves great merit is called Yu. His ancestor was Zhuanxu, and his father was Gun;
he was thus the great-grandson of the Yellow Emperor. He was conceived for two months during the fifty-eighth year of Yao’s reign, in the sixth month of the Wuxu year.
He was born on the sixth day of the month in the town of Shiniu in Baidao. He grew up among the Western Qiang tribes. He ruled as king by the virtue of Earth (*tǔdé*).

He established the calendar with the month of Yín (the second lunar month) as the first. He reigned for one hundred and six years before passing away at Kuaiji. During the time of Yao, the great flood reached the heavens;
Gǔn’s efforts to control the waters were unsuccessful. Shùn then appointed Yù to continue his father’s work. He lived abroad for thirteen years to open up the Nine Provinces. Three...

He passed by their gates but did not enter; thus, the calamity of the waters was finally stilled. He received the abdication of Shun and established his capital at Anyi, founding the state known as Xia.
Yu was a man of quick wit and diligent industry; his virtue was unswerving, his benevolence approachable, and his words trustworthy.
His voice resonated with the *zhong* pitch, and he regulated his person according to the laws of propriety. Thus, Confucius praised him, saying: "His food and drink were simple."
Yet he manifested filial piety toward the spirits. He wore coarse clothing, yet displayed the finest beauty in his ceremonial robes and caps.

He kept his palace humble, yet exerted all his strength in the construction of irrigation canals and ditches. Regarding Yu, I find nothing to criticize. In ancient times, Emperor Yao wore plain clothes to cover his body and deer skins to ward off the cold;
his garments and shoes were not replaced until they were worn out. Emperor Wen of Han likewise wore dyed coarse cloth himself, and his inner curtains were made of felt.
His tent was without ornamentation. When Emperor Wu of Jin burned the pheasant-head fur robe, he still issued an edict forbidding the offering of such items.
There have been many such sagacious rulers regarding extraordinary crafts and exotic garments; I cannot enumerate them all. Gongsun is his surname and Hong is his given name.

Emperor Wu of Han summoned him as a *boshi* (erudite). The Son of Heaven, observing his sincerity and integrity, subsequently appointed him as Grand Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (*Yushi Dafu*).

In his meals he did not eat meat twice; he ate plain millet porridge and used a cloth quilt. His stipend was entirely given to those who relied on him for food, leaving nothing remaining in his household.
At that time, Ji An memorialized, saying: "Huang Hong holds the rank of a Senior Duke (San Gong), yet he uses a cloth quilt;
this is a deception. The Emperor questioned Huang Hong, and Hong apologized, saying: "It is true. It truly addresses my own failing. For one of my status as a Senior Duke..."
The Duke used plain cotton for his bedding; in reality, he was practicing hypocrisy to fish for fame. Furthermore, he lacked the loyalty of Ji An. How could Your Majesty have heard such words?
The Son of Heaven regarded him as modest and treated him with even greater favor.
He appointed Hong as Chancellor and enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Pingjin. He died at the age of eighty.

How could those who observe the four monastic precepts be practitioners of the Way? On the contrary, they greedily crave ornamental finery. It is only fitting that they wear robes of dyed colors and clothe their bodies in refuse-rags.

As for the "rag-robe" (*pāṃśukūla*), there are ten types according to the Vinaya:

these are items discarded by worldly people that are no longer used, and because they are regarded as being like refuse, bhikṣus collect them, wash and dye them to the color of the *kaṣāya*, and sew them into the three robes to cover the body.
Substance consists of contentment and progress on the Path; it quiets the mind of restless seeking and severs thoughts of arrogance and indulgence. Thus, it is said, "it is truly appropriate.
Formerly, when a bhikṣu washed his refuse-rag robe by a river, the devas took the wash-water and used it to cleanse their own bodies.
He did not decline the unclean task; next, as an outsider, he took a clean cloth to wash [the Buddha’s feet]. The devas obstructed him from afar, saying, "Do not defile the waters of the pond.
Thus we know that they valued his virtue, not his material things.
5. To cite an example from antiquity:
there were eminent monks who wore a single pair of shoes for thirty years; how much more so should this be true for ordinary people?
"Eminent monk" (gāosēng) is a title for one who dwells in the mundane world without being defiled by it, possessing profound virtue and great dignity. A pair of shoes is called *shuanglǚ*.

[The term] *liǎng* (a pair of shoes). The *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Tang* states that when Dharma Master Huixiu left home at the age of sixteen, his studies encompassed the sutras and śāstras;

he was particularly proficient in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, yet regarding the Vinaya section, he had not yet had the leisure to examine it thoroughly. He thought to himself, "The precepts can be sought through practice."

Upon reading it, he understood immediately without the need for a teacher’s instruction. Later, however, when he opened a single fascicle, his nature and understanding were at a loss; only then did he regret his previous judgment.
He then requested the *vinaya* from Master Ti-ping, following Master Hong to listen to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* more than thirty times.

Looking at his disciples, he said: "In the past, when I listened to the sutras and śāstras, I would enter into their profound spirit after a single reading; now, in listening to the *vinaya* section, it exceeds [the former]."
This increases and surpasses [the darkness of] ignorance. Is it not the case that while principles may be sought in vain, the actual facts are difficult to reconcile?

For this reason, I once heard Master Li lecturing on the Vinaya, and he said: "Dharma Master, you are a Great Virtue in your later years; why do you still exert yourself so diligently in the Vinaya-piṭaka?
Daohui replied: "I recall the beginning of my renunciation: I came from the jaws of a tiger. How could I, even in my old age, allow myself to be separated from it for even a moment?"

Yes. I have long regretted that I could not hear this constantly. Today’s later scholars possess a meager knowledge of literary phrasing, yet their grasp of the essential tenets remains vast and obscure;

they immediately presume themselves to be teachers and models, which is why I sigh deeply throughout the long nights. You, however, are reverently cautious in the three karmas and devotedly practice the six periods of worship.
You honor the prohibitions and guard the Way, becoming more earnest as you grow older. As for clothing, you obtain what merely covers the body; your robes hang suspended from the wall.
He wore a single hempen sandal for over thirty years; whenever he encountered soft ground, he would go barefoot.

When people asked him the reason for this, he replied, "It is difficult to consume the offerings of the faithful. The Emperor repeatedly summoned him to the capital, but he firmly declined on the grounds of illness. He lived to the age of eighty-eight.
Furthermore, after attaining great enlightenment, Chan Master Tonghui of the Tang dynasty sewed his coarse cotton robes together, wearing them through both winter and summer.
It was simple. In his later years, he possessed only one skirt and one blanket. For over twenty years, he wore a single pair of hemp sandals;

he would wear them when encountering sandy ground out of fear of harming the physical remains left by his parents, but he would walk barefoot on soft ground out of fear of damaging the offerings of the faithful.
Third, the exhortation to refrain from drinking: "Is it not fitting to observe this precept?
The *Uttaramātṛ-sūtra* states: "The bhikṣu Uttara honored the Buddha and delighted in the Dharma; he did not even touch alcohol."
[He observed] the precept of not eating after midday. He never applied incense, flowers, or cosmetics to his body. His mother had become a hungry ghost (*preta*).

Udāra placed water in a jar, inserted willow twigs into it, and covered the top with his dharma robes. He then provided a meal for the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) and recited the names [of the Buddhas] while offering prayers of merit.
Thus, his mother was freed from her grave transgression. The *Aśokarāja-sūtra* states: "In South India, there was a man who..."
Having gone forth in the Buddha-dharma, he was one of few desires and contentment, taking no pleasure in honor or fame.

He did not anoint his body with ghee or oil, nor did he bathe in warm water; he did not consume ghee or oil, nor did he desire floral ornaments. Constantly fearing birth and death, he traveled to the kingdom of Mathurā to pay homage to Upagupta.
Upon hearing the Dharma once, he applied himself with diligence and reflection, and attained [realization].
The Fruit of Arhatship.
Seventh: The Precept Against Singing, Dancing, and Watching Performances (divided into two parts). First, the title:
Seventh, one shall not sing, dance, or engage in theatrical performances, nor go to watch or listen to them.
Commentary: "Not singing or dancing" means that body and speech are free from transgression. "Not watching or listening" means that the eyes and ears are pure.

In studying the Way, taking the cultivation of the self as the foundation, one should guard the mouth like a sealed jar and defend the mind like a fortified city, devoting oneself solely to single-mindedness.
One must apply oneself with diligence to cultivate the Way. Yet, within the three realms, every lifting of a foot and every movement of a step is nothing but sin and suffering.
As the ancients said: "To be absent for even a moment is to be like a dead person. If one's practice of the Way is not yet perfected, what joy can there be?
Once the initial resolve is lost, regret is difficult to remedy later. Therefore it is said: "One must not engage in singing, dancing, or performances, nor go to watch or listen to them."
I have often discussed how the ears and eyes, in relation to sounds and forms, most easily cause human spirit and wisdom to become clouded, yet they can also trigger the mechanism of awakening.
Thus, the Immortal [Liu] lost his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) because of them, while Master Lou opened the ground of his mind because of them.
If one traces the source of this clouding and awakening, it is said that being carried away by sounds and forms is called "flowing with the current. As for "flowing":

This is the lower [approach]. To investigate the root of awakening, one must not be carried away by sounds and forms; therefore, it is called "flowing against the current. To flow against the current means to ascend.
Among the ordinary people of the world today, those who are not carried away by sounds and forms are few;

thus, they drift further and further from the Way day by day. For this reason, a beginner should avoid sounds and forms as if they were swords and blades, and regard laughter and play with such caution.
It is like weeping; singing and dancing are like madness. When one does not indulge in external objects, the inner mind naturally becomes tranquil.

Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, bodhisattvas of great authority, moved by the Buddha’s grace and virtue, manifested in the forms of devas and humans, constantly praising the Buddha with *brahmaghoṣa* chants.
Sometimes they performed melodies on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, causing all sentient beings to be moved.
Realizing the eternal and constant, one causes the water birds, trees, and forests to all proclaim the wondrous Dharma;
how could this be compared to the worldly performances of song, dance, and theatrical entertainment?

Second, the explanation of the meaning (divided into three parts): first, the exposition of the Vinaya; second, the citation of scriptural evidence; third, the summary exhortation. Within the first [part], there are two sections. First, the clarification of the objects and their definitions:
"Singers" refers to those who produce songs with their mouths. "Dancers" refers to those who perform theatrical dances with their bodies. "Performers" refers to lute players (*vīṇā*).
This refers to instruments such as the se, the xiao, and the guan. Regarding "songs" (gequ):
it means drawing out sounds and elevating melodies to chant and harmonize with musical tunes. The *Music Book* (*Yue Shu*) states:
"In music there are songs; in songs there are tunes; in tunes there are lyrics. Thus, the *Book of Poetry* says, "Poetry expresses the will; song chants the words. The *Erya* says: "Long..."
To draw out the sound and compare it to the lute and zither is called "song" (*gē*). When the sound of song is heard from afar, it is called "ballad" (*yáo*).

Thus, a skilled singer possesses tones that contain the *shāng* note and emit the *jiǎo* note. As for "dancing performers," they are like those in the *níshāng* dance, adorned with lotus-patterned ornaments, moving with elegant grace and fluttering flight, manifesting transformations of body and head, leaping and bounding with hands and feet.
"Entertainers" (*chàngjì*) are the same as the *líng rén* (court musicians). It is said that...

They are able to play instruments such as the *qín*, the *sè*, the *xiāo*, and the *guǎn* for entertainment. Furthermore, the *qín* and *sè* belong to the category of stringed music (*sī-lè*), while the *xiāo* and *guǎn* belong to the category of wind music (*zhú-lè*).
Regarding the *qín*, the *Commentary on the Erya* (*Ěryá Sū*) states: "Fuxi carved paulownia wood to make the *qín*. It further says:
Shennong established it; its alternative name is Li. The larger version has twenty-seven strings; its length is not clearly specified. The *Guangya* states:
"The qin is three feet six inches and six fen long, representing the three hundred and sixty days of a year to harmonize Heaven and humanity.
It is six inches wide, representing the six realms of existence. Its waist is four inches broad, also representing the four seasons. The front...

The broadness at the back and the narrowness at the front represent the distinction between the noble and the humble. The circular face and square back represent Heaven and Earth. The five strings represent the Five Elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*).

The thirteen bridge-pins (*mushen*) represent the twelve pitch-pipes (*dvādaśa-lakṣaṇa*) with the remaining one representing the intercalary month. Later, King Wen added the "lesser *gong*" and "lesser *shang*" strings.
It has two strings, or seven; some say it adds two strings for civil and military affairs. The *Zihui* states: "The large [zither] is eight chi and one cun long;
the medium is three chi, six cun, and six fen long. The *Shiyi* states: "The 'Phoenix Pond' is four cun, representing the four seasons;
the 'Dragon Pond' is eight cun, representing the eight winds. Furthermore, there is another explanation stating that the *qin* has thirty-three strings, which are strung together.

The *sang* was made for this purpose: to cultivate the person and refine their nature, returning to their original state of truth (*tianzhen*). It is an error for people today to use it merely for amusement.
Regarding the *se*, the commentary on the *Erya* states that Fuxi originally made it with fifty strings, which Huangdi subsequently reduced to twenty-five strings.
The ancient diagrams of the Rites (*Litu*) state that the *yase* (elegant *se*) is eight chi and one cun long and has twenty-three strings. Its...

Regarding those commonly used: nineteen strings. As for the remaining four strings, the *Sòngshè* (Lute of Praise) is seven chi and two cun long and has twenty-five strings, all of which are employed.
Zheng’s commentary states: "The large *shè* is also known by the name *sǎi*. Furthermore, the *Lǜshì Chūnqiū* says:
"In the era of Zhūxiáng, there was much wind throughout the world; the yang energy did not accumulate, and fruits and grains did not ripen. Therefore, [Zhūxiáng]..."
King Jian fashioned the five-stringed *se*. Gu Sou created the fifteen-stringed version, and Shun added eight strings.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han, his singing girls produced the twenty-five-stringed instrument. The *Baihutong* states: "The *qin* means 'to restrain.
It is used to prohibit depraved thoughts and to rectify the human mind and will. The *se* means 'parsimony' and 'restraint'; it is used to punish anger and block [evil impulses]."
Desire is the virtue that rectifies the person. Regarding the *xiāo* (flute), the *Fēngsú Tōng* states: "Shùn created the *xiāo*;
it is made by binding together small bamboo tubes so that they are uneven and jagged, imitating the wings of a phoenix. The *Bóyǎ* states: "The larger version consists of twenty-three tubes."
The large ones are fourteen *chi* long; the small ones consist of sixteen tubes and are twelve *chi* long. The *Erya* states: "The large ones are called *yan*;
the small ones are called *jiao*. The *Shiming* says: "As for the *xiao*, it means 'solemn' (*su*), for its sound is solemn and clear.
Furthermore, the *Liji* states: "Nüwa created the *sheng*. The *Shuowen* says: "As for the *sheng*, it resembles the nest of a phoenix; the large one is called a 'nest' (*chao*')."
The *huang* has nineteen reeds; the smaller version is called the *he*. The *huang* with thirteen reeds has a tube one foot long and one inch in circumference, made of lacquered bamboo;
it has six holes like a flute and represents the sounds of the twelve months. The larger version is called the *jiao*, and the smaller is called the *miao*.
It is blown vertically, like a *xiāo* (flute). Its shape is like that of a *chí* or *yuè*. The *Zhou Li* states: "The *chí* is made of bamboo; it is one chi and four cun long and has seven holes;

it is blown horizontally. The *Mao Zhuan* states: "The *yuè* is made of bamboo; it is like a *dí* (flute) with three holes; it is blown horizontally. Regarding the music of King Wen, the *Fengsu Tong* says:
"As for the *dí*, it was created during the reign of Emperor Wu by Qiu Zhong; it is one chi and four cun long and has six [holes]."

The *kǒng* (holes) may be seven in number. As for the *dí* (flute), it means "to cleanse" (*dí*); it is so called because it serves to sweep away depravity and impurity, leading one toward the refined and correct.

The *Yuelü Shū* (Book of Music) states: "Cutting the frost-streaked bamboo of Yunmeng, one emulates the extraordinary tones of the dragon’s cry. In the present day, the body of the *xiāo* resembles that of the *dí*;

they are distinguished only by whether they are held horizontally or vertically. That which is held vertically is called the *xiāo*, while that which is held horizontally is called the *dí*. Regarding this:
Other instruments, such as the lute (*vīṇā*) and the harp (*kṣapaṅka*), all belong to the category of musical performances. Second,
it is manifest that one must not perform these oneself, nor may one go to watch or listen while others are performing them.
Commentary: "One must not perform for oneself" means that one must not personally sing songs or chant and recite scriptures like the Brahmins, such as the sounds of composing poetry or reading aloud.
Furthermore, one must not engage in physical performance or dance, such as appearing on stage in the graceful *nielang* (霓裳) style or assuming roles in theatrical narratives;
this includes even such gestures as swinging the arms, crossing the hands, or brandishing a sword.
Brandishing a halberd and the like are all impermissible. Therefore, when one goes with intention, one incurs transgression at every step;
yet if one encounters [the situation] without intention, staying there constitutes an offense.
2. Citing Scriptural Authority (divided into four parts). First:
An ancient seer who wished to harm [others] suddenly lost his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) upon hearing the subtle and exquisite voice of a woman singing.
If such is the harm caused by merely listening, how much more so for those who act themselves?
"Shi" (釋) means to explain. "Ju" (遽) means immediately. "Shenzu" (神足) refers to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of the divine immortals (*ṛṣi*).
First, the power of the divine ear (*divyaśrota-abhijñā*): because one is able to hear all sounds of suffering and joy. Second, the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-abhijñā*):

because one is able to see all forms and colors, as well as the signs of the death and rebirth, and the states of suffering and joy of all sentient beings. Third, the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*).
The fourth is the power of knowing the deaths and rebirths of others (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), because one is able to know all the deeds performed by oneself and others throughout many lifetimes.
The fifth is the power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*), because one is able to know all the thoughts of good and evil within the minds of others.

The sixth is the power of supernormal feats (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), because one can manifest transformations at will, travel through the air with mastery, and perform all actions without any obstruction. — *Mahāvibhāṣā* [Śāstra].
The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* states: "In the past, King Jitaśatru took his palace women and went to Mount Jalavāhana.

Having removed all men, he was accompanied solely by women. They burned various famous incenses and performed the five kinds of music; they danced in the nude as the musical sounds were pure and exquisite, and the fragrance was rich and pervasive.
At that time, there were five hundred rishis who, by means of their supernatural powers, were traveling above."
Some saw forms, some heard sounds, and some smelled scents; they all lost their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and fell down simultaneously, like birds with broken wings that can no longer fly.
The King saw them and asked, "Who are you? The sages replied, "We are seers (*ṛṣi*).
The King said, "Have you attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)? The sages replied, "We have not. [The King] questioned them further, and so on.
The King asked, "Have you attained the first dhyāna? The seer replied, "I once attained it, but have now lost it. At that, the King spoke in anger:
"How can one who has not abandoned desire gaze upon my palace women and handmaidens? He then drew a sharp sword and severed the hands and feet of five hundred seers.
Among those seers, some fell away from the faculty of the eye, and some fell away from the faculty of the ear.
They regress from the faculty of the nose; therefore, they fall all at once. Thus it is said: "The harm of sight and hearing is such as this, how much more so when one acts upon it oneself.
This refers to the fact that as soon as a single thought of desire arises, one immediately loses the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Second, exposing the delusions of the foolish people of this age: because the *Lotus Sūtra* contains the phrase regarding the lute, gong, and cymbal, they have taken it upon themselves to study music at will.
However, the *Lotus Sūtra* refers to making offerings to the Buddhas; it is not for one's own amusement.
[The] Explanation: This present age is the period of the Final Dharma (*mappō*). There are fools who are not conversant with the teachings;

they do not know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and that the lute (*pípá*) is a Hu-style zither (*qín*) measuring three feet and five inches. Its [three-and-a-half-foot length] symbolizes the Three Powers (*sancái*) and the Five Elements (*wǔxíng*).
Its four strings symbolize the four seasons. "Náo" refers to clamor; it means that when it sounds, the musical tones are tumultuous and noisy. In antiquity, this was used...
It is made of gold and is also a *nāga* (gong). It signifies "stopping. Whenever military law is enforced, the soldiers always hold the *nāga*;

at the first sound of the golden *nāga*, the drumbeats immediately cease. The *paṭaha* (cymbals) signify "assistance," meaning that when they are struck, they assist the musical sounds. *Yū* means "joy" or "pleasure."
This refers to those who have newly entered the monastic life but lack the aspiration for spiritual advancement;
they fail to realize that the essence of renunciation is most sublime while worldly customs are exceedingly base.

Hearing only the passage in the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding the lute, gongs, and cymbals, they immediately indulge their hearts and minds in playing them at will to seek pleasure, failing to understand that such music is a cause of suffering. Yet, the *Lotus Sūtra* is—
If one causes others to perform acts of making offerings to the Buddhas, one plants the causes for attaining Buddhahood in the future.

If a person who has received the precepts is indeed able to maintain their conduct with rigorous discipline, how could they not receive the protection and assistance of the devas? Even if one recites sutras and performs repentance rituals, these may still be termed "Dharma-giving.
However, if one indulges in coarse or subtle music, there is fear that the mind will give rise to attachment; therefore, such things are not permitted.
Furthermore, even ignorant and deluded fools, failing to study the Vinaya, perversely interpret the Sage’s intent.
They borrow phrases from the *Lotus Sūtra* to indulge in their own whims, using flutes and cymbals as entertainment. How are they any different from professional performers?
Thus, the Jewel of the Sangha is lost and the causes for rebirth in hell become profound. As the Vinaya states: "Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana..."
Even after the Parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣus themselves performed music, blowing instruments and chanting praises as an offering. The Buddha said, "You should not do so.
The bhikṣus, being cautious and apprehensive, did not dare to have laypeople perform music. The Buddha then granted permission for this.
Thus, the Buddha’s regulations can be understood. Question: The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is without contradiction;
both the *Lotus Sūtra* and the Vinaya are the Buddha’s words. Why, then, is the *Lotus Sūtra* permitted while the Vinaya is not?
However, one must understand that for those within the Vinaya, if they regard music as a meritorious act, then the Vinaya itself transforms into the *Lotus Sūtra*. If...
If those within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* entertain themselves with music, then both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the monastic discipline (*vinaya*) will fail to be fulfilled.
While it may still be permissible to perform rites for the human realm as a ritual site at the Sanfu Zhengyingyuan, now, for the sake of birth and death, one must renounce the secular world.
Having left the household life, how could one fail to cultivate the primary task and instead seek out the arts of music and performance?
"Śrāvastī" refers to a monastery where offerings are received from donors and where Buddhist services are performed.
"Human affairs" indicates that these are not the supramundane, ultimate Buddhist services. A place for practicing the Way in leisure and tranquility is called... [a *vihāra*].
Regarding the *bodhimaṇḍa*: because the Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*, this place was designated as the field for attaining the Way.

Now, when a human site is designated as a *bodhimaṇḍa* through ritual affairs, it is likewise due to the devotion of donors and believers who respectfully invite the Triple Gem to seek merit and benefit;
therefore, wherever one makes offerings to the Buddha and turns the wheel of Dharma, that place becomes such a field.
It is called a "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa), yet it is not the primary site of enlightenment. That it can still be undertaken is a modest concession, not a full endorsement.
Regarding the ritual activities of yoga, in ancient times these were all performed by great Dharma masters who excelled both in practice and virtue;
however, today they are not comparable to those former times. To sever attachments and bid farewell to kin is what is meant by "renouncing the secular world."

One departs from the house of afflictions; therefore, it is called "birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra*). Observing the precepts, practicing meditation and recitation, and performing prostrations—diligently cultivating merit and wisdom—are termed the "right tasks.
To fail to cultivate these right tasks and instead devote oneself exclusively to the arts and music is to further increase the burdens of birth-and-death.
It is difficult to digest the offerings of the faithful, and one's time is spent in vain; how then shall one confront birth-and-death?

The four types of games that reform abuses, up to and including *weiqi* (go) and *luobo* (chess), as well as activities such as dice-throwing and *chupu* (backgammon), all disturb the path of the mind and increase transgressions and evils.
Regarding *weiqi*, the *Bowuzhi* states: "Yao created it to instruct Dan Zhu; it has three hundred and sixty points."
First: It consists of nineteen rows both vertically and horizontally. According to local dialects, what is east of the Pass is called *yi* (chess).
The *xiangqi* (elephant chess) has thirty-two pieces, which are adorned with ivory; hence it is called *xiangqi*. It is traditionally said that Yao invented *weiqi* (go).

The *xiangqi* (elephant chess) was created by warriors; it is so called because it simulates battles between elephants. Some say that in antiquity, Shennong used the sun, moon, stars, and constellations as its pieces.
The Tang Prime Minister Niu Sengrou, however, employed chariots, horses, generals, and soldiers, adding cannons to serve as mechanical devices.
Regarding *lubo*, the commentary to the *Hanshu* states it refers to moving chess pieces. Bao Hong’s *Bojing* says there are two types of pieces.
It is divided into black and white, each half being cast. "Dice" (zòu) refers to the dice used as implements for land-based gambling games (*lùbó*).

Furthermore, *lùbó* refers to the game of *shuanglù* (double-six chess), also known as the game of *bósè*. During the Wei dynasty, Cao Zhi fashioned a *shuanglù* board and used five wooden pieces as dice.
There are five outcomes—*xiāo*, *lú*, *zhì*, *tú*, and *sè*—which determine victory or defeat; thus, people carved [these marks] upon them.

One die is shaped like a *xiāo* (owl) bird; obtaining it constitutes the highest victory. Furthermore, there are six counting-sticks (*zhù*) and six pieces moved; this is called *liúbó* (six-fold play).
"To throw" (*zhì*) means to cast, to toss, such as throwing stones, tossing arrows into a jar (*tíuhú*), or tossing balls and jumping coins.
In ancient times, stone was used for *tóuhú* (arrow-tossing), while today arrows are used; one wins by hitting the mark. *Chūpú* refers to the gaming counters (*chóu*).
Now it is called *húlú* (calling for the dice). Taking a pure color as a victory, six pieces are used as horses;
people today cast them as a game, which is also a general name for board games and gambling. This refers to what is called "a single throw of the *chūpú* wins a million."
The word "etcetera" (等) summarizes all such playthings and diversions. As stated above, none of these are the deeds of a son of the Buddha;
they merely disturb the mind intent on the path of cultivation, increase ignorant and evil karma, and cause one to sink into the sea of suffering with no time of liberation.
A person of resolve would rather maintain simple and rustic integrity, willingly sit upon a *pútuán* (grass mat), and devote themselves exclusively to the three robes and a single alms bowl.
Regarding the training in the precepts: if one seeks only minor, worldly skills yet violates the Buddha’s precepts, how could this be the conduct of one who has left home with a sincere heart?
Generally, good and evil are counterparts; like the tips of two arrows meeting, it is ultimately easier to fall into evil.
To do good is difficult; to do evil is like releasing a horse without a halter. To do good is like rowing a boat against the current.
A boat going against the current may gradually make progress, but once a horse without a halter has galloped away, it is difficult to recover.
This is also what those of like mind have said. When Tao Kan of the Jin dynasty was the Governor of Jingzhou, he saw an official...

Regarding the implements for gambling games, he said: "Go-boards were used by Yao and Shun to instruct their ignorant sons. Gambling boards were created by Yin Zhou. You gentlemen are all vessels of state;
why do you occupy yourselves with these? It is further said: 'The sage Great Yu cherished even an inch of shadow [of time].
As for ordinary people, they should cherish even a fraction of that shadow. Therefore, assistants, do not let games cause you to neglect your duties. He then took them away.
As for *chuppo* (dice): he cast them into the river, saying, "Chuppo is merely a game for swineherds' slaves.
Three times he exhorted [the people] with this; how could one not take it as a warning?
Commentary: The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states that when Dharma Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty was eleven years old, he left home to become a monk.

Observing the other śrāmaṇeras engaged in boisterous talk and playful antics, he said to them: "Those who have left the household life do so for the sake of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

How can you continue to indulge in childish play? This may be called a mere waste of a hundred years. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The characteristics of sound do not remain; as soon as it is heard, it immediately perishes."
Foolish people do not understand that the characteristics of sound are impermanent and subject to change and loss; therefore, they falsely give rise to attachment toward sounds.

Regarding sounds that have already passed, they dwell upon them and develop defiled attachment. A person of wisdom contemplates the arising and ceasing of sound, seeing that the preceding and succeeding moments do not coexist and that no characteristic can reach across them.
Knowing it thus, they do not become defiled or attached. It is like this.
As for human beings, even the music of the devas cannot disturb them, let alone the voices of men.

For various reasons such as these, one should censure the faults of sound so as not to become attached to it. Consider how even those such as the Venerable Kāśyapa rose to dance upon hearing the celestial king playing the lute, unable to remain composed;
how much more then should ordinary people not exercise self-awareness? One should distance oneself [from such attachments].
The Patriarch said: "If one acts with a distracted mind, all such actions constitute unrighteousness.
The eighth precept concerns sitting on high, wide, or large beds (divided into two parts). First, the title:
Eighth, not sitting on high, wide, or large beds.

Commentary: Regarding "not sitting," it means that the body is detached from the sense-object of touch. This refers to the disciples of the Buddha who, relying on the precepts in their practice, should maintain contentment in every matter among the four modes of deportment.
They must not take pleasure in beds and cushions, thereby giving rise to arrogance and indulgence, nor become lazy in the cultivation of meditation and recitation.
If one harbors preferences and attachments, one will not attain what is correct. The *Śīla-sūtra* says: "Constantly seek the three..."
Take ignorance as your bed and wisdom as your seat. With a single-minded resolve for the Way, do not act like worldly people by greedily seeking pleasant enjoyments.
If even a single breath does not return, one becomes like ash and soil; what use then are such attachments?

The *Madhyama Āgama* records that the brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked the Buddha, "What is suffering for one who has left the household life? The Buddha replied, "For one who has left the household life, [suffering lies in] oneself..."

Lack of mastery is suffering; that is to say, it follows upon desire, hatred, and delusion, and because one does not maintain the prohibitions and precepts, one consequently suffers from anxiety and confusion.
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asked, "What constitutes happiness? The Buddha said, "For those who have left the household life, lack of mastery is happiness.
This means that in training on the Path, one does not follow desire, hatred, or delusion, but takes the precepts as one's own [refuge]."
If one exercises restraint, there will be no strife; if there is no strife, there will be no resentment, hatred, sorrow, or suffering.
Because these benefits exist, one regards the lack of autonomy as a form of happiness.

II. Explanation of the Meaning (divided into three parts): First, the exposition of the Vinaya; second, citation of scriptural evidence; third, the concluding exhortation. Regarding the first [exposition of the Vinaya] (divided into two parts), the initial section clarifies the established rule and its interpretation, stating:
The Buddha decreed that the height of a corded bed (*rajjupīṭha*) shall not exceed eight finger-breadths of the Tathāgata; to exceed this constitutes an offense.

*Śikya* (a hanging rope rack) is one of the eighteen types of articles. It refers to a rope threaded through [a loop] and hung in a forest or beneath a tree for the purpose of dwelling there to avoid dampness and low-lying ground.
As for the term *Tathāgata*, it means one who has come (*āgata*) by means of the path of suchness (*tathatā*) to deliver sentient beings.
In the Vinaya, it is recorded that King Bimbisāra offered the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove to the Buddha and the Saṃgha. All...
The great elder constructed various dwellings and spread out floor coverings.

When it rained, the ground became very damp, and sick bhikṣus were unable to sit or lie down upon it. The Buddha said, "I allow you to construct beds. At that time, snakes, scorpions, and centipedes entered the rooms;
those who had not yet abandoned desire were all terrified upon seeing them. The Buddha said, "I allow you to install legs, one chi in height."
Six *cun* is equivalent to the eight fingers of the Tathāgata. There are two kinds of beds: first, the rope bed, provided for those who travel;
second, the wooden bed, provided for those who practice seated meditation. What is referred to here as a "seated" bed is the wooden bed.

The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the Tathāgata’s eight fingers measure approximately one foot and six inches in height, which is equal to one cubit (*hasta*) of an average person. When sitting, the feet [rest...]
It does not hang in the air. That which exceeds this measure is called "high. That which can merely accommodate the body’s turning and shifting is called "broad.

Because it is both high and broad, it is termed "large. The Great Master, fearing that beginners and students might become lax in body and mind and thereby increase their transgressions and evils, has spoken thus in accordance with the regulations established for the great monks.
Second, regarding ornaments for the precepts, such as lacquer and paint, carving and engraving, as well as items like silk curtains and cushions—these too are not appropriate to use.
*Śīla* explains: "Lacquer" refers to ash-lacquer; "paint" refers to decorative coloring. "Carving" means hollowing out the interior; "engraving" means chiseling the exterior.

Silks and gauzes are all materials produced through the taking of life. Such items as these are prized by kings, ministers, and laypeople, but they are not things for those who have left the household life to employ.
To use them violates the Buddha’s clear precepts, diminishes virtue, and invites transgression;
therefore, they should not be used. If a donor offers them, one should merely store and protect them, rather than using them. If the Sangha...
"On long connected beds, it matters not whether one sits or lies down. The *Kuixue jiyu* states: "When Shun made food vessels, he flowed lacquer and ink over them;
those in the state who did not submit numbered thirteen. When Yu made sacrificial vessels, he applied ink-lacquer to their exterior."
The interior was painted in vermilion. Among those who were not submissive to the state, there were thirty-three persons.
Yet, although Shun and Yu were sage-rulers, their use of lacquer for vessels was not an excessive indulgence, for they had worthy ministers to offer admonitions;

this was likely because they feared that the officials and common people would waste resources without restraint. Today’s monastics, however, adorn their private chambers and refine their utensils with such care.
The vessels [of the monasteries] have lost the admonitions of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; their enjoyments are equal to those offered to kings and lords.

Those who offer loyal words that are harsh to the ear and speak with direct remonstrance are treated as contrarians; those who fawn with hunched shoulders and sycophantic smiles are the ones who find favor.

This is why the monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*) decline day by day and the Dharma-gate falls into decay. The *Chūxuéjì* states: "The palaces of mugwort and the pillars of reed-grass truly brought prosperity to the state."
