Such pure principles as these—jade mats and pearl-embroidered robes—are but the corrupt customs of a precarious state.
(II. Citing Evidence, divided into three parts. First, to provide an analogy:
in ancient times, people used grass for seats and slept beneath trees; that we now possess couches and stools is already a great improvement. Why [should we not use them]?
Even higher. To indulge the illusory body to its full extent.
[Commentary: This citation of antiquity serves as a mirror for the present, precisely clarifying the benefits of maintaining the precepts and ceasing greed.
That which may be sat upon or reclined upon is called a *cang* (bed); that which is narrow and long is therefore called a *ta* (couch). The *Wu Yuan* states: "Shennong first..."
As for the making of beds and mats, previously these did not even exist. Yet, there is none more honored or noble than a king, and none more supreme or holy than the Buddha.
When the World-Honored One left the royal palace, he sat exposed in burial grounds and took shelter beneath trees;
upon attaining Buddhahood, he used grass as his seat and spoke these words: "If I do not attain perfect enlightenment, I shall never..."

Rising, he sat in the full lotus posture. This is the model for the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world. Now that there are couches and beds, one has already surpassed dwelling under trees or sitting on grass mats;
why then would one further elaborate them with carvings? Even if one were to cast aside this physical form, how could one be willing to return to the thought of practicing the Way?
As for the "illusory body," it means that this body is formed by the combination of the four great elements; it arises when conditions assemble.
When conditions disperse, they perish; they are like dreams, illusions, or flowers in the sky—false, unreal, and insubstantial. Therefore, it is called an illusory body. Fools do not understand this;
they grasp at it as real, indulging their emotions and yielding to their desires, thereby increasing the roots of outflows (*āsrava*).

Consequently, they remain long submerged within the three realms of existence, wandering back and forth without end. Master Huirong of Donglin addressed the assembly, saying: "To avoid the Ten-Thousand-Wagon [Emperor]..."
Noble and honored, he endured six years of hunger and cold without leaving his grass mat, until he attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment and delivered immeasurable multitudes.
This "Yellow-Faced Elder" is the model for those who leave the household life. Later generations forget their origin and instead pursue the comforts of mouth and body.
As the Buddha said: "Those who are śramaṇas should abandon worldly wealth and possessions; they should beg for food until satisfied, eat but one meal at midday, and dwell beneath trees."
He stayed for one night more; be careful not to do so again.
As for the Venerable Ekasāṭaka, throughout his life he never let his side touch the mat. Chan Master Gaofeng Miao made a vow for three years [not to lie down].
"Stained the bed and chair.
Explanation: The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that the Venerable One was a native of Central India.

His original name was Durlabha, because he was born only after being in the womb for sixty years. At the age of eighty, he entered the monastic life under the ninth patriarch, Upagupta. At that time...
A young bhikṣu derided him, saying, "The practice of one who has left the household life consists of two things: first, practicing meditation; second, reciting the sūtras.
Now that you are old and decrepit, what progress can you possibly achieve? Upon hearing this, the Venerable One made a vow: "If I do not master the Tripiṭaka..."
He did not cease from severing the three delusions; he attained the six supernormal powers and was endowed with the eight liberations.
He never allowed his side to touch the mat. While serving at the side of the Ninth Patriarch, he never slept. By day he studied the Tripiṭaka, and by night he sat in meditation.
Within three years, he fully realized all that he had vowed and became the Tenth Patriarch. People of the time revered him, and he was known as—
The Venerable Xie explains that "one lifetime" begins with his renunciation of the household life. Originally, Chan Master Gaofeng, whose name was Yuanyao, was the son of the Xu family of Wujiang.
His mother dreamed of a monk coming by boat before she conceived him. Once he had outgrown his swaddling clothes, he delighted in sitting in the lotus posture;
whenever he saw a monk enter the gate, he would immediately wish to follow him. At the age of fifteen, he left the household life at Miji Temple in Jiahe.

At age fifteen, he entered Yin Temple; at sixteen, he shaved his head; at seventeen, he studied the teachings of the Tiantai school. At twenty, he changed his robes and entered Jingci Monastery, where he established a three-year limit for his practice.
During this time, he did not bathe his body, did not shave his head, and did not touch a bed or a chair; he forgot both mouth and body.
Later, at Simha Rock on Mount Tianmu, in the West Stone Cave, he constructed a small hut shaped like a boat and inscribed it with the name "Gate of Death.

He severed all contact with attendants; as the cave could not be ascended without a ladder, he cast away the ladder and cut off all means of access, so that even his disciples rarely had the opportunity to behold him.
The verse for manifesting nirvana says: Coming, one does not enter the barrier of death; Going, one does not exit the barrier of death.
An iron snake drills into the sea, Toppling Mount Sumeru.
The three joys are transgressions.
Even one who awakens to the Way and receives a seat of fragrant sandalwood may still diminish their merit and invite retribution.
Explanation: The Dharma Master Zhihuan of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Chen. He had mastered the three studies [of Vinaya, Sūtra, and Abhidharma], and his reputation was preeminent in his time.

His extraordinary deeds were numerous; thus, he was known in the world as "Chen the Bodhisattva. At the age of five, he was already able to compose poetry; at fourteen, he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The *Pán jīng*. In a poem presented by Lǐ Shāngyǐn, it says: "A fourteen-year-old śrāmaṇera can lecture on the sūtras;

though his age is but that of a novice, he carries only his water jar. When the śrāmaṇera preaches the Dharma and the śramaṇas listen, it does not depend on years of seniority, but on spiritual nature.
Emperor Yìzōng bestowed upon him a precious sandalwood throne over twenty feet high. Emperor Xīzōng conferred upon him the title National Teacher Wùdá. (2)

The Emperor made offerings to him with extraordinary generosity. Later, while in meditative concentration, he suddenly saw the Bodhisattva descend and place his hand upon Huanxuan’s crown, expounding the profound and wondrous Dharma to comfort him.
Upon finishing his words, the Bodhisattva vanished. Shortly thereafter, a pearl was seen entering the left thigh of Huanxuan;
it swelled up with extreme pain, and upon it were the two characters "Chao Cuo. It subsequently became a facial ulcer, and Huanxuan—prior to this—[had been ill].
"This body is that of Yuan Ang of the Han dynasty. I executed Chao Cuo by beheading him in the Eastern Market. For ten generations, my descendants have been eminent monks.
Yet Chao Cuo has sought retribution without success until now. Because he encountered the favor and patronage of a sovereign, a single thought of fame and profit arose, which diminished his virtue;
thus, I was able to harm him. Fortunately, he encountered the Venerable Kanakavatsa of Western Shu, who washed him with the three..."
One who is ignorant attempts to dissolve it with water; therefore, it becomes a source of affliction. The details are as found in the original biography.
Third, the exhortation:
Alas! Is it not necessary to exercise caution?
Commentary: This bed, seat, canopy, and matting constitute one of the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).

By being content with these, one is able to advance in the practice of the Way and realize *sambodhi*; therefore, they are called "noble lineages. If one lacks contentment, one will have no share in the fruits of the Path, and the noble lineage is lost.
For example, National Preceptor Wudao’s insight transcended his time, yet his spiritual station remains unfathomable.
Due to a lack of contentment, a single thought arises; virtue diminishes and calamity arrives.
Who among us are we that we do not take this as a warning? Alas! The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: A certain śramaṇa stayed by a river under a tree and practiced the Way for twelve years.
Yet, his greedy thoughts were not eliminated; while his body remained still, his mind wandered, never finding rest, and he was unable to attain the Way. The Buddha—
He transformed himself into a śramaṇa and went to that place. A tortoise emerged from the river and came beneath the tree.

There was also a water dog, wandering about in hunger seeking food, which intended to devour the tortoise. The tortoise drew in its head, tail, and four legs, concealing them within its shell, so that the dog could not devour it.
The Buddha said, "I consider the people of this world; they do not compare to this tortoise. They give rein to their six [senses]..."

When the external demons find an opportunity, the physical form perishes and the spirit departs; birth and death have no beginning, as one revolves through the five realms of existence amidst hundreds of thousands of sufferings.
Then he spoke in verse: "Hide the six senses like a tortoise; guard the mind like a fortress. With wisdom, do battle against the demons;
victory brings no further affliction. Upon hearing this, the śramaṇa immediately attained the fruit of the Path.
The Ninth Precept: Abstaining from Eating at Improper Times (divided into two parts). First, the title:
The ninth is "not eating at improper times.
Explanation: "Not eating at improper times" means eating at the midday hour, as the Tathāgata did, so that one’s mouth does not commit an offense.

To depart from this is called "untimely. The first eight [precepts] and the last one are called "precepts" (*śīla*); this abstention from untimely food is called "fasting" (*upavāsa*). "Fasting" means "to level" or "to align.
It refers to leveling oneself with the practice of not eating after midday. Among the five "middles," the Tathāgata abides: he was born in the Middle Kingdom; at midnight he left the city;
at midday he took his single meal; at midnight he attained Buddhahood; and he taught the Middle Way. This is the Vinaya.
It is said: The nature of the Tathāgata is free from eating at improper times. From his birth in the royal palace until his parinirvāṇa, he never once ate at an improper time.
The *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra* states: By not eating at improper times, one obtains five kinds of benefits:
first, freedom from all covetous desires; second, a clear and refreshed spirit; third, the ability to repel the demon of sleep; fourth, [the advancement of] the path of practice...
Easy to understand. Five. Increasing merit and longevity. The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"If a donor builds a monastery and provides generous provisions for the renunciants, yet [a renunciant] seeks food at an improper time from the food steward;
what offense does the one who gives it and the one who eats it incur? What merit does the donor obtain? The Buddha said: "Eating at an improper time is a violation..."
One who observes the precepts is a person who commits theft; one who gives at an improper time is likewise a person who breaks the precepts and also a person who commits theft.
This is because they steal the property of the donor (*dānapati*), and since it is not the intention of the donor, the donor gains no merit, just as if they had lost their own goods.

There is only the merit of the initial resolve to establish [the gift]. The *Xi yang za zu* (Miscellaneous Records of Xiyang) states that during the Zhenyuan era, there was a monk at Tianchong Temple in Jingzhou.
Zhiding constantly upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When he fell ill and was on the verge of death, his disciples noted that his hands and feet remained warm;

not daring to enshroud him, they waited for seven days until he returned to life. He said: "Initially, I saw the King of the Netherworld. I joined my palms in reverence, and as I descended the steps, he questioned me, saying:

'Because of the merit you have gained from upholding this sūtra, your lifespan is extended by ten years, and you are exempted from the cycle of birth and death. He further asked: 'Regarding the assembly of monks in the human world...'"
Taking medicine as food at midday or in the evening, and eating *yīyǐrén* (coix seed), greatly violates the fundamental teachings. Dēng said, "The Vinaya contains both allowances and prohibitions.
The King said, "This was added by later generations; it is not the Buddha’s intention. Nowadays, among the monastic community in Jingzhou, there is no one who drinks medicine after midday."

Second, the Explanation of the Meaning (divided into three parts): First, confusion regarding the Vinaya; Second, citing scriptural evidence; Third, the concluding exhortation. Within the first part (divided into two), first is the determination of the time.
Regarding the term "improper time" (*akāla*): it refers to that which has passed noon, the period when the Saṃgha does not eat. This is the division [of the day]. The various devas eat early.
The Buddha eats at noon; animals eat after noon; ghosts eat at night. Monks should emulate the Buddha by not eating past noon. Explanation:
The term "noon" (*riwu*) follows the conventional language of this region. According to the sūtras and vinaya, it should be called "midday" (*rizhong*).
If the sun has passed its zenith and the dawn light (*mingxiang*) has not yet appeared, this is termed "improper time" (*feshi*). Therefore, it is said that this is not the time for monastic meals.
This is because the hour of *wu* (noon) consists of eight *ke*; the first four are designated as "time" (*kāla*), while the latter four are "non-time" (*akāla*).
Fearing that people might confuse these categories, it does not say "noon" (*wu*) but rather "midday" (*zhong*). As for the gods who eat early, "early" takes the sense of being pure and superior.

Regarding "gods" (*tian*), it means "natural" (*tianran*); that is to say, by practicing the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action, one receives this naturally pure and superior [existence].
Because of merit, the purity, excellence, and utmost sincerity of those among humans also manifest early. Heaven opens for them at dawn;
therefore, the fasting ritual for the heavens is performed in the morning. All the devas rejoice in the purity, excellence, and utmost sincerity of humans, and thus naturally accept their offerings.

Regarding the Buddha’s midday meal: it is because the midday meal is taken as the "Dharma-food. In the *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra*, King Bimbisāra asked the Buddha, "For what reason does the Buddha eat at noon?
The Buddha said, "The various devas eat in the early morning; the Buddhas of the three periods of time eat at noon;
animals eat in the afternoon; and ghosts and spirits eat at dusk. The Tathāgata wishes to sever the six [senses]."
This is the cause for [attaining] the [right] destination and leads one into the Middle Way; therefore, it is the same as the meal of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
As for the fact that animals eat after midday: the Sanskrit term is *tiryañc*, which here means "animal," referring specifically to the six domestic animals.

This means that because of actions committed during their causal phase that opposed heaven and contravened principle, they were reborn in this realm; thus they carry the weight of heaven upon them and eat after midday.
Regarding "ghosts and spirits who eat at night": "ghost" (kuei) means fear; it refers to those who are empty and timid, possessing much dread.

"Spirit" (shen) means capability. Those with great power can move mountains and fill the seas; those with lesser power can conceal and manifest themselves, undergoing transformations. This arises from a mind of flattery and deception.
Regarding the deeds one performs, fearing that others might discover them, one consequently experiences this path of darkness and feeds upon it.
As for the statement that "the Sangha should learn from the Buddha," it means that the Buddha is a world-transcending sage who has long since severed the causes of the six realms of existence.

Now, having resolved his mind and received the precepts, he aspires to attain Buddhahood. If one wishes to become a Buddha and emerge from the effects of the six realms, one must first sever the entry [into them].
This is the cause for [beings in] the six realms to become equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, constantly partaking in the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna.

After midday, they do not eat. In various sūtras, the Buddha has said that there are five blessings in not eating after noon: first, little lust; second, [little anger]; third, [little delusion]; fourth, [fewer afflictions]; fifth, [longer life].
One sleeps little; third, one attains single-mindedness; fourth, there is no downward-moving wind; fifth, the body attains tranquility and does not fall ill.
Now, precepts are like a person’s clothing and food. If one lacks clothing and food, how can a person survive? Therefore, they are essential.
The Mahāvinaya states: "The Piṭaka of Vinaya is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma. As long as the Vinaya remains in the world, so shall the Buddha-dharma endure for a long time.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he repeatedly instructed and admonished [his disciples], saying: 'After my parinirvāṇa...'"
"You all should take the precepts as your teacher; were I to remain in the world, it would be no different from this.

Therefore, Mahākāśyapa and the others practiced them throughout their lives, transmitting them from master to disciple, all of whom followed the Buddha’s injunctions without ever having transgressed."
Second, when practicing compassion for hungry ghosts, one hears the sound of their bowls and basins, whereupon fire rises from within their throats; therefore, even at midday meals,
one should maintain silence, let alone after noon.
Explanation: Regarding "hungry ghosts" (preta): they are called "hungry" because they are oppressed by hunger and thirst; they are called "ghosts" because they are characterized by constant seeking.

That is to say, these hungry ghosts perpetually seek food and drink from others in order to sustain their lives. This is due to their past stinginess and greed, whereby they failed to practice generosity.
Therefore, they fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). Their throats are as narrow as needles, while their bellies are as large as drums; they are constantly tormented by hunger and thirst.

While the World-Honored One was at the Jetavana Monastery, he saw from within meditative concentration the hells and hungry ghosts, with flames rising from their throats and spreading throughout the Iron Enclosure (*Cakravāḍa*) mountains.
Having questioned them and learned the cause—namely, that the sound of bowls and basins in the human world [disturbed them]—the Buddha [acted accordingly]. Great!
Maitreya cautioned his disciples: "Whenever you eat, you should remain silent; you must not allow your bowls or basins to make noise.
Since one ought to maintain silence even before noon, how much more so during the afternoon, which is precisely the time when ghosts eat?
How could one bear to let the sound of clattering bowls and basins reach their ears, causing their fires to flare up and subjecting them to the suffering of being consumed by flames? Indeed...
In the causal state of their existence as hungry ghosts (preta), they plundered the food of others to sustain their own lives, causing them to suffer from hunger;
because they committed these karmic deeds upon bowls and alms-basins, they receive retribution upon bowls and alms-basins.
II. Citation of Scriptural Evidence (divided into four parts).

First: Formerly, there was a high monk who, upon hearing his neighbor in the adjacent room raising the cooking fires after midday, could not help but weep, grieving for the decline and decay of the Buddha-dharma.
Explanation: A "high monk" (gaoseng) is one who takes the Buddha-dharma as his own responsibility. *Cuan* means to kindle fire to cook food.
*Bi* refers to nasal discharge; weeping without sound is called *qi*. Formerly, when Chan Master Fahui resided at Ye Temple, he heard a bhikṣu in the adjacent room cooking after midday.
He was grieved that the Buddha-dharma was entering its autumnal decline; moved by this ruin, he lamented with such sorrow that he could not help but shed tears.

Tears moistened their robes. Since people today lack the spirit of the ancient virtuous ones who protected the Dharma, they instead give rise to slander, claiming that spiritual practice does not lie in this [Buddhist path].
Can they remain at ease without shame? Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty was deluded by the demonic words of the Daoist Lin Lingsu and changed the name of the Buddha to that of the Dao.
The Dharma Master Yongdao submitted a memorial to offer remonstrance; the Emperor... [was greatly moved].

The magistrate was enraged. He arrested Dao and handed him over to the prison of Kaifeng. The Governor of Chongling said to the Master, "A practitioner of the Way subsists on vegetarian food and does not eat past midday;
this is truly not a plan for self-preservation. You ought to consume meat and blood. The Master smiled broadly and said, "I shall die if I must, but I cannot violate the prohibitions of the Buddha."
Second, regarding the treatment of illness:
people today are physically weak and frequently afflicted by disease. Those who wish to eat multiple times a day may find it difficult to maintain this precept;
therefore, the ancients referred to the evening meal as "medicinal stone," taking the sense of curing illness as its underlying purpose.
Commentary: "People nowadays" refers specifically to the sick person; it does not mean that everyone in general is frequently ill.

"Frequently ill" means that the body is emaciated by hunger and physical strength is diminished; it does not refer to having only one kind of illness. "Repeatedly" means eating at successive intervals.
"Perhaps" expresses doubt, meaning one suspects that one cannot maintain this precept. "Medicine and stone" (referring to solid food) is an ancient term...
In ancient times, acupuncture used stone as needles; nowadays, iron is mostly used. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
At one time, various bhikṣus had taken emetic and purgative medicines and failed to eat at the proper time, so their bellies became empty and distressed. A physician instructed them to eat.

The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha ordered that they boil water with rice husks and permitted them to eat outside of the prescribed mealtime. When this did not suffice to cure them, the Buddha permitted [the use of...].
He filled a bag with grain and boiled it to make a broth for him to drink, yet he could not be cured. The Buddha permitted him to fill a bag with rice and boil it to make a broth for him to drink;
his condition showed slight improvement, yet he was still not healed. The Buddha then compassionately allowed him to boil rice into gruel.

Since he could not form characters while painting, he was instructed to take it in a secluded place. Once the illness was cured, he was to perform repentance. The ancients referred to this as "eating late."
Regarding "using [food] as medicine": this means that when a sick bhikṣu eats congee, it is equivalent to taking medicine.
Just as one uses a stone needle to treat the body, it is for the purpose of curing illness; it is not for the sake of merely nourishing the mouth and belly.

Furthermore, a stone is not something that can be eaten, used here as a metaphor to show that late meals are not to be consumed. If one indulges in eating at will under the pretext of being ill, [it is improper].
This is a great violation of the Buddha’s teachings. It is like a worldly king’s decree: who would dare to oppose it?
The Tathāgata’s establishment of the precepts is likewise. Tiantai said: To destroy the precepts for the sake of one's illness is like tearing open a life-preserving float;
to cherish this body of pus and blood while destroying the essence of the pure precepts—there can be no greater sin. Thus, the Vinaya says: "When a bhikṣu is ill..."
First, one should abstain from food and drink until recovery is achieved; this is called being a "celestial physician.

Whether ill or healthy, one should constantly contemplate this body as the root of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and the source of all suffering. One should deeply reproach oneself and restrain one's passions. An ancient saying goes:
"If a person constantly contemplates the day they will fall ill, their worldly mind will suddenly cease. If a person constantly contemplates death..."
When the day comes, the thought of the Way should arise spontaneously; yet instead, you indulge those roots of craving and increase the very source of suffering for yourselves.
You do not fear the calamities of kalpas on end, but worry only about the span of a single lifetime.

To eat to satiety and sleep in peace, breaking the fast and eating at night—thereby the donor loses the merit of timely giving, and the assembly of monks diminishes the virtue of the fertile field. Furthermore, regarding medicine taken outside of the proper time...
Various fruit syrups are all prohibited by the Buddha. Those who have left the household life with a sincere heart should rely on the Dharma and not on persons;
only then may they be called true sons of the Buddha possessing right view.
Third, one must feel shame and remorse;
knowing that one has violated the Buddha’s precepts, one should give rise to great self-reproach. One should keep in mind the suffering of hungry ghosts and constantly practice compassionate relief.
One should not eat in excess, nor eat fine foods, nor eat with a restless mind; only by doing so can one hope for success.
[The author] explains: "One must know that this violates the Buddha’s regulations" refers back to the preceding text.

This means that although eating late in the day is permitted as an accommodation for illness, it ultimately constitutes a violation of the Buddha’s regulations. Since one knows that eating while violating the regulations is improper, one must not cling to the provisional [expedient] while being deluded regarding the ultimate reality, thereby treating it as a standard practice.
One must instead give rise to great shame and remorse. As for "shame" (*hrī*), it is the dread of transgression.

In Buddhism, "shame" (hrī) refers to feeling ashamed of eating at improper times. Because of this sense of shame and remorse, one should naturally reflect upon the suffering of hunger and thirst endured by hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Thus, one does not eat at improper times with a restless mind, nor does one allow the bowls or alms-bowl to make noise;

this is precisely the mind of compassion and altruistic salvation. Because of this compassionate salvation, one does not indulge in eating excessively, nor does one crave fine flavors or succumb to greed.
One eats with a sense of preference, yet what is eaten is not much and is not delicious; this is called eating with an unsettled mind.
"Shujǐ" (庶幾) is a term meaning "perhaps" or "it may be possible," implying that if a person possesses the aforementioned sense of shame and remorse, they may then be permitted to listen.
Regarding the four offenses, if one acts otherwise than prescribed, the offense incurred is even more grave.
The commentary explains: "If one acts otherwise than prescribed" means lacking the supreme sense of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*), neglecting the Vinaya, and being gluttonous in drinking.
"Eating" means nourishing the physical body. "Mī" (彌) means "extremely"; it refers to the gravity of the offense being very heavy.
Some say that the Buddha provided an opening for exceptions, such that one does not commit an offense when ill; however, this shows a lack of understanding of the Vinaya laws.

Indeed, within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are seven types of exemptions found in the precepts concerning separate assemblies (*pṛthaggaṇa*), yet regarding the precept against eating at improper times (*akālabhojana*), not even a hair's breadth of allowance is permitted, except in cases involving a donor (*dānapati*).
Because it was so requested, the Tathāgata intentionally permitted [the practice] for a separate group. This occurs before noon, not after noon.
One should know that while ordinary speech lacks foundation, the words of the Sage are based on evidence; thus, one must not speak recklessly regarding the Vinaya scriptures.
Why do you alone fail to mention that when a bhikṣu is ill, he first abstains from food and drink? In the past, Master Fu was an emanation of Maitreya Bodhisattva; every...

When practicing the pure fast (*śuddha-anaśana*), one does not eat for the entire day; one reduces one's own food to give to the poor and hungry. Now, you eat your fill at both meal times and yet feel no shame.
Thus, you violate the Buddha’s regulations, fail to observe the virtue of the patriarchs, and disregard the destitution of others.
How can you be called one who has resolved to receive the precepts?
Third, the exhortation to refrain from eating at night: "How can one not observe this precept?
The commentary explains that the *Mahāvinaya* states: "A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya, would rather break his own belly than eat at night. This applies to śrāmaṇerīs as well.
The *Śīla-sūtra* states: "If a king or a householder offers food after midday, one must not eat it;

until death, one must not violate this. The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* asks: "Regarding eating at the proper time (*kālabhojana*), if there is food remaining from the proper time that is eaten at an improper time (*vikāla*), or if one receives food at the proper time but eats it at an improper time, does one still obtain merit? The Buddha replied: "For one who is pure regarding eating at the proper time..."
This is the field of merit; this is the renunciant; this is the Saṃgha; this is the virtuous friend of gods and humans; this is the guide for devas and men.
Those who are impure are like precept-breaking, plundering hungry ghosts; they are a den of sin.
One who solicits at an improper time, or one who gives at an improper time, is called a Māra who retreats from the Path; such a person is called evil.

This exposes the vessel [of the recipient]. Because it destroys wholesome fruit, those who are like lepers—namely, the various Brahmins who do not eat at improper times, and even the non-Buddhist brahmacārins who do not consume forbidden food—let alone my disciples, should know that one must practice according to the Dharma.

If one steals or receives what has been stolen—even a single lump, a single pinch, a slice of salt, or a bit of vinegar—one will die and fall into the Hell of the Scorched Entrails. (From the *Gaoseng*)
The tradition relates that Shi Zhishun of Yunmen Monastery on the northern side of Liangshan was so severely ill that he did not eat for many days.
When the day had come to an end, his disciple Tanhe, noting that Shun had been abstaining from grain for a long time, secretly boiled half a measure of rice and offered it to him.
Shun swallowed it but immediately spat it out; he then sought water to bathe and said to He, "You shall leave Yunmen forever."
One must not return and dwell there, as described above; it causes one's hair to stand on end and one's bones to tremble.
Why, for the sake of a single meal, should one leave such a legacy of suffering? Should not those who possess wisdom exercise profound caution?
The Tenth Precept: Prohibiting the Handling of Gold, Silver, and Precious Objects (Divided into two parts). First, the title: The tenth [precept] states:
"One shall not handle or possess raw or wrought gold, silver, or precious objects.

Explanation: "Not handling" means being devoid of a mind of covetous desire. This implies that it is not merely a matter of not physically grasping gold and silver; rather, [it refers to the internal state].
One must not grasp any vessels, hairpins, bracelets, or other items fashioned from gold or silver.

Having left the household life to cultivate the unconditioned Dharma and proceed toward the path of purity, one should distance oneself from defiled attachments and sever the mind that hoards out of greed, thereby perfecting the pure and white holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If one grasps and holds such things, one will store them away; storing them gives rise to greedy attachment, which leads to craving for the world.
As for material wealth, one will lose the spiritual riches of the supramundane Dharma; the life of wisdom will be mutilated; an evil reputation will spread; one will be despised by the world;
and even benevolent deities will no longer provide protection. As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "There was a bhikṣu..."
He took a śrāmaṇera with him to visit his relatives. On the way through a vast wilderness, a non-human being manifested in the form of a dragon;

it circumambulated the śrāmaṇera to the right, scattered flowers over him, and praised him, saying, "Excellent! You have gained great benefit by leaving home and going forth, not grasping gold, silver, or coins.
When the bhikṣu arrived at his relatives' house and had finished his greetings, he was about to return. At that time—
A relative’s wife said to the śrāmaṇera, “Return now; you may take this money and purchase whatever you require.
The śrāmaṇera accepted it and tied it to the collar of his robe. On the way, a non-human being saw the śrāmaṇera carrying the money walking behind the bhikṣu.
The non-human being then transformed himself into the form of a dragon, circled the śrāmaṇera to the left, threw earth over him, and spoke as follows:
"You have lost a great benefit. Having left the household life to practice the Way, you have grasped silver coins. The śrāmaṇera then wept. The bhikṣu asked him what was the matter.
The śrāmaṇera cried out, "I did not intend to commit a transgression; I have been troubled for no reason. The teacher asked, "What is it that you are holding?
He replied, "I am holding these coins. The teacher said, "Discard them! Thereupon, the non-human spirit again made offerings as before.
One can see the benefits and harms [of this practice] to be as such.

Second, the explanation of the meaning (divided into three parts): first, the description of the precepts; second, the citation of evidence; third, the conclusion and exhortation. Now, for the first part, the commentary states:
"Jeweled" (*jīng*) refers to gold. "Image" (*xiàng*) means resemblance. That which resembles gold is silver. This refers to the original substance of the golden color.

"Yellow" refers to silver, which can be dyed yellow so that it resembles gold. "Jewels" refers to the category of the seven treasures; all of these increase greed and obstruct the abandonment of worldly affairs for the sake of the Way.
Regarding this, Nanshan says: "In Sanskrit, *jātarūpa* means 'gold and silver' in Chinese; therefore, *jāta* (生) refers to gold. This is excellent.
The commentary states: "Born color" (*janshik*) refers to "resembling color" (*sishik*). Since "resembling" means "an image," it says: "That which resembles gold is silver.

This means that while gold is yellow by its very nature of birth, silver can be dyed to resemble yellow. Thus, it says: "The color of gold is yellow by its original birth; silver can be colored to resemble yellow."
Therefore it is said: silver can be dyed yellow so that it resembles gold. Furthermore, "produced" (*jāta*) refers to naturally occurring gold and silver;
"refined" (*vikṛta*) refers to processed gold and silver, such as when gold and silver are melted into ingots or cakes, or forged into ornaments, figures, and the like.

All are termed "images" (xiàng). However, gold is the primary name, while silver is distinguished by its color. Furthermore, gold, silver, copper, iron, and tin are collectively called "gold," as this term is used to signify their nobility.
Among these five metals, yellow gold is supreme. As stated in the *Zhen-di za-ji* (Miscellaneous Records of the True Dharma):
"Because it possesses four virtues: first, its color does not change; second, its essential nature is unstained."
Third, it transforms into unimpeded [manifestations]. Fourth, it can enrich the poor. These serve as metaphors for the four virtues of the *dharmakāya*:

permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*). As for "jewels," they refer to the seven treasures: first, gold; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that it is produced from mountain rocks, sand, and red copper.
Second, silver; it is produced from scorched stones and is known in the world as white metal. Third, *vaidūrya*; in the language of China, this means "blue-colored."

4. *Vaidūrya* (lapis lazuli). In the Chinese language, it is called "water-jade" (*shuiyu*), which refers to green jade (*cangyu*). This is because its substance and color are translucent and lustrous. 5. *Musāragalva* (amber).
Its substance is hard and its color is bright. 6. *Aśmagarbha* (agate). Its color is reddish-white, resembling the brain of a horse; it is named for this reason. 7. Red pearl.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this jewel emerges from the belly of fish and the head of snakes.
Among them, its color is luminous and translucent, making it the most preeminent. These seven types are all noble objects, rare in the world, and are collectively termed "jewels" (*ratna*).
Furthermore, "jewel" refers to the raw material, while "object" refers to the form;
for example, when jewels are carved into the shapes of birds, beasts, flowers, grasses, and so forth. Other items such as coral, amber, and *maṇi* gems are also all jewels.
This refers to such things as these. If one grasps them, one is turned about by others; therefore it is said that they all increase greed.
If one holds onto them, one cannot cultivate the Way; therefore it is said that they obstruct and cause the abandonment of the work of the Path.
As it is said: "If one grasps precious objects, the life of wisdom is destroyed; afflictions increase and right mindfulness is lost. For this reason, they are prohibited.
II. Citation of Scriptural Evidence (divided into five parts). First, citing ancient precedents:
During the Buddha’s lifetime, the Sangha all relied on alms-gathering; they did not maintain hearths for cooking. Their clothing and dwellings were entirely dependent upon external conditions.
Gold and silver were relegated to a state of uselessness; even their possession was prohibited. Thus, their purity is evident.
Commentary: Begging for alms is the fundamental regulation for śramaṇas. The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to practice impartial teaching and transformation.
This means carrying a single bowl to a thousand households and traveling alone across ten thousand *li*, receiving sustenance according to conditions to support one’s physical life.
Thus, there are three meanings: first, to subdue one’s own arrogance and conceit; second, to benefit the donors (*dānapati*).
For these reasons, there are three [principles]: first, one must understand the hardships of material sustenance so as not to sit idly while consuming offerings of faith;
second, for this reason, no "pure kitchen" (jìngchú) is established, and thus there is no smoke from cooking fires; third, those who study the Way must necessarily exert their sinews and bones.

Only by emaciating one's body and skin can one ascend the Path. If those who practice the Way were to seek abundant clothing and ample food, then the Tathāgata would not have had to leave the royal palace.
Clothing and dwellings are collectively termed the four noble lineages (*catur-ārya-vaṃśa*).

This means that having already traveled for alms in all directions, he would settle wherever there was benefit to be gained through随缘 (following conditions) to transform and deliver beings; thus it is said that he "entirely relies on external conditions.
Even if a donor were to offer gold or silver, he would have a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) manage it to provide offerings to the Triple Gem.
If it were not for the Triple Gem, nor for bestowing upon sentient beings to rescue them from suffering and hardship, what use would there be in hoarding it?
Therefore, it is said that one places gold and silver in a place of no utility. Formerly, when the World-Honored One descended Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, Ānanda saw a hidden treasure in a pit.
Ānanda said, "World-Honored One, it is a poisonous snake. The Buddha said, "It is a poisonous snake; the Tathāgata..."
After he had departed, the woodcutter heard of this and came to look. Seeing the gold and silver in the pit, he said:
"I only wish that this snake might poison me for the rest of my life. He then took it back and constructed a multi-storied pavilion; within a single year, all manner of things were completed.
At that time, the King went out hunting and saw it, and addressed his ministers, saying: "Last year I observed that this was originally..."
"In this desolate wilderness, why is it so lush and flourishing today? He immediately summoned a woodcutter and questioned him regarding the cause.
The woodcutter reported the matter in detail to the king. The king said, "Under heaven, there is no land that is not the king's soil; all hidden treasures belong [to me]."
"All these are state property. Why have you stolen them? He was immediately handed over to the authorities. Upon interrogation, he was found guilty of a capital offense.
As he was being led to the place of execution, he called out, "World-Honored One! Ānanda! The authorities reported this fully to the King, who said, "You have stolen state property."

"What is the use of recollecting the Buddha? The woodcutter then related the matter of the venomous snake in detail. The King said, "Since you have found this hidden treasure from the side of the Buddha, I grant you your life;
however, the wealth shall enter the royal treasury. One can see that gold and silver possess such great risks and benefits.
Therefore, the Tathāgata prohibited the handling of them in order to cultivate the path of purity. Thus it is called 'pure'."
This can be understood. When the Great Master explains this, one reads it unconsciously, as if being led into the realm of the Buddha.
Second, to cite an analogy:
even secular scholars still disregard gold while plowing; how much more so for a Buddhist disciple who calls himself poor—what use would he have for accumulated wealth?
Commentary: Regarding "not looking back," the *Shishuo xinyu* states: "During the Han dynasty, Guan You’an (styled Ning) was weeding vegetables in a garden with Hua Xin.
Seeing a piece of gold on the ground, Guan swung his hoe as if it were no different from a tile or a stone; Hua picked it up and threw it away.
People of the time used this to determine the relative superiority of Guan and Hua. Thus it is said: 'Even the Confucian scholars of the world are like this.'"
Furthermore, Yangzi of Le once encountered a discarded gold ingot while traveling on a road. He took it back and gave it to his wife.
His wife said, "I have heard that a man of resolve does not drink from the waters of Robbers' Spring, and a person of integrity does not accept food brought with the cry of 'Alas!
How much less would one pick up gold for profit and thereby defile their conduct? Yang was deeply ashamed; he then cast the gold away in the wilds. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Scholars*).
The Duke in the Fur Cloak was a man of Wu. When Ji Zi of Yanling was traveling abroad, he saw gold left on the road. It was the fifth month;
seeing the Duke wearing a fur cloak and carrying firewood on his back, Ji Zi looked at him and ordered him to pick up the gold.

The Duke threw down his sickle, glared with wide eyes, and brushed his hands together, saying: "How can you, sir, dwell so high [in status] yet look down upon one who is lowly? In the fifth month, one wears a fur cloak..."
"Carrying firewood—how could one take up a stray piece of gold? Jizi was greatly startled and asked his surname.

The man said, "You are a man who judges by the surface of the skin; why should I tell you my name or clan? As for 'Śākyaputra' (Shizizi), since ancient times those who have left the household life have been called by their teacher's clan name.
The Dharma Master Dao'an of the Jin dynasty studied under Fotudeng and addressed him as 'Master. Since there is no one superior to the Buddha, he simply called him 'Buddha.'"

Having abandoned secular life to enter the monastic order, one ought to be called a "Son of Śākya. It was only after the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* arrived in the Eastern Land that it became known that during the Buddha’s lifetime, everyone was called a Son of Śākya.
To call oneself "poor" (pin) is a term of self-reproach, meaning: "I feel ashamed before the sages of old regarding my Way."
Because one is largely destitute of the seven kinds of noble wealth of the sages, what is the point? Why is this so?

Since it is said that one is impoverished regarding the Way, if one accumulates money and wealth, one’s words and actions will contradict each other, and the Way will remain far away. Therefore it is said: "What use is there for accumulating wealth?
Yet even Confucianists do not regard it as essential; why then should I accumulate it? The ancients were concerned with the Way, not with poverty.
Therefore, the Venerable Kāśyapa said in verse: "The food one eats shall not exceed one *śīrṣa* of rice; for sleeping, only a single small bed is required;
two pieces of felt cloth are sufficient to cover the body; everything beyond this is but a thing of folly.
In the past, Meditation Master Huiman upheld the dhūta practices and kept only two needles. In winter he would beg for thread to mend them; in summer, he would discard them. His mind—
He was free from fear. When he slept, he had no dreams. Wherever he went for alms at a monastery, he would split firewood and repair his sandals.

He stayed only one night; he never remained for a second. Later, he sat without illness, refining himself through practice until he was spontaneously transformed. As the ancients said: "If you cherish a single coin, you will not be worth even a single coin.
This is a famous saying that has endured for a thousand ages.
Third, as for the present day,
people are unable to practice alms-gathering together. Whether they enter monasteries, reside in hermitages,
or travel to distant regions, they cannot avoid the expense of gold and silver.

Commentary: As for those who cannot do so today, it is because during the age of the Final Dharma (mofa), people have little faith, making it difficult to compare with the time of the Buddha’s presence.

Furthermore, the people of Jambudvīpa sustain their lives through wealth; therefore, it is difficult to subsist by begging for alms. The Sanskrit term *vana* is translated here as "thicket" (*conglin*).
Grass gathered together forms a thicket, while wood gathered together forms a forest. It is where dragons and elephants rush to take refuge.
A *chù* (abode) is a place where the assembly of monks settles their minds to cultivate the Way. It is like a great tree with dense thickets; its pure shade extends far and wide.

Thus, a place where the Sangha gathers is called a *cónglín* (grove). Furthermore, when grass does not grow in disorder it is called a *cóng*, and when trees do not grow in disorder it is called a *lín*.
This signifies that within it there are laws and regulations. As for *ān* (hermitage), it means "peace" (*ān*). The minds of the ancients were open and...
"An" (Peace/Security). Covering one's head with thatch to shield against wind and rain, living in pure poverty while delighting in the Way, both body and mind are at ease; hence it is called "an.
When monks and laypeople in the Western Regions practice their cultivation, they frequently construct dwellings of woven grass in *araṇya* (hermitage) locations. As for "yuan" (monastery):...
This is also a meditation hall. Generally, any courtyard or residence enclosed by walls is called a *yuan* (monastery);
this is also another name for a monastic community (*conglin*). For those from distant regions who seek teachers and inquire after the Way, traveling far to other lands requires more than mere words;
thus it is said that they cannot avoid the expense of gold and silver.

Fourth, one must certainly know that other forms of relief contradict the Buddha’s prohibitions; thus, one should give rise to great shame and remorse. Mindful of the poverty and destitution of others, one should constantly practice giving.
One should not engage in seeking profit, nor hoard wealth, nor engage in trade. One should not use the seven precious gems to adorn clothing, vessels, or other items. In this way, may...

This is acceptable. Explanation: Regarding "generosity" (*dāna*): to bestow grace upon others is called "dispensing" (*bu*); to extend benefit to them is called "giving" (*shi*). This means that when one sees another in poverty, one who has surplus should relinquish it;
one must not hoard much. "Managing" (*ying*) refers to managing and directing; "seeking" (*qiu*) refers to planning and deliberating.
"Seeking" means that one does not manage the affairs of the donor, but instead misrepresents circumstances to convert others for the sake of scheming to obtain gain and support.
As the ancients said: "A *sengchu* (monastic youth) is like a phoenix chick; one should cherish its feathers and plumage and allow it to develop naturally.

If one begs piteously and demands with hardship, then one loses the essence of the *kāṣāya*. Regarding "hoarding": "hoard" (*xu*) refers to greedy accumulation, and "accumulate" (*ji*) refers to gathering together.
This means that when a donor makes an offering and uses it to venerate the Triple Gem, they personally obtain wholesome fruits while also causing the merit of their giving to increase further.
It is improper to keep such items in chests or bags and store them on high shelves, thereby giving rise to the greedy thoughts of others; this brings calamity upon oneself and harms others.

Moreover, having merely ascended to the level of the precepts, one ought to devote oneself single-mindedly to the study of the Path. One must fear that allowing such things to proliferate will cause greed to run wild.
Gold and silver do not pass through his hands; how could he accept or accumulate them? Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Do not hoard impure treasures. If others offer them, do not accept them;
if you do accept them, do not keep them, but distribute them to relieve the poor. This is what is meant by constantly preaching to others the virtue of non-attachment.
As for "buying and selling": to purchase at a low price and sell at a high price is called "buying" (fàn); to seek profit by means of goods is called "selling" (mài).
This means that one must not buy low and sell high, thereby impairing pure conduct and seeking profit from profit, which violates the Buddha’s physical demeanor and decorum.

Thus, the *Yeyu* (Excerpts from the Vinaya) states: "If, with a deviant mind and involvement in greedy defilement, one sells the Dharma for the sake of gain—whether it be the offerings obtained from bowing to the Buddha, reciting scriptures, or fasting—all such items are termed 'objects of wrong livelihood. One must not use the seven treasures for adornment."
As for adorning one's robes, vessels, and other articles, these are not appropriate for those who are sons of the Śākya.
For these increase the root of craving and result in out-flowing (*sāsrava*) karma. That which is permissible refers only to supreme objects;
even this is spoken as a concession and is not the word of the Buddha.
If one acts contrary to the five fixed rules of conduct, the offense incurred is even more grave.
"Contrary" (*bùrán*) is a term meaning the opposite; it refers to the absence of the thought of supreme generosity and the failure to give rise to the Great [Vehicle].
Shame and remorse: if one who has received the precepts harbors a mind of greedy attachment and seizes [possessions], the offense is extremely grave.

A person who has received the precepts should advance along the Path according to conditions and practice with contentment. When the three poisons are stilled, the observance of the precepts is complete;
when the ten unwholesome actions are purified, one is spared from the three miserable realms. If the four requisites of food and drink are already fully provided, then as for wealth and property...

These matters equally confuse the Way-mind. If you claim that the Hīnayāna is merely for self-benefit and does not benefit others, or if you say that after receiving the precepts one is permitted to handle [money], there is no such statement in the Vinaya. One must understand this as the Bodhisattva path.
Taking the salvation of sentient beings as the primary concern, one regards wealth and resources as secondary to the ten directions.
Since there is no means by which to accumulate them, they do not belong to oneself; therefore, while the grasping and handling of them is not prohibited, their hoarding and storage are forbidden.
Thus, Master Sishin said: "The Way and profit do not plot together. Those who seek profit cannot be given the Way; those who seek the Way cannot be given profit."
Indeed, it is not that these two types cannot coexist; rather, their conditions cannot be maintained simultaneously.
If profit and the Way were practiced together, then even merchants, butchers, tavern-keepers, and those commoners who carry goods through the villages would all be able to seek them.
Why, then, would the ancients have had to renounce wealth and status, forget fame and achievement, and extinguish their will and intellect within the vast mountains and great marshes?
In the midst [of this], one drinks from mountain streams and eats from the trees for the rest of one’s life.
Alas, how can one not be cautious regarding these three exhortations? How could one fail to exercise restraint?
Commentary: These produced images, precious objects, and the like are extremely capable of clouding the divine wisdom of humans and causing them to lose their resolve for the Way;
therefore, the Tathāgata compared them to a venomous snake. If one were to seize and hold it, there would be the peril of losing one’s body and life—should one not be cautious?
It is like an ancient mirror: originally bright and pure, it cannot tolerate even a single speck of dust upon it. If...
If even a speck of dust settles upon it, its radiance will be obscured. The essence of the precepts is likewise:
one must not harbor even a trace of covetousness. If one harbors even a trace of covetousness, the essence of the precepts will become corrupted.
Therefore, Huìtáng said: "A single speck of dust flies up and obscures the heavens; a single mustard seed falls and covers the earth.
This very point of greedy mind immediately shuts down immeasurable Dharma-gates. From this moment on, one misses [the Way];
how could it be limited to only one or two lifetimes? An ancient worthy said: 'I do not worry about swords and halberds falling like stars; I only fear being bound to death by a lotus fiber.'"
Regarding this, the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* states: "Wealth and treasures cause people to give rise to affliction; one should not possess them at all.
Even if they bring comfort, separation from them is inevitable. Just as when bees produce honey, others obtain it while the bees themselves do not, so it is with wealth and treasures."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "If I did not maintain the precepts, I would fall into the three evil realms;
I would not even obtain the body of a lowly human being, let alone be able to mature sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, and perfect all-knowledge.

Therefore, you should know that it is better to sacrifice one's body and life, even to the point of being ground into fine dust, than to violate the prohibitive precepts and fall [into the lower realms]."
One falls into the three miserable realms and forever loses the seed of Bodhi. Regarding the ten precepts above, the first four are *prakṛti-sāvadya* (natural offenses).
"Nature" (*prakṛti*) means reality; that is to say, even if one has not received the Buddhist precepts, according to the laws of the world, these acts are inherently sinful.

The precept against alcohol is half-natural and half-prohibitory (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). It is half-natural because it can sever the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom; it is half-prohibitory because...

This is because they are not prohibited by secular law; that is to say, worldly people only know [the consequences of] ruining their families and destroying their nations, but do not know of the bitter retributions in the three miserable realms.
The latter five are offenses of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*); because the Buddha prohibited them, one is not permitted to violate them.
Therefore, if one commits a transgression, one must not conceal it, but must immediately give rise to deep shame and remorse, confessing and repenting before a teacher.
After repenting, one may again attain purity. As the treatise states: "Among these, four are actual evils;
alcohol is the gateway to all calamities; the remaining items are conditions for negligence. If one commits the first four, it is called breaking the precepts (*śīla*);

the ninth is called breaking the fast (*upavāsa*); the rest are called breaking the rules of decorum (*airyāpatha*). Furthermore, these ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera* are [identical to those of] a bodhisattva..."
The precepts are largely the same, with only minor differences. Among the ten grave precepts of a bodhisattva, the precept against killing is primary;

likewise, among these śrāmaṇera precepts, the precept against killing is placed first. Among the forty-eight light precepts of a bodhisattva, the precept on respecting teachers and friends is primary;
likewise, among these twenty-four categories of śrāmaṇera deportment, the precept on respecting great śramaṇas is ranked first. Therefore, the sutra states:
It is said: This precept serves as the staircase for the bhikṣu precepts and the root of the bodhisattva precepts, leading all the way to the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi;
therefore, it must be maintained with purity, without allowing even the slightest transgression. The explanation of its characteristics is hereby concluded.

Regarding the meaning of "the teachings for a lifetime": this refers to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma. From beginning to end, it is called "a lifetime.
"Time" refers to the period when the Buddha and his disciples were in harmonious union of teaching and listening. "Teaching" refers to the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment by coming to perfect enlightenment through the path of reality as it is; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.

Section Two: Explaining the Two Codes of Deportment. This is divided into two parts: first, stating the titles; second, explaining the meanings. Now, the first: the Gate of Deportment.
Regarding majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*): majesty is manifested through virtue; it is not the majesty of power or force. Deportment is expressed through conduct; it is not a deceptive display.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata dwells in the world, he profoundly understands the capacities of sentient beings.

Whatever he performs, he invariably takes majestic deportment as primary. Internally, he harbors the virtue of a lion; externally, he manifests the majesty of a Dharma King. Thus, humans and devas revere him.

Looking upward, divine dragons are awed and submissive; this is truly the essential task for gathering sentient beings and benefiting their lives. Furthermore, "majesty" (*wei*) means possessing a majesty that inspires awe, thereby subduing sentient beings.
This arises from strictly maintaining the practice of the precepts; because one’s manifold virtues are majestic and solemn, one becomes someone whom others find awe-inspiring.
"Dignity" (*yi*) means possessing a dignity that inspires reverence, thereby gathering in sentient beings. This arises from [the harmony of] movement and stillness...
Their conduct was harmonious; their advancing and retreating were serene and composed, and thus they were worthy of veneration.

It is said that pure practice is perfected through the ritual of the Way, and purity is brought to completion within the categories of the precepts. Just as Aśvajit walked with dignified grace along the path, inspiring the peasantry to leave the household life out of faith and joy;
and as Śāriputra begged for alms with serene composure, converting non-Buddhists to return from error to the right path. Therefore it is said:
Dignified deportment is a teaching beyond words, capable of inspiring faith in sentient beings. Furthermore, dignified deportment is called "taming and guiding.
This means taming the body so it does not move recklessly, the mouth so it does not speak recklessly, and the mind so it does not harbor reckless thoughts.
When these three karmas are thus harmoniously tamed, the six sense faculties are naturally restrained. Indeed, the dignified deportment of one's person is itself the mark of a renunciant.

The Buddha ordained that when a śrāmaṇera has reached the age of twenty and wishes to receive full ordination (upasampadā),
if he is unable to answer all questions regarding his conduct as a śrāmaṇera, one should not grant him full ordination.
The Buddha’s regulation is as stated above. When a *śrāmaṇera* reaches twenty years of age, it means that since the period of time has been completed, he stands in the position of a man;

he is thus capable of enduring cold and hardship and is fit to perform the duties of a *bhikṣu*. This is just as in the world, when a man at twenty undergoes the capping ceremony, reaching adulthood and establishing his career.
"Desires" (*iccha*) means "to lead toward"; "receiving" (*pratigraha*) refers to taking in and accepting. [This constitutes] the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
This refers to the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the ten precepts, which are not yet complete;
only the bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī precepts are called "complete. This describes the person who, with a mind of perfection, aspires to the wholesome Dharma.

Because one attains the nature of a bhikṣu at the conclusion of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual proclamation), according to your own established treatise, it is subsumed under four constituent meanings:

First, the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*). This refers to the person receiving the precepts: their petition is free from error, they do not forget their name, their mind and object correspond, and their mental application is all-pervasive.
Having previously received the ten precepts, they now seek full ordination and listen with their ears to the *karmavācanā*.

His life story is clearly detailed in the *Xiangru ji* (Record of the Fragrant Milk). Indeed, during the first century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who transmitted the Dharma in the Western Land [India] were all masters of the Tripitaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma (or Dhyāna, Vinaya, and Abhidharma).
This was due to the five disciples of the Fourth Patriarch, the Venerable Upagupta.
Each adhered to their own views and expanded upon the *Vinaya*, dividing it into five schools; thus, the core principles became exceedingly difficult to maintain.

Thereafter, in the transmission of the Dharma, only the Chan school and the various sutras and śāstras were taught. From that time forward, the lamp of the Vinaya gradually dimmed and the life-force of wisdom hung by a thread.
During the High Tang, Master Xuanzang composed the *Xing-shi-chao* (Commentary on Practice and Affairs) and established the Nanshan school, thereby reviving the Vinaya teachings.

Fearing that those who have newly received the precepts might not be familiar with their practice, and in order to provide protection for the observance of the Vinaya and to instruct beginners in guarding the *vinaya*, Master Yunqi has drawn from this work all passages that correspond to the rules for *śrāmaṇeras* to supplement what was lacking.
Therefore, it is said: "Although these instructions are addressed to newly ordained *bhikṣus*, there are aspects applicable to *śrāmaṇeras* as well."
As for the "Universal Version," it is also an abridgment. It extracts the essentials according to the capacities of beings (the original text notes:

this is because the sentiments of people in the age of the Dharma’s end are largely characterized by indolence; hearing what is voluminous leads to weariness). For this reason, the redundant was deleted and the essential was retained.
Essential. Nevertheless, it is categorized for the sake of ease in reading and study.
"Truly" (*liángyǐ*) is an expression of lamentation and sighing. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma passes through three periods:

namely, the *saddharma* (True Dharma), the *pratirūpakadharma* (Semblance Dharma), and the *paścimadharma* (Final Dharma). The *saddharma* lasts for a thousand years; during this time, the faculties of human beings are pure and robust, and they hear the Dharma.

This is the period of the Semblance Dharma (Saddharmapratirūpaka), lasting for one thousand years. During this time, although it resembles the True Dharma (Saddharma), those who hear the Dharma are many, while those who practice and realize it are few.
This is the period of the Final Dharma (Pashāṇḍa-dharma), lasting for ten thousand years. During this time, strife and contention are firm and entrenched, and false views increase.

Most people at this time harbor thoughts of being reborn in the higher realms; they follow along with negligence and indolence. Regarding worldly dharmas, they weary of the simple and long for the complex; regarding the transcendental...
Regarding worldly dharmas, one grows weary of complexity and seeks simplicity.

For this reason, within the *vinaya*, sūtras, and codes of pure discipline that constitute established models, the Great Master has excised redundant texts and distilled them into essential summaries to suit the needs of the times.

He has divided these into twenty-four categories so that they do not overlap with one another. Why is this? If one considers it from the perspective of principle, the substance of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*) is one.
If one infers by way of their subject matter, the characteristics differ; therefore, they must be classified.
This allows beginners who are practicing to find their starting point; thus it is said that they are further classified to facilitate reading and study.
The four meanings should be supplemented [to the original], as there were some omissions. One or two points have been added according to their significance.
Regarding the phrases "intermediate," "middle," and "incomplete," they precisely demonstrate the Master’s earnest concern for people. That is to say, these two...

Within the fourteen sections of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), wherever there are matters that are incomplete or where the Dharma is not fully provided, one should examine the precious volumes of the canon and supplement them according to their meaning.

Thus, the principles will be thoroughly resolved and the precedents established; the rituals and the Dharma will be without error, and the practice of beginners will be perfected in both excellence and beauty.
It is hoped that the dignified deportment of Aśvajit may be seen once more, and that the regulations of Upāli may be restored.
The model still remains; the single assembly at Vulture Peak is as if it has not yet dispersed.
Furthermore, regarding the complete work (the original), those who take pleasure in extensive reading should naturally consult the full text themselves.
"Joy" refers to desire. "Broad surveying" means that one does not stop with this alone. For the ocean of Vinaya is vast and deep; one may probe it, yet its bottom remains unfathomable.
The mountain of its meaning is lofty and expansive; one may gaze up at it, yet its peak is difficult to behold.

Therefore, I have extracted the essentials and pruned the redundancies so that they may be used according to one's capacity. This is done so that beginners do not turn back in dismay like those gazing out upon the vast sea. If one can indeed...
Those with superior aspirations who wish to propagate the study of the Vinaya should examine the entirety of the śrāmaṇera’s deportment, the various sūtras on the ten precepts,

the *qinggui* (rules of purity), the *chengfan* (models of conduct), and so forth, so as to become thoroughly familiar with their details; one must not consider a small measure of knowledge to be sufficient.

Regarding "reverence" (*jing*): it means respect and faith; it carries the sense of honoring. This refers to one who necessarily believes what is said and certainly follows what is taught, not daring to treat [the teacher] with contempt or arrogance.

There have never been any miscellaneous trees there; how could there be any ordinary beings at the assembly on Vulture Peak?

It is only for fear that those who have not received full ordination, upon hearing this, might fail to understand the Buddha’s compassion and instead act unwholesomely, thereby undermining both internal and external paths.
Whether out of fear that the precepts are too strict or by disparaging matters such as dependent origination, those who might consequently lose their wholesome resolve—just as if one were to...
