The Great Māra. The *Mahāvinaya* states: "Whatever speech a person who has left the household life utters should be for the sake of benefit;

one must not privately harbor resentment and speak of it to others. The *Śāstra* says: "If one speaks of a bhikṣu’s transgressions to laypeople (avadātavasana), it will cause people to lose their faith and reverence toward the Buddha-dharma.
It would be better to destroy stupas and damage images than to speak [of such matters] to outsiders."
This speaks of the faults and evils of a bhikṣu. If one speaks of grave offenses, it destroys the Dharma-body. Regarding the passage "if one sees the fault of a great śramaṇa and does not rise":
this refers to a great śramaṇa who is a descendant of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; to treat such a śramaṇa with contempt is to treat the Buddhas and Patriarchs with contempt.
Furthermore, even when one encounters the faults of a superior in ordinary circumstances, one ought still to rise and offer greetings.
How much more so when one encounters a Great Śramaṇa? How could one sit at ease without rising? This phrase places emphasis on the word "to see.
Filial piety is called the precept; priority and respect must be observed. To sit idly watching without rising fosters one's own arrogance and provokes anger in others.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "In the past, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, whenever he saw the Triple Gem..."
Regarding stūpas, images, teachers, monks, parents, and elders or virtuous friends, there were none to whom he would not incline his body and yield precedence.
Consequently, from the time he attained Buddhahood, all people and animals in the mountains and forests alike held him in profound admiration and took refuge in the Buddha. The *Book of Rites* says:
"Arrogance must not be allowed to grow; desire must not be indulged; ambition must not be overfilled. The *Xinghu* (Conduct Protection) says: "When seeing..."

One should stand up; when sitting, one must yield one's seat. If one encounters another on the road, one should immediately step aside onto the path and stand to one side, waiting until they have passed before proceeding.
Whenever there is instruction or benefit to be gained, one should listen with hands joined in reverence and offer a prostration in thanks.
If one is reprimanded, one must not stare back with angry eyes, but should instead speak with gentle words and repent of one's faults. As the *Sūtra of the Adorned Jewel King* says: "If..."
Those who treat the Saṃgha with contempt shall fall into birth within poor and lowly families. In whatever place they are born, their physical faculties will be incomplete;
they will be hunchbacked, crooked, and deformed. After casting off this body, they will again be born into places where they suffer from many illnesses and emaciation;
their hands and feet will be cramped and paralyzed, and pus and blood will flow profusely over their bodies, causing their flesh to waste away for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes.
For a year, one undergoes this retribution of suffering.
One sits [in meditation] except for five occasions:
when reading scriptures, when ill, when shaving the head, when eating, and when performing communal duties.
Regarding the time of reading scriptures: because the Dharma is held as paramount, one should regard the scriptures as if they were the Buddha;

reciting them with the mouth and contemplating them with the mind, one penetrates their meaning deeply, and thus there is no need to rise. Regarding the time of illness: this refers to when the four elements are out of harmony and the body is afflicted by severe suffering;
therefore, there is no need to rise. Regarding the time of shaving the hair: this refers to when receiving and upholding verses or mantras, or using a sharp blade.
Regarding "at the head": if one moves, there is a fear of causing an error; therefore, one need not rise. Regarding "at the time of eating":
this refers to the three ladles and five contemplations while receiving food according to the Dharma; therefore, one need not rise.

Furthermore, because the Buddha prescribed eating in a single sitting, when performing various tasks, one must prioritize the permanent and essential duties; rising would hinder and cause the abandonment of such effort. Therefore...
It is not necessary to rise. Unless there are circumstances such as those mentioned above, one shall not be permitted to leave.
Third, regarding the preliminary knowledge of the teacher’s rank and conduct:
it is said that from five summer retreats (vassa) upward, one holds the rank of ācārya; from ten summer retreats upward, one holds the rank of upādhyāya. Although...
Regarding the duties of a bhikṣu, a śrāmaṇera should anticipate them in advance.
"Summer" refers to the summer retreat (varṣa), meaning the number of years since one received full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).

Having diligently practiced the precepts for that many years of retreat, one's moral qualities become firm and one’s understanding of what is permitted and what is prohibited becomes clear; thus, one is capable of serving as a teacher to guide others and benefit sentient beings. It is not otherwise.
This refers to speaking in general terms. If one is not conversant with the aforementioned methods, one must still rely upon others;
how much more so for one who is capable of acting as a teacher? *Upādhyāya* is the formal name; it was transmitted to Khotan and translated there as *Heshang*.
Upon arriving in this land, Master Kumārajīva translated it as "One Who Gives Birth by Power" (*Lìshēng*). The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "Now..."
One who has left the household life abandons the house of their parents—the realm of birth and death—and enters the gate of the Buddha to receive the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
this is due to the power of the teacher. They cause the Dharma-body to grow, produce the wealth of merit, and nourish the life-force of wisdom;
no service is greater than this. Some call him *upādhyāya*; Master Yi Jing translated this as "Preceptor" (*qīn jiàoshī*), because he is able—
The Upādhyāya is so called because he leads others out of worldly affairs. Furthermore, it is said: "To dwell together with those of different surnames is called *ho* (harmony);

to always abide facing the sun of the Buddha is called *shō* (to honor). This means that the transmission of the Dharma and the benefiting of sentient beings continue without interruption, and his pure moral virtue is widely renowned.

Regarding the Ācārya, the correct name is *Ācārya*, which is translated here as "transmission" (*denju*). In the Tang language, it means "model" (*kikon*). This refers to one who is able to serve as a model.
It is for the purpose of guiding junior students; in the Sui language, it means "correct practice" (*zhengxing*). The *Nanshan Shichao* states:
"This refers to being able to rectify the conduct of one's disciples. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The *upādhyāya* is like a father, and the *ācārya* is like a mother.

Since one has abandoned one's biological parents, one must seek the parents of the supramundane path. If one abandons the *upādhyāya* and the *ācārya*, it is termed 'abandoning the precepts' (*śīla*)."

"Ji" (即) means "to attain. To honor and manifest one's virtue and the Way is called a "position" (*wei*). This refers to having studied the precepts and the Vinaya for five years and being capable of serving as a model;

therefore, it is said: "one attains the position of an *ācārya*. After ten years of strictly purifying the *vinaya*, one is qualified by the Vinaya rules to ordain others; therefore, it is said: [one attains the position of a *upādhyāya*].
This refers to the position of the *upādhyāya*. Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* clarifies five kinds of *ācāryas*:

first, the one upon whom one relies for ordination and thereby becomes a renunciant; second, the one who confers the precepts and performs the *karmavācanā*; third, the one who instructs and admonishes regarding dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*);
fourth, the one from whom one receives the scriptures, whether it be the explanation of their meaning or even as little as a four-line verse.

Five. Regarding the *niśraya* (dependence): even for one who relies [on a teacher] for only a single night, the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) and the *niśraya* (dependent teacher) are generally those with ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*).

For the four aforementioned teachers, they are generally those with five years of seniority (*pañcavarṣa*). As explained above, these dharmas all pertain to the domain of the great monks (*mahābhikṣu*);
therefore, they are called "matters of a bhikṣu. A *śrāmaṇera* will not long remain on the platform before receiving [the full ordination].
[End of] section. By practicing and maintaining [the precepts] gradually, one also enters that stage; therefore, it is said, "one should know this in advance. Question:

Previously, during the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) for the great *saṃgha*, it was not permitted to hear [the recitation] in advance. Why is it now, on the contrary, required to know it beforehand? Answer:

The fortnightly *Poṣadha* proclaims the characteristics of offenses; fearing that wrong views might arise, hearing it was not permitted. What is now called the "Teacher’s Dharma" (*śāstṛ-dharma*) refers to its name.
Regarding rank: it means that a bhikṣu who has devoted himself to cultivation for five years or ten years is immediately able to serve as a teacher and model for humans and devas.
A śrāmaṇera is still but a junior member of the assembly; one must not treat the great saṃgha with contempt.

Regarding the phrase "serving one's teacher": serving refers to attending with tireless devotion; a teacher refers to one who instructs others without weariness.
The *Tàipíng yùlǎn* states: "A teacher is the foundation for dispelling ignorance. That a student has a teacher is like a tree having roots.
Yet, once great wisdom is perfected, one is further able to bring lesser wisdom to fruition, just as a tree root produces seeds, and those seeds in turn [produce new trees].
Roots of virtue are established; they arise one after another in succession so that their lineage remains unbroken. Therefore, it is said: "The teacher provides guidance and instruction;
the friend provides mutual refinement through critique. Both mundane and supramundane vessels of the Dharma rely entirely upon teachers and friends;

they must be revered and honored. If arrogance is harbored, the merit and wisdom of a lifetime will be extinguished. For this reason, one is cautioned to act as Sadāprarudita did, even selling his heart and liver."
To study Prajñā, O Bhagavat, is to sacrifice one’s entire body for the sake of seeking even half a verse.

The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "Ordinary beings lack wisdom and cling to a self; they further adhere to the view of self, being arrogant and conceited. Unashamed of their ignorance, they falsely exalt themselves.
Seeing what is good, they do not follow it; they refuse instruction and admonition. They do not associate with the worthy, and thus they remain very far from the Way."
The Vinaya states: "When a disciple attends upon his preceptor, he should maintain four mentalities: first, affection; second, reverent compliance;
third, apprehension of difficulty; and fourth, respect. In serving and supporting him, they should be like a minister or a son attending upon a sovereign or a father.
By thus successively honoring, respecting, and looking after one another, they can cause the True Dharma to abide long, increasing and expanding it. △ [End of section] When.
Regarding those who rise early: they rise early for all matters, ensuring that every task proceeds in its proper order, so as not to fall into haste or agitation.

As the ancients said: "If one rises even slightly late in the morning, a hundred affairs will all go awry. One's clothing will be disheveled when donned; opening the door, one regrets the slowness of one's hands.
The tea and soup for the Buddha offering have grown cold; the incense burned has become like ash. One bows in hurried prostration, while at the kitchen hearth..."
The sound of the wooden board urges you on. If a monk rises early, he will find advantage in every matter. According to the Vinaya, the night is divided into three parts:

the first watch, the last watch, and the middle watch. One should apply oneself diligently to the Buddha-way during the first and last watches. During the middle watch, one is permitted to rest. If the middle watch has passed, one should immediately rise;
having washed and rinsed one's mouth, one should then prepare tooth-sticks, water for bathing, and so forth, awaiting whatever the teacher may require.
Furthermore, "early" means first. As a disciple, it is reasonable that one should rise first. Regarding the instruction to "strike the fingers three times before entering the door":

this means that whenever a disciple enters their teacher's quarters, they should remain outside the door to observe whether there is movement or stillness, fearing that they might disturb the teacher’s meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*).
One should first snap the fingers three times to alert the teacher, and only then enter. Not so.
One may act with urgency. △ Regarding the phrase "if there is a fault," etc.: to deviate from the Middle Way is called a "fault.
If one has committed a fault when a teacher reprimands and instructs them, one should lower one's head and accept it.

If one instead speaks back in opposition, this is a fault upon a fault; such a person cannot be taught. Even after [the teacher] has departed, one should still reflect upon it and always maintain a sense of shame.

With a sense of shame, one should contemplate repaying the four debts of gratitude and provide support for all beings within the three realms of existence. To fail to comply with the teacher’s words is equivalent to committing an act of rebellion;

therefore, it is said: "One must not respond with contrary speech. As the Sūtra states: "To slander the teacher, to revile the teacher, to hate the teacher, or to envy the teacher is a great demon within the Dharma—the very seed of hell.
Regarding the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya, one should regard them as one would the Buddha. This means:
The Buddhas of the past have already passed away; those of the future have not yet arrived; it is only the present Buddhas who preach the Dharma.

Those who act as the Buddha’s representatives in proclaiming the transformation [of sentient beings] are none other than the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya. Therefore, it is said: "One should regard them as one would the Buddha. Chengfan says:
"If there are many disciples, each should fulfill their respective duties and serve in succession without fail. △ If one is sent out...
"Unclean vessels" refers to receptacles for excrement and urine, as well as spittoons and the like. "Anger" (*krodha*) means harboring resentment in the heart;
"wrath" (*pratigha*) means being filled with indignation. This means that while there is resentment in the heart, one does not yet express it through indignation, and thus spits upon [the teacher].

However, since everyone fears and avoids such foul odors, it is contrary to the principle of filial conduct toward a teacher to do so. Having already removed these [impurities] for the sake of the teacher, one should not...
One may give rise to a sense of revulsion, manifesting signs of anger and spitting out phlegm and saliva.
At such times, one should reflect that this body is a collection of manifold sufferings and that everything within it is impure. If the teacher is thus, so too is the disciple.
By removing this impurity, one removes the three poisons of the afflictions. If one can contemplate in this way with true discernment, then both self and others will become pure.
This is truly how one emerges from an impure vessel.
Second, regarding the method of prostrating at the proper time:
if the teacher is sitting in meditation, one should not prostrate; if the teacher is walking in meditation (caṅkrama), one should not prostrate; if the teacher is eating... the teacher.

When the teacher is reciting a sutra, combing his teeth, bathing, or sleeping, one should not perform prostrations in any of these instances. When the teacher has closed the door, one should not perform prostrations outside the door.
If one wishes to enter the room to perform prostrations, one should snap the fingers three times; if the teacher does not respond, one should depart.
Regarding "prostration" (*li-bai*): Tiantai says that the ritual rules for the four modes of deportment are called *li*, while the act of reverent homage through the body is called *bai*.
The *Baihutong* asks: "Why do people prostrate to one another? It is to express their feelings and manifest their intentions, bending the joints in humble ritual to honor what is venerable.

When a teacher is practicing seated meditation (*zazen*), one should not prostrate to them, for fear of disturbing their meditative accomplishment. If the teacher is walking in meditation (*jingxing*), [one may prostrate].

If the teacher is engaged in formal mindfulness, one should not pay respects, for fear it might interfere with that mindfulness. If the teacher is receiving food, one should not pay respects, for fear it might distract from their contemplation.
If the teacher is expounding the sutras, one should not pay respects, for fear it might interrupt the flow of the Dharma’s meaning.

If the teacher is cleaning their teeth, one should not pay respects, for fear it might cause them to neglect the recitation of verses and mantras. If the teacher is bathing, one should not pay respects, for their physical appearance will be disarrayed.
When the teacher is sleeping or resting, one should not prostrate because it may startle him awake. Regarding the phrase "and so forth":

when the teacher is shaving his head, washing his feet, or otherwise occupied with affairs and unable to attend to others, or when he is receiving guests; if the teacher has closed the door, one should not perform a prostration outside the door.
This means that performing a prostration at a closed door does not constitute respectful conduct. When wishing to enter the room, one should first snap one's fingers.
Three times. One must not enter hastily or without authorization; if it is not permitted, one should simply return in silence and must not force the matter.
Thus, one knows that prostrating oneself is not as good as obeying a command.

Third, when serving food and attending to the master’s meals, one should always support the vessels with both hands. Upon finishing the meal, one should carefully clear away the utensils. One must stand slowly [and respectfully];
one must not stand facing the master, nor stand at a high elevation, nor stand too far away; one should position oneself so that the master can speak in a low voice.
I have heard that one should not exert great effort;
rather, one should hold the food with both hands as a supreme expression of reverence. Serving food and drink to one's teacher is equivalent to making offerings to the Buddha.

It should be held level with the eyebrows. One must not allow coarse breath to touch the pure food. "Gather" (liǎn) means to withdraw or collect oneself. This should be done slowly and in accordance with one's dignified demeanor.
This means that when collecting the bowls, one must act with composure and delicacy; one must not be coarse or rough, nor allow the bowls to make noise. The Vinaya states:
"In all matters of serving food and drink, one must ensure they are neither too cold nor too hot. Chengfan says:

"When preparing food for one's teacher, regardless of whether it is coarse or refined, it must be pure and clean, and must suit the teacher’s disposition. Furthermore, when offering tea or soup, one must not use one's fingers [to hold the vessel].
Insert it into the bowl. When both hands are held level, present it to the teacher. When the tea is finished, receive the bowl as before. The attendant says:
"If salted tea, medicine, or any food is served, you should consume it all; present it at each respective time.
If fresh fruit is presented, it must first be purified—either by touching it with fire, cutting it with a knife, or using [other means]."

Regarding the peeling of fingers: if they are unfit to serve as seeds [for planting], then purification is unnecessary. As for attending upon a teacher: "Attending" (*shi*) means to receive [instruction] in close proximity.
If one stands directly facing the teacher, there is no distinction between the superior and the subordinate, which fosters arrogance.

If one stands at too great a height, there is a total lack of ritual propriety, resulting in a loss of reverence. If one stands too far away, the minds do not connect and speech does not meet the occasion.
Xinghu said: "One must not stand upwind, nor stand too close. One should remain at a distance of about seven chi from the teacher’s temple;
thus, one can hear their soft speech without taxing the teacher’s effort. Chengfan said:
"One must not turn the body or lower the head, nor speak in a low voice or laugh lightly. One should maintain a solemn and respectful mind and body, and must not manifest signs of fatigue."
Furthermore, one must not stand with hands hanging down like a layperson before the teacher.
One must not speak useless words, scratch an itch, or rub the face with the tips of one's fingernails. One must not put on socks or wash one's feet in the presence of the teacher.
4. The Method for Requesting Instruction and Reporting Matters:
If one wishes to inquire about the causes and conditions of the Buddha-dharma, one should adjust one’s robes, prostrate, join the palms, and kneel with the right knee on the ground.

When the teacher speaks, one should listen with a clear mind and contemplate deeply. If one asks about ordinary domestic matters, there is no need to prostrate or kneel; one should simply stand upright.
The student stands to one side and reports the matter according to the facts. If the teacher’s body or mind is weary and instructs him to leave, he should depart;
he must not show displeasure in his heart or let it appear on his countenance.
"Requesting" means to seek. One who wishes to seek the Dharma must subdue their own mind and contemplate the Noble Path;

they must humble themselves and pay respectful homage, serving their teachers and elders with reverence—this is what is meant by "honoring the teacher and valuing the Way. Yongjia said: "The Right Path is silent and solitary;
though one practices it, it is difficult to realize. The Deviant Paths are noisy and cluttered; though there is nothing to practice, they are easy to approach. To humble oneself...
Xie Bo questioned those who possessed prior realization; by concentrating his spirit within his heart throughout the day and night, he was finally able to understand.

Regarding the "causes and conditions of the Buddha-dharma," these refer to the events introduced in the Sūtras and Vinayas, or the public cases (*gong'an*) and circumstantial encounters (*jīyuán*) of past masters.
The *Sutra on Skillful Reverence* states: "If you have any doubts, you should first consult and inform [your teacher]. Only when you see that the teacher grants permission..."

Regarding the subsequent inquiry: "Adjusting one's robes, prostrating, and kneeling with palms joined" means that the hands, originally at the left and right, are brought together as one to signify single-minded devotion.
Placing the right knee upon the ground is called *juei* (kneeling). The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* clarifies that there are three reasons for placing the right knee on the ground:
first, the right knee possesses strength, allowing one to remain in the kneeling posture for a long duration.
2. The right knee possesses strength, making rising and sitting easy. 3. The right knee is restless; when it touches the ground, it brings stability.

If both knees touch the ground, this is called *jang-kwei* (long-kneeling). However, when a disciple seeks instruction or resolution from a teacher, there has never been a case of doing so while seated;
therefore, Subhūti, Śāriputra, and others, whenever they had questions to ask, invariably rose from their seats.
Baring the right shoulder, prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, kneeling with palms joined, listen attentively to what is being said.

Because deluded thoughts do not arise, it is called "clarifying the mind. To listen attentively is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); to contemplate is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); to penetrate deeply is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
This means that through hearing one realizes the principle, and by grasping the principle one unifies it with the mind. When the teacher is sitting alone, [it is] appropriate...

When [the teacher] is walking, or when his countenance is serene, one should immediately ask questions. One must stand to one side, with a relaxed expression and a calm mind, inquiring with utmost sincerity.
Each word should be articulated clearly, and one should listen with an open mind; thus, one will naturally be able to penetrate deeply.

△ Regarding "household matters," these refer to the ordinary daily activities of the monastic community. As for "not needing to prostrate or kneel," it means that in the household there is no fixed [formality].
This is the ritual propriety. Standing upright at the side of the master ensures that one does not deviate from the standard model.

One reports matters directly according to the facts; therefore, it is said: "to present a statement based on reality. If one does not base it on reality, there is fear of misleading the assembly and failing in the regulations of the monastic community.

△ Regarding "those whose body and mind are weary": this means that when meditative reflection exceeds its limit, the mind becomes exhausted; when rising and sitting are too frequent, [the body becomes weary].
When the body is weary, whenever you inquire about the scriptures or engage in dialogue, you should wait for the teacher’s disposition; you should not seek your own convenience.
If the teacher’s body and mind are fatigued and lack the spiritual presence to respond, you should be instructed to leave for a while.

If you instead harbor inner displeasure that manifests on your outward countenance, first, you will incur transgression; second, all matters will fail to be accomplished. As the ancients said: "Reading..."

In the *Shu* (Book of Documents), it is said that transforming one’s temperament and disposition must be the priority. In studying the Way, obeying the teacher’s instructions must be paramount. The *Wushi Song* (Fifty Verses) states:
"One should always admire the teacher’s virtue and not look for minor faults; by following them, one attains accomplishment, but seeking out faults only brings self-injury.
The *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) says: "In seeking a teacher, one must focus on their ultimate excellence; in serving a teacher, one must forget the teacher’s [shortcomings]."
[This is] a transgression. The *Sūtra on Good Reverence* states: The Buddha said, "A disciple must not use coarse language toward their teacher.

When the teacher rebukes them, they should not respond in kind. Unless the teacher asks a question, they must not speak of their own accord. Whenever they are commanded to do something, they must not disobey.
If one does not give rise to reverence toward the teacher and speaks of the teacher’s faults or shortcomings, that person..."
Foolish people should be dealt with according to the law. If a teacher actually has a fault, one must not speak of it; how much less so when there is none.
If one fails to show respect toward a teacher, one will fall into a separate minor hell called *Tui-po* (The Beating).
There, one shall have four heads on a single body, with the entire body likewise [multi-headed], appearing like a mass of fire emitting fierce, blazing flames.
Blazing without ceasing, in that place of hell there are further venomous insects with hooked beaks that constantly suck at the root of the tongue.
Upon emerging from hell, they are born among animals, where they perpetually consume urine and excrement. After casting off that body, although they may be born among humans...
They are constantly born in remote borderlands where their skin does not resemble that of humans; they cannot possess the complete physical form of a person.
They are perpetually despised, slandered, and humiliated. Being separated from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they are forever devoid of wisdom.
After dying there, they fall back into hell, further encountering immeasurable and boundless states of suffering and affliction.
5. Approaching the Master to Seek the Method of Repentance:
Whenever there is an offense against the precepts or similar matters, one must not conceal them. One should immediately go before the master and piteously beg for repentance.

If the master grants permission, one should disclose everything with full sincerity and reform with earnest devotion; thus, one shall regain purity. [One must] not interrupt the master while he is still speaking.

Regarding the term "concealment" (*paticchādana*): "concealment" (*paṭicchādeti*) means to hide; "to cover" (*paṭicchādeti*) means to wrap up or conceal. As the Sūtra says: "To wrap up and conceal one's flaws is not permitted by the Buddha.
Confessing prior transgressions is what is esteemed by the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*. Therefore, it is known that when there is an offense against the precepts, one must not conceal it.

*Saṃvara* means to conceal or hide. *Kṣipram* means to go quickly; it signifies going in haste before the teacher to beg for instruction and to earnestly entreat forgiveness so as to avoid the further accumulation of the offense of concealment.
*Deśanā* (confession) is named for the act of laying bare all faults and exposing one's transgressions.

"One dares not conceal or hide [one's faults]. 'Repentance' (*huì*) means the mind that severs the continuity [of transgression]; it is the wearying of regret, the relinquishing and abandoning [of faults], and the discarding of both the agent and the act.
Therefore, it is called *chànhuǐ* (repentance). Regarding 'if the teacher grants permission, one should disclose everything with full sincerity':

this means that once the teacher has granted compassionate consent, one must overturn [the past] from the very depths—like clouds parting to reveal the moon, or sunlight shining to melt frost—without leaving even a single thread [of secrecy]."
"Hao" (毫) means sticky attachment. Regarding "one who sincerely repents": "Jing" (精) means single-mindedness and purity; "Cheng" (誠) means utmost sincerity without deception;
"Hui" (悔) means regretting what one has committed; "Gai" (改) means reforming former errors so as not to commit them again.
Therefore it is said: "One thereby regains purity. Xinghuo says: "If you are reviled or scolded, you must hold yourself accountable and speak with gentle words."
One should offer repentance and express gratitude, cultivating precepts and meditative concentration to repay the kindness of the teacher. Chengfan says:
Whenever there is an error or transgression, even if the teacher displays anger and reproaches one in various ways, one must not use clever words to gloss over one's faults.

As soon as one perceives the teacher’s anger, one should immediately feel awe and fear, composing one's countenance and kneeling before the teacher. With a heart full of shame, one should accept the reprimand; having committed a fault, one must reform it.
"Remaining silent when there is no fault. Regarding "one must not speak while the teacher’s words are unfinished":

this means that in ordinary conversation with others, one must wait until they have finished speaking before responding; how much more so when it concerns the teacher’s instruction? If the teacher’s speech is not yet concluded, [one must remain silent].
To intermingle one's own words with the instructions of the Master in this manner results in losing both one's own benefit and the respect [accorded to the teaching].
Once the proper sequence is lost, where is the model? The Vinaya states: "One must not seek victory by disputing over principles."

Sixth: Regarding the etiquette for delivering letters while attending upon one’s teacher, one must not sit playfully in the teacher’s seat, nor lie upon the teacher’s bed, nor wear the teacher’s robes or hat.

When acting as a messenger to deliver letters for the teacher, one must not privately open them to read them, nor show them to others. Upon arriving at the destination, one should respond appropriately to any questions asked.

If it is a matter of substance, one should answer; if it is not appropriate to answer, one should politely decline. If the other person persists and cannot leave, they should remain standing, focusing their mind single-pointedly on the teacher while looking toward him.
The "teacher’s seat" is the position of honor for a disciple who has received instruction. If one sits upon it with a frivolous mind, [it is improper].
Then one's transgressions will not be few. To revere the position of the teacher is to revere the teacher himself; do not treat him with negligence or contempt.

As for his bedding, clothing, and hat, these too must not be treated lightly. Whenever you draw near to the teacher, you must always maintain a sense of respect, remaining the same whether in his presence or behind his back.
If you allow yourself even a moment of casualness, you will ultimately lack any real foundation. What benefit would that bring to your practice? △ *Chida* (Running Through)

Regarding "letters" (*shuxin*): they are dispatched for delivery; their meaning lies in conveying matters to inform another, hence they are called "letters" (*shu*) because they manifest one's trust (*xin*).
Thus, when a letter is dispatched beyond a thousand li, reading it is as if one were meeting face-to-face.

Generally speaking, the correspondence composed by those in the Way (monastics) merely serves to attend to the affairs of the monastery and involves the exchange of inquiries and responses; there is nothing therein that cannot be shared with others.
As for those who look [at the letter]: since a special envoy has been dispatched, there must be a matter of great importance.

To open the sealed envelope privately or to show it to others is something both monastics and laypeople avoid; it is most certainly inappropriate. Nevertheless, having received my teacher’s command, I must take up this heavy responsibility.
Deliver it with utmost sincerity to that destination. If you open it to inspect it midway or show it to others, first, it will delay the journey;
second, there is a fear that the message may be lost or intercepted. Therefore, one must be cautious and discreet.
Furthermore, regarding letters entrusted by others, one must hand them over clearly and complete the task for the sender; one must not betray the trust placed in them. If one acts privately...
To tear [a letter] and show it to others, exposing another’s affairs, damages one's virtue and invites transgression. Xinghuo said:

"Even regarding letters from outside, one must not read them together with the Master. In the spring of the Dingwei year, while I was serving as an attendant in Huashan, the Abbot was reading a letter.
I looked on from a distance. My Master turned his head and rebuked me, saying: "Go away! Kneel before the incense burner. From this day forward..."
These instructions are a model for future days. To this day, my knee pain has not ceased; since even a distant request is not permitted, how much less so a private reading?
Formerly, when Fu Bi was an envoy to the Qidan, he received a family letter but did not open it, instead burning it and saying, "It would merely disturb one's mind.
If even a family letter was not opened, how much less so any other letter? △ Arrive.
Regarding those who come with questions: generally, when a disciple is sent out on an errand, the preceptor must provide instructions concerning what should be answered and what should not.
The essential point is to adapt according to the circumstances. If one answers what should not be answered, it will contradict the written instructions and result in a futile round trip.
Furthermore, while there, one must not look at other people's writings.
Regarding the inspection of registers, the unauthorized movement of vessels, brushes, and inkstones, as well as the perusing of clothing and hats, and the damaging of crops:
if one must leave and cannot remain, there are three considerations: first, measuring the matter; second, measuring the time; and third, measuring the road.
Regarding the thought of longing for the teacher’s return: it is like a filial son’s mindfulness of his compassionate mother; he cannot, even for a moment, forget her presence by his side.
As the Sūtra says: "One should go directly forward and return directly back; one should recognize what the teacher says, and one should also recognize the words of others in response."
One must not be negligent.
When seven guests come to attend, the Dharma Master stands facing them;
they may stand in their usual places, or beside the Master, or behind the Master, ensuring that their ears and eyes remain in mutual communication.
Upon meeting [the teacher], one should attend to whatever the teacher requires.

In ordinary service to the teacher, one must be most reverent and respectful to fulfill the way of filial piety; even when guests are seated [in the presence of the teacher], one should likewise maintain such reverence.
Master Cishou Shen said: "When encountering a monk in the corridor, one must offer a greeting; when meeting [a guest] at the gate..."
When guests call for one another, those who have left the household life should maintain an attitude of humility and courtesy; do not emulate the ignorant who lack proper etiquette.

When standing at a constant distance—neither too far nor too near—one stands at the proper measure. Thus, the ears and eyes remain in contact, and body and mind respond to one another without missing the opportune moment;
all this is for the sake of attending to the needs of the teacher. For example, if asked for *saindhava*, one should immediately respond.
Chengfan said: Whenever a guest arrives, one should give rise to reverence and not harbor feelings of aversion or arrogance.

One must wash the cups and brew tea to await the moment for serving. If the master calls out loudly while facing a guest of high status, it is a waste of mental energy and reveals a lack of strictness in the family’s internal discipline; where, then, is the way of serving one's teacher?
The eight attendants served the Dharma Master during his illness with meticulous care, attending to each detail of his treatment. Matters concerning his quarters, bedding, medicines, and congee,
as well as the handling of his robes, the provision of sandals, and their washing, drying, and ironing, are fully detailed in the Vinaya and are not recorded here at length.

The teacher is the parent of the Dharma-body. Just as a child in this world cannot be without parents for even a single day, so too a renunciant who has transcended the world cannot be without the teacher and the Dharma for even a single day. Therefore, one should reverently follow the teacher and the Dharma.
Serve your parents as you would serve a teacher. If they fall ill, you should attend to their treatment with a focused mind.
Even if the teacher becomes angry or scolds you during their illness, you should remain calm and patient, serving them from beginning to end without ever becoming weary or disheartened.

You should reflect that the body is the root of suffering and that having form makes it difficult to avoid such conditions. Thus, provide for their external needs through housing, bedding, and clothing, and treat their internal needs with medicine, tonics, and congee.
This refers to the fact that all necessary medicines for the illness, food, and appropriate utensils must each be prepared.
Zen Master Yue Tang Chang said: "When Huanglong resided at Jicui, he was ill for three months and did not come out of his room.

Zhenjing Wen served as the head of the administrative office (jianyuan) and prayed earnestly night after night, even to the point of burning his crown and cauterizing his arms, looking upward to pray for spiritual assistance. Huang... [text continues]
Upon hearing this, Long reprimanded him, saying, "Life and death are surely my own lot.
Zhenjing responded with composure, "The monastic community may do without Ke-wen, but it cannot do without the Master.

Those who understood him remarked that Zhenjing’s reverence for his teacher and gravity toward the Dharma reached such a point of sincerity that he would surely become a great vessel in the future. Thus he was named Cheng (Accomplished).
Fan said: "One should prepare and adorn the chamber, avoiding locations that are windy or damp. The bedding and mattresses must be thick and soft.
One should observe the teacher’s facial expression and assist him with a staff when entering or leaving. Soup, broth, medicine, and food should be prepared and cooked according to the proper methods.

Upon even slight recovery, one should feel joy. One should always serve him with filial devotion and a harmonious countenance. When guests arrive to inquire after his health, one should skillfully speak on his behalf; one must not engage in clamor."
The assembly should maintain solemnity and tranquility. If the illness is grave, one must not wail or weep. Upon the Master’s parinirvāṇa, one must not violate his sincere instructions;
everything should be carried out exactly according to his teachings. Among the eight fields of merit, caring for the sick is foremost.
Since the Master is a field of reverence (*gurutva-kṣetra*), one should pay him even greater heed. △ As for those who hold the Master’s robes, they should slowly push them upward with one hand.

Grasp it with one hand and place it upright upon the left shoulder of the teacher. Once the teacher has placed it on, look again to see whether the upper and lower patterns are aligned according to the Dharma.
When folding it, do not hold it in your mouth; you must observe the upper and lower parts so that it does not touch the ground.
Return it to its usual place and cover it with a clean cloth; do not cover it with other garments or clothing. Hand over the sandals.
One should first shake out the robe and brush away the dirt, doing so without making a loud noise. One should inspect it and compare it [with the others] before proceeding.
Once the hands have been washed, one may then take up the garment. In all washing, one must ensure it is thoroughly clean, yet one must not waste water. As for the method of drying the dharma robes:

One should wait for it to dry. If there is urgent business requiring departure, one must not leave it unattended; it should be entrusted to another person. Upon completion of the task, one should return it immediately.
Other matters, such as the washing of bowls and utensils, are fully detailed in the *Vinaya-sūtra*; as the text is extensive, I shall not record them here at length.

However, although the descriptions of serving a teacher in the Vinaya are broad in their terminology, they can be summarized in a single word: sincerity, and in another: filial piety. When serving a teacher, one should at all times...
If sincerity and filial piety reside within the heart, then all acts of service will naturally accord with the Dharma.
Between teacher and disciple, they will blend like water and milk, and the Way will be found therein.
II. The Ritual for Attending (divided into two parts; the first part concerns the method of showing respect through the three types of activity).

In general, when attending upon a teacher: 1. Unless commanded to sit, one must not dare to sit. 2. Unless questioned, one must not dare to respond. 3. [Except] when one has a personal matter that one wishes to ask.
In general, when standing in attendance: One must not lean against a wall or rest against a desk. One should maintain an upright posture with feet together and stand slightly to the side.
○ If one wishes to prostrate and the teacher stops them, one should comply with the teacher’s command and not prostrate.

○ Whenever the teacher engages in discussion with guests concerning matters of the Way that are beneficial to body and mind, one should take note of them all. ○ When the teacher has a task to be performed, one should attend to it promptly;
one must not be negligent or disrespectful. ○ In all instances of sleeping, one must not precede the teacher. ○ When others ask questions...
Regarding the Master’s name, it should be stated as "Upper [Name], Lower [Name].
"Fu" (附) means to entrust; that is, to entrust matters to complete the text. This is where the Great Master’s compassionate heart was most earnest;
therefore, whenever there were matters concerning śrāmaṇeras beneficial within the sūtras and vinaya, he selected and extracted them all to supplement the text, according to the vinaya.
I, [the author], do not dare to intermingle [these matters]. Thus, I have raised this point clearly. Regarding the rule that one does not dare to sit unless commanded to do so:
when a disciple stands in attendance before a teacher, moving about to his left and right, it is indeed their proper duty.

However, if the teacher takes pity on the disciple’s long-standing standing and physical fatigue, and thus commands them to sit, this is an act of compassion. That the disciple respectfully obeys the teacher’s command and sits down is the proper ritual.
To sit without being invited is an act of arrogance. Regarding "not daring to respond when not asked": this refers to the dialogue between teacher and disciple;
if one does not understand the flow of the discourse, then one's words will lack foundation. Talk that lacks foundation is like a tangle of hemp with no end to its threads.
Apart from matters concerning oneself, one must not inquire arbitrarily.

However, when the ancients engaged in question and answer after their awakening, it was like threading a needle with lightning-fast speed—thread coming and thread going—or like ripples on water and scattered blossoms adorning the surface.

Although these were but everyday expressions, one must know that there are thorns hidden within the mud. △ As for those who lean against walls or rest against desks, this refers to being biased or partial.
It is said: "Leaning" means to rest one's body at an angle; "relying" means to lean against something. To stand askew means not to face [the teacher] directly. The *Fifty Verses* states:
"Furthermore, one should not manifest signs of physical fatigue before the teacher, snap the joints of the fingers, lean against pillars or walls, nor step upon the threshold.
This is what is meant by the saying: "To be reverent without propriety leads to exhaustion. Master Sengzhao said: "One should maintain reverence and accord with [the teacher’s will]."
Regarding the attendants of the Buddha, they are called *upasthāyaka*. The *Bodhisattvāvatīraṇa-sūtra* states: "An attendant possesses eight qualities:
first, firmness of faith; second, a mind that seeks progress; third, freedom from physical ailments;

fourth, diligence; fifth, possession of mindfulness; sixth, a mind free from arrogance; seventh, the ability to achieve concentration and wisdom; and eighth, the full possession of the wisdom of learning."
△ If one wishes to pay homage and the teacher restrains them, one must comply with that command.

If one were to disregard the teacher’s command and insist on prostrating, even though one has prostrated, it is as if one has not prostrated at all. If one follows the teacher’s command and does not prostrate, this is superior to prostrating.
△ Whenever the teacher converses with a guest, every word is a karmic occasion for the Buddha-dharma. To understand its profound subtlety, one should observe it.
In the ordinary course of daily life, "discourse on the Way" refers to talk concerning the Way; that is, Dharma-talk.
However, while manual labor and service build the foundation of one's own merit, hearing the Dharma and committing it to memory moistens and nourishes the ground of the mind.
Thus, it is said to be beneficial for both body and mind. This is truly the meaning of serving one’s teacher. Chengfan said: "Or when the teacher inquires of a guest..."
Answer: When the master answers a question, one must not hear something different and be startled or alarmed; one must not see him smile and laugh along with him.

One should instead discern the meaning of his words and grasp his fundamental principles, studying them with a sincere heart. If you should have a point of realization, you ought to present it to the master once again.
In the past, Yunmen Wenyan’s preaching was like clouds and rain; he did not permit it to be recorded. He would invariably scold and drive away anyone who saw him recording his teachings.
He said, "Your mouth is useless; instead, you record my words. In time, you will surely sell me out.
These words spoken within this room—Xianglin used paper as clothing and recorded them as he heard them.
The ancients were so attentive to their practice that they later shook heaven and overturned the earth. Looking at this, there is nothing in all matters that can be accomplished without study."
**Completion (Chéng) △:** When the Master has a command and one ought to perform it immediately, this means that upon hearing the task assigned by the Master, one should act at once.
One must fear that another command might be heard before the current one is finished; "preparation" (*bàn*) refers to making ready. To fail to comply is called "disobedience" (*wéi*);
to lack reverence is called "arrogance" (*màn*), which is also synonymous with indolence. Chengfan says: "Whenever you hear the Master call, you should respond accordingly."
Upon his arrival, if there was anything required, he would bestow it according to the Dharma. To have even the slightest negligence resulted in the offense of transgression and arrogance.
Regarding the rule that one must not sleep before the teacher: "sleeping" (*shui*) refers to dozing while seated, while "sleeping" (*mian*) refers to closing the eyes.
Among the afflictions of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), this is the foremost; because it shrouds and obscures both body and mind, it prevents wholesome dharmas from arising.
Long submerged within the three realms, one must gradually subdue them. Now that you have become a disciple, you ought to rise before your teacher and lie down behind him.
The character *xiān* (先) should be read with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). Originally meaning "to be ahead," it is called *xiān* because one was originally in front but is now [behind];
thus it is said to be *xiān*. The Vinaya states that there are five faults of excessive sleep: first, having many bad dreams.
2. The devas do not rejoice; 3. the mind does not enter the Dharma; 4. one does not contemplate the signs of light; 5. one dreams of losing seminal purity.

Regarding the question of why ordinary people inquire after a teacher’s *huì* (諱): *Huì* means to avoid, to shun, or to conceal. What is called a "name" (*míng*, 名) during life is called *huì* after death.
When people nowadays ask about another's *huì*, they are concealing the two characters of their formal name (*fǎmíng*, 法名), meaning they dare not ask for the actual name.
Yet it is called a "taboo name" (*huì*). Although this is a misnomer, it carries the sense of reverence; thus, the Great Master supplemented the text here.
Because a disciple may not directly address their teacher by name, he added the two characters "upper" and "lower.
If one asks for the teacher’s title, one should answer, "Venerable [Name] Upādhyāya," or "My Root Teacher [Name]," without the need for the two characters "upper" and "lower. Now...

Regarding the proclamation of one's seniority during the conferral of the precepts, this is a designation used for disciples. If asked for the name of one's teacher, one should say, "My teacher is [Name].
As stated in the *Fifty Verses*: "Furthermore, one should not casually utter the name of one's teacher."

If there is someone who asks insistently, one should show them the single character [of their courtesy name]. If they ask about the master’s years since ordination (*śrāmaṇera-lakṣa*) or the name of their prefecture and county, each of these must be answered.
The *Helin Yulu* says: "The ancients considered addressing someone by their courtesy name to be most undignified;

the disciples of Confucius addressed their Master as Zhongni. In the present day, equals address each other by courtesy name, while those who are slightly more honorable [address others by their given names]."

Consequently, one dares not utter their personal names; this differs from ancient practice. The *Fayuan* states: "To invoke the names of the various Buddhas and pay them homage brings forth blessings and merit;
for the most part, this depends upon the mouth and the mind. If it issues from a mouth of reverence," [the merit is great].
This will bring merit; however, if it issues from the mouths of the frivolous, it will become a calamity.
Second, regarding the method for seeking a teacher and choosing a place:
all disciples should select an enlightened teacher and remain in close attendance for a long time, not departing from the teacher too soon. If the teacher is truly...

[This point is] unclear; one should seek a separate, virtuous guide. Should one be separated from the teacher, one must remember the teacher’s instructions and must not indulge one's own whims or act independently.
One must not follow the improper practices prevalent among worldly customs. Furthermore, one must not dwell in marketplaces or noisy places;
one must not dwell in shrines or temples; one must not dwell in private residences; one must not dwell near nuns' monasteries; and one must not [dwell] apart from the teacher.
While dwelling [in the world], one may commit all manner of evil deeds within the worldly dharmas;
therefore, one must select an enlightened teacher—a teacher whose Dharma-eye is opened and clear.

One should remain in close proximity to such a teacher for a long time and must not depart from them arbitrarily, for the Buddha-dharma is not easily obtained and is difficult to encounter over the long term. Thus it was in the past...

Chan Master Duanya addressed the assembly, saying: "For twenty or thirty years, I have been in close proximity to Gaofeng, constantly striking through to the very marrow of my bones, never once giving rise to a single thought of desire to leave. Such was the conduct of the ancients.
Within the Vinaya, there are four ways of being in close proximity to one's teacher: first, having both the Dharma and food, which is called 'dwelling with joy'; second, having the Dharma..."
Three: having no food, it is called dwelling in suffering. Four: having food but no Dharma; one should offer an apology and depart.

Five: having neither Dharma nor food; one departs without taking leave. As the ancients said: "When a bird seeks to rest, it must choose its forest; when a person seeks the Way," [they must likewise choose their teacher].
One must certainly select one's teacher, for the teacher is the model and standard for a person. When a model and standard are upright, excellent vessels will surely emerge;
therefore, one must choose with care. If it were otherwise, one should seek elsewhere:

a fish that swallows a boat does not hide in a shallow stream, and a tree with a trunk of several arms' span does not grow on Mount Danqiu. How could the Great Peng, when spreading its wings across ninety thousand li, [ever find such a place]?
If a swiftlet rests upon a single branch, yet a *śrāmaṇera* fundamentally has no rule for departing from his teacher, it is because he truly lacks clear understanding.
A "virtuous guide" refers to one who is well able to lead others to reach the ultimate Way; this is as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*:

"By following and studying under such a teacher, one shall attain the vision of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. If one does not seek [instruction] elsewhere, I fear one will revere a monkey.
The monkey took Śakra to be his lord; he took rubble to be a bright pearl. To take rubble as one's object of veneration is to be ignorant of the Dharma;
to revere a monkey is to be ignorant of people. If one is ignorant of the Dharma, the eye of wisdom is lost; if one is ignorant of people, one falls onto a false path.
Therefore it is said: "Since your teacher has fallen, you too shall follow in his fall. This is what that means.

As for the instruction, "Even if you leave your teacher, you should always remember your teacher's teachings," this means that although you may depart from your teacher, you must constantly recall the words of instruction he gave you during your time with him.
It is as if one were being instructed by ear and face-to-face; for the rest of one's life, one dares not transgress. The *Zhongxin jing* (Sutra on the Mind’s Core) states:

"The Buddha said that those who recognize their teacher’s kindness, when they see the teacher, should serve and make offerings to them; when they do not see them, they should contemplate the teacher’s instructions. This is precisely what is meant.

If one indulges one's own whims and acts according to one's own will, it is because one does not remember the teacher’s admonitions; thus, performing improper deeds is merely following the ways of the world.
This refers to worldly people. Regarding "one must not dwell in bustling marketplaces": a place where goods are accumulated for trade and where people congregate is called a "market" (*shi*).
Since ancient times, markets were often established at water wells; thus, they are termed "market-wells" (*shijing*).
Because the market is noisy and chaotic, it is called a "bustling place. Unless one is a person of great power and capacity, one should not enter such a marketplace.

Hanging down the hands. To be harmonious yet not flow with the world, one must not remain [attached]. This is because if the external environment causes disorder, the body and mind will follow in disorder.
Regarding "not remaining in a shrine": shrines offer sacrifices of wine and meat; if one were to do so, the monastic decorum would become lax and one would be held in contempt by others.
Therefore, those who have left the household life—during the Buddha’s lifetime—lived in reliance upon the Buddha; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [they rely upon the Dharma].
Therefore, one should dwell relying upon the Buddha image. For this reason, those who uphold the precepts do not prostrate to ghosts and spirits; rather, they are revered by them.
If one dwells in a shrine to a deity, one will be held in contempt by those very spirits. As it was said of old: "When monks dwell in city shrines, the Buddhas and Patriarchs rebuke them;
the ancient sages all hid in mountain caves and gullies. When mountain springs flow out into the human world, they become clear water."
It remains turbid waves. △ Regarding those who may not reside in inhabited dwellings: this is a distinction between the monastic and the lay.

It means that because one is often near noisy places, there is fear of hindering the Path. As the *Āraṇyaka-gāthā* says: "One who desires diligence in the One Vehicle should first select their dwelling place.
If one does not distance oneself from the marketplace, afflictions will be like knives and saws. Until one reaches the gate of No-more-learning..."
When one studies with focused concern, beneath the forest trees or by the water’s edge, impurities are naturally filtered away.
Relying upon a thatched three-bay hut, spread out a single *pútuán* (grass mat) and gaze steadily with a vacant mind; wherever you touch, it is the ground of the Way.
I now feel much regret for not having relied upon these words. △ Regarding the prohibition against dwelling near a nunnery: this refers to [the presence of] men and women.

This is a distinction. Regarding the adage "the melon field and the plum tree," one must avoid giving rise to suspicion and shame. △ It is not permissible for the teacher and disciples to reside separately;

this means that the gathering and dispersing of teachers and disciples is a natural principle of reason. However, if one simply practices according to the Buddhist teachings and does not follow worldly conventions, then there will be no obstruction.
△ As for "evil deeds," this refers to those who, with hunched shoulders and sycophantic smiles, seek fame among the gentry and scholars.
Forming alliances and frequenting one another; belonging to powerful and influential clans; studying extraordinary arts; being employed as actors;
serving as envoys to the four quarters; engaging in trade for profit; and dwelling near nuns' temples, shrines, or private residences—all these are not the deeds of a son of the Buddha.
Therefore, it is said: "These are all evil matters within the ways of the world."
Section Three: Following the Teacher on an Excursion (Nine Items in Total; Divided into Two Parts). Part One: The Proper Protocol (Divided into Four). Item One:
On the Road, one must not pass by or enter people’s houses. Item Two: One must not stop by the side of the road to converse with others. Item Three: One must not [walk] to the left...
Looking back to the right, one should keep the head bowed and follow behind the teacher.
To "follow the teacher" means to pursue and follow; that is to say, when the teacher goes out, the disciple should follow along with his staff and sandals.
Regarding the phrase "one must not pass through people's houses": *li* (歷) means to traverse or walk through. This means that while the teacher is at one house, the disciple [must not enter].
The disciple may also walk one house further, though this deviates from the path of following closely.
Even if it passes by the parents' home or the donor's household, if the teacher does not permit it, he must not enter. The Vinaya states: "One must not go so far as to be out of sight;
one should remain at a distance of one *śu-shou* (the reach of an extended hand). If there are dangerous elephants, oxen, or horses ahead, one should inform the teacher first and avoid them."
Regarding the location: one must not say that one has delayed or made an error. One must not stop by the side of the road to converse with others.
"Road" (道) refers to the path. If you encounter relatives, friends, or acquaintances on the road, you should politely decline their company.
If you engage in conversation, you will lose the decorum of being an attendant; where then would you place your teacher? Furthermore, one must not look left or right.

"Gu" means to look back. This refers to ordinary coming and going: one should gaze level ahead and proceed straight forward, maintaining dignified deportment in accordance with the Dharma so as not to violate monastic regulations.
When following behind one's teacher, one should be especially solemn and orderly, attending to their every movement and stillness.

If one looks east while gazing westward, one will be ridiculed by the laity and cannot avoid being criticized for having no family discipline (*jiafa*). Yet, the disciple is unable [to maintain this].
To comfort one's teacher with the practice of the Way, yet instead reproach him with worldly matters—how can one’s heart find peace in such a burden upon the teacher?

Xinghuo said: "Among the three thousand dignified demeanors (*sāhasrika-iriyāpatha*), conduct is foremost. If one looks about on all sides and is reviled by the laity, one is not a vessel of the Right Dharma.
As the Book says: "When the will is sincere, the mind becomes correct; when the mind is correct, there is nothing that is not correct."

Second, when arriving at one’s own home or the home of a donor, one should stand to one side. When the teacher instructs one to sit, one should sit. When arriving at another temple, if the teacher pays homage to the Buddha, one may do so as well;
however, one must not strike the *qing* bell on one's own initiative.
Regarding the meaning of the name: *dāna* is a Sanskrit term. Translated [into Chinese], it means "giving.

This refers to one who is able to practice giving and make offerings to the Triple Gem, thereby crossing over this ocean of poverty and suffering in the future; thus it is also called *dānapati*, which means "donor.
The Mahayana treatises state that it is so called because it can lead to the accumulation of merit. As for "should stand to one side," it means:
One should never be separated from [the teacher] by his side. As for the instruction to sit when one should sit, it is out of respect for the Dharma and respect for the teacher.
Chengfan says: "If circumstances require you to sit, do not extend both legs; always maintain all dignified deportment.

When the teacher rises, you should rise immediately. The *Book of Rites* says: "When an elder offers a seat, one should announce that one will sit before sitting. △ Regarding the teacher’s prostration to the Buddha: the Buddha...
These are those who have attained awakening first; the teacher is one who awakens later. Because one awakens others by virtue of having awakened first, one must pay homage upon seeing a Buddha.
As for those who prostrate themselves, it is because "near vermilion, one becomes red. Regarding the prohibition against striking the *qing* bell arbitrarily:
"arbitrarily" (*shàn*) means to act with personal autonomy. The bell and the *qing* are the eyes and ears of humans and devas, and the signal-call of the monastic community.
Each shall have its appointed officials in charge. Upon entering the monastery, one must strictly observe its regulations;

do not fail in the etiquette of a guest, for only then will the rules governing host and guest be seen. Should one act impulsively, it will cause the entire assembly to stir and bring shame upon the master.
What benefit is there in following him?
When he ascends a mountain or travels across a mountain, one should carry the sitting mat and follow him; if traveling a long distance, one must not be separated from him by too great a distance.
"If traveling by mountain, one should carry a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*).

This means that because mountain paths are difficult to traverse, one should carry a sitting mat, a rush cushion (*kūrpa*), or whatever object is used for sitting, prepared to lay it out for the teacher to sit upon, lest the teacher become weary from the journey and desire a brief rest.
△ "One must not stay too far away" means that if one stays too close, one might step on the teacher.
[The shadow] may move as he walks, stirring up dust; if it is too far away, one will not hear the teacher’s call.

Once their respective locations are lost, the two will no longer be in sight of one another, and there is fear that the task will be compromised. Therefore, in all actions one undertakes, one must look back and forth so as not to leave both sides hanging in anxious suspense.
Fourth, regarding crossing water or using a ferry:
one should hold a staff and carefully test the depth. Carrying a water flask, a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), and so forth, is detailed as prescribed in the Vinaya;
the text is too voluminous to be recorded here.
The Vinaya states: "There are two causes and conditions for which the Buddha permitted the keeping of a staff:

first, because of being old, emaciated, and lacking strength; second, for striking the path and testing the water. By testing it slowly, one avoids the fear of danger and peril. If the water is shallow, one assists the teacher across;
if it is deep, one requests someone to carry him on a shoulder-palanquin. Regarding serving the teacher, a verse says: "If upon a dangerous path..."
Having already acted as a guide, when crossing streams or ravines, he tests the depth with his staff—what is called "wading across if deep" and "lifting the hem if shallow.
Regarding the carrying of the *kundika* and the *khakkhara*: the Sanskrit term *kundika* translates here as "vase.
There are two types: first, the pure vase (*śaucakundika*); second, the bathing vase (*snānakundika*). This is the bathing vase, meaning it is used to store water for personal use while traveling.
Because the hands must be clean: those made of ceramic or tile are called "for pure use," while those made of copper or iron are called "for contact use.
Regarding the pewter [staff], this is the pewter staff (*khakkhara*); when carried by a teacher, both sound and noise must necessarily be silenced, as detailed in the Vinaya.
In the *Daśa-śīla-sūtra*, there are fifteen matters concerning the carrying of the teacher’s water flask (*kuṇḍikā*) and seven matters concerning the carrying of the staff; the text is extensive.
Because it was not recorded [in the main text], those who wish to study this extensively should personally examine the scriptural text; then they will know it completely.
Part Two: Supplementing the Meaning (divided into two). First, regarding the appointment of a time:
if one makes an agreement with another practitioner to meet at a certain place, one must not arrive later than the appointed time.

Regarding "going out on an errand": "on an errand" means "occasionally" or "as the occasion arises. This refers to one who, having a sudden need or circumstance and wishing to go out for a short time, must first seek permission.
One should agree to wait at a specific location; even if obstructed by other circumstances, one must return to report before departing again.
"One must not remain behind" means that one should first go to the appointed place to await the teacher and must not act according to one's own whims.
I have been negligent in my intentions, which is why I have delayed so long; I hope that you, Master, will arrive first, for I am looking forward to you with great anticipation.

During the second meal, when the Dharma Master receives the offering, you should stand in attendance as he emerges from the hall. When the meal is finished, you shall again stand in attendance as he collects the offerings.

Regarding "giving birth" (to the practice): it means that once the offerings have been completed, one should follow the Tathāgata’s instruction by first setting aside a portion of the food to bestow upon the spirits and sentient beings.
The meaning is as clarified in the *Xiangru ji* (Record of Fragrant Milk). When the attendant delivers the food, it must be placed in a clean vessel.

Settle [the image] in a clean place. The recitation of mantras and visualization must both be performed with utmost sincerity. Regarding *dakṣiṇā*: this refers to the items bestowed by a donor (*dānapati*). Chengfan states:

"Wait until the master has finished his meal, then collect the master’s *dakṣiṇā*. If a *śrāmaṇera* observing the ten precepts is attending the master, one should have another person collect the *dakṣiṇā*.
The Sanskrit term is *dakṣiṇā*, which here means "offering" (*shī*); in terms of the Dharma, it is as follows:
It is said: "The gift of Dharma. Regarding material goods, it is called the "gift of wealth. Laypeople should practice the gift of wealth;

those who have left the household life should practice the gift of Dharma. *Yilan* says: "Only when both the gifts of wealth and Dharma are perfected, and both merit and wisdom are complete, does one become a Buddha.
*Chengfan* says: "When the master has finished eating, he requests that the bowl be put away and the offering accepted; this is the full extent of the disciple’s etiquette."
Yixing said: "Upon hearing that the Master has returned from abroad, you should go out to welcome him.

You must respectfully receive his robes and bowl, prepare tea and soup, as well as water for washing the feet, attending to each detail with the utmost sincerity and ensuring that no distracting thoughts arise."
Entering the Assembly, Part Four (Thirty-two Matters; Divided into Two). First, the Proper Protocol (Divided into Seven). First, regarding humility and virtue: one must not contend for a seat.
Second, one must not call out to, speak with, or laugh with others from across the seats.
Third, if there is a lapse in decorum within the assembly, one should conceal faults and proclaim virtues. Fourth, one must not boast of one's own hardships or manifest one’s own achievements.

The Vinaya states: Whenever one wishes to enter the assembly, one should be endowed with five dharmas. First, one should possess a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Second, one should humble oneself, like a dust-cloth;
that is to say, just as a cloth gathers filth upon itself to allow things to become clean, so too should one act.
Third, one should know the rules for sitting and rising; that is to say, if one sees a senior (*sthavira*), one should not sit at ease; if one sees a junior, one should not... [sit at ease].
4. One should stand up. When a small group of *śrāmaṇeras* sees those who have received full ordination (*upasaṃpanna*), they should all stand up.
5. One should not be distracted within that assembly; that is, while in the midst of the Sangha, one does not engage in worldly conversation with others.
6. If one sees something unbearable occurring within the Sangha, one should remain silent. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The noble disciples of the Buddha..."
Because one dwells in harmony, there are two kinds of dharmas: first, the speech of the noble ones; second, the silence of the noble ones.

Nevertheless, relying on the process of smelting and refinement, one must certainly provide service. Like a furnace and bellows for forging and tempering, it is appropriate to enter the assembly first.

When the utility of conforming to the dust is uniform, the merit of saving sentient beings will naturally be universal. Although a śrāmaṇera has not yet reached this stage, because of the Buddha’s regulations—
Food is distributed according to the assembly, and the Dharma is received from the assembly; therefore, this ritual protocol is established. △ Regarding "one must not contend for a seat":
it means that even sitting without courtesy is improper, let alone contending. However, in the monastic community (saṃghārāma), seating positions each have their proper order.
Śrāmaṇeras sit according to the sequence of their precepts. If there is anyone who contends, they lose the integrity of the monastic community.

This is the Dharma regulation. △ Regarding "calling out and laughing from afar": "calling out from afar" means shouting from a distance. "Speaking and laughing" refers to speaking while accompanied by laughter.
This is no different from the assemblies of Brahmins; it does not constitute the essence of the *saṃgha*.

If there is an urgent matter, one should snap one's fingers to awaken others and speak softly so they may understand. If one laughs, speaks, or calls out from afar, it is as if one does not exist to those nearby.
If a person loses their decorum and causes a stir among the assembly, the transgression is no small matter.

"Losing decorum" refers to such acts as calling out to one another from afar or laughing, as described above. "One should conceal evil and promote good" means that one ought to hide the faults of others and bring forth their virtues.
By concealing evil, one naturally increases one's own virtue; by promoting good, one inspires the assembly.

[This] enhances its brilliance. National Master Yan said: "The ancients delighted in hearing their own faults, took joy in doing good, were long-suffering in embracing the coarse, and generous in concealing others' evils.
They were humble in befriending others and diligent in aiding the multitude; they did not allow gain and loss to divide their minds."
Therefore, its radiance is vast and great, illuminating both the present and the past. Lingyuan said: "The Sages have spoken thus:

'Those in this world who are clever and profoundly observant, yet come near death, are those who love to discuss the faults of others. Those who are erudite, eloquent, and grand, yet bring peril upon themselves, are those who love to expose the evils of others.
For one who has left the household life, there is nothing more powerful than not seeking to know the affairs of others."
In all affairs: do not be empty-minded and haughty; do not use strength to oppress the weak; do not benefit yourself at the expense of others;
do not be arrogant toward the younger because you are senior; do not treat elders with contempt because you are young; and do not claim "I am right" based on a mere fragment of ability.

Do not, upon a slight understanding, immediately criticize the faults of others. Instead, apply your mind diligently toward the Buddha-dharma and strive to eliminate afflictions within the realm of sensory objects.
To lose one's human form beneath the *kāṣāya* is truly a great suffering. Therefore, one should conceal one’s own shortcomings and promote what is good.
Regarding the instruction "one must not boast of one’s toil or manifest one’s own merit": *fa* (伐) means to boast. To have accomplished something in one’s deeds is called "merit" (*gōng*).
"Lao" means to claim one's own merit for oneself, which is called "va. This refers to the inability to boast of one's own abilities to manifest one's achievements.

However, when one has merit, it is naturally promoted by the mouths of the multitude; what need is there for self-claiming? It is precisely because one does not claim their merit that their achievement becomes even more manifest.
As the ancient sage said: "He who is self-righteous is not illustrious; he who is self-boastful does not grow; he who claims his own merit has none."
This is merit.
Second, as for one's general conduct in all places: when sleeping, do not be ahead of others; when rising, do not lag behind others.
"To sleep not before others and to rise not after others" refers to practicing the Way with diligence.

However, when wakefulness and stillness mutually illuminate one another, then in every matter one acts ahead of others, and in every action one does not fall behind them. First, one naturally distances oneself from indolence;
second, one has no distracting thoughts. Thus, our Founder, the Venerable Master Jianyue, addressed the assembly:
It is said: "Diligence is the treasure for cultivating the Way. It is through this that Buddhas and Patriarchs are realized, and it is because of this that afflictions are severed.
As a son of the Śākya, how can one be indolent? The Pure Regulations state: "When the bell is about to strike at the fifth watch, rise quietly first and sit upright.
One must not fan the wind to cause others to become distracted."
3. Cherishing Merit:
When washing the face, one must not use excessive water. When brushing the teeth and spitting out the water, one must lower the head and let the water flow downward;
one must not spray or splash water onto others. One must not make loud noises, blow the nose, or vomit. One must not [perform these acts] within a temple hall or at a stupa.
