Therefore, one should first study the precepts, the discipline, and proper decorum. "Lectern" refers to the lecture hall.
This refers to the place where the Dharma assembly is held. If one arrives too early, there is concern that the mind will lack stability and the foundation of practice will not yet be firm;
like a rudder overturned by the wind, this may lead to the denial of cause and effect, thereby inviting the grave retribution of the Avīci Hell.
Chapter Eight: Training in the Scriptures (Nineteen Items; Divided into Two Parts). Part One: The Proper Protocol (Divided into Three). Part One: Learning the Sequence.
One should first study the Vinaya and subsequently study the Sūtras; one must not transgress this order. Generally, when studying any scripture, one must first...
He informs his teacher. When the recitation of the sutra is complete, he informs him again, saying he will study a different sutra;
this is called "practice" (xi) because it does not lose the maintenance [of what was learned]. To receive the Dharma with single-minded diligence is called "study" (xue).

It also means "awakening" (jue) and "emulation" (xiao); that is to say, those who awaken later must necessarily emulate what those who have already awakened have done, and only then can they clarify what is good. If one does not study, then one does not [attain this].
To know the Buddha-way: one should first study the Vinaya. The precepts and discipline (*vinaya*) are the method for taming the body and mind.
*Sūtra* is translated here as "scripture" (*jing*). A "scripture" (*jing*) means a path; it is the path traversed by the sages of the Three Vehicles.
One should first study the Vinaya, like planting seeds below to nourish the root, and only thereafter study the Sūtras.
If one irrigates its sprouts so that the roots become deep and firm and the branches and leaves flourish, then the fruit of sagehood may be expected.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "It is like a person learning archery; first they steady their feet, and only afterward do they practice the technique.
It is also like having a foundation for manual labor, or a source for drawing water. If one studies the scriptures first, it is like irrigating without seeds.
If one irrigates it, since the seed is already gone, from where can one seek the fruit? Therefore, one must proceed by stages;
knowing what comes first and what follows brings one close to the Way. △ Regarding the requirement to first inform the teacher when studying a scripture:

this refers to a śrāmaṇera whose understanding of the Buddha-dharma is not yet extensive and whose insight is not yet broad; such a person does not know the depth of the Dharma or the proper sequence of study, and thus must inform the teacher.
For those who study later in life, by rehearsing what is old they come to know the new, and thus there is daily progress and benefit. An ancient saying goes:
"If a practitioner of the Way spends two days on worldly crafts, then one day is wasted. Time passes easily, yet the work of the Way is difficult to accomplish;
one must not slacken even slightly.
2. When revering the Dharma and honoring others, one must not blow dust from atop the scriptures with the mouth. One must not conceal tea dregs or miscellaneous items on the scripture table.
When someone is reading the scriptures, one must not walk back and forth (caṅkrama) near their table. Whenever any scripture or text is damaged, it should be promptly repaired.
Supplement:
Wherever the scriptures are located, it is as if the Buddha himself were present. If there is dust upon the sutras, one should brush it away with a clean cloth.
To blow on them with the mouth involves two faults: first, the foul breath touches the scripture; second, it causes one to lose a heart of reverence. — Mañjuśrī.

Question: A sutra states that those who blow dust upon any kind of ornamental offering with their mouth will fall into the Utpala Hell, and as a secondary retribution, they will become a Wind Deity King.
Regarding the practice of concealing tea leaves and miscellaneous items on a sutra table:
this is to defile the sutras and stain the table. For any sutra table, cleanliness is paramount; one must sweep away the dust early each morning.
Ashes and dust are still to be brushed away; how much more so miscellaneous items!
The *Chinggui* (Rules of Purity) states: "To privately store tea dregs is to invite derision from onlookers.

Furthermore, one must not place worldly texts, any secular books, impure objects, nor items such as head-caps, fans, handkerchiefs, or prayer beads upon the Buddhist sutras and vinaya. When a person reads the scriptures...
One must not walk past the scriptures before the desk. That is to say, when reading the scriptures, one must contemplate with clarity and stillness.
If one walks around in front of them, it will distract the mind of another and disturb their contemplation, which constitutes a fault.
Regarding the prompt to "quickly repair damaged scriptures and texts": "scriptures and texts" refers to the sacred scriptures; these are the [teachings] of the sages and worthies.
The *dharmaparyāya* is likewise our parent; if it is damaged, it must be repaired with urgency. When one's parents are ill, how could one afford to be negligent?
As the Sūtra says: "If the covers and spines fall off, the volumes lose their order, or the paper and ink become torn and broken, and one does not repair them, one incurs sin in every case."
The Three Teachings take the pursuit of the fundamental as their goal;
since a śrāmaṇera’s primary vocation has not yet been perfected, he must not study external texts such as the *Zi* and *Shi* histories or the secular codes of governance.
His "primary vocation" refers to his own fundamental duty, just as a Confucian scholar of the world must first master the Five Classics before proceeding further.
One should study this fundamental scripture first, and then other scriptures in succession. If one does not master this fundamental scripture, all other scriptures will become obstructed and blocked.
It is the same for a śrāmaṇera: as long as the ten precepts are not yet pure and the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*) are not yet complete, one may not study other teachings.
"The Hundred Schools" refers to the various masters of the hundred schools of thought; "History" refers to the historical records of successive dynasties; and "all" refers to whatever [exists].

Every dynasty of rulers and ministers must have its own dynastic history. What is called "history" records the traces of what was lawful and what was unlawful, as well as instances of success and failure during that time.
It is compiled to warn future generations and to ensure credibility for those who come after; therefore, it is called a "credible history" (*xìnshǐ*).
As for "external books," these include the canons of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, as well as the records of Confucius and the Duke of Zhou.

Extending even to the Four Books and Five Classics, they teach how to regulate the family and govern the state, cultivate the person and nourish the nature, and assist the nation while benefiting the people;
thus they are called the "classical statutes for governing the world. Because these are the words of worldly governance, they are termed "external.

As for the "internal scriptures," they refer to the holy teachings of the Three Vehicles, which instruct one to purify the mind, eliminate delusions, and perceive one's own original nature; all are intended for transcendence.
Because it is the dharma of the world, it is called "internal. The *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "In the future, there will be bhikṣus who delight in reading external scriptures.
When preaching the Dharma, they will embellish their prose and rhetoric to please the assembly.
These people will be deluded by Māra; their eye of wisdom will be obscured and blocked. Deeply craving gain and offerings, they are like a herd of blind men, deceived by trickery. (*Fuxing*)
It is said: If, for the purpose of subduing non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), one is permitted to study non-Buddhist texts during one period among the twelve periods of the day—Section Two:
Supplementary Regulations (divided into four parts)—First, prohibiting the study of counterfeit and superficial attachments:
One must not select [texts] that merely appear to conform to the Way for the purpose of attending ritual assemblies; nor must one study forged scriptures.
Regarding the prohibition against selecting those who have already mastered the scriptures for attendance at the ritual site:

this refers to the profound sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, which require individuals to receive, uphold, study, and practice them for the sake of benefiting both oneself and others. To say now that they "may not" [be selected] is an error resulting from such selection.
"Zi" (Character): This means one must not exclusively train for the purpose of selecting candidates for others' invitations to ritual sites (*maṇḍala*).
Since the fundamental practice of a *śrāmaṇera* is not yet perfected, there is a fear that latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) may manifest; thus, one must not forget the precepts for the sake of profit.
"Must not train in the forgery of scriptures": This means using fabricated words to falsely claim they are the Buddha’s teachings, thereby deceiving the ignorant.
Furthermore, scriptures such as the *Xuèpén jīng*, the *Miàoshā fēnzhū jùkǔ jīng*, and others are all not the word of the Buddha. Thus, a sutra states:
"In future ages, there will be many evil spirits who take birth among humans;

constantly harboring malicious intent, they will frequently engage in contentious debates and each seek fame and material gain. They will falsely compose scriptures and various incantations, praising themselves..."
To disparage others so that those practicing the Way do not know where to turn, becoming blind regarding the correct eye and losing their right view— this is it.
Second, to prohibit the study of non-Buddhist texts.
One must not study books on astrology, physiognomy, medicine, military strategy, divination, astronomy, geography, or prophetic diagrams;

nor books concerning alchemy, the transformation of base metals into gold and silver, miraculous wonders, ghosts and spirits, or talismanic water. One must not study the recitation of scrolls or the composition of gāthās.
One must not study the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths, except when one possesses sufficient intellectual capacity to do so.
For those who wish to discern the depth or shallowness of internal and external teachings, they may peruse these works; however, do not harbor the thought that they are for the purpose of study.

As for books on destiny—referring to texts such as *Zi Ping*, the five planets, Yin-Yang, and the Seven Luminaries—which discuss human longevity, misfortune, or success and failure for the sake of seeking profit:
those who have left the household life ought to cultivate the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and thus have no need for them.
This is not beneficial. The ancients said: "For those who do good, a hundred blessings descend; for those who do evil, a hundred calamities descend. But from where are these calculated?

As for physiognomy books—referring to works such as those by Māyī and Liǔ Zhuāng—they examine one's physical appearance and spirit to discuss poverty, wealth, nobility, and meanness for the sake of seeking profit.
However, physiognomy follows the mind; fortune is... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

Cultivated and accomplished. Furthermore, from what source does this characteristic arise? Regarding medical texts: these refer to the various treatises on major and minor pulse diagnosis, as well as internal and external medicine.

Beginning with Shennong, who investigated the cold and warm natures of herbs and plants and distinguished the propriety of the "sovereign," "minister," "assistant," and "messenger" roles [in prescriptions], he composed medicinal formulas to treat the ailments of the people.
Later, however, many practiced this for the sake of profit; therefore, its study was not permitted. If...
Reflecting on the suffering of illness, one should not seek profit. Regarding the "exceptional circumstances" permitted by the Buddha:

as for military treatises—referring to the *Six Tactics* (*Liùtāo*) of Jiang Taigong, the *Three Strategies* (*Sānlüè*) of Huang Shigong, the thirteen chapters of Sun Wu, and so forth—all are books concerning warfare and military formations;
they are not that which a son of the Śākya (a Buddhist) should study. As for books of divination and astrology, the *Wùyuán* states: [text omitted].

Fuxi divined by means of tortoise shells; Shennong practiced divination with the *shī* stalks. The *shī* grass grows from the tomb of Fuxi and Wen Wang; its clusters must number one hundred, and each stem must be ten feet long.
Above it covers the azure clouds, and below it guards the numinous tortoise. The *Baixi Tong* states: "The *shī* of the Son of Heaven is nine feet long;
that of the feudal lords is seven feet; that of the Great Officers is five feet; and that of the scholars is three feet. It is used for divining and verifying good fortune and misfortune."

Regarding fortune and misfortune, one may know their events in advance. As the ancients said: "Fortune and misfortune have no fixed gates; they are summoned only by oneself. Where, then, is there any need for divination?
The Jin official Yan Han once remarked when Guo Pu wished to perform divination for him: "One's years are determined by Heaven, while one's position depends on man.
To cultivate oneself yet find that Heaven does not grant success is destiny (*ming*). To uphold the Way yet find that others do not recognize it is one's nature (*xing*)."

One possesses one's own destiny; there is no need for the divination of milfoil stalks or tortoise shells. Even the Confucian scholars of the world are unwilling to do this, let alone those who are disciples of the Buddha.

△ Regarding books on celestial phenomena (*tianwen*): these refer to books that observe the atmospheric signs of heaven to predict in advance the good fortune, misfortune, and transformations of time.
Because they seek profit, they are not what a disciple of the Buddha should practice. △ Regarding books on geomancy (*dili*): these refer to... [text continues]

Guo Pu’s *Zangjing* (Book of Burials), Yang Yunsong’s *Dili Daquan* (Great Compendium of Geomancy), Huang Shigong’s *Bazhai* (Eight Houses), and the *Zhou Shu* (Book of Zhou), among others, are all treatises on geomancy (*kan*) and fengshui for selecting auspicious dates;
because they seek worldly profit, they are not what a follower of the Buddha (*shizi*) should study.
△ Regarding books of diagrams and prophecies (*tuchen*): "diagrams" refers to the *Hetu* (River Diagram) from the time of Fu Xi, when a dragon-horse bore [the markings]...
It is illustrated and explained therein. A "prophecy" (*chan*) is a book that foretells the future of a state and provides verification through unerring correspondence;

its significance is no small matter, and it is not something those who have left the household life should read. △ As for the "yellow and white" of the furnace fire, this refers to the alchemical arts of the immortals regarding yellow and white [gold and silver].
The *Lianzhen jing* (Scripture on Refining the True) says: "When cinnabar is refined, upon the first reversal it becomes white silver. Second...
Upon its completion, it turned into gold. Formerly, Zhongli of the Han dynasty transmitted the elixir to Lü Dongbin.

Once the elixir was perfected, stones were transmuted into gold, a feat capable of being passed down through generations. Lü asked, "After this elixir is perfected, what will ultimately become of it? Zhong replied:
After five hundred years, the original [elixir] would return to being stone. Lü said, "If the original returns to being stone, it will ultimately harm the world;
it is not true elixir. He then abandoned the cauldron. Yet, although Dongbin abandoned the cauldron, the true elixir was accomplished.

How could the Buddhist disciples be inferior to those of the secular world? △ Regarding spirits and ghosts: those with blessings who possess spiritual power are called *shen* (spirits); those without blessings...
What is called a "mei" (魅) is a "gui" (鬼). Furthermore, "gui" means "deception," so called because they deceive people to take their food and drink.
"Strange and marvelous" refers to those who invoke spirits and capture ghosts, draw talismans and spray water to cure illnesses, or manifest events through circular halos;
they perform such arts and use deceptive speech to delude the masses. When people see these strange wonders, they all believe them; therefore, they are called "spiritual marvels."

Regarding ghost stories, talismans, water for exorcism, and the like—these are written texts. A śrāmaṇera should diligently study the Buddha-dharma; he must not emulate these practices in order to seek profit.
△ As for those who "roll out scriptures" (*xuàn juǎn*) and "strike verses" (*dǎ jì*), they belong to the non-Buddhist Way of Non-action (*wúwéi*).
It is said that there are five sections and six volumes. One person recites the verses while the multitude all join in harmony; hence it is called "striking verses. A śrāmaṇera is a Dharma King.
This person must not fall into this [category]. Regarding "the books of non-Buddhists" (tīrthika): it means that their minds wander outside of principle and their knowledge and views are divergent;
thus they are called "non-Buddhists. There are ninety-five types in total. Because their path and practice lie outside of [true] principle, their books are likewise external;
therefore, one must not study them. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "To study and learn non-Buddhist texts is like using a knife..."
It is like cutting through mud; the mud is not formed into anything, yet the blade is damaged by itself. The *Śīlasūtra* states:

"If a Bodhisattva does not read and recite the true scriptures of the Tathāgata, but instead reads and recites worldly treatises, prose, verse, commentaries, or sub-commentaries, they commit an offense—except for those whose intellectual power is sufficient.

This refers to those for whom the fundamental teachings and the Vinaya are unified, and virtue and wisdom are both manifest; whether entering the realm of Buddhas or Māras, there is nothing they cannot master."

Because it remains, it is said to be "with remainder. If there were even a hair's breadth of non-comprehension, then no further power would remain. The internal and external teachings have been explained as before.
Their depth and shallowness distinguish their relative superiority and inferiority. "Traversing" (*shelie*) is merely another name for "passing through.
However, if one wishes to know the depth and shallowness of the teachings, one should merely glance over them for a moment; one must not become attached to them. Therefore, it is said:

"Do not give rise to the thought that this is a practice to be studied. In the Vinaya, because the two venerable ones, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, were seated on high seats to defeat the non-Buddhists, they taught newly ordained bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras to study the books of the non-Buddhists.
The Buddha, knowing this, established a prohibition. Subsequently, when newly ordained bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras engaged in debate with the non-Buddhists, [the rule was reaffirmed].
None of them could answer. The non-Buddhists laughed derisively. The Buddha asked them the reason for this.
The bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras replied, "Because we were concentrating our minds on our primary practice. The Tathāgata then granted them leave.
Regarding the three precepts for worldly affairs:
one must not practice or study poetry and prose; one must not set one's heart on learning calligraphy to seek artistic excellence. It is sufficient merely to write with upright and clear characters.

Poetry is the manifestation of one’s intent through speech; prose is the expression of that speech through writing. The *Records* state that calligraphy, mathematics, divination, worldly classics, and literary odes are all mundane dharmas.
For those who have left the household life, before their footing is even steady, thirty or fifty years may already have passed in the blink of an eye.
If the Great Matter remains unclarified, it is as if one has lost one’s parents; how could there be [time for such things]?
In one's leisure time, does one study poetry and prose? Regarding "regular script" (*duānkǎi*): "regular" (*duān*) means upright; "script" (*kǎi*) refers to *kaishu* (square script).
However, these two characters for "regular script" are not easily mastered, for they relate to whether one's character is upright or deviant, and whether one’s lifespan is long or short.
This was created by Wang Cizhong of Shanggu; it is sufficient to proclaim the texts and manifest their meanings. It need not—△—be [neglected].
Furthermore, one must strive for excellence in clerical, seal, and cursive scripts. For those who have left the household life, every matter must be authentic;
even the slightest degree of superficiality or pretension becomes a cause and condition for obstructing the Path.
4. To revere the orthodox teaching, one must not hold scriptures with defiled hands; one should regard the scriptures as one would the Buddha and must not laugh or joke;
one must not leave the volumes in disorder upon the table; one must not raise one's voice to disturb others; and one must not borrow scriptures from others.
Do not look upon [the scriptures] with indifference, nor fail to treat them with reverence, lest they be damaged.
The scriptures are the pure and wondrous Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata; they must be received and upheld only when one’s three karmas are pure.
The *Sūtra on Cause and Effect* states: "If one touches a scripture with the hand while requesting it, one shall fall into the retribution of becoming an insect in a latrine. Ānanda requested...

The *Śīla-śāstra* states: "If monks, nuns, or laypeople read or recite the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Śāstras while conversing and holding the scrolls in their hands, they will, according to the reckoning of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, receive the retribution of an animal and fall among the species of deer or wild asses, where they will constantly have their backs broken, enduring unbearable suffering.
Even if it is for neutral purposes or idle chatter, grasping the Sūtras, Vinaya, or other scriptures likewise invites this aforementioned retribution."
△ Regarding the Sūtras: As with the Buddha, one should regard the Sūtras as the Buddha’s word; therefore, the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all make offerings to them.

They are rarely encountered in a thousand lifetimes and difficult to meet even in ten thousand kalpas. Even if one cannot understand their meaning upon reading them, reciting them will surely plant roots of goodness.
Thus, one must show them exceptional respect; how could one treat them with derision or laughter? (Vinaya)

It is said: "Be careful never to recite the scriptures while lying down. If you feel even the slightest fatigue or a mind of indolence arises, you must immediately reflect with urgency upon the fact that human life lasts but a breath, and rouse yourself to diligence as if your head were on fire.
How could you possibly afford to be lax? Regarding the rule against leaving the volumes in disorder upon the desk: this refers to the practice of binding the scrolls together into a fascicle.
The term "disarrayed" (*langji*) is used as a metaphor for manifestation. This refers to the food eaten by a wolf:

because its belly is small while its mouth is large, it tears open the ground everywhere until the scattered remains are uneven and unsightly, much like a sutra scroll spread out in disorder upon a table.
When ancient scholars were reading the *Shi* or *Shu* and had not yet finished, even if they were in a hurry, they would invariably wait until the scrolls were neatly bound and arranged.
Thereafter, one should rise from one's seat; for fear of causing damage, how much more so regarding the Buddha-dharma—should one not maintain solemnity?

Regarding "one must not raise one's voice and disturb the assembly": this means that whenever reading the sutras or the vinaya, one must understand the phrasing and the rules of intonation, ensuring that the Chinese and Sanskrit are clearly distinguished.

When chanting along with the assembly, the voice should be harmonious and measured; one must not rely on one's own prowess. However, when practicing or studying on one's own, [one may proceed as appropriate].
The voice must be low and soft; do not let distracting thoughts arise. Master Masu Chan said: "When raising the Buddha’s voice, it is like water flowing over a weir;
chanting sutras and walking in meditation is like geese traveling in formation. Looking ahead and behind, move your steps lightly; turning left or right, half-closing your eyes.
Placing hands together at the chest is like cradling water; standing upright with head held high is as if balancing oil. Such is the majestic deportment.
Whether in motion or stillness, it is always thus. Do not falsely act as a bhikṣu among humans.
Regarding the phrase "one must not borrow a scripture to read and fail to return it," etc., this means that the Dharma of the scriptures is the parent of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles;

one should cherish it equally and must not harbor distinctions between self and other. If there is disrespect, or if it is damaged or destroyed—[the karmic retribution for] damaging [it is as follows].
One incurs the offense of arrogance regarding the Dharma. If one borrows something with the intentional purpose of not returning it, one immediately incurs the offense of theft. As the Sūtra says:
"When borrowing or lending, one must be clear and explicit; do not violate the appointed date, lest you breach the covenant of trust."
Entering a Temple, Part Nine (Seven Items in Total; Divided into Two Sections). First, the Sequence for Entering the Gate:
When entering the temple gate, one must not walk through the center; one must walk along the left or right side. When walking along the left, the left foot must lead.
Circumambulating to the right, one begins with the right foot.

As for the term "temple" (si), in the Western Regions it is called *saṃghārāma*, which here [in China] is translated as "Garden of the Community" (*zhòngyuán*); this refers to the garden where the community of monks resides.
From the twenty-fourth year of the Jiayin cycle of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, on the eighth day of the fourth month... as [it was said].
At the time of his coming birth, this region all saw a crimson light piercing the sun, and the rivers overflowed their banks.
The King questioned his ministers, and the Grand Astrologer Suyou reported: "A sage has been born in the West; a thousand years hence, the Dharma shall flow into this land.
The King commanded that this be engraved upon stone and buried before the Tianci Temple at the Southern Suburb. Later, Yu Mu...
In the fifty-third year of King Ren-shen, on the fifteenth day of the second month, at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, a violent wind suddenly arose;
the earth quaked and the heavens grew dark. Twelve white rainbows shot straight up toward the sky. The Grand Astrologer Hu-duo said:
The sages of the West have passed away; therefore, Confucius later sighed, saying: "Why was my birth so late? Why did Nirvāṇa come so early?
Not seeing Śākyamuni, my heart is constantly filled with distress. It reached the second sovereign of the Eastern Han, Emperor Xiaoming;
in the third year of Yongping, the cyclical year being Gengshen, the Emperor dreamed of a sixteen-foot golden man.
A radiance like the sun emerged from his neck and flew into the palace courtyard.

The Emperor questioned his ministers, and the Grand Astrologer Fu Yi replied, "I have heard that there is a deity in the Western Regions called Buddha; what Your Majesty has dreamed must surely be of him.
In the seventh year, the Jiazi year, the Emperor issued an edict to the Langzhong Cai Yin, the Zhonglangjiang Qin Jing, the Bohshi Wang Zun, and others.
Eighteen men traveled westward in search of the Buddha-dharma and reached the kingdom of India.
They invited Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, who carried the scriptures upon white horses and brought with them a painted image of Śākyamuni Buddha.

In the tenth year of Yongping, the year of Dingmao, they arrived at Luoyang and temporarily resided at the Honglu Temple. This temple was originally established for the purpose of receiving envoys from the four directions and distant lands.
It was originally his residence. Later, as the number of monks gradually increased, a separate hall and temple were constructed to house them.

When the two monks moved into their new quarters, they retained the name of the monastery to commemorate its origin. Furthermore, because a white horse had carried the scriptures, it was named the Baima Temple (White Horse Temple).
The *Jiegu lü* (Brief Account of Examining Antiquity) states that in the fourth year of the Chiku era, the Tripiṭaka Master Kang from the country of Kangju...

Senghui arrived in Wu and constructed a thatched hut where he installed an image of the Buddha and practiced the Way. When the people of the country first saw the śramaṇa, they were struck with wonder and astonishment.
An official reported this to the throne, and Lord Sun Quan of Wu remarked, "This is the lingering influence of the Buddhist Way regarding the dream of Emperor Ming of Han.
Sun Quan then asked the Grand Tutor Kan Ze, "In what year of Emperor Ming of Han did Buddhism enter China?"
The Master of the State asked, "For what reason has it not reached the East?
Zai replied, "Since the Buddha-dharma first arrived during the Yongping era, calculating up to the fourth year of the Chigu period, one hundred and seventy years have passed.

In the fourteenth year of Yongping, the Daoist practitioners of the Five Peaks, including Chu Shanxin and others, requested to debate the Dharma with the Western monks. Thereupon, Shanxin died out of shame for his false pretenses."
Generally speaking, it was not permitted for those from the Middle Kingdom to leave the household life, and thus there were no people to propagate [the Dharma].

Furthermore, having fallen into turmoil, it took many years before they reached their own country. Quan said, "Confucius established rites and classic instructions to transform and educate future generations;

Laozi and Zhuangzi cultivated themselves for personal enjoyment and roamed freely among the mountains and forests—why should one serve the Buddha? Ze replied, "The teachings of Confucius and the two [Laozi and Zhuangzi] follow Heaven."
"Regarding the application of regulations: we dare not disobey Heaven; the Buddhist teachings command the various devas to practice them, and they dare not disobey the Buddha.

From this, the relative superiority [of the two] can be seen. He then issued an edict to summon [Huiyuan] to interrogate him regarding his conduct. Huiyuan replied: "The Great Master Tathāgata has been in extinction for a thousand years;
yet his sacred relics and śarīra manifest divine responses without limit. Formerly, King Aśoka honored them as..."

There were eighty-four thousand stupas; these were the remnants of his transformative influence. Sun Quan took this as an opportunity to boast of himself, saying, "If the śarīra can be obtained, you shall build a stupa for it.
If there is no proof, the state shall impose its regular punishments. Senghui requested a period of seven days, but there was no sign;
when two weeks had passed without result, Sun Quan said, "Go ahead and cook them. Senghui silently recited the Buddha’s name, thinking of the True Compassion.
"Could he truly have abandoned me? I request another seven days. When the fifth watch arrived and he was still not seen, blood burst forth from his eyes.
Suddenly, he heard a clanging sound; looking up at the jar, he saw brilliant light flashing forth. At dawn, he presented it [to the Emperor].
Quan, along with the high officials, gathered to observe it and sighed, saying, "A rare omen for this age! Thereupon, a stupa and a temple were constructed, and an assembly was convened.

He resided there. This was the beginning of temple pagodas in Jiangnan. Furthermore, the *Monastic History in Brief* (*Sengshi lüe*) states that in the first year of the Shiguang era of Emperor Taizu of the Later Wei, a monastery was established and named Chātī (Zhāotí).

During the Daye era of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty, it was renamed Dōjō (Dàochǎng), and upon reaching the Tang dynasty, it was restored as a *sì* (temple). Regarding the prohibition against traveling through the center: this refers to...
One must not proceed straight ahead through the center. The Confucians say: "When entering, do not go through the middle door;

when walking, do not step upon the threshold. If one walks along the center, it is a rash act lacking respect. Therefore, one must proceed with circumspection; one must walk along either the left or right side.
"Along" (yuan) means "toward. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "First place the heel down, then place the toes down," proceeding from the hall...
At the right side of the gate, one first steps forward with the left foot; upon completing the task, one returns by the left side of the gate, originally stepping out with the left foot.
If the great assembly gathers together, they may be divided into left and right ranks, in which case these rules do not apply.
2. One must ascend the hall according to the prescribed ritual;
one must not ascend the main hall or wander about for no reason. One must not ascend the pagoda for no reason.

When entering a hall or a pagoda, one should circumambulate to the right; one must not turn to the left. One must not spit or snot inside a hall or a pagoda. When circumambulating a pagoda, it may be done three times.
Circumambulate seven times, or even up to ten or a hundred times; one must know the full count. One must not lean a hat, staff, or other items against the walls of the hall.
Whenever one wishes to enter the hall, unless it is for burning incense, offering flowers, prostrating to the Buddha, reciting mantras, or performing ritual acts, [one must not do so otherwise].
As for this matter, all other [procedures] are unsuitable. It is like when a worldly sovereign ascends the hall to deliberate on state affairs;

the civil and military officials must wait for an imperial summons before they dare to approach. When the Han general Huo Guang assisted Emperor Zhao, whether entering or leaving the inner palace gates, he never strayed even an inch from the steps of the hall;
this was the height of his reverence and awe. How much more so, then, regarding the precious hall of the Dharma King—how could it possibly be [treated otherwise]?

"Is it not improper to wander about without purpose? The *Sīyù sì tú* (Illustrations of Monasteries in the Western Regions) states: "When entering or exiting [a shrine], one always turns one's face toward the Buddha.
When paying homage to the Triple Gem, one should contemplate that their essence is but one: that which is called the 'Buddha' is the perfection of the realization of the Dharma;
the path realized is called the 'Dharma'; and those who study the Buddha-way are called the 'Saṃgha. Thus, the essence of all ordinary beings and sages is identical."
There is no duality. However, because [the conditions] are absent, one may not enter; because they are not absent, one may ascend the stupa.
This means that the stupa is a banner and sign for humans and devas. If there are no śarīra relics or Buddha images, it is already improper to ascend, let alone when they are present.
If one enters the hall or the stupa without making offerings of flowers, banners, incense, or lamps, one incurs the offense of arrogance upon entering.
Regarding the practice of circumambulating a temple or stupa to the right, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"When paying homage to a Buddha-stupa, one should circumambulate it to the right, just as the sun, moon, and stars revolve around Mount Sumeru; one must not turn to the left.
When the Tathāgata was born, he took seven steps, proceeding from south to west. Therefore, when entering a temple or stupa, one should proceed from south to west, and then from west to east.
Furthermore, circumambulating to the right signifies the ultimate degree of deference and compliance. When one defers to and complies with all matters, then no undertaking will fail to succeed.
The *Wenju ji* states: "Circumambulating to the left is partial and biased; therefore, it is considered inauspicious, as it symbolizes evil."
Turning to the right is convenient; therefore, it is auspicious, signifying goodness. The Buddha’s hair curls to the right, whereas that of ordinary people curls to the left;
thus, one should follow the Buddha. △ One must not spit or snot inside a temple or stupa, because this clearly demonstrates the distinction between sin and merit.
The *Saṃgharakṣita Sūtra* states: "If one spits or snot on the pure ground of the Buddha or the Sangha, by this causal condition, one enters [hell]."
In the hells, one’s nose is sliced off with knives and one suffers the pain of being burned by fire without ceasing, as described in detail in the sūtras.
Regarding the phrase "circling the stupa three or seven times," the three circumambulations symbolize the purification of the three karmas and the making of offerings to the Triple Gem.
It severs the three poisons and extinguishes the three evil realms. Seven circumambulations symbolize the removal of the sevenfold offenses and the attainment of the seven factors of enlightenment.

Ten circumambulations symbolize the removal of the ten proclivities and the attainment of the ten powers of a Buddha. One hundred circumambulations symbolize the removal of the hundred afflictions and the attainment of the hundred Dharma gates;
therefore, it is said that one must know the number of revolutions. While circumambulating, one should recollect the Buddha and keep him in mind. Thus...

Not falling into the two extremes of indeterminate conceptualization, one immediately attains single-mindedness without distraction. This single-mindedness without distraction is what constitutes the true circumambulation of the stupa.
△ One must not lean a hat, staff, or other items against the walls of the hall. For a śrāmaṇera, there is fundamentally no rule for possessing a staff;
it may be carried only when traveling a great distance or when aged or ill. If one encounters the two teachers or an elder, [one should act with due respect].
The venerable seniors all set down their staffs and rain-caps upon the ground before offering their greetings.

If they carry a staff for their two teachers, when the teacher has something to inquire about, they must first embrace the staff and then respond. The *Lüshi Chunqiu* states that this was the practice of the disciples of Confucius.
To carry the staff while inquiring after one's father; to lean on the staff while inquiring after one's brothers;

and to drag the staff while inquiring after one's wife—these reflect the distinctions between the honorable and the humble. If one were to lean the staff against the wall of the hall, one would incur the offense of irreverence.
Formerly, the twenty-fifth patriarch, the Venerable Vasubandhu (Po-xie-si-duo), was destined to realize the second fruit [of the śrāvaka path] seven kalpas ago, yet because he...
He leaned his staff against the wall of the palace hall. Due to this transgression of pride, he subsequently lost two fruits of his spiritual attainment.
The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states: There was a worthy man who had the marks of a king upon his face. When a physiognomist saw this, he gave his daughter in marriage to him.

Later, when the worthy man entered a monastery, he leaned his staff against the wall of the temple. Because he gave rise to arrogance, he lost the marks of a king and fell into the great hells. One should [be wary of such things].
How heedless! Xinghu said: "One must not nail holes in walls; one must not write characters on doors or walls;
one must not recite poetry in the corridors; one must not wear wooden clogs; nor should one enter a temple or pagoda while carrying wooden clogs or boots.
[Otherwise,] one will be reborn with the retribution of having horse-hoofed feet."
Entering the Meditation Hall with the Assembly, Part Ten (Seventeen Items; Divided into Two Sections). First, the Formal Protocol (Divided into Three).
First, Mindfulness and Compassion:
One must not shake one’s robes or bedding on the mat, nor make noise or fan the air, causing those on adjacent mats to be disturbed in their thoughts. When descending from the bed, remain silent.
The verse of recollection says: From the morning dawn until evening, may all sentient beings protect themselves.
If one should lose their life beneath my feet, I pray that you be reborn immediately in the Pure Land.
Regarding the *cān-táng* (meditation hall): "Cān" refers to gathering the mind so that it does not scatter; "táng" refers to a hall where the eminent and virtuous are refined.

It need not be restricted solely to the Chan school. For instance, if one practices seated meditation with earnestness, studies the teachings (*śāstra*), or studies the Vinaya, the mind will naturally not scatter.
This depends entirely on each individual’s self-respect. If the monks are respected, the Dharma is respected; if the monks are slighted, [the Dharma is likewise slighted].
This is a slighting of the Dharma. Master Xiaoweng said: "After the morning gruel, offer a *vaṃdana*; after the midday meal, serve tea.
At the conclusion of the session, take your medicinal food; do not be noisy. Entering the hall or leaving the quarters must accord with the pure regulations (*qinggui*);

only then will you see a true master in the monastic community. △ One must not shake one's bedding on the meditation seat. Those who make noise or fan the air commit three transgressions: first, they are coarse themselves.
1. Restlessness. 2. Stirring up dust to defile others. 3. Causing others to become distracted in thought. △ Regarding "descending from the bed": previously one was on the single mat;
this refers to descending from the bed. "Silently reciting" means the turning of the mind. If one speaks loudly, first, it will not conform to the hall regulations;
second, one has not yet rinsed one's mouth. Therefore, one is instructed to recite silently. From the dawn of the morning hour of *yin* until evening, all...
Regarding sentient beings protecting themselves: although humans and other sentient beings differ in form, their nature is truly without distinction.
When a human moves, a sentient being also moves; when a human breathes, a sentient being also breathes. Thus, although I have no intention to harm them, [they may still be harmed].
Furthermore, it is essential that one first protect oneself.

If one’s body were to perish beneath [the practitioner's] feet, the phrase "May you be reborn immediately in the Pure Land" means that despite having just caused injury by mistake, one relies on the power of this verse and mantra to be reborn immediately in a place of peace and happiness.
This generally expresses the intention to cease evil and practice compassion, as explained in detail in the *Xiangru ji* (Record of the Fragrant Milk).
2. To guard against wrongdoing and exercise caution with the mouth, one must not speak loudly or raise one's voice. When lifting a curtain, move the hand lightly and ensure the hand hangs behind it.
One must not let sandals make noise when removed. One must not cough or clear the throat loudly. One must not converse head-to-head or whisper with those in adjacent seats. To lecture:
To speak of worldly affairs:

the meditation hall (*zhandang*) is a place for testing the "dragons and snakes" (discerning the worthy from the unworthy). Whenever one enters the hall, everything must conform to the established rules.
If one speaks loudly or at great length as if no one else were present, it appears like the behavior of a madman; how much more so if one person speaks loudly while the assembly remains silent?
If others join in this, the hall will become noisy and chaotic, obstructing those who are practicing their cultivation; there is no greater transgression than this.
When a śramaṇa speaks, he must be humble, respectful, and gentle to accord with the pure regulations. △ To lift the curtain with a light hand, one must keep the back of the hand down.
As for the "curtain" (lián), it means a screen used to conceal shame. The Son of Heaven has an outer screen (*wéipíng*).
The feudal lords used inner screens; the great officers used curtains (*lián*); and the scholars used hangings (*wéi*).

When lifting a curtain with both hands, one must not let the hands trail behind. This is for two reasons: first, to prevent the curtain from being dropped suddenly or pulled too tight, thereby damaging it; second, because coarse and turbid sounds would disturb the assembly.
When rolling up the curtain, the face must be turned outward, ensuring that both ends are level and straight. When letting it down...
"Hand-deliver [the sandals] to the ground. (△) "One must not allow sandals to make noise. Regarding this, *Xinghu* says: Whenever putting on shoes or sandals, first ensure the heels touch the ground;
do not allow them to make any sound. (△) "One must not make loud sounds by coughing or clearing the throat."
That which has phlegm but no sound is called *kai* (coughing); that which has phlegm but no sound is called *che* (snoring).
If one cannot restrain oneself, one should cover the mouth with the sleeve of one's robe. One must not lean heads together or whisper to neighbors in the same quarters.
Even when discussing the Buddha-dharma, it is inappropriate to lean heads together and whisper; how much more so for worldly affairs? There are three reasons for this: first, [it causes] loss...
1. One must maintain dignified deportment. 2. One must avoid situations that give rise to suspicion. 3. One must not forget right mindfulness.
Regarding these three points, whether in public or private, one must observe the regulations.

Even if there are fellow practitioners with whom one has a close personal relationship, one must not engage in lengthy conversation within the hall; instead, one should invite them to the woods or by the water.
Only then may one incline the heart toward discussion. If reading the scriptures, one must straighten the body, clarify the mind, and contemplate in silence;
no sound should be made. When the second board sounds, one should promptly enter the hall. Upon returning to one’s seat, silently recite the verse:
"Sitting upright with the body straight, I vow that all sentient beings shall sit upon the Bodhi-seat, their minds free from attachment."
Regarding those who look upon one with the affection of a fellow traveler on the Path: this is because natural affinity is most profound, and there is none that surpasses that of one's parents.
Now that you have left your kin to study the Way, you ought to take the Way itself as your kin.

As for those with whom you pour out your heart in discussion, they must be individuals of true caliber before you can devote your whole mind to weighing matters with them; if we were to discuss worldly conventions, such talk would be nothing less than a defilement to the lips.
A kiss—yet I fear it would defile the forest springs. As the ancients said: "The lofty mountains and flowing waters hold a profound meaning;
there will naturally be those who understand and smile with nodding heads. Master Chan Shi Cishou Shen said:
"If they are former companions on the path or close kin from afar, one may lead them to the woods and by the water to converse with an open heart; as for closing a deal or making a purchase..."
To sell [one's time] and attract miscellaneous people is entirely not the conduct of a *śramaṇa*. △ If one is to study the scriptures, one must clarify the mind and contemplate them in silence.
"Contemplate" (*wan*) means to visualize and reflect. When studying the scriptures within the hall, one should grasp their meaning silently; the mind must not be distracted.

If one expresses it through sound, there will be no way to contemplate the meaning of the scripture. Therefore, clarify the mind and realize it in silence. In this way, the meaning of the scripture [is grasped].
From this, one attains clear understanding; secondly, wisdom arises from this. Therefore, one must not raise one's voice.
△ Second, regarding the sounding of the board: one should promptly enter the hall. The bell and board were established by Baizhang;

he once carried them on his back while traveling through the wilderness, maintaining the rules without slackening. Thus, the monastic communities have followed this practice to this day. As for the "second board," it refers to:
When the second board sounds, one should immediately relieve oneself and enter the hall; this should not take longer than the time it takes to drink a cup of tea.
When the third board sounds, silence is established and the meditation hall doors are closed; those within do not go out, and those outside do not enter.
After a short delay, even those who are outsiders [are expected to remain]. "Sitting upright with the body straight" refers to the physical posture, the seat of Bodhi.
This is precisely the realization of one's own original awakening to the throne of the Empty King. This throne is inherently possessed by every person, yet it has not yet been awakened to;

therefore, it is said, "one should aspire. Because it is like a lotus flower that is unstained, it is called "non-attachment," meaning that the four marks are all empty—like a dream, like an illusion, like a flower in a mirror, and like the moon in water. If there is any attachment, it is no longer so.
Bodhi. Appendix II: Ritual Procedures for Entering the Hall.
One must not pass straight through the hall. Whether ascending or descending from one’s mat, one should always act with meticulous care so as not to disturb one’s neighbors.
One must not write characters on the *dan* (separate mat). Except when the assembly is reading the scriptures, one must not gather together on the *dan* to serve tea.
One must not engage in idle chatter while sitting at night. One must not sew or patch clothes or bedding on the *dan*.
One must not sleep or lie down on it. Nor should one converse with those on neighboring *dan*s to disturb the assembly.
The assembly within the hall each has their assigned duties: practicing contemplation, sitting in meditation, reciting sutras, or studying the Vinaya.
To pass straight through the hall with such levity and restlessness not only leads to one's own loss, but also disturbs the minds of others.

Even if there is a pressing matter, one should proceed along the front or back corridors. The admonition states: "To pass straight through the hall—how shameless! One must walk respectfully around the halls."
Fearing the incurrence of meager merit: regarding "single-layered mats above and single-layered mats below," these are all matters of fine conduct.

This means that the Śākyaputrīyas originally possess three thousand dignified deportments and eighty thousand rules of fine conduct. In every movement or gesture, one must first exercise caution of mind;
do not be coarse or flighty, lest you disturb the thoughts of others. One must not write texts upon a single-layered mat, for the scriptures are the Tathāgata’s...
As stated: copying [texts] on single sheets invites the fault of arrogance toward the Dharma; if one composes poems or verses upon them, the transgression is even more severe.
This is permissible only when the assembly is reading the scriptures, meaning when there are many people in the hall but few seats.
△ One must not gather on single sheets to serve tea or engage in miscellaneous talk while sitting at night. There are three faults in this: first, it causes agitation...
1. Distract the minds of others; 2. Scatter one’s own mind; 3. Violate the rule against improper times.

Even if one possesses medicinal food that may be taken at improper times, one should not sit up late at night engaging in idle chatter; how much less so when one’s own business remains unfinished—how could one afford such vain procrastination?

Regarding "one must not sew or patch robes and bedding": this refers to the communal meditation benches (*zànchuáng*), which are not places for sewing or patching. First, it would attract [criticism].
Miscellaneous Discourse on People. Second: Regarding the construction of meditation platforms (zànchuáng). △ One must not sleep or lie down, nor converse with those in adjacent quarters.
As the Sūtra says: "When eating, do not speak; when lying down, do not talk; when sitting, engage in meditative reflection; when rising, recite the scriptures."

Such is the conduct of those who claim to be true disciples of the Buddha. If they converse with their neighbors while lying down as if asleep, the assembly will harbor suspicions and their teachers will reprimand them.
One who conducts themselves in such a manner will ultimately become a useless person.
Section Eleven: On Handling [Objects] (Twelve Matters; Divided into Two Parts). Part One: The Proper Protocol (Divided into Three). First:
Regarding Reverence for the Sangha’s Property—One should cherish the property of the Sangha.
One must follow the instructions of the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) and must not act in opposition to them. Generally, regarding washing...
Vegetables: one should change the water three times.
Wherever there is a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), there must be a large assembly; where there is a large assembly, there must be communal affairs;

and where there are communal affairs, the large assembly must take part in the manual labor. △ Regarding those who should cherish the property of the Sangha, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Great Vinaya) says: "Protect..."
Regarding property belonging to the permanent Sangha: it should be protected as one would protect one's own eyes. A precept for practice states:

"If there is any loss or waste of the property of the Three Jewels belonging to the permanent Sangha, one must provide compensation. Formerly, at the White Pagoda Temple in Yangzhou, the śramaṇa Daochang was in charge of the monastic property.
He arbitrarily appropriated and used it for himself. Suddenly, several officials from the underworld entered his room during the day and dragged him away.
The official of the lower realm descended to sever his head. Seng-chang cried out in terror, begging for his life. The official spoke in a stern voice:

"If you return all the property and wealth of this entire room to the monks, I shall release you and let you live. Seng-chang prostrated himself and said, "I dare not disobey your command. He immediately struck the bell to assemble the community;

they gave away all their clothing and belongings to commission the making of images and to provide offerings. After three days, the official of the underworld arrived once more and saw that Seng-chang was [still there].

With one alms bowl and a single robe, he departed without a word. From that time on, Xuanchang exerted himself in diligent cultivation and ultimately achieved both clarity of insight and virtuous conduct.

Regarding the instruction that one must follow the commands of the administrative officers (*zhishi*) and not act in opposition: "Opposition" (*wei*) means to act contrary to or disobey; "contrariness" (*li*) refers to being stubborn and refusing to submit.
Those who hold administrative positions in the monastic community (*conglín*) are selected based on their abilities and talents. Whenever there are communal affairs, one should speak with kindness.
If one informs the assembly and they hear it, they will immediately emerge; thus, those within and without will be like water and milk.
If, however, one hears yet acts as if not hearing, thereby defying instructions and causing the assembly’s affairs to go astray, such a person is an unrighteous man.

△ Regarding the washing of vegetables, one should change the water three times. The *Weiyi* (Ritual Protocol) states: First, examine them to remove insects and ants; second, cut off the roots; third, trim [the ends].
First, the head. Third, one must not allow blue and yellow [colors] to mix. Thereafter, wash with water and change [the water].
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "The first time removes only coarse impurities; the second time, fine impurities are not yet exhausted; the third time, the vegetables become pure."
2. Regarding water for cleaning food:
whenever drawing water to wash one's hands, one must carefully examine it to see whether there are insects or not. Only after filtering it through a fine strainer (*sūkṣmajāla*) should it be used.
During the severe cold of winter, one must not filter the water too early; one must wait until the sun has risen. Regarding the lighting of the hearth: [text continues]
One must not burn rotten firewood. When preparing food, one must not allow the dirt from under the fingernails to remain.
Washing the hands before drawing water is an expression of the utmost sincerity; only by having clean hands is one fit to offer water to the Buddhas and the Sangha.
Regarding the use of water, there are two types: first, for food and drink; second, for washing.
Regarding "washing": one must examine [the water] with close attention. Whether it be river, pond, or well water, all contain living beings whose forms are extremely minute;
therefore, one must carefully observe it. One must not wash hands, faces, or perform defecation or urination within it.
Only after filtering it through a *micra* (strainer) may it be used. This is the essential practice of the sages for protecting life and practicing compassion; thus, the Vinaya states:
It is said: "If one travels five *li*, one should not go without a water bag. There are five kinds of water filters (*parisrāvaṇa*):
first, a square filter of fine silk; second, the *yīnyáng* (yin-yang) jar; third, the *jūnzhī* (kumbha) jar—these two both have their mouths covered with silk and their necks tied with fine cord.

4. Submerge it in water and wait until it is full before pulling it out. 5. The water-strainer (jala-śodhana): use a square piece of silk about two *tala* [the span of a thumb and forefinger] in size;
either tie it over the mouth of a jar or place it atop a bowl to filter the water before use. One must wait for the sun to rise.
This means that on cold days one should filter [water] early, fearing that insects might freeze to death. Regarding "one must not burn rotten firewood":
this refers to wood that is decayed and naturally harbors insects; therefore, it is prohibited. The Sūtra states: "Nor shall one burn green firewood or damp firewood.
Regarding "when preparing food, one must not have fingernail dirt": the Vinaya stipulates that one must not keep long fingernails.
If it is as long as a single grain of barley, one should immediately trim it. To prepare food while wearing filth and remaining impure results in rebirth as a ghost dwelling in a latrine.
The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states that when preparing offerings, one must first wash the hands, rinse the mouth, and purify the vessels; otherwise, all prayers and petitions will lack efficacy.
The ancients said: "If one prepares food uncleanly and feeds others, people will surely resent it, and the deities will likewise loathe it as defilement."
To leave food uneaten is equally a waste of resources. The *Piyū jīng* (Sutra of Parables) states: "There was a śramaṇa who prepared *mopoli* rice.
A bhikṣu, while distributing curd and ghee, placed them on his hand and wiped his hand against a pillar; the pillar immediately split apart. One must not fail to be cautious."
Third, regarding protecting living beings according to the teachings:

when discarding wastewater, one must not do so on the path, nor should one splash it by raising the water high with the hands. One should discard it at a height of four or five inches from the ground, doing so slowly and steadily.
Regarding the sweeping of floors: one must not sweep against the wind, nor should one pile up dust and soil near the door.
After fanning [the body], wash the undergarments; one must pick out lice before washing them. During the summer months, once the water basin has been used, it must be turned upside down;
if left facing upward, insects will breed within it.
"Dirty water" refers to the water used for washing vessels or rinsing clothes. This means one must not discard it on the path where people walk;
rather, it should be held four or five inches above the ground so as not to splash. One should dispose of it slowly so as not to soil one's robes.
Regarding the phrase "sweeping the ground and so forth," one should sweep with the wind; otherwise, the dust and debris will fly up and strike the faces of people. It is improper [to do otherwise].
This is a person of wisdom. He gathers ashes and soil and places them behind the door leaf. That person has a beginning but no end; the final outcome will later become visible. As the Sūtra says:
"When sweeping the ground, one should make it clean so that no tracks remain. If tracks appear, they must be swept away immediately.
The *Śatapañcāśatkā-pratyaya-sūtra* states: "Sweeping the ground yields five kinds of merit. First, one personally removes the defilements of the mind."
2. To remove the defilements of others' minds; 3. To eliminate arrogance; 4. To subdue the mind; 5.

To increase merit and attain rebirth in a favorable realm. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Sweeping the monastic grounds of all Jambudvīpa is not equal to sweeping a single palm-sized area of the Buddha’s ground.
Regarding the washing of undergarments and the necessity of picking out lice: this refers to avoiding the fault of harming living beings.
The small ones are called *kīṭa* (nits); the large ones are called *yūka* (lice). Regarding the rule of cleaning and not being subject to reproach:
during the summer months, after using a water basin, it must be inverted. This means that if the basin is left face-up, there will be residual water; where there is water, insects easily breed.
One must not wash one's feet or lower garments in the same basin used for washing upper robes. When drying them on a rack, they must not touch one another.
Before spraying water upon the Dharma robes, one must first rinse one’s mouth.
Appendix II:

Rituals for Repairing Faults One must not pour hot water onto the ground. Regarding all grains, flour, fruits, vegetables, and so forth, one must not discard them carelessly or leave them in disarray;
they must be treated with care and respect.
One must not pour hot water onto the ground, for this would harm living beings. Nor should one douse a fire with hot water to extinguish it.
An ancient saying goes: "To cast foul water aloft or to pour hot water on the ground—where can the minute insects find refuge?
Their bodies are as vulnerable to water and fire as if entering a seething cauldron. To inflict such severe punishment upon them pointlessly is unjustified.
My own merit does not increase, while their evil is recorded forever; therefore, it is said one should proceed "gradually.

Regarding all rice, flour, fruits, vegetables, and so forth, one must not discard them carelessly or leave them in disarray. This means that if one does not cherish things in this life, there will be nothing to enjoy in future lives;
how much more so for the property of the Sangha, which dwells eternally—how could one fail to cherish it with deep care? (Ancient Record)

It is said: "The celestial granaries and the five grains are among the twenty-eight lunar mansions; they are presided over by the constellation Wei (Hazard). Since humans take food as their heaven, the sages made agriculture their priority and valued the grain.
The Son of Heaven personally plowed the fields to encourage the farmers and offered prayers for the harvest to the Supreme Deity during the spring and summer.
Yet people remain unaware of the grace of Heaven and Earth in nourishing and sustaining them; how then could the five grains be cast aside?"
How much more so for a son of the Śākyas, who ought especially to be mindful of the grace of those who offer gifts in faith; he should treat them with even greater respect.
Section Twelve: Entering the Bath (Ten matters in total, divided into two parts). Part One: The Proper Ritual (divided into two). Part One:
What Must Be Known Regarding Purity and Impurity.
First, wash your face with warm water, proceeding from top to bottom and washing slowly; do not be coarse or impulsive.
Do not splash hot water or wash-water onto your neighbors. Do not relieve yourself in the bathhouse.

The Buddha established the rule that one should bathe once every half-month. However, due to the request of the youth Jīvaka, it was permitted during times of illness—specifically when a bhikṣu eats much food and cannot recover without bathing.
Subsequently, it was further permitted for those engaged in manual labor or traveling long distances.

Furthermore, regarding the practice of first washing the face with warm water: because the face is the most honored part of the body, whenever entering the bath, one should first take the [soap] from the bottom...
Once the robe-hanger has been lowered from the pole, wrap the lower body securely with a bath towel before removing the upper garment and hanging it back on the pole.
Next, wash yourself clean with water, and then enter the pool. Recite the verses and mantras silently while washing slowly from top to bottom;
do not neglect the proper ritual for bathing. One must not be coarse or impetuous, nor splash water or hot liquid about.
"Neighbors" (lín-rén): "Splashing" (jiàn)—the pronunciation is *jiàn* with the departing tone—means to sprinkle or scatter.

This means that when bathing, one should act with refinement and must not be coarse or impetuous, causing the hot water to splash onto neighbors and disturb their thoughts. △ "One must not relieve oneself in the bathhouse":
"Relieving oneself" (xiǎo-yí) is also called "minor evacuation" (xiǎo-háng), "minor urination" (xiǎo-jie), or "minor purification" (xiǎo-jìng). Or it is said...
One must urinate. However, it is improper to discharge waste even on clean ground, let alone within a bathhouse. For bathing is originally intended to purify the body;
if one urinates in the bathhouse, seeking purity instead results in defilement. Having defiled oneself, one further defiles the assembly;
thus, all acts such as worshipping the Buddha and reciting sutras become impure. This is a most grievous offense. — *Senghu* (Saṃgharakṣita)

The Sūtra says: "If a bhikṣu defecates or urinates on pure ground without choosing a proper place, by reason of this cause and condition, he shall enter hell and become a well in a flesh latrine, suffering incessantly as it is scorched by fire."
Second, one must avoid suspicion;

one must not converse or laugh with others. The *Rendian baojian* states: "A śrāmaṇera once entered the bathhouse and laughed and played, whereupon he was reborn in the Boiling Water Hell as retribution.
One must not wash in secluded places. Whenever one has sores or skin rashes, one should remain at the rear.

When bathing, if there are any fearsome sores, one should especially avoid them to prevent pricking people's eyes. One must not bathe for an excessive length of time at will, as this obstructs those who follow.
Speech and laughter are the very roots of dissipation. Little do they realize that while the impurities of the body have not yet been cleansed, the impurities of the mind have already arisen;
all this is due to a lack of shame and remorse, and thus such retribution is incurred. Those who bathe must each prepare themselves with propriety.
The warning for the bathhouse says: "One must not splash water upon one another, nor should one waste water excessively."

One may wash one's clothes inside [the monastery]. When entering, one must not precede the teacher. Furthermore, one must not bathe in front of the *upādhyāya* (senior monk). The Inscription on the Bathhouse by Wanfeng says:
"The mountain peaks are distant and the paths long; thus one brings firewood there. Boiling the cauldron and kindling the fire, one exerts diligent labor.
To bathe several times a month is rarely heard of in the monastic groves (*saṃghārāma*). Śrāmaṇeras play and laugh, pouring boiling water over themselves. [This is for] washing the mind."
Purify your thoughts; renew yourself day by day. How can one repay such virtue? Suddenly, one realizes that "the private parts" refers to the areas for urination and defecation.

This means that one should first wash these areas clean before entering the bath; it is unnecessary to wash them again during the bath itself, as doing so would violate the protocol of proceeding from top to bottom.
Nevertheless, even if the lower body suffers from hot rashes, itching, or scabies, [one must still observe this rule].
Furthermore, one must not bathe beforehand. Regarding those with sores or scabs, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There was a bhikṣu suffering from leprosy who sought medical treatment. The physician Jīvaka told him, 'You may bathe and you will be cured. The bhikṣu replied:"
The Buddha had not yet permitted entry into the bathhouse. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then allowed the Saṃgha to bathe after [the others] had finished washing.
Therefore, it is said that one should bathe last. Regarding "frightening sores": these include carbuncles, abscesses, and all other malignant sores;
one must avoid them oneself, or take water to wash separately so as not to prick the eyes of others, or remain at the very edge.

One should bathe last; otherwise, one will diminish merit and incur transgressions. "Not bathing at will for a long time" means that one should cherish the communal property and show consideration for the assembly.
One must not indulge one's desires or let one's mind run wild by bathing for a long duration, thereby obstructing those who follow.
Appendix II: Rituals for Donning and Removing Robes. Don and remove robes with composure and ease. Before bathing, first wash yourself clean; this must be done with meticulous care.
Do not pour the water used for washing into the bath cauldron. If the water is too cold or too hot, strike the wooden gong according to custom; do not shout loudly.
"Tranquil and self-possessed" means one must not be flighty or hasty. Regarding "first washing oneself before bathing":
this means that prior to bathing, one must first wash oneself according to the proper ritual; only then may one enter the pool. Since this method was omitted previously, it is now supplied here.
"One must not pour the water used for washing into the bath cauldron": *kǒng* (釜) refers to a large cooking pot.
Furthermore, it means that one must not pour water used for washing away filth into the bath cauldron. Regarding the striking of the wooden mallet (*bāng*) when the water is cold or hot:
this refers to adhering to the established regulations of the monastery; one must not shout loudly, as that would be like a worldly person.
In ancient times, small wooden boards or small mallets were placed inside the bathhouse; when the water was cold, they were struck twice.
"Down" refers to the two characters for "lukewarm. "Hot" means to strike three times, which signifies "do not burn.
If one wishes to add water, strike once; when the attendant hears this, they will understand the intent to increase or decrease the amount and prepare it according to the proper method.
Furthermore, the bathing implements should be kept clean and used in accordance with the rules.
One should act in accordance with the Dharma.
Chapter Thirteen: Entering the Toilet (Sixteen Matters; Divided into Two). First: The Proper Ritual (Divided into Three).
First: Knowing the Time and Proceeding.
When you wish to defecate or urinate, you should go at once; do not wait until you are pressed by internal urgency and act in haste.
Hang your *zhiduo* (straight robe) on a bamboo pole or a peg, folding it neatly and securing it with a handkerchief or a waist-belt. First, mark it so as to recognize it later;
second, lest it fall to the ground. You must change your footwear; you must not enter the latrine wearing clean shoes.
The *Jizhu-men-jingxun* states: "The rules for using the toilet are clearly detailed in the Vinaya.

This is intended to ensure that one maintains strict purity of the physical vessel, thereby facilitating close proximity to the sages and worthies. Therefore, there are specific regulations for both cleansing and washing the hands.
If these various methods are not fully observed, then all acts such as ritual recitation, burning incense, or handling scriptures will be considered impure."
Regarding "If one wishes to defecate or urinate, one should immediately go": this means that for one who possesses a body, it is necessary to rely on food and drink for nourishment.
When there is food and drink, light qi ascends and heavy, turbid matter descends;
thus, the discharge of feces and urine occurs. This is something unavoidable. Whenever one intends to go, one must prepare oneself. If such matters become urgent, [one must act immediately].
If one acts [in this manner], there will be the fault of violating proper decorum. Therefore it is said: "Do not wait until you are driven by internal urgency before acting in haste.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One should know the proper time; when wishing to go, one should go immediately. One must not cover the head while urinating or defecating, nor act with such panic and confusion as to make mistakes.
Regarding the phrase "hanging the *zhiduo* (outer robe) and other items on bamboo poles," this is because one observes that the performance of tasks requires meticulous care. Not... [text ends]
This results in some loss [of propriety]. Regarding the *zhiduo* (straight robe):

tradition holds that when predecessors saw monks who had a *pianshan* (slanted-sleeve shirt) but no skirt, or who had a skirt but no *pianshan*, they combined these two garments to create the *zhiduo*. △ One must change one's shoes and sandals.
*Jue* (屩) is pronounced "jue" and refers to straw sandals. This is verified by comparison with the *Qinggui* (Rules of Purity), which states that one ought to remove them.

One should remove clean shoes and change into straw sandals before entering the latrine. Furthermore, one must not wear footwear that has been in contact with defilements when treading upon the monastic grounds, nor enter the hall for prostrations or recitation;
the offense incurred is no small matter. As the ancients said: "To ascend the privy while bare-chested, or to roam the mountains in straw sandals."
Do not step upon the Dharma Hall. Yield respectfully to the senior monks.
Second, when the Preacher is present, maintain a mind of utmost propriety.
Third, snap your fingers to let the inner attendants know [the time]. Do not urge the inner attendants to come out. Once [they have emerged],...

When resting, one should further snap the fingers three times and silently recite: "At the time of defecating or urinating, may all sentient beings cast off greed, hatred, and delusion, and eliminate all unwholesome dharmas.
One must not lower the head to look down; one must not hold grass to draw on the ground;
one must not force the breath to make a sound; one must not converse with others through a wall; and one must not spit against a wall.
"Three snaps of the fingers" means to startle and awaken those within. However, those within should likewise make a sound so that [the visitor] knows;
if those within do not come out, one should naturally avoid them or go elsewhere.
"One must not press or urge those within" means one must not make noise or movement toward them to force those within to come out. Above is the section on "Ascending."
This refers to the latrine. Furthermore, one should snap the fingers three times because one fears injuring the spirits who consume filth within the latrine;
therefore, one must first startle them awake. The *Piyū jīng* (Sutra of Similes) says: There was once a śramaṇa who did not snap his fingers when entering to relieve himself.

His excrement splashed onto the face of a spirit in the latrine. The malevolent spirit became greatly enraged and wished to kill the śramaṇa. However, because the śramaṇa maintained the precepts, the spirit did not [harm him].
When one finds an opportunity, one should silently recite [the mantra]. Regarding the phrase "when defecating or urinating, one should wish for all sentient beings":

this means that because Bodhisattvas take the benefit of living beings as their primary concern, every single thought they raise is a vow to deliver them. As for "discarding greed, anger, and ignorance, and eliminating sinful dharmas":
it is because these three poisons defile the body and mind, acting like shackles that bind one to sinful dharmas so that one cannot attain mastery over oneself. Therefore...
It is like filth; saying "I now cast off this filth" is according to the dharma for removing sin. Being pure and stainless, I also wish that all sentient beings may likewise be pure and stainless.
△ One must not lower one's head to look downward; this means one must not look at the private parts.
△ One must not hold grass and draw on the ground; in the Western customs, reeds are used as toilet grass, hence [the prohibition against] such foolishness.
Indeed, ignorance leads to great calamity, as illustrated by the story of one who drew characters on the wall of a latrine.

If one writes upon the wooden panels or walls of a latrine, one will be rebuked by the Creators of All Things (*zuowu*). The *Bishan* (Pen-scan) states: "The Daoist Pan of Mingzhou was of exceptionally sublime Daoist arts.
One day, he drew talismans on a latrine wall. Suddenly, the Heavenly Official arrived and asked what he was summoning for. [Pan] had no answer."
Yi Yingzhi said, "Move the tree in front of the gate and plant it behind the house. When the man was about to leave, Yi Yingzhi said, "This is but a small matter;
why did you summon me with such casual intent? He then nodded his head with a flaming brush and departed. Subsequently, pus and fluid never ceased to flow from the gentleman's head.
Whenever there are those suffering from sores or abscesses, the mendicant shall apply the pus and discharge [from his own sores] to them;

there will be no lack of efficacy. △ One must not exhale forcefully or make sounds. "Forcefully" (*nu*) means to exert effort. However, although the removal of filth is a coarse practice, if one exerts oneself too much, one’s vital energy (*qi*) will be lost.
△ One must not converse with others across a wall. The Mañjuśrī Sūtra states: "Whether large or small... [and so forth].

At the time of using the toilet, one’s body and speech should be as motionless as wood or stone, and no sound should be made. This is for the sake of maintaining the purity of body and speech. An ancient saying states:
