"To converse with others while on the latrine is the mark of the most base and lowly. Furthermore, one must not spit against the wall; there are two faults in doing so:
first, when the caretaker sweeps it up, one diminishes one's own merit; second, when others see it, they become suspicious, which causes the spirits to be startled.
*Wei Leshi zhuan* states: Song Jingbo of Nanyang was walking at night when he encountered a ghost. The ghost asked, "What are ghosts most averse to?
He replied, "They simply dislike human saliva."
Regarding these three matters, one must not bow when encountering people; it is appropriate to sidestep and avoid them. One must not walk along the road with one’s robe belt tied.
Upon finishing [the task], one should wash one's hands thoroughly. Until they have been washed, one must not handle objects. When washing the hands, recite silently while using water.
When washing the hands, one should wish: "May all sentient beings obtain pure hands to receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
*Oṃ Cukāraya Svāhā* (recite three times).
To perform prostrations while wearing undergarments is contrary to proper decorum; one should turn the body aside to avoid it. This is the correct principle. [One must not...]
Regarding "tying one's waistband while walking along the path": this means that at other times, even if one has removed one's garment and tied the waistband, one should not walk along the path;
how much less so when entering the latrine with the body exposed? Although one must not linger for long in such a defiled place, one must nevertheless fasten the belt securely before departing.
If one ties it while walking along the path, the state of frantic agitation will be difficult to observe. △
"Having finished" means that the task of removing filth is completed. The reason it says "washes the hands" rather than "cleanses [the anus]" is due to an abbreviation in the text.
The *Vinaya Daily Use* states: "If one has only urinated, it is pure by simply washing the hands once with water.
If it is after defecation, one washes the hands after removing the filth, using either ash, mud, or soap."
He washed it with water. The Buddha said, "The method of washing for purification brings great benefit. All who take me as their teacher should perform this washing.
If one does not wash according to the Dharma, one should not circumambulate stupas or practice walking meditation;
it is improper to prostrate to the Buddha or recite sutras; one should neither prostrate to others nor accept the prostrations of others; one should not consume food, nor sit among the Sangha."
Bedding. One should not enter the assembly [with these]. Any dhāraṇī methods one maintains will all lack efficacy. Regarding "not holding objects until one has washed":

this means that if the hands are defiled, the objects held are likewise defiled. △ Washing the hands while silently reciting: rinsing the palms with water, one should make the vow, "May all sentient beings...
This refers to benefiting both oneself and others. Obtaining pure hands to receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma pertains to both the phenomenal and the noumenal.
This is indicated by both [the preceding and following passages]. Recite the mantra seven times. The *Qinggui* (Pure Rules) states:

According to the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the *Āṭānāṭīya Sūtra*, and other texts, if one does not recite this mantra when entering the latrine or washing the hands, even if one were to wash with the waters of ten Ganges Rivers until reaching the very limits of the vajra-ground, [the defilement would remain].
One must likewise not relieve oneself [in an impure state]. This is explained in detail in the *Xiangru ji* (Record of Fragrant Milk).
Regarding the two supplementary protocols:
when relieving oneself, one must also roll up one’s sleeves; furthermore, one must not wear a tight-fitting shirt (*bianshan*) while relieving oneself.
"Jie" (解) means "to loosen. This term originates from the *Liji* (Book of Rites), which states that the deportment of the hands should be reverent.

When a gentleman rises or sits, he always maintains reverence and does not dare to let his hands hang loosely or swing his arms. However, when it comes to the times of urination or defecation, one cannot help but temporarily loosen them.
Nevertheless, as one's sleeves cannot be washed constantly, whenever one must relieve oneself, one should first roll up the sleeves; this is appropriate.
[The text] explains [the rules for] using a bucket: one must not aim directly into the bucket to make a splashing sound, thereby causing a foul odor to permeate others.

Nor should one engage in conversation or laughter with others. As for the *biànshān* (short-sleeved robe), it was originally not ordained by the Buddha; rather, it was created in this region. Zhu Daozu said:
"During the Wei dynasty, when monks were invited into the palace for offerings, the palace ladies saw that the monks had bared their right shoulders. He did not [approve of it].

It was considered virtuous. Consequently, a *biānshān* (tunic) was made and bestowed; it was attached to the left side over the *fùjiānyī* (shoulder-covering robe), thereby covering the right shoulder.
Because of this, it was named the *biānshān*. Today, the name *fùjiānyī* has become obsolete, and those with two sleeves are generally referred to as *biānshān*.
Sleeping and Lying Down, Chapter Fourteen (Seven items in total; divided into two parts). Part One: The Proper Ritual (divided into two).
Part One: Mindfulness of the Body.
One should lie down according to the ritual, specifically on the right side; this is called the "Auspicious Sleep. One must not lie on the back, lie face down, or lie on the left side.
Lying on the right side is the legacy of the Buddha; it is called the reclining method for śramaṇas. One should lie like a lion king:
resting on the right side upon a mat, with feet stacked and mouth closed, the head resting on the right hand, and the left hand extended along the body.
Without abandoning mindfulness and wisdom, one contemplates the Triple Gem. Thus, evil dreams will not arise and the mind will not become inverted; therefore, it is called auspicious.

"Xiáng" (祥) means to sleep. To lie on one's back is the posture of a corpse; to lie face down is the posture of one who is prostrate. The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states: "Lying on one's back is the posture of an asura;
lying face down is the posture of a preta; lying on one's left side is the posture of a person of lustful desire."
Lying on the right side is the manner of reclining for one who has left the household life. However, when lying down, one must have a pillow; alternatively, one may rest the head upon the bent arm.
The head must not touch the mat. The *Huangting jing* states: "Above is the Yellow Court (*huangting*), below is Guanyuan; in front is Youguan, and behind is Miming.
If one lies on one's back or face down, then the vital energy of the Miming gate and the Dantian will not [circulate properly].
Because [the qi] is extended, there arise states of chaotic dreams and inverted perceptions. The *Lingshu Jing* says: "Heaven is not full in the northwest;
therefore, the right ear and eye are not as clear and sharp as the left ear and eye. Earth is not full in the southeast;
therefore, the left hand and foot are not as strong and healthy as the right hand and foot. Thus, one who sleeps for auspiciousness leaves the left side empty in order to fill the right.
Second, one must distinguish between the honorable and the humble;
one must not share a room or a bed with one’s teacher. Even if sharing a room is permitted, one must not share a bed.
Nor may one share a bed with a *śrāmaṇera* who performs the same duties. Furthermore, when hanging up shoes, sandals, or small garments, they must not extend above the height of a person’s head.
"Facing [the teacher]" means one must not share a room or a bed with the teacher; this is because one follows the Buddha's regulations.

Alternatively, "sharing a room" refers to cases where there is a danger to the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); if there is no such danger, it is not permitted. "Sharing duties" means performing the same tasks as a *śrāmaṇera*.
Regarding the performance of rituals: there were those who had studied under the same teacher as the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita.

He saw two śrāmaṇeras in the midst of hell, lying down and embracing one another while their bodies were scorched by fierce flames, suffering without respite. The bhikṣu asked the Buddha, "By what offense was this caused?
The Buddha said, "During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, these two śrāmaṇeras were embracing one another within a single bedding."
Because of this cause and condition, they fall into hell, where their bedding and quilts are scorched by fire as they suffer while embracing one another;

this misery continues without end to this day. As for shoes and small garments—these are items of the lower body—if they exceed the height of a person’s head or face, they diminish merit and invite transgression;
therefore, they must not be hung too high.
Appendix on Rituals for Repairs:
One must not lie down with one's inner robe removed. One must not sleep on a bed while laughing or speaking in a loud voice.
One must not carry a urinal or chamber pot past sacred images or in front of the Dharma Hall.
Those whose will is set upon the Way have little time for sleep and much time for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), or they may lie down for a brief moment when they reach the utmost exhaustion.
This is why the ancients used a round log as a pillow to alert themselves. As for the inner robe:
Regardless of one's seniority, the name is determined solely by the garment worn closest to the body. If one removes it while lying down, one will become negligent and sleep excessively;
therefore, it must not be removed. △ Laughing and speaking in loud voices is no different from the regulations for sleeping and speaking in the Zen hall previously mentioned;
the only difference lies in the private quarters. When sleeping, the sound of speech is detested by gods and ghosts. One should recite the Buddha’s name and maintain mindfulness.
Incantation. Regarding the "divine images" (shèngxiàng) that receive the protection of spirits and ghosts: these are the images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and Patriarchs.

As for the "Dharma Hall" (fátáng), it is a place where ordinary beings and sages intermingle to expound the Dharma. Regarding the "urinal" (nìqì): the *Zhou Lǐ* states that the Heavenly Palace says... [text ends]△.
The Grand Marshal (Taishi) presides over the King’s informal attire and personal articles of hygiene. Zheng Sannong stated: "Informal" refers to the chamber pot;

it is called *huzi* (tiger-child) and also named *fuhu* (crouching tiger). This indicates that such vessels for excretion and impurity—being unclean objects—must not be carried past one's teachers and elders, let alone before sacred images.
Section Fifteen: Gathering Around the Fire (Four Items; Divided into Two Parts) First:
To avoid suspicion, one must not speak with others by whispering head-to-head or ear-to-ear. Second: One must not flick ashes or grease into the fire. Third:
One must not warm or dry shoes or socks over the fire.
In the bitter cold of winter, one may sit by the fire for the sake of warding off the chill. However, if one leans head-to-head or whispers into each other's ears, one loses one’s dignified decorum;
if one engages in idle chatter, one neglects one’s primary practice. Furthermore, such behavior is the root of disputes.

Moreover, if one tosses greasy filth into the fire, or roasts shoes and socks over it, causing their foul odor to permeate the air and disturb the thoughts of others, the resulting loss of merit will not be slight. Therefore:
The Vinaya states: When warming oneself by a fire, one must not place hair, nails, snot, saliva, skin, blood, cakes, fruit, or poison into the flames;
to do so incurs an offense in every case. The *Chinggui* (Pure Regulations) states:
One must not warm shoes or sandals over the fire, nor stir the embers so as to scatter ashes and dust into others' eyes.

Second, once you have finished [using the fire], you must not remain by the fire for too long, lest you hinder those who come after you. When you are somewhat warmed, it is best to return to your place.
Living together in the sixfold harmony, one shares equally in both cold and warmth. To remain by the fire for too long is to act not for the sake of the community; therefore, you should know this.
This is appropriate. The *Zhenguī* (Admonitions) states: "When shaving the hair and gathering around a brazier, the proper etiquette requires humility and yielding.

According to the Buddha’s words in the Vinaya, there are five faults in facing a fire: first, it causes one to lose their healthy complexion; second, it causes one to lose physical vigor; third, it causes one's vision to grow dim;
fourth, it causes many people to gather in a noisy crowd; and fifth, it leads to much talk of worldly matters. Thus, it brings harm rather than benefit.
Section Sixteen: On Conduct Within the Quarters (Six Matters in Total; Divided into Two Parts). Part One: Respectful Interactions and Mutual Inquiries; Knowing Seniority.
When intending to enter with a lamp or torch, one must first announce to those inside the quarters, saying, "I am entering with fire.

When intending to extinguish the lamp or torch, one must first ask the fellow residents, "Will you need more light? [If not,] one shall extinguish the lamp or torch. Part Two: Extinguishing the Lamp or Torch. [The procedure for extinguishing the lamp or torch is as follows:]... [not to be extinguished].
One may blow [on the ashes] with the mouth. When reciting mantras, one must not speak loudly.

"Mutually" means that they take turns. Regarding "inquiring," it refers to speaking words of inquiry; specifically, one should first inquire after [the other's] year of birth and their years since ordination (*kṣetra*).
If one is senior to oneself, one should inquire whether their daily life is peaceful and secure; if one is junior to oneself, one should inquire whether their studies are progressing daily.
Therefore it is said: "One must know who is senior and who is junior. Xinghuo says: "If there are words concerning gain or loss, one must immediately seek the other's joy;
one must not allow the matter to remain overnight so as to incur the burden of transgression. One should act thus toward one another."
Praise them; do not speak behind their backs with disparagement or engage in mutual mockery.

[The reason for] holding up a lamp as a signal is to avoid causing others to lose their decorum through haste. [The reason for] asking if the lamp is extinguished beforehand is to take advantage of one’s fellow resident;
one must not act according to one’s own convenience. Regarding the prohibition against blowing out the lamp with the mouth, there are two meanings. First, [it is to protect] the lamp...
There are minute insects that fly and gather upon the flame, taking fire as their object; they are invisible to the human naked eye.
If one blows upon them with the mouth, they fall into the flames and die because they have lost their compassionate mind. Second, the lamp is presided over by the Fire Deity.
In the birth of a person, there is none who does not rely on it to dispel darkness and bring forth light, thereby maturing and sustaining life.
If one blows on it with the mouth, there will be foul odors due to a lack of reverence; nor should one fan it out with the hand to extinguish it.
One should instead remove the remaining wick with a lamp-stick and gently submerge it in a water vessel. One must carefully inspect the candles and lamps so as not to let them go out.
When reciting, one must not raise the voice; the meaning is as previously explained in full.
Second, regarding mindfulness:
if there is a sick person, one should care for them with compassion from beginning to end. If someone is sleeping, one must not strike objects to make noise, nor speak or laugh loudly.
One must not enter another’s room or courtyard without a valid reason.
"Sickness" refers to the disharmony of the four great elements, where the breath is labored and constricted, and the body becomes the root of suffering; who can escape this?
For the fivefold assembly of those who have left the home life, there is no one else upon whom they can rely. Therefore, the Tathāgata repeatedly instructed them, saying:
"If you wish to make offerings to me, you should make offerings to the sick. He further told the bhikṣus: "Attending to the sick must be complete in five aspects."
Virtue: First, knowing what food a patient may or may not eat; second, not loathing or despising the patient’s excrement, urine, mucus, or saliva;
third, possessing a heart of compassion and acting not for the sake of fame or profit; fourth, being able to manage medicines until the patient recovers or passes away;
fifth, being able to preach the Dharma to the sick person to inspire joy in them. Therefore, one who possesses a compassionate heart is able [to fulfill these duties].
This refers to tending to the sick. "From beginning to end" means the long-term resolve for the Way. As the Buddha said in a verse in the *Sūtra on the Good Birth*:
"A person should care for the ill and inquire after those in peril; good and evil have their retributions, just as planting seeds yields fruit."
The World-Honored One is the father; the sutras and the Dharma are the mother; fellow practitioners are the brothers.
It is through these that one attains deliverance. When someone is sleeping, one must not strike objects to make noise, nor speak or laugh loudly.
To strike objects and make noise, or to speak and laugh loudly, is to disturb the stillness of others and to lose one’s own subtle refinement.
Practice. An ancient said: "When others are sleeping, one should maintain love and respect. In all movements, the mind must remain tranquil.

One must not laugh or speak loudly, strike objects to make noise, or cause others to lose sleep; such actions provoke the affliction of anger and pile up obstacles of ignorance, driving the true nature far away.
One must not enter another’s room or courtyard without cause. This means there is no fault in doing so [when there is a valid reason].

One must not enter [a room] for the purpose of seeking instruction, inquiring after one's teachers, examining the causes and conditions of an illness, or attending to matters concerning the permanent residence (sangha property).
As the ancients said: "To enter another's quarters without cause is never for the sake of conversing in plain speech; it is surely for the sake of drinking tea."
The foolish draw near to them; the wise keep their distance. Those who study the Buddha-way will certainly not do so.
Chapter Seventeen: Arriving at a Nunnery (Ten items in total; divided into two parts). Part One: Proper Protocol (divided into two).
Part One: Avoiding Suspicion.
One may sit only on a designated seat; one must not sit where there is no designated seat. One must not engage in talk that is untimely.
Furthermore, upon returning, one must not speak of another's virtues or faults.
Regarding the term "ni" (bhikṣuṇī): the *Sudarsana* states that it means "woman. One uses "ni" rather than "woman" in order to distinguish her from worldly women;

furthermore, it is intended to inspire faith, reverence, and respect among the people of the world. If one were to use the same term as for worldly women, namely "woman," she would be treated with contempt by others and unable to inspire faith or reverence.
The *Huizheng ji* states: "Fourteen years after the Tathāgata attained enlightenment..."
Six years later, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with five hundred women of the Śākya clan, requested ordination and entry into the homeless life.

Because this would cause the True Dharma to decline for five hundred years, the Buddha did not grant her request. Mahāprajāpatī and the others walked until their feet were cracked and their bodies were covered in dust;
weeping, they would not depart. Ānanda pleaded on their behalf three times, and the Tathāgata, out of compassion, acted for their sake.

He established the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*). He declared: "If you can practice these, you shall be ordained and enter the homeless life. Ānanda, following these instructions, proclaimed them;
Mahāprajāpatī and the others replied three times that they could uphold them, and thus their ordination was permitted. The Vinaya states:

"Because the nuns were able to practice the Eight Rules of Respect, the True Dharma of the Tathāgata was restored for another thousand years. This was the beginning of the bhikṣuṇīs. As for the nunnery (*bhikṣuṇī-ārāma*), it was likewise...

This was during the time when Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty burned scriptures; as a response to the Buddha-dharma, palace women resolved to leave the household life, marking the beginning of the establishment of three monasteries for the ordination of nuns.
Regarding the phrase "those who sit on separate seats": "separate" (yi) means specially provided. This refers to the fact that these are not the regular seats where nuns sit.
As for the rule that those without a separate seat may not sit [in the assembly], it is because of the distinction maintained between men and women.
△ "One must not engage in untimely discourse" means that if it is not an appropriate time for preaching the Dharma, one should not speak.
However, the speech used in preaching the Dharma cannot be non-verbal. When the sun has passed the meridian, one must not remain for long.
△ Furthermore, "one must not discuss its merits or defects" means that one must not deliberate upon its right or wrong, or its excellence or inferiority.
It is improper to [discuss] evil, as well as the physical characteristics such as height and stature.
Second, to remove doubts, one must not engage in the coming and going of letters or notes, nor in borrowing, cutting, or washing [clothing]. One must not perform purification with one's own hands.
"Regarding 'hair' (matters concerning hair): one must not sit together in a secluded place;

nor engage in the exchange of letters (*śāstra*) and the like. This means that "letters" (*śu*) are used to convey one's intentions, while "notes" (*shū*) are used to express one's feelings to another.

"Borrowing" (*ka*) means to take on loan. "Cutting and patching" (*sai-katsu*) refers to sewing and mending. "Washing" (*sen-nan*) refers to laundering clothes. As for "and the like" (*tō*): it refers to these and similar activities.
These remaining words are all spoken out of fear that [the practice] might become gradually corrupted and invite public ridicule and slander.

Although one’s observance of the precepts may be as pure as ice and both mind and environment may be tranquil, it is better to strictly prohibit such things for the sake of excellence. △ One must not use one's own hands to shave the hair.

This means that one must distance oneself from worldly dust and transcend the mundane; one’s character and standards must be lofty. Within the supramundane Dharma, the status of the *saṃgha* must be held in high esteem.
If one were to shave the heads of nuns with one's own hands, the nuns would sit while the monks stand, thereby ruining the Dharma-gate and ultimately becoming mere worldly men.

Chengfan says: Furthermore, one must not teach the manner of shaving while holding hands, nor enter the kitchen to teach the preparation of food and drink unless specifically commissioned by the teacher.
Even when passing by the gate of a nunnery, one must not enter arbitrarily.

Regarding the prohibition against sitting together in a secluded place, there are two reasons: first, it gradually gives rise to defiled thoughts; second, it causes others to harbor suspicions and slander.
Appendix II: Rituals for Replenishment 1.
One must not enter alone; two persons are required and may not proceed singly. 2. One must not exchange gifts with one another. 3.

One must not entrust matters to nuns, nor enter the homes of the wealthy and noble to solicit for alms, nor request that they recite sutras or perform repentance rituals on one's behalf. 4. One must not associate with nuns.
When monks prostrate to their parents, sisters, or fellow practitioners (dharma-friends), they must not enter alone;
this is to avoid giving rise to the suspicions of others. They must not exchange gifts with one another.
This means that because one must sever worldly attachments and abide in equanimity, one must not entrust nuns with matters such as entering the homes of the wealthy and noble to solicit for alms.
This implies that although the flourishing of the monastic community relies upon the generosity of donors, all comings and goings must be conducted with due respect;
one must not engage in intrusive solicitation or scheming that causes donors to withdraw their support. If there are those whose virtue is lofty and eminent, and whose conduct...
As for the reality of karma, it arrives spontaneously without being contrived. For example, if one solicits alms by associating with powerful or wealthy families, one will be seen through by others.
If one seeks to perform recitations and repentances, one loses one's own integrity and loftiness.
One considers this a source of honor, while others look down upon it. If this can be endured, what cannot be endured?

Yet the wise feel shame for such things, and those who have attained realization do not necessarily believe in them. △ One must not perform the ritual of "kneeling to parents" (*jièbài fùmǔ*) with a nun.

Regarding the term "sister-fellow practitioners" (*dàoyǒu*), there are two meanings. First, it would give rise to worldly suspicion; second, it places undue weight on the karmic fruits of birth and death.
This is most certainly not the conduct of one who has left the household life. As the ancients said: "When parents are not kin, who else could be more kin?
To obscure the true mind and bow to a woman—how can such a person wield the 'hair-pulling sword' across the universe? (From the *Zhengfeng*).
Sweeping away all [worldly ties], he beholds his celestial kin. Hanshan said: "Leaving one's kin to become a renunciant, yet upon renouncing the world, one instead forms ritual bows of fealty.
Though there may be affinities in the secular world, within the Sangha there is none but the rogue. This single robe of the Tathāgata has, in the end, been sold by him."
Producing this ruinous child, even the Buddha can do nothing about it.
Chapter Eighteen on Visiting Lay Homes (The Twenty-First Section, divided into two parts). Part One: The Proper Ritual (divided into four sections). Section One:
Observing Capacities and Adapting the Teaching.

If there is a separate seat, one should sit upon it; it is not appropriate to sit in a mixed manner. When asked about the sutras, one should know the proper time; be careful never to deliver discourse at an improper time.
"Separate seat" refers to the seat of the *upādhyāya* (preceptor). "It is not appropriate to sit in a mixed manner" means that one must not sit together with laypeople.

This refers to sitting in a mixed manner. One should sit on a separate seat; one must not squat, sit with legs spread like a winnowing basket, sit with legs crossed at the shins, sit swaying the body, sit swaying the feet, or repeatedly stand up and sit down.
Regarding "when people ask about the sutras, one should know the proper time": this means one should be mindful of the appropriate occasion.
That is to say, one should observe the faculties and capacities of the person before them to determine what Dharma they are fit to hear, whether much or little;
one must not speak beyond their capacity. Be careful never to give teachings at an improper time.

If a layperson does not have faith in the Triple Gem, does not bow at one’s feet, takes no pleasure in seeing the Sangha, and has no desire to cultivate merit, they are not the right person for such instruction; do not preach recklessly to them. One should...

This concerns the gravity of the Dharma. The *Yize jing* (Sūtra on Ritual Precepts) states: "If one preaches the Dharma inappropriately to the recipient, others will not hold it in high regard upon hearing it;
at the end of life, such a person will undergo great suffering. The *Dalü* (Mahāvinaya) states: "There are five kinds of people who inquire about the Dharma to whom one should not preach:

first, those who ask as a test; second, those who ask without doubt; third, those who do not ask for the sake of repenting their transgressions; fourth, those who do not intend to accept the words [spoken]."
5. Regarding questions posed with the intent to challenge or find fault, one must not provide an answer.

However, if the person before you truly possesses a kind heart and does not possess the aforementioned five [faults], and their intention is to give rise to goodness and extinguish evil, then one may employ skillful means according to the occasion and speak with a kind heart.
Yet, if one’s own understanding is not yet clear, or if one has doubts regarding the Dharma, then one must not explain it for them, lest it cause harm to that person.
There is the fault of erroneous transmission; both parties incur offense. A Great Sūtra states:

"If one receives, upholds, reads, recites, transcribes, or proclaims [the teachings], yet does so at an improper time or in an unsuitable land, or speaks without being requested, with a disrespectful mind, disparaging others while praising oneself, or teaches haphazardly—this will instead extinguish the Buddha-dharma and cause immeasurable people to die and fall into hell. This refers to the assembly.
This gives rise to evil associates. However, for one who possesses faith, even the teaching of worldly dharmas is itself the Buddha-dharma;
for one who lacks faith, even the teaching of the Buddha-dharma becomes a worldly dharma.
2. Be cautious in demeanor and maintain strict discipline;
do not laugh excessively. 3. When the host provides food, even if it is not a formal dharma assembly, do not neglect the proper ritual procedures.
4. Do not commit the offense of traveling at night. 5. One must not sit or converse with a woman in an empty room or in a secluded place.
One must not engage in the exchange of letters or similar correspondence, as previously stated.
As for laughing: this always arises from a distracted mind and negligence. When a renunciant goes to the residence of a donor (*dānapati*), they must protect the dignity of the Sangha.
Even when discussing the Buddha-dharma to the point of great joy, one must not allow laughter to become audible. It is not permitted.
Laugh much, but do not laugh with delusion, laugh wildly, or laugh without cause; nor should you feign joy through artificial means.
You should cherish yourself and avoid being ridiculed by others. When the Tathāgata smiles with a joyful countenance, there must be a specific cause and condition for it.
As for the phrase "the host provides food and so forth," it refers to the sincere offering made by a donor.
Regardless of whether they are great or small, all are fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). If one fails to observe the proper ritual procedures, one will damage the offerings of faith made by others.
Wherever a practitioner of the Way arrives, that place becomes a Dharma assembly; wherever the host possesses faith, that place becomes a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Since the offering is made with faith, the recipient ought to receive it with sincerity. Xinghu said: "If one enters a lay household, one must maintain a dignified demeanor in both sitting and rising."

In one's deportment, speech should also be characterized by kindness and compassion; it must not be coarse or violent. One should not discuss worldly affairs, but should instead speak of the Dharma to increase their wholesome resolve.
One should restrain the six sense faculties and not allow them to become lax. △ Regarding those who do not violate the rules concerning nighttime conduct:
when going out, it is not appropriate to be too early; when returning, it is not appropriate to arrive too late at night. One should act when the sun rises and return before sunset.

If one ceases [such activity], then there will be no affliction. Yet, even when practitioners of the Way walk with great rectitude and luminosity under the clear blue sky and bright sun, they still encounter scrutiny from others; how much more so when walking at night?

Regarding the passage "One must not [sit] in an empty room, nor in a secluded place," etc., it means that if the location or the person is inappropriate, one should not speak, let alone sit. As for sitting:
Regarding transgressions such as those concerning nuns (ni): one must not engage in the exchange of letters or documents, and so forth, as previously described.
This means that the principles regarding entering a nunnery are no different from those previously explained.
Third, generating faith through the observance of ritual decorum.

If you go to visit your relatives in the secular world, you should first enter the central hall to pay homage to the Buddha, or to the sacred images in the family shrine, greeting them with dignified composure.
Next, you should offer greetings to each of your parents and kinsmen one by one.

You must not speak to your parents of the strictness of the monastic discipline, the hardships of leaving the household life, or of its solitude, austerity, toil, and subjugation. Instead, you should explain the Buddha-dharma for their benefit, causing them—
Giving rise to faith increases merit.
Regarding those who visit their relatives in the secular world, the Buddha said: "In this world, no debt of gratitude is heavier than that owed to one's parents.

Even if a person were to carry their father on the left shoulder and their mother on the right shoulder, and even if they were to carry them upon their shoulders until the end of a hundred [eons], while discharging excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva [upon them]..."
Even after a lifetime, one still cannot repay the kindness of a single moment. You all ought to be filial and respectful toward your parents; therefore, this ritual exists.
As for the reason that those in lay attire who possess faith enter the central hall first to pay homage to the Buddha:

it is because there are many images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas enshrined in the central hall. Question: Since they are visiting their relatives, what is the significance of paying homage to the Buddha first?
Answer: Having bid farewell to one’s kin and severed worldly attachments to leave the household life, one’s parents are the primary donors (*dānapati*) and one’s relatives are the supporting patrons.
Since one relies upon the Buddha-Dharma to benefit these very relatives, one pays them homage first. Regarding the sacred images in the family shrine:
when greeting these images of the ancestral hearth and deities, one should simply join the palms and bow the head; however, for parents and others, one should offer a more formal salutation.
This is a question regarding their well-being. △ Regarding the instruction that one must not speak to one’s parents of matters such as the strictness of the Master’s laws:

this refers to the intent of visiting one’s kin. One should comfort one’s parents with words concerning the advancement of the Way, exhorting and guiding them so that they may find joy in the Way and forget their anxieties.
If one were to speak of desolation, suffering, or grievances, it would cause one’s parents... [to feel distress].

One gives rise to a mind of indulgence and fails to conceive thoughts of reverence and esteem toward the Triple Gem; consequently, one sinks long into the ocean of suffering, which is not a way to delight one's parents.
If, however, one speaks of the Buddha-dharma, it will cause them to give rise to faith and deep respect, increase their merit and wisdom, and transcend saṃsāra.
This is how one delivers one’s parents from the bitter ocean of birth and death. Therefore, one pays homage.
The Record states: "To be able to lead one's parents to the Way is the ultimate expression of filial piety;
therefore, it is said that one should explain the Buddha-dharma for them, so as to inspire faith and increase their merit."
One should maintain the fourfold mindfulness without deviation and must not sit or stand for long periods with kinsmen or small children, nor engage in idle chatter or laughter with them.

Furthermore, one must not inquire into the affairs, right or wrong, good or bad, within the family. If one stays overnight when it is late, one should occupy a single mat alone; one should sit much and sleep little.
Lying down, one should mindfully recite the Buddha’s name. Once the business is concluded, one must return immediately and not linger.

Regarding the phrase "relatives, small children, and so forth," this refers to visiting laypeople specifically to visit one's kin. According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, whether they be elders, juniors, or close relatives, all such associates are considered *dānapati* (donors);
one should treat them with equal respect. However, one should not sit or stand with them for a long time, nor engage in miscellaneous conversation.
To engage in jesting and laughter is not the path of the renunciant. To inquire about the clans' merits and demerits, or their likes and dislikes, is not a virtuous intention.

As the ancients said: "The worldly dust and the net of craving have no end. Having already left home to renounce the world, one does not wish to see them again; how much less should one inquire after such matters?
△ Sitting alone upon a single mat is for the purpose of guarding against obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); by sitting much and sleeping little, one causes [wholesome states] to arise.

Out of faith and reverence, one should mindfully recollect the Buddha with single-mindedness. Because one must remain free from a mind of deluded conceptualization, one should return immediately upon completing one's business and not linger.
As for śrāmaṇeras, since their power of precepts is not yet deep and their power of the Path is not yet firm, they should not stay overnight at the houses of laypeople.
Because one cannot take leave with even a single word when visiting one's parents, it is necessary to stay overnight.
Nevertheless, one must not share a bed, covers, or mats with servants or maidservants while staying there.
II. The Ritual for Restoration (divided into two parts). First, the expulsion of the heterodox and the manifestation of the orthodox, with appended rules:
One must not look to the left or right with a sidelong glance. One must not engage in idle chatter. If one speaks with a woman, one must not speak in a low voice or in secret;
one must not speak at length. One must not feign dignified deportment or falsely assume the appearance of a practitioner of meditation (*dhyāna*).

In seeking their respect, one must not deceive by falsely claiming to understand the Buddha-dharma, nor answer others' questions in a confused manner, nor sell one's own erudition to seek their respect.
Regarding "evil glances," this refers to a mind that is not upright. As the ancients said: "If you wish to know a person, observe the pupils of their eyes. Generally speaking, the pupil...
The disciple is not upright; his mind is not rectified. △ Idle talk: to plagiarize the common parlance of the world is like tangled silk entangled in thorns—utterly devoid of coherence.
It is like the hooting of an owl in a desolate mound, filled with many strange and eerie sounds;
there is no one who does not grow weary of hearing it. Because it violates the orthodox teaching, it is not permitted. Do not speak in a low voice.
"Esoteric speech" means that there is no private [hidden] intent. "Not speaking much" means that the words uttered are in accord with the truth.
One must not falsely manifest dignified deportment or feign the marks of meditation. This refers to the fact that the dignified deportment of a śramaṇa inherently possesses the marks of meditation.
Yet they falsely manifest artificial adornments, seeking fame and respect; therefore, this is not permitted. Guishan said: "When one is habituated to the ordinary state, it is natural;
what need is there to affect a pose or put on airs? Hanshan said: "Dignified deportment values its own fundamental nature;

false manifestation is not reality. The mark of Chan is fundamentally markless; how could that which is markless be adorned? Even if one were to succeed in adorning it, it would be difficult [to maintain]."
Fleeing from reality while claiming to possess discernment is like a monkey learning to sit in meditation; outwardly it appears correct, but inwardly the mind is utterly distracted.
As subtle winds of sensory objects arise, they playfully steal away the fruit of realization. Behold those noble persons: their clarity and concentration are profound and silent for long.

It is as if they were in a red furnace, yet true gold does not change its color. △ One must not deceive others by speaking of the Buddha-dharma; this is because, through lack of understanding, one has lost it.
To answer with a distracted mind is to speak without logical coherence; because one desires respect, one peddles one's own extensive learning.

Since there is no underlying principle, answering others' questions with such confusion not only causes others to treat one with contempt, but one also fears that the karmic retribution will be difficult to repay.
2. One must distance oneself from evil conduct:
one may not accept gift boxes; one may not emulate the social interactions of laypeople;
one may not manage household affairs; one may not sit together at banquets; one may not prostrate before laypeople to treat them as parents or sisters. One must not...
Regarding the faults within the Sangha:
one must not present gifts in boxes. To emulate the coming and going of laypeople—meaning the practice of sending gifts and receiving returns—is something done by secular households;
it is a worldly entanglement and is not the conduct of a son of the Śākya. Nevertheless, those living at home should make offerings to the field of merit.
Yet those who have left the household life, on the contrary, go so far as to offer service to laypeople.
How can such perversity be as extreme as this? Moreover, they feel joy when others give to them, yet harbor resentment when others do not; thus they give rise to slander, which is therefore improper.

As for the retribution for the karma of such offenses, the scriptures explain it in detail. Regarding the prohibition against managing household affairs: this refers to even those who are one's closest kin by nature, yet one must endure [the consequences].
Cut through your attachments with the heart. For the sake of seeking the Way, you must eliminate all worldly entanglements and study with fierce diligence;

only then will there be ground upon which to repay your debt of gratitude. If, though you have left the household life, you remain no different from the laity—going today to the home of such-and-such a lord to discuss affairs, and tomorrow to the home of such-and-such a gentleman to seek patronage—then your own fundamental duty is utterly neglected.
Do not take it up. One day, when old age and illness entwine you and you lie bedridden, neither your lord nor your noble sir can relieve you of it.
△ Do not sit idly at banquets: the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* prescribes the abstention from alcohol.
Furthermore, this is not permitted; sitting together in a mixed manner is especially inappropriate. This is because within wine shops, there are many who are wild and reckless.
Even if one does not drink with them, it is possible that one might be slighted by such frivolous people, thereby bringing disgrace upon the Dharma-gate; therefore, it is not allowed.
△ One must not prostrate to laypeople (baiyi) by treating them as one's parents or sisters. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Fahua Wenju*) states: "Abandoning what..."

To abandon one's parents, cast off affection and love, dwell in an araṇya, and practice samādhi, yet further bind oneself with those of a different surname to act as brothers, parents, and so forth—this is the height of perversion.
All this arises because the initial thought of leaving home was not true, and one failed to reflect upon oneself.
△ Regarding "one must not speak of the faults within the Sangha": this means that when conversing with laypeople, one should employ words of sincerity and truth.
Regarding that faith: if one speaks of the faults within the Saṃgha, it is as if using a sharp blade to sever the root of one's faith.
Yet, since people are not sages or philosophers, who could be without fault? Kāśyapa rose up in dance, while even Yao and Shun were plagued by their own shortcomings.

Lacking the eye of wisdom oneself, how can one examine the errors of others? The virtue of the Saṃgha is like the ocean, and even the Buddha personally praised it; if one gives rise to slander, [one harms oneself].
It invites retribution of suffering. The Vinaya states: "There are five faults in going to the homes of laypeople: first, frequently seeing women; second, gradually drawing near to them;

third, becoming increasingly intimate with them; fourth, gradually giving rise to lustful thoughts; and fifth, frequently committing grave offenses. The *Mingxiang ji* (Records of Miraculous Signs) states:
"The Song dynasty monk Senggui was invited by Zhang Yu of Jingzhao to receive offerings at his home. Suddenly, [Zhang] became free of illness..."
He died suddenly and revived only after two days, saying: "Five men bound me and took me to a city. An official sat with a pen, examining a register.
Another man in a crimson robe and black cap came and said, 'There is no person by this name on the register.
The official said, 'Executioner, why have you brought a person here in error? He then whipped him. Shortly thereafter, a messenger arrived, claiming to be from Heaven."
The Emperor summoned him. The practitioner arrived immediately. The Emperor said, "You are a śramaṇa; why do you not apply yourself diligently to your practice?
Why have you been seized crosswise by a minor spirit? Since your life has not yet ended, you shall now return to life. You ought to be diligent and energetic; do not frequent the homes of laypeople.
Spirits who kill people often cause wrongful and excessive harm, as was the case with those like you. Having finished speaking, he then sent him away.
Sending an Attendant to Return; Returning to Master Yu’s House;
Begging for Food, Part Nineteen (Ten Items in Total, Divided into Two). First: Proper Etiquette (Divided into Two).
First: Entering and Exiting with Awareness of Prohibitions.
One should always be accompanied by elders; if there is no one to accompany one, one must know where it is appropriate to go.
When arriving at a person’s door, one should carefully examine one’s conduct and must not lose one’s dignified demeanor. If there are no men in the household, one must not enter the gate.
"Begging for food" means that while communal meals are finite, begging is inexhaustible.

Disciples of the Buddha receive this inexhaustible food in order to cultivate the Dharma of the inexhaustible. Furthermore, there are four meanings: first, to bring benefit and merit to all living beings.
2. To subdue pride; 3. To realize that the body is subject to suffering; 4. To eliminate attachment—for these reasons, the Buddha established this rule.
△ "One should travel with an elderly person" refers to one who maintains the precepts and is trustworthy. One should travel with such a person.
Thus, no faults will arise. Regarding the places where one may go, the *Āgama* (Scriptural Teachings) states that there are five types of households to which one must not go for alms:
First, the household of professional singers (*kīrtaka*). This refers to those who sing songs and melodies solely for the sake of entertainment;

because they can disturb meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one should not go there. Second, the household of prostitutes (*veśyā*). This refers to those whose conduct is impure and whose reputation is improper; they are a fundamental obstacle to the Path.

Therefore, there are three [prohibitions]: 3. Visiting households that serve alcohol; this means that alcohol is a causal condition for the arising of transgressions and is capable of destroying wholesome dharmas.
4. Royal palaces; this refers to the inner courtyards of strict prohibition, which are not places where one may intrude. 5. Butchers' shops;
this means that the intent to kill is extremely great, and seeing such a place causes injury to compassion, as there is no root of faith. If one is not accompanied by an elderly person...
Knowing that one is free from these five households, this is a place where practice may be undertaken. Regarding "conduct" (jucuo), it refers to movement and stillness.
This means one should observe the movements and stillness of the donor (*dānapati*). If there is an offering, one should accept it in accordance with the Dharma;

if there is none, one should proceed to the second household. One must not stand for too long. Whether [the offering] is present or absent, one should rise and depart; the ritual decorum must not be lost.
△ Regarding the rule that one may not enter a house where no male is present: first, it would cause others to harbor doubts and slander;
second, there is the fear of losing one's integrity. Therefore, one must not enter.
Second, regarding sitting and speaking:
if one wishes to sit, one should first inspect the seat. If there are weapons or blades, one should not sit; if there are precious objects, one should not sit;
if there are women’s garments, bedding, ornaments, and the like, one should not sit. When wishing to preach the sutra, one should know what is appropriate.
Regarding the time for speaking: one should not speak at an improper time. One must not say, "Give me food, so that you may obtain merit. This refers to observing and examining.
The previous statement said there were no men and thus one could not enter the gate;

this statement says that even if there are men, one should still examine the seating place before sitting. Regarding weapons: these are instruments of misfortune. If one sits [without precaution], one fears they may cause harm.
[One should avoid] being injured, or causing others to give rise to anger. As for sitting upon precious objects: first, one fears the arising of greedy attachment;
second, one guards against loss and the incurrence of transgressions. One should likewise avoid women’s clothing, ornaments, and the like, to escape censure and ridicule.
Regarding the proper time for teaching: there may be faithful men or elders who are capable of discerning the Dharma.
Regarding the meaning and terms such as "good" and "evil," one should speak them in order to increase faith and reverence; therefore, they ought to be spoken. As for times when one should not speak:
this refers to when there are no persons such as those mentioned above nearby, or when one is asked in jest;

therefore, one should not speak. Regarding the statement, "Give me food so that you may obtain merit": one must reflect for oneself—what virtue or what practice of mine could cause another to obtain merit? One [should thus refrain].
It is improper to praise [the donor] while seeking food, nor should one beg piteously or press them for it.

Furthermore, when begging for alms, one must not speak extensively of cause and effect in order to entice others. *Appendix on Supplementary Rituals:* In all instances of begging for food, one must not lament or plead in distress. One must not engage in lengthy discourses on karmic causality with the hope of [eliciting generosity].
If you receive much, do not give rise to greedy attachment; if you receive little, do not give rise to distress.
Do not exclusively seek food from the houses of donors or at the monasteries of your personal acquaintances.
Begging for alms is the method of practice for Buddhas and patriarchs. This has been handed down from antiquity as something most supreme and noble.
If one begs piteously, one loses the very essence of a monk; how is this different from a beggar? If one demands with hardship, it causes others to feel aversion; such a person is like an enemy.
It is precisely for these reasons that the work of conversion and guidance fails to proceed. △ Not permitted.
He spoke extensively on cause and effect. Regarding those who give much, it is the constant law of all Buddhas to preach the Dharma for them;
yet even after the Buddha has preached the Dharma, he does not accept their offerings, much less accept them with a mind of expectation. Xinghu said:
"One must not employ wrong livelihood to convert others or incite laypeople to bestow gifts. The Buddha prescribed begging for food as a means of maintaining solemnity and reverence."
Regarding one’s deportment: limit the daily visits to seven households and proceed through them in succession. Maintain a distance of three feet from the eaves.

Empty the mind of all worldly concerns and accept whatever is offered according to one's lot, regardless of its quantity. Remain upright, silent, and composed; even speaking is considered inverted, let alone engaging in extensive discourse.
To give rise to various cravings and afflictions is like the rivers and lakes [of the world]. To speak of, record, or seek out [worldly matters] brings disgrace upon my Dharma-gate;

the offense incurred is no small matter. The mendicant must strive diligently and not regard these things with contempt or disdain. Regarding the principle that "one should not give rise to greed when obtaining much, nor give rise to distress when obtaining little"—this refers to even a single bowl of gruel or a single meal, down to a grain of rice or a single coin.
Although these are called the fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for this present life, [one must remain detached].
This is truly due to the planting of conditions in the past. If there is much, one must not become attached to it and give rise to greed;
if there is little, one must not worry over it and suffer distress. To accept things according to conditions is precisely what constitutes right livelihood.

△ To beg for food from those with whom one has a mature affection means to be ignorant of contentment. Because of this ignorance of contentment, one repeatedly approaches such acquaintances, lacking any sense of shame.
Therefore, whenever someone requested food from him, the Buddha said, "Even animals fear being asked for alms; how much more so should humans? As the ancients said:
"To encounter fragrant rice when hungry is truly a blessing; one should know to value it and exercise self-restraint within.
Even if invited with lax etiquette, a man of integrity will never accept food brought with a sigh of contempt.
Entering a Village, Chapter Twenty (Seventeen Matters; Divided into Two). First, the Proper Manner (Divided into Three).
First, the Ritual for the Matter:
One must not enter [a village] without having eliminated all urgent causes. One must not walk with a galloping gait. One must not walk shaking the arms. One must not...
Frequently looking aside at people and their movements.

Regarding "village" (*grāma*): a gathering of many is called a "gathering" (*grā*); a place of residence is called a "settlement" (*ma*). That is to say, a place where many people dwell together is termed a "village.
Regarding "all circumstances": for the sake of the Three Jewels, for the permanent [Dharma], and for visiting one's teachers, elders, parents, and the Dharma.
Entering the gates for matters of utmost importance is not for the purpose of soliciting alms or for one’s own private affairs.
Unless there is such urgent and essential business, one must not enter lightly; how much less so when entering a village where sounds and sights are intermingled?
If one’s power of the Way is not firm and stable, how could one avoid being dazzled and deluded by them? Thus, Hanshan said: "The monastics of future generations, speaking of their emotions..."

Deep-seated ignorance: originally seeking liberation, one instead endures the toil of worldly pursuits. All day long wandering through lay dwellings, performing rituals and recitations as a mere display of decorum;
earning money to buy wine to drink, one ends up becoming a hired laborer. As the *Buddha-ghosa-sūtra* says:
"When a bhikṣu remains in a village, though his body and speech may be diligent, all the Buddhas grieve for him. When a bhikṣu dwells in the mountains, setting aside affairs and resting in peace..."
"All Buddhas rejoice" (諸佛皆喜) means they gallop forth, as if a horse were running at full speed. "Waving the arms" (搖臂) refers to dangling the hands and swinging the arms;
it is a manner of unrestrained abandon. The *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma) says: "The five hindrances cover the mind, and the gates of dhyāna are already closed.
The six sense-objects dwell in one's thoughts, and distracted imaginings constantly gallop about. This is like a mad elephant without a hook, or similar to a playful monkey."
While walking beneath the trees, one has not yet seen swift movement; rather, there is a graceful gait.

Therefore, when lifting the feet, they should be neither slow nor hurried, neither too light nor too heavy, but steady and measured, like a white crane in a field of *zhī* grass, or a blue lion moving through a stone cave, or like clouds entering a deep forest, following the hidden birds without startling them, or like a boat traveling with the current, moving in harmony with the fish.
There is no hindrance. Those of noble resolve should reflect upon this deeply. △ "Frequently looking sideways" means frequently, without interruption;
"sideways" refers to glancing to the left and right. When a practitioner walks, they go straight forward and straight back;
yet to cause bystanders to marvel, one might look left and right. Xinghuo said: "One should keep one's gaze on the ground for seven feet, so as not to step on and harm insects."
Ants. Second, one must not shift from right mindfulness;
one must not walk about engaging in idle chatter with śrāmaṇeras or children; and one must not follow behind or precede a woman.
When walking, one must not walk with a bhikṣuṇī before or behind her in mutual succession. One must not walk with a drunkard or a madman before or behind them in mutual succession.
One must not gaze intentionally at women, nor look at women from the corners of one’s eyes.
1. If one walks while chatting and laughing with a śrāmaṇera or a young child: (i) it causes one’s own body and mind to become distracted;

(ii) it causes those who see this not to give rise to faith or respect. The *Qinggui* states: "One must not walk together holding hands. [This applies to] discussing the right and wrong of worldly matters.
△ One must not walk back and forth following a woman or a bhikṣuṇī. This refers to women and bhikṣuṇīs exiting [the premises].

When traveling, one must avoid the bustle and clamor of the marketplace, for such environments provoke the vocal karma of agitation. If one’s presence is mingled with that of monks, one cannot escape suspicion and debate;
therefore, one should keep a great distance from them. One must not travel before or after those who are intoxicated or insane, as there is a fear of causing them harm.
If one encounters such persons on the road, one should immediately avoid them by taking a different path. This applies equally to those in vehicles, horses, wild beasts, and so forth.
As well as rabid dogs and the like, one should likewise avoid them. Regarding "one must not intentionally gaze at women," this means one must not look at them on purpose.
As the Buddha said in a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "It would be better to have red copper wire wound around one's eyes than to look upon the forms of women with a distracted mind.
To look askance from the corners of the eyes is "evil gazing" (*viṣama-darśana*). The Sūtra says: "Prohibit..."
Close the six sense-faculties. Let the mind harbor no thoughts of lust; let the mouth utter no words of flirtation. Do not follow one another’s tracks. Do not share a boat.
If you encounter one another on the road, do not converse. If you hold some unusual object, do not look at it closely.
Maintain a sincere and upright demeanor of mind;
if you encounter elders or close acquaintances, stand to one side and first offer a greeting with a respectful expression.

If you encounter performances of illusion or strange spectacles, it is not appropriate to watch them. Always walk with your body upright and your gaze directed straight ahead. Whenever you encounter a puddle of water...
[Text missing. One must not leap over [obstacles]. Where there is a path, one should walk around it; where there is no path, it is permissible for the entire assembly to leap over.
Except in cases of illness or urgent business, one must not ride a horse, nor even urge it along with a whip out of a playful mind.
Regarding venerable seniors and close acquaintances: this refers to ordained elders who are spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), as well as lay elders and relatives.
If one encounters them on the road, one must always step aside from the path, lower the head, join the palms, and inquire after their welfare before proceeding.
One must wait until they have passed before continuing on; one must not simply walk straight past them. △ Or, if one encounters performers of illusions or strange wonders...
"Et cetera" (*ādi*) refers to those encountered by chance who go about for the sake of jesting; this "jesting" (*parihāsa*) means singing songs or performing all manner of playful antics.
"Illusion" (*māyā*) refers to magical arts, meaning the various wondrous transformations that delude the minds and eyes of people.
As for these "things," they are like passing clouds or flowing water, which do not linger once they have gone; if one encounters them on the road, one must not [engage with them].
"Standing and observing: 'Only those who walk with the body upright and on the correct path'—the ancient sages did not take by-ways, for they saw that movement must always be correct.
How could one travel upon deviant paths or dangerous tracks?

"Whenever encountering pits or chasms, one must not leap over them"—this demonstrates the dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) of the Śākya disciples. For instance, there was the Bhikṣu Asaṅga... [text continues].
A lay devotee of faith invited [the bhikṣu] for a meal and wished to offer him a fine robe. On the way, they encountered a water pit;
as he was about to leap across it, the devotee thought that because of this leaping, the robe would be reduced by half.

The bhikṣu, possessing the supernormal power of knowing others' minds, understood the devotee's intention. Upon seeing the water pit again, he leaped across it three times. The devotee’s thoughts were further diminished until—
He had no clothes and left behind only a single meal. As the bhikṣu walked forward, he saw a puddle of water and did not step over it.

When the layman asked for the reason, the bhikṣu replied, "If I were to step over it again, I fear I might lose my meal. The layman was struck with awe and realized he had met a man who had attained the Way;
he invited him to return and provide offerings. If even one who has attained the Way acts in this manner, how much more so should an ordinary person? When there is a path, one should go around it.

"Practitioner" (*yōgyō*) means principle. Regarding "if there is no path and everyone leaps over, then one may obtain [the benefit]": although leaping over is permitted, one must also exercise self-reflection.
△ Regarding "riding a horse at a gallop": the character for *shū* (驟) is pronounced *sō*. To gallop a horse is called *chi*; to move with great speed is called *shū*.
The *Mahā-vinaya* permits those who are elderly or infirm to ride, provided they do not ride mares or female animals.
Appendix II:
Rituals for Visiting Lay Authorities Whenever one encounters government officials, regardless of their rank or status, one should always yield the way.

When encountering those engaged in a quarrel, one should likewise keep a wide distance and must not remain to watch. One must not return to the monastery to boast about what was seen, such as the splendors of the city.
Regarding such matters, whether the government office be large or small, all should observe avoidance; this is to comply with the regulations established by the Tathāgata.

If one encounters them on the road, one should either avoid entering by going to the entrance of another's house, stand upright beneath a eaves, or stand respectfully with hands clasped by the roadside.
One must wait until the contest has ended before proceeding. Regarding those who engage in fighting, there is nothing more than the brandishing of fists and the rolling up of sleeves;
such actions often bring misfortune upon bystanders. To watch may cause a loss of decorum or even invite calamity. The *Mahā-vinaya* states:

"If one watches elephants, horses, oxen, or sheep, or even roosters fighting, or witnesses human quarrels, one incurs an offense. As for excessive finery and beauty, these corrupt the hearts and eyes of people.
Robbers! They are the causes for wandering through the suffering of birth and death.

In antiquity, those who did not meet with indecent sights with their eyes nor speak the vulgar talk of marketplaces and alleys were guests of the world-transcending realm; they were untainted by worldly dust—what is there to boast of?
One should only contemplate suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self; this alone is what is fitting for a son of the Śākya.
Section Twenty-one: On Buying Goods (Five Matters in Total; Divided into Two Parts). First: To follow the honest path and avoid suspicion, one should not dispute over the value of goods.
One must not sit at a woman’s stall. If one is wronged by another, one should skillfully avoid them and not seek restitution from them.

The *Qishi jing* (Sutra on the Arising of the World) states: "Regarding all goods traded by the people of Jambudvīpa—whether for money and treasures, grain and silk, or various precious gems—the gods of the Desire Realm, such as those in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, likewise engage in trade and enjoy excursions to delight their spirits;
however, their goods differ from those of worldly people. The *Xiangfa jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma) states:
In future ages, all worldly people will despise the Triple Gem precisely because bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs do not act according to the Dharma.
Though they wear the dharma-robes, they manage mundane affairs;

they may frequent marketplaces to trade for their livelihood, or travel on roads as merchants seeking profit, thereby forgetting their primary vocation. As the ancients said: "A true hero does not stand in a row."
This refers to going to the marketplace. Regarding "those who do not dispute over value or worth": this means that because pearls and jade are scarce, they are precious;
whereas tiles and rubble are abundant, they are cheap. Therefore, as for the value of goods, the market master sets the fixed price himself. No buyer may demand a reduction.
To cause them loss would be improper, nor should one give excessively, thereby wasting the permanent offerings of the faithful. One must follow the current market price;
if one suppresses or inflates the price, disputes will inevitably arise, often leading to the loss of the greater for the sake of the smaller.

Therefore, sons of the Śākya do not set their own prices in the marketplace, but rather procure what they need based on prevailing market rates. △ There are no women sitting at the stalls, meaning that [the goods] are displayed...
A shop for goods is called a *si* (market stall). It refers to a shop where women conduct trade; one must not sit there.
Even if one were as pure as jade and without flaw, if one were to sit there, it would be difficult to avoid the clamorous chatter of the marketplace.
Therefore, it is inappropriate to sit. An ancient saying goes: "Guarding against the mouths of others is more difficult than damming a river. If one is offended by another, that is an offense.
"Encroaching" (*āghāta*) also carries the sense of "returning. "Value" (*mūlya*) refers to price. "Seeking" (*anveṣaṇa*) means to deliberate and seek.

This refers to when goods are in a shop and their high or low value has not yet been determined; once a person returns with an offer, a fixed amount is established, and thus it is called "encroaching.

If the previous person has not yet completed the purchase of an item and I go there again to solicit a price, this constitutes "seeking" or "striving for value," which gives rise to right and wrong. Even if...
"Even if the owner invites me, I shall not purchase it; I will go elsewhere. Thus, it is said that one should skillfully avoid it and not seek its price from him;
this refers to avoiding both the previous person and the owner.

Second, having already promised to give a certain item to someone out of faith and conscientiousness, even if that item subsequently becomes cheaper, one must not abandon it to take up another, thereby causing the owner resentment. Furthermore,
one must be careful never to act as a guarantor, lest one incur fault and liability.
When a transaction is concluded, one says "ji" (already). "Jia" (first) refers to the beginning. Throughout the world, people are ranked in order by characters such as Jia, Yi, and so forth.

This means that once one has returned the goods to the first house, even if the goods at the second house are cheaper, one must not abandon the previously purchased expensive ones to buy the later cheap ones;
this is to prevent the original owner from giving rise to feelings of resentment. As the *Shishuo xinyu* says: "If one abandons that to take this..."
It is like killing one’s own parents; where then is the mindfulness of the path of renunciation? Regarding "guarantee" (*bao-ren*):
it means seeing that someone has borrowed an object and cannot repay it, and thus acting as a guarantor (*bao*). Furthermore, "taking responsibility" (*ren*) means taking it upon oneself, meaning:

"If the other person does not return it, I shall repay it in their stead. "Fault" (*qian*) refers to violating what was promised. "Breach" (*fu*) refers to failing and sinking [into debt]. From oneself...
This invites calamity and entanglement. Whenever one acts as a guarantor, there will inevitably be many transgressions, debts, resentments, and slanders.
Hanshan said: "There is a certain kind of person in this world whose nature is constantly prone to trouble. All day long they frequent the streets and neighborhoods, never leaving the wine shops.
They act as guarantors for others and offer explanations on their behalf. Yet when a single misfortune occurs, the entire blame falls upon you."
In all matters one undertakes, one must not act on one's own authority. (Twenty-second [Eleven Matters;
divided into two parts]) First, the Proper Protocol (divided into two):

First, regarding the duty of not acting independently—when entering or leaving, or when coming and going, one should first inform the teacher. When making new Dharma robes, one should first inform the teacher. When putting on new Dharma robes...
When putting on robes, one should first inform the teacher. When shaving the head, one should first inform the teacher. When taking medicine for illness, one should first inform the teacher.
When performing affairs for the Saṃgha, one should first inform the teacher. If one wishes to privately possess items such as paper or pens, one should first inform the teacher.
If one intends to chant the sūtras or perform Buddhist hymns, one should first inform the teacher.

Regarding all actions performed, those that may not be undertaken according to one’s own will refer to the fact that this body has surrendered its life to the teacher and is no longer one's own possession.
In all matters, one must follow the teacher’s instructions and dare not act as the sole authority.

Therefore, in ordinary movements and conduct, one must report everything to the teacher to fulfill the practice of filial piety. However, the eleven subsequent rules concerning acting on one's own authority are merely stated in brief here.

Among these matters, there are those that may be reported to the teacher and those that may not; the essential point lies in exercising discretion according to the specific circumstances. The *Nanshan Shichao* states:

"That the Buddha-dharma increases and expands is truly due to the mutual support of teachers and disciples, their mutual encouragement and assistance, and their provision for one another in both material goods and the Dharma.

As days and months pass, practices become deepened and long-standing achievements are firmly established—all of this relies upon this very principle. (Regarding reporting matters to the teacher when entering or leaving.)
This term has two meanings. First, the meaning of consolation, which refers to the teacher’s knowledge of what should be entered and what should be withdrawn.

Second, the meaning of requesting a decision, which refers to requesting the teacher’s instruction on whether an action may be performed or not, so as to avoid error. If one acts according to one's own whims, [one will fall into mistake].
Should there be any error, one must inform the teacher afterward; by then, it will be too late for regret. For this reason, one ought to inform the teacher first.
△ Regarding the making of new Dharma robes: those who wear new Dharma robes refer to the *maṇḍala* robe (the single-layered robe). This refers to its substance and color.

Regarding measurements: because its dimensions conform to the Dharma, it is called "Dharma-robes" (*dharmakāṣāya*). Even if they are not Dharma-robes, as long as they are new, one must inform the teacher.
The teacher should examine their provenance as well as the construction and dimensions of the robes to determine whether they accord with or deviate from the Dharma before permitting them to be worn.
Regarding shaving the head: one must first inform the teacher out of fear that this might become a pretext for idle chatter and derision.
Miscellaneous Remarks. Regarding the administration of medicine for illness: one must first inform the teacher. This means that medicine must not be administered haphazardly;
one must understand the origin of the ailment, its underlying nature—whether it is of a "void" or "solid" (vāta/pitta/śleṣman) type—and the cold or warm properties of the medicine before taking it.
If one does not inform the teacher and administers medicinal substances indiscriminately, it will instead aggravate the illness. △ [End of section] Practice.

Regarding matters concerning the community of monks (*saṃgha*), one must first inform one’s teacher; this refers to affairs pertaining to the resident monastic assembly. If one does not inform the teacher, there may be errors or omissions.
Regarding the private possession of paper and brushes, one must first inform one’s teacher; this is because one fears it might neglect the primary duties of meditation and recitation.
Regarding the chanting of sutras and hymns (*geya*), one must first inform one’s teacher; this is because [the teacher] oversees the chanting.
This is the Brahma-voice. When a śrāmaṇera’s fundamental practice is not yet perfected and he first begins to recite, he must first inform his teacher.
Second, regarding wisdom borrowed from the teacher:
if another person gives an object as a gift, one should first inform the teacher before receiving it; if one gives one's own object as a gift to another, one should likewise [inform the teacher].
First, inform the teacher. Only after the teacher has granted permission may one borrow from another person.
One must first inform the teacher; only after the teacher has granted permission may one do so. If one wishes to borrow an object from another person, one must first inform the teacher.
Whether the teacher grants permission or not, one must perform a prostration. If permission is not granted, one must not harbor feelings of resentment.
If a person offers material gifts with wisdom, they should first inform their teacher, meaning that one should ascertain whether the gift may be accepted or not.
If it is acceptable but one does not accept it, one blocks the gateway of giving and severs the path of virtue.
If it is unacceptable yet one accepts it, it may lead to calamity and misfortune; the consequences are no small matter. Therefore, one must inform the teacher to avoid censure.
To deliberate on this later is an error born of regret. When one intends to give one's own belongings as a wise gift to others, one must first inform the teacher;
this means ensuring that one knows what may or may not be given, thereby avoiding the error of private partiality. △ When others come to borrow from oneself, one must first inform the teacher;

this means that items belonging to the permanent endowment (*sangha*) or for the common use of the ten directions (*daśadig-sādhāraṇa*) must not be lent arbitrarily. When they ought to be lent... [text ends]... one must inform the teacher.
When one is about to give something, one must inform the teacher; there is no deliberation required. When one wishes to borrow an object from another, one must always inform the teacher;

this means one should request permission as to whether it may or may not be granted. Regarding informing the teacher and whether they grant or deny permission, one must in all cases perform a prostration;
this means one must not act with haste or negligence. If permission is denied, one must harbor no resentment; this is to admonish one to maintain a spirit of obedience and compliance.
...and so forth. Second, the Supplement to the Rituals,
including matters such as traveling abroad, attending lectures, joining the monastic assembly, guarding the mountains, or undertaking [construction projects].
Regarding matters arising from circumstances, one must always inform one’s teacher and may not act on one’s own authority;

"great matters" refers to anything other than minor affairs. "Traveling abroad" means visiting and seeking instruction from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), which requires identifying those who are truly eminent and wise.

"Listening to lectures" means hearing and studying the sacred teachings, which requires that understanding and practice be in accord. "Entering the assembly" means joining the community of great monks (*bhikṣu*).

Within the assembly, one must understand the protocols of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*). "Guarding the mountains" means protecting the forests, bamboo, trees, flowers, fruits, and so forth; these must not be disturbed at will.
"Creating conditions" refers to the construction of monasteries, the casting of statues, and similar works; one must clearly understand the distinction between cause and effect.
As stated above regarding such matters as practice and implementation, one must not act according to one's own private whims. Therefore it is said:
