All such matters should be reported to one's teacher. However, traveling abroad was originally not the business of a śrāmaṇera; a śrāmaṇera should properly focus on training in the Vinaya.
It is only because he encountered certain circumstances that he is treated as an exception in this case.
Section Twenty-Three: On Visiting Teachers (Total of Five Items; Divided into Two Parts).

First, the Proper Protocol for Traveling Afar Requires a Virtuous Companion. Those of the ancients whose realization had not yet been fully penetrated would travel thousands of miles to seek a teacher.
"Visiting teachers from all quarters" (*sān-fāng zhě*) refers to visiting and paying homage to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in various regions.

Those who wish to become superior persons must undergo a thorough refinement—being ground and forged a thousand times within the great furnace and bellows—before they can emerge above the heads of others.
As the ancients said: "If you wish to pass over the heads of a thousand people, you must first walk upon the feet of ten thousand."△

A "good friend" (*liang-peng*) refers to a virtuous companion. This means that because such a person’s character is upright and their speech and conduct are worthy of emulation, they are called "good.
The *Book of Rites* states: "Those of the same kind are called 'companions' (*peng*); those with the same aspirations are called 'friends' (*you*). The *Treatise on Following the Correct* states:

"A virtuous friend can serve as the foundation for all wholesome practices. Thus, Master Guishan said: "One embarking on a long journey must rely upon a good friend; repeatedly [associating with them] purifies one's mind."

Regarding the ears and eyes: it is said that those who give birth to us are our parents, while those who bring us to fulfillment are our friends. By relying on friends to assist in the cultivation of benevolence (*ren*), one may evaluate and discern people;
thus, virtuous friends possess the merit of mutual refinement and polishing, serving the purpose of fashioning them into vessels of the Dharma.

It is like crossing a great ocean, where the sail and the rudder are mutually indispensable. As the *Huanyu jing* (Sutra of Joyful Delight) states: "A virtuous friend is the source of ten thousand blessings."
It is the foundation [of liberation]. In this life, one avoids the king’s prison; at death, one closes the gates of the three miserable realms.
To ascend to heaven and attain the Way—all is due to the assistance of a virtuous friend. Thus, the *Shiyuan ming* (Inscription on Abandoning Conditions) says:

"A false teacher and an evil friend are feared like wolves and tigers; a good guide and a fine companion are cherished like fire-drills. Chengfan says: "Choosing a friend is like [choosing] Yunyan; the Way..."
Wu, Xuefeng, Yantou, and others were truly genuine and virtuous friends. The *Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground* states:
"All Bodhisattvas who cultivate the holy path should know these four essential dharmas: first, drawing near to virtuous friends; second, hearing the true Dharma;
third, reflecting according to principle; and fourth, practicing and realizing according to the Dharma."
This constitutes the fourth [point]. All the great holy lords of the ten directions cultivate these four dharmas to realize bodhi.
The *Inga-kyō* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) states: "Friends have three essential dharmas: first, when seeing a transgression, one should immediately admonish and counsel;

second, when seeing good deeds, one should deeply give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); third, when [a friend] is in distress or peril, one must not abandon them. For this reason, one travels afar.
One must rely upon virtuous friends. Regarding "ancient worthies": these were people of virtue from antiquity.
It is said that when the minds of ancient worthies were not yet enlightened, they sought out spiritual teachers (*kṣetrajña*), not considering even a thousand *li* too far.
They would go directly to anyone who possessed the True Eye (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). For example, Chan Master Xuefeng went three times to Touzi and ascended Dongshan nine times.
This refers to Mount [Shan]. Chengfan said: "In seeking a teacher for the sake of the Dharma, one must certainly exercise careful discernment.

If you have not yet clearly perceived his depth or gained true insight, you should be cautious not to follow the mere rumors of others and hastily judge the gravity of his status or the intimacy of your relationship with him."
II. The Ritual for Replenishing (divided into two parts). First, regarding those whose emotions are attached to the Dharma:
being young and of shallow precepts, they are not permitted to travel far. If they must travel, they must not do so in the company of unwholesome persons.
They must seek out teachers and inquire after the Way to resolve the matter of birth and death; it is inappropriate to merely view mountains and waters, seeking only [worldly pleasures].

To travel through vast distances and display one's prowess to others while still young—when one’s vital energies (*ojas*) are not yet settled and one’s precepts (*śīla*) are shallow—is feared to result in a lack of resolve and strength; therefore, long journeys were not permitted.
Nevertheless, there is a compelling necessity to go, and one must certainly choose a virtuous friend as a companion. An unvirtuous one...
Those who do not cultivate the precepts and practices are evil friends; fearing that one might gradually be infected by their influence, one should therefore distance oneself from them.
Guishan said: "Associating with the wicked fosters evil views and insights; creating evil day and night, one receives retribution immediately. After death, one sinks into the depths;
once lost, this human body will not be regained for ten thousand kalpas. The Fayuan zhulin states: "The House of Hua..."
The king possessed a white elephant capable of destroying his enemies; if anyone committed a crime, he would have the elephant trample them to death.

At that time, the elephant’s stable was consumed by fire, so the elephant was moved near a monastery. There, it heard the monks reciting a verse from the *Dharmapada*: "By doing good, one is reborn in heaven."
"Those who commit evil fall into the abyss. His mind then became gentle and compassionate; he gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion.

Later, when the elephant was handed over to the condemned man, it merely sniffed him with its trunk and licked him with its tongue before departing. When the King saw this, he summoned his ministers. A minister said, "This elephant stays near the temple."
It is because of hearing the Dharma that this occurred. When [the bird] moved closer to the butcher’s stall, its cruelty increased even further.
Later, it proved those words true. One should know that the dispositions of all sentient beings are not fixed; if even animals are like this, how much more so humans?
Therefore, the wise ought to be aware of this: when they see evil, they must abandon it. The *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning) of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* says: "For example, it is like incense..."
Fragrant Herbs. *Yóu* is a foul-smelling grass. When fragrant herbs and *yóu* grass are mixed together, their qualities interact;
even after ten years, the stench remains. Once the fragrance has vanished, the stench persists. This means that goodness cannot stop evil, whereas evil can destroy goodness.
△ Those who seek teachers and inquire after the Way desire to attain unsurpassed *bodhi*. It is not through mere acquaintances...
No one can provide guidance for you; therefore, you must seek out teachers and inquire after the Way. On the long journey through birth and death, delusion and awakening depend upon yourself;
thus, you must personally exercise discernment. What benefit to body or mind is gained by gazing at mountains and playing with waters?
What does boasting of vast distances add to the flavor of the Path? For those who are preoccupied with birth and death, what leisure is there for such things?
Regarding the method for entering the gate and reaching one's destination:
upon arriving, one must set down their luggage and may not enter the hall directly. One person shall remain with the luggage while another enters first to offer a greeting;
only after receiving instructions from the monastery authorities may the luggage be brought inside and settled.
"Traveling goods" (xínglǐ). It is also written as "traveling principles" (xínglǐ); both are commonly used. Some call them "packing bags," which refers to travel trunks.
If a person travels far, they must certainly have these. Because the regulations of various regions differ and their rules vary, there is no single fixed etiquette;
one must act according to the circumstances. Therefore it is said: "Only by observing the constant rules for movement and rest can one properly set down one's traveling goods."
Entering within, the ancients said: "Before it grows late, seek lodging; enter the forest and listen to the evening bell. Upon reaching the gate, one must discern the host;
in greeting, one must be composed. One may spread grass upon the ground as needed; for what heaven is not a drifting gourd?
The moon tonight upon the rafters of my hut serves merely to console my neglectful idleness."
Section Twenty-Four: Names and Characteristics of Robes (Nine items in total; divided into three parts). Part One: Names and Characteristics of Robes (divided into three).
Sub-part One: The Five Robes (divided into two). Sub-sub-part One: Characteristics and Uses.

The five-strip robe (*pañcaka*). In Sanskrit, it is called *antarvāsa*; here it is called the "innermost robe" (*zhongsu yī*), also called the "lower robe" (*xiayi*), and also called the "miscellaneous robe" (*zayī*).
Making Robes: Whenever one performs manual labor or service within the monastery, or travels on the road coming and going, one should wear this garment.
"Robe" (cīvara) means "reliance"; it refers to relying upon this to shield oneself from cold and heat. The *Cīvaravastu* states:
The Buddha saw various bhikṣus traveling on the road carrying many belongings, and he thought: "I should establish a regulation for the bhikṣus."
Regarding the quantity of robes: one must not keep more than is permitted. At that time, the Buddha sat in the open air during the first watch of the night wearing a single robe.
When it grew cold during the middle watch, he put on a second robe. During the final watch, feeling cold again, he put on a third robe and then dwelt in comfort.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "I permit my disciples to receive and maintain three robes."
It is permissible to possess [robes]. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains: "Laypeople seek pleasure, and thus they possess various kinds of clothing;
non-Buddhists practice asceticism, and thus they go naked without shame. Therefore, the disciples of the Buddha abandon these two extremes and abide in the Middle Way;
being of few desires and contented, they possess only the three robes. Regarding the five strips (*pañcaka*), this is the characteristic of the robe. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The Buddha..."
While walking back and forth before the Śakra Cave in Rājagṛha, he saw the distinct boundaries between the rice paddies and the frogs.
He said to Ānanda, "The robes of the Buddhas of the past were like this. From now on, let the three robes be fashioned according to this."
The disciples of all Buddhas of the past wore robes such as these; the disciples of all Buddhas of the future shall also wear these robes.
Just as I do today, they are made from cloth cut with a knife to form the robes of a śramaṇa, so that they cannot be plundered by enemies or thieves.
This is the garment of liberation; it is the robe of the field of merit. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all wear this robe.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to even a single evil thought toward the Buddhas of the three periods, the Pratyekabuddhas, or the Arhats..."
And for one who shows disrespect toward those wearing dyed robes, the offense incurred is immeasurable. Why is this? Because robes of discolored hue are the outward sign of the noble ones (ārya).
If one can resolve to develop a heart of reverence toward those wearing dyed robes, the merit obtained will be immeasurable. Regarding "those who dwell nearby" (madhyama-vasin):

it refers to those who reside close to one's person. Regarding "lower robes" (adhovāsas): it refers to those worn beneath the seven types of robes. [This concludes] the section on miscellaneous matters.
Regarding "robes": it means that for all light tasks whatsoever, one should wear them; regarding "performing labor and service":
it means performing the labor of the great assembly; regarding "wearing them when entering or leaving on the road": it is because this manifests the characteristics of a śramaṇa.
The two verses of the mantra:
"Excellent is this robe of liberation, the supreme field of merit. I now receive it upon my head; may I never be parted from it in life after life.
Oṃ siddhya svāhā. (Recite three times.)
"Excellent! These are words of praise, meaning that the merit of the robe is inconceivable.

Because it unties what is sticky and removes what binds, it is called "liberation" (*vimukti*); that is to say, one is liberated from the afflictions of birth and death by means of this. It is "unsurpassed."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "As for this robe, none of the ninety-five types of non-Buddhist practitioners know its name;
only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has revealed this unprecedented dharma, and thus it is called 'Unsurpassed. Regarding the 'Field of Merit' (*puṇyakṣetra*):

it means that when a donor plants merit, the disciples of the Buddha manifest the appearance of the field through the marks of the robe; hence it is called the 'Field of Merit. Regarding 'wearing on the crown': it means..."
Knowing that the robe possesses such merits as these, one should place it upon the crown of the head and carry it upon the shoulders to manifest the height of one’s reverence.
It was through the utmost devotion and respectful veneration of this robe born of faith that I attained Buddhahood.
"Never to be parted from it in life after life" means that one should not only honor and maintain it with such respect in this present life, but vow to do so in every successive birth.

One must not abandon them. Since one’s vow is thus, and seeing that the robe and bowl cannot be separated from oneself, the Tathāgata has issued earnest admonitions regarding this in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Vinayas.
One should recite the mantra three times; this is called "constant wearing and use. The verse-mantra is as follows.
If one discards the old and receives a new one, one should follow the textual prescriptions of the Vinaya.
II. The Seven-Striped Robe (divided into two parts). First, regarding its characteristics and functions:
the seven-striped robe (*saptaka-cīvara*). In Sanskrit, it is called *uttarāsaṅga*; this is translated as "upper garment" (*shangzhuoyi*) or "robe for entering the assembly" (*ruzhongyi*).

Whenever one worships the Buddha, performs repentance rituals, recites sutras, practices seated meditation, attends a vegetarian feast, listens to lectures, or participates in the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā* ceremonies, one should wear this robe.
"Upper robes" refers to those worn over the five monastic robes. "Assembly robes" refers to those donned when entering the assembly.
*Poṣadha* is translated here as "Purification through Growth"; *Pravāraṇā* means that when one has committed a transgression, one freely allows the Saṃgha to point it out.
On such occasions as these, one should wear this robe.
The two verses for the incantation:
"Excellent is this robe of liberation, the unsurpassed field of merit. I now receive it upon my head; may I always wear it throughout all lifetimes.
Oṃ. Tūṣa tūṣa. Svāhā. (Recite three times.)

"To always obtain that which one wears" means the intention of never abandoning [the robe]. The remaining meanings are as previously explained. The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states:
In the fifth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a disciple of Dharma Master Huiguang of Anxiang Temple.

His mother was impoverished and lacked even small undergarments. She entered her son’s room, took an old *kāṣāya*, fashioned it into a garment, and wore it while visiting with other neighboring women.
While she was laughing and chatting with her companions, she suddenly felt heat rising from her feet and gradually ascending to her waist.

In an instant, there was a clap of thunder, and she was hurled more than a hundred paces away. Mud and earth clogged both her ears, and she remained unconscious for a day before finally regaining consciousness.
As for the robe she had been wearing, it was struck dead by the lightning; scorched and curled by the fire, the words "Because the use of this dharma-robe was improper" were inscribed upon its back.
Because of the Dharma, his son collected and enshrined [the remains], which were then shaken out again; only after being exposed beneath a tree did they finally dissolve and vanish.
Thus we know that for those dragons who uphold the Dharma robes and possess wisdom and the Three Refuges, faith is not in vain.
The Three Great Robes (divided into two parts). First, regarding the characteristics and functions of the twenty-five-fold robe:
in Sanskrit it is called *saṃghāṭī*; this is translated as "combined," also as "layered," and also as "variegated or many-patched robe.
One should wear this robe when entering royal palaces, when ascending the seat to preach the Dharma, and when going on alms-round through villages. Furthermore, this robe...
The nine grades: the lower grade consists of nine, eleven, and thirteen strips; the middle grade consists of fifteen, seventeen, and nineteen strips;
the upper grade consists of twenty-one, twenty-three, and twenty-five strips.
The *saṃghāṭī* is the king among robes. It is called "great" (*mahā*) because it ranks above the five, seven, and two types of robes.
It is termed "combined" (*saṃghāṭa*) or "double-layered" (*dvi-guṇa*), meaning that after being cut into pieces, they are subsequently joined together.

As for the "miscellaneous small robes" (*pāṃśukūla*), these are made by sewing together scraps; they are so named because they consist of many strips. One wears them when ascending the seat out of reverence for the Dharma.
Regarding those who wear the robes for begging alms: it is to inspire reverence and respect. As for the nine grades, these are the characteristics of the *saṃghāṭī*.
That the length is greater than the width symbolizes the increase of the noble ones and the decrease of the ordinary. The *Śīlakaṇḍa Sūtra* states: "The five-strip robe cuts off greed;
it pertains to the body-karma. The seven-strip robe cuts off anger; it pertains to the speech-karma. The great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) cuts off delusion; it pertains to the mind-karma. Thus, the Flower...
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Those who don the *kāṣāya* abandon the three poisons and purify the three karmas.
Two verses of praise for the mantra:
"Excellent is this garment of liberation, the supreme field of merit. I now receive it upon my head to extensively deliver all deluded beings."
Oṃ mahākāpota-siddhe svāhā (three times). The preceding two verses pertain to self-benefit;
this one verse pertains to the benefit of others. Because all Buddhas have already attained awakening, they are called "Greatly Awakened" (Mahābodhi);
because sentient beings are still deluded, they are called the "multitude of the deluded. This refers to donning these robes and directly taking up [the burden].
Bearing the life-force of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, one transforms and benefits all sentient beings. Thus, the Treatise states: "For five reasons, one dons this robe:
namely, to ward off cold and heat; to eliminate shamelessness and lack of modesty; to beg for food in villages;
to give rise to wholesome states while traveling on the road; and because its deportment is pure. These three robes are originally the dharma-robes of a bhikṣu. Now, wishing to...
To ensure that śrāmaṇeras understand in advance the distinction between the names and characteristics [of the robes], they are appended here at the end. The *Ekottara-karman* states:
"The saṃghāṭī is the garment for those who seek tranquility (śrāmaṇeras). In these present degenerate times, people are unacquainted with the Vinaya texts;
consequently, they all cause śrāmaṇeras to wear the five- or seven-panel *kaṭhina* (cut-and-sewn) robes. This has even extended to laymen and laywomen, whom they likewise cause to wear them."

[This practice] is deeply offensive and constitutes a grave transgression against the lands of the Divine Continent (Jambudvīpa). This custom has long been propagated, violating the Buddha’s teachings and disrupting the Dharma;

the Vinaya contains severe condemnations of it. This is because the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Tang Dynasty personally traveled to the Western Regions and observed the territories of the Five Indias as well as the various Vinaya texts, finding that nowhere did śrāmaṇeras wear the cut-and-sewn robes of bhikṣus. Specifically...

This instruction is offered to initiate a discourse for all ages. Since it has been stated that this constitutes an unlawful practice, those who act as teachers must not fail to understand this, and those who act as disciples must likewise exercise great caution.
II. The Characteristics of the Alms Bowl (divided into two). First, the designation of the name:
The Sanskrit term is *pātra*, which here is translated as "vessel of proper measure. This refers to the fact that its substance, color, and dimensions all conform to the Dharma.
"Patra" (bowl) is a term derived from the Sanskrit *pātra*; it is an abbreviation that omits the two syllables *tara*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"The bowl is the emblem of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; it is not an ordinary utensil for domestic use.

One must not store miscellaneous items in it, nor employ it for improper purposes or for washing hands. One should revere it as one's own eyes. These are all the earnest instructions and admonitions of the Tathāgata.
All who receive and uphold [this] should cherish and protect it. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The almsbowl is the vessel of those who have left the household life.
It is for those of few desires and contentment; it is not suitable for worldly persons. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The Tathāgata commanded the bhikṣus..."
Regarding the practice of receiving food with an alms bowl: this was because there were heterodox practitioners (tīrthika) who used sewn leaves as vessels and ate with their hands clasped.
This was not the appearance of a monastic field of merit (puṇyakṣetra); therefore, the Buddha established this regulation.

Second, the explanation of the substance and its function. The two materials used are iron and ceramic. Regarding the color, it is treated by fumigation with medicinal smoke. Regarding the dimensions, they are divided into superior, middling, and inferior grades.
As for the substance being the two materials of iron and ceramic, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "The Buddha was traveling through the country of Suma when he saw..."

In that land, the soil was fine and smooth. Without sparing even *tūla* cotton-wool, he took the earth with his own hands and fashioned it himself into the mold for a bowl, establishing it as a model for future use.
He then entrusted it to a potter, who fired it into this bowl, which possessed a precious luster and was perfectly beautiful.
The Buddha permitted its acceptance and possession; one should know that this bowl is the supreme dharma-vessel transmitted from Buddha to Buddha.

It is most precious. Regarding the iron alms bowl: according to the Vinaya, while the World-Honored One was inspecting the dwellings of the bhikṣus, he saw a bhikṣu lying with his arm bent, distressed and unhappy.
The Tathāgata, knowing this, asked him intentionally, "Are you at ease?
The bhikṣu replied, "World-Honored One, I am old and my movements are clumsy; I shook my hand and lost my bowl, which fell to the ground."
[The Buddha] broke it; therefore, he did not approve [of such behavior]. The Buddha said: "From now on, I permit elderly and infirm bhikṣus to accept and maintain iron alms bowls.
You should know that the earthenware bowl is the superior bowl, while the iron bowl is a concessionary provision (*kai-en*).

However, one must not, out of self-indulgence or negligence, intentionally accept and maintain an iron bowl merely to settle into a coarse and agitated state. The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-vinaya* (or *Sudarsana-vinaya*) states: "The Noble Ones of the Three Vehicles..."
All people should hold earthen alms bowls and rely on begging for food as their livelihood. The use of other miscellaneous bowls made of jewels, copper, tin, wood, or stone is strictly prohibited.

Regarding treatment by medicinal smoke: crush hemp seeds and apricot kernels, apply the paste to the interior and exterior [of the bowl], and fumigate it with bamboo smoke until it takes on the color of a dove’s neck or the color of a peacock. That which is thus fumigated—
What is meant? It refers to ensuring that the rice does not spoil and that the bowl is not stained by grease or filth.

Regarding the Western Regions (India), even earthenware bowls must be fumigated; this is because in those countries, soup and rice are both eaten from the same bowl, and they fear that oiliness and impurity will attract many insects and ants.
However, in this land (China), since the bowl contains only rice, it is not necessary to fumigate the earthenware bowl. As for...
Painted designs, as well as colors such as lapis lazuli, are the styles of non-Buddhists and must not be used at all. Regarding the superior, middling, and inferior [sizes]:
according to the Chinese *dou*, the superior bowl is one *dou*, the middling bowl is seven and a half *sheng*, and the inferior bowl is five *sheng*.
Although there are these three types, the Buddha instructed that one should use whichever size is appropriate to one's own capacity.
III. The Three Names and Characteristics (divided into two parts).
First, the designation of the name: In the Sanskrit language it is called *niṣīdana*; this is translated here as "sitting mat" (*zuòjù*).

It is also called "foot-covering cloth" (*suízú yī*). It is termed a "sitting mat" because one spreads it out and sits upon it; it is termed a "foot-covering cloth" because one spreads it out to cushion the feet.
Furthermore, it is said that what has the shape of a felt mat is called a "reclining implement" (*śayanāsana*), and what has the shape of a quilt or blanket is called a "bedding implement.
The *Shisao* states: The Buddha said, "For the sake of the body, for the sake of clothing, and for the sake of bedding, I have prescribed their possession.

Regarding "for the sake of the body," it is because one fears that sitting on the bare ground might cause injury. Regarding "for the sake of clothing," it is because one fears that without a protective layer, the three robes (*tricīvara*) would easily become damaged.

Regarding the bedding cloth (*śayanāsana*): fearing that bodily impurities might defile the monastic beds and mats, it is two and a half *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha in length and two *vitasti* of the Buddha in width.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One *vitasti* of the Tathāgata is two chi and four cun.

This is calculated according to the small *chi*; if based on the large *chi*, it would be approximately two chi. It may not be used as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*), nor may it be purified (*pariśuddha*).

One may use [the bedding] for giving, for gathering firewood or grass, for holding miscellaneous items, or solely for spreading as a seat. If traveling on a road, one may take it to a place where one sits and use it there.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "For new [bedding], two layers [of cloth] are used; for old, four layers. One should not accept a single-layered item;
to remain overnight with such is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: "The Buddha was at a monastery and went to inspect all the rooms."

Seeing that the sitting mats were in disarray, he therefore instructed the bhikṣus: "One should take a piece of old [material] one span (vitasti) in length and breadth and patch it onto the new mat for the purpose of discoloring it.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that one should patch the four corners; the current mention of the "Four Heavenly Kings" is an error.
The *Vinaya-daily-use* (*Vinayopayoga*) states that neither the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* nor the *Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan* mentions this.
It is permitted to use [the robe] for prostration and for spreading out. In the five regions of the Western Regions (India), such a practice is rarely seen or heard of.

As for this land (China), the timing of when the custom of using it for prostration and spreading arose is unknown. If one follows the sacred regulations, not using it for these purposes is considered correct.

However, if one discusses it as a garment, there is no hindrance to using it for prostration while it is spread out. This matter is clearly auspicious; let students act according to their circumstances.

The second verse is a mantra for consecrating the bedding and the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat). It nurtures the seed-nature of the mind, unfolds it so as to ascend to the ground of the sages, and upholds the command of the Tathāgata.
Oṃ. Dambha dambha. Svāhā. (Recite three times.)
*Śayanāsana* (bedding) and *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) are terms that express both the Chinese and Sanskrit meanings together. The *Jietan jing* (Sutra on the Ordination Platform) states:
"The *niṣīdana* is like the foundation of a stupa; the body receiving the precepts represents the stupa of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*).
This is because the fivefold Dharma-body is nurtured through the precepts, and right concentration and wisdom are produced from the precepts; therefore, it is said to 'nurture the mind.'"

The sprout is its nature. Thus, when right concentration and wisdom can nurture it, one spreads out this sitting mat, whereupon the clouds of delusion suddenly part, and one directly perceives the original source, the ground of the mind.
Therefore, it is said: "Spreading it out, one ascends to the ground of the sages.

Having perceived the original source, the ground of the mind, one should likewise open the path of the mind-ground for all sentient beings. Therefore, it is said: "To uphold [this] as the Tathāgata does."

This is the decree. As explained extensively in the *Gandhadugdha-vyākaraṇa* (The Record of Fragrant Milk), regarding the aforementioned deportment (*īryāpatha*), if one acts intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession;
because it was done intentionally, one further commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anairyāpathika*).
If not done intentionally, one commits only a *duṣkṛta* offense. Although these articles are said to comprise twenty-four sections, in reality, they are three.
The thousand modes of deportment and the eighty thousand subtle practices all derive their foundation from this. It enables one to uphold the True Dharma and establish the monastic community.
I pray that my fellow practitioners will together protect and preserve it, so that the Vinaya may endure for a long time and the True Dharma may flourish forever.

The Dharma does not propagate itself; it must rely on people to propagate it. People cannot establish themselves independently; they must rely on the Dharma to establish themselves.
Therefore, both worldly and world-transcending beings alike revere the Dharma. Yet, there has never been one who could propagate the Dharma without having studied it.

In the year Jiachen, I ascended Mount Hua to seek the precepts, but due to illness, I did not succeed. It was not until the spring of the Bingwu year that I finally attained full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).

Reflecting upon how difficult it is to encounter the rules of discipline (*śīla*), I resolved to maintain them with steadfast intent and devoted myself to the study of the Vinaya. I sought to verify [the teachings]...
Though I am not quick-witted, my mind has never wavered. Through the humid heat and the biting cold, I have never allowed myself to slacken.

Since assuming the abbacy of Zhaokeng in the spring of the Jiazi year, I have constantly cherished the memory of the late Master, who founded this Dharma gate; for while his great achievements and profound virtues are known to all, I fear that with the passage of time—
Because [the teachings] gradually became obscured, I have recorded the essential points of the *Vinaya* by writing them in fragrant milk.
As the commentaries on the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* are numerous and complex, causing students to weep at the crossroads of uncertainty, I have summarized the primary principles to guide them.

Since the *bhikṣu-karman* (monastic rituals) are scattered throughout the Vinaya texts and difficult to consult when needed, I have set forth the formal procedures to assist them. Regarding the full ordination sought by the community of nuns, both divisions of the Saṃgha shall confer it together.

This has been rarely heard in the world; therefore, I have compiled these rules and regulations to transmit them. The *Essentials for Śrāmaṇeras* is concise in wording yet profound in meaning, such that beginners are unable to comprehend it;
thus, I have explained its meaning in detail to clarify it. All of this continues and recounts matters previously unspoken by my late preceptor and Dharma brother.
Although his words were not exhaustive, they directly revealed the essential characteristics of the phenomena; however, as for their underlying meaning—

In principle, there is no contradiction in opening and clarifying the mind. For those of vulgar nature who read this, my wish will be fulfilled if they can grasp the meaning through the text and maintain strict observance of dignified deportment.
As for the hope that it might bring widespread benefit to future generations, I do not yet dare to expect such a thing.
Recorded in the hand of Yuge regarding the matters and meanings of the *poṣadha* on the first white fortnight of the winter season in the forty-seventh year of the Kangxi era.
Internally harboring the virtue of a lion— *saṃgha* in the Sanskrit language, which here means "lion"—
just as when a great lion roars and all the young lions hear it they become courageous and robust while the hundred beasts hide away, so too when the Buddha roars the lion's roar,

the various bodhisattvas hear it and their spiritual powers increase while the hosts of Māras scatter in fear. Because one is a disciple of the Buddha and trains in the Buddha’s majestic deportment, it is thus called.

Internally possessing the virtue of a lion, externally manifesting the majesty of an elephant king—*Gaja* in the Sanskrit language, which here means "elephant. When an elephant king turns its gaze, its entire body rotates along with it.
Likewise, when the Tathāgata, the Great Being, observes anything, both his body and mind turn together; for this reason, he is revered by humans and devas.
Looking up, the hosts of māras were struck with terror; thus it is said that externally he manifested the majesty of a Cakravartin King.

The five schools are as follows: 1. Dharmaguptaka (translated as "Dharma-Secret"). Its Dharma is called the *Four-Part Vinaya* (*Caturvarga-vinaya*).

2. Sarvāstivāda (translated as "All Exists"). Its Dharma is called the *Ten Recitations* (*Daśabhāṇavāra*). 3. Kāśyapīya (translated as "View of Repeated Emptiness"). Its Dharma is called the *Vimukti*. 4.
Mahīśāsaka (translated as "View of Non-attachment to Existence and Non-existence"). Its Dharma is called the *Five-Part Vinaya* (*Pañcavargika-vinaya*). 5. [The fifth school is] the... Vātsīputrīya.
Cāṇūra; this is translated as "Vatsa" (Calf). He did not come to the original Vinaya, so together there are five schools.

*Pán* (pronounced *mán*) and *hán* (cut by *xǔ gān*, pronounced *hān*) refer to a large face;
it denotes one who is indolent and takes no action.

He climbed a tree and retrieved him. [The king] took him as his son. At the age of seven, he followed the Dhyāna Master Sengjian of Mount Zhong to leave the household life.

He left the household life at the age of seven and recited a thousand verses daily. He was also thoroughly versed in the essential meanings [of the scriptures] and served as a translator of Buddhist scriptures since the time of the Seven Buddhas.
Sadāprarudita, whose Sanskrit name is *Sadāprarudita*, wept in sorrow for seven days and seven nights in order to seek the Dharma;
therefore, he was called "Ever-Weeping.
Long ago, when the World-Honored One, as a bodhisattva, entered the mountains to practice the Way, Śakra, wishing to test him, manifested...
He became a yakṣa and spoke half a verse, saying: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. He requested that the latter half of the verse be spoken.
The yakṣa said, "I am famished in my belly; what leisure have I to speak? He asked, "What food do you desire?"
He replied, "What I eat is nothing but human flesh and blood. [The man] said, "I pray that you will explain this for me;
I shall sacrifice my body as an offering. He then spread out a seat and requested him to speak. The yakṣa said, "When birth and cessation have ceased, nirvāṇa is bliss.
The Bodhisattva inscribed this verse throughout the mountain rocks. He climbed a tree and sacrificed his body, but the yakṣa caught him with his hands. [Thus he] acted...
He performed the funeral rites and departed.

*Śatadru* is a Sanskrit term that possesses four meanings: salt, water, a vessel, and a horse; only a wise minister is able to discern them.

For instance, when the king is about to eat, he calls for *śatadru*, and the minister immediately serves the salt; when it is time to wash, he serves the water; when it is time to work, he serves the vessel;
and when it is time to go out, he serves the horse. A disciple attending upon a teacher is likewise like this wise minister; therefore, it is said: "Immediately..."

As for the small jiao-liao bird, it nests upon the tips of reeds, binding them with its feathers; though it leaps and bounds, it does not exceed a few *ren* in height, soaring only amidst the *peng-hao* weeds.
This too represents the ultimate extent of its flight. By this, one may compare the petty person who lacks great ambition.
Regarding the veneration of the monkey as Śakra in a past life: there was once a foolish man who did not recognize monkeys.
He entered a great forest and saw a troop of monkeys gathered together in one place. This man had previously heard of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Thinking them to be the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he immediately emerged from the forest and returned to his native village.
In the midst of a great crowd, he spoke these words: "Have you ever seen the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?
The people replied, "No. He then said at once, "I have already seen them. Do you wish to see them? They all said they wished to see them. He then led the great multitude to that place.
"In the forest, he pointed to the monkeys and said, 'You all look at these Trāyastriṃśa devas. The people all said, 'These are not Trāyastriṃśa devas;
these are monkeys. Because of your folly, you do not recognize monkeys, yet you claim they are Trāyastriṃśa devas and falsely summon us.
This was used as an analogy for those who do not recognize people."

Regarding the taking of rubble for a bright pearl, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "These people, during the month of spring warmth, were traveling by boat for recreation when they lost a lapis lazuli gem.
They immediately entered the water together and scrambled to seize tiles and stones, each claiming it was the lapis lazuli bead."
None of these are true jewels. Because this pearl is within the water, it is like looking up at the form of the moon in the void;
it stands alone, remote and transcendent, not something grasped by the multitude. This is a metaphor for not recognizing the Dharma.
